10088-thaumaturgia-or-elucidations-of-th:
An Oxonian, writing in 1835, called his book Thaumaturgia, or Elucidations of the Marvellous. Its epigraph comes from Hudibras, about Bombastes, who kept the devil's bird shut in his sword's pommel and taught it the pranks of mountebanks past and future.

The chapters treat wonders, marvels, and the inferior deities said to attend mankind from birth to decease, in the curious, learned manner of early Victorian antiquarianism. Readers get a cabinet of marvels: magic, spirits, and strange beliefs, examined with both wonder and skepticism. The book treats marvels as beliefs worth recording, not proofs.
10093-gutta-percha-willie-the-working-ge:
George MacDonald's Gutta Percha Willie follows a working genius from childhood. It opens with who he was and where he was, his education, and his being turned into something he never was before. Willie serves an apprenticeship and goes to learn a trade.

He learns to read before he knows his letters, digs and finds what he did not expect, and sees sights on the way. He hatches a new scheme and makes a nest in the ruins, with his grandmother near. MacDonald, with pictures by Arthur Hughes, celebrates a boy's inventive mind. Young readers get a hero who learns by doing.
10212-peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-circus:
George W. Peck, already known for his Bad Boy books, sent the boy and his father off with a circus in this 1905 comic novel. Pa takes a job as circus manager, which gives his son a whole new stage for mischief. The book is told as a diary-style chain of pranks, mishaps, and close calls under the big top.

The Bad Boy teases animals, upsets acts, and lands Pa in trouble with clowns, managers, and crowds. A rogue elephant, a bobcat, a midget, a giant, and an ostrich that swallows a diamond stud all play parts in the chaos. Readers get broad, good-natured humor about a father who can never quite control his son.
10574-the-history-of-england-volume-i-fr:
David Hume, the Scottish philosopher, wrote his History of England in the eighteenth century, and this first volume runs from Julius Caesar's invasion of Britain to the Revolution of 1688. Hume tells the story reign by reign, covering Roman rule, Saxon kingdoms, the Norman conquest, and the long growth of Parliament and law.

His account stresses politics, religion, and the clash between kings and subjects, leading up to the settlement that limited royal power in 1688. Hume wrote in a clear, balanced style that made his history widely read for generations. Readers still use it as a vivid, if old-fashioned, guide to how England became a parliamentary state.
1060-grass-of-parnassus:
Andrew Lang, the Scots scholar and ballad lover, gathers his early lyrics in this book: verses on old books, lost loves, spring fields, and the gods of Greece. The poems are light, learned, and musical, with a classicist's love of form and a Scotsman's eye for weather and hills.

Lang writes as a man of letters at ease, trading quatrains with friends and saluting the poets he loved. The book is modest in aim and sure in craft. It suits readers who like short, polished verse and the company of a witty, well-read mind.
1106-titus-andronicus:
Titus Andronicus is a Roman general home from war. He falls into a feud with Tamora, Queen of the Goths, and the revenge spirals. Murders and mutilations lead to a final banquet where Titus serves Tamora her own sons baked in a pie. William Shakespeare's earliest tragedy is his bloodiest.

The play borrows Seneca's horrors and piles them high, yet its verse already shows Shakespeare's power. Aaron the Moor, the plot's smiling villain, steals scenes with his wit. The tragedy shocked and thrilled its age, and modern stages revive it as a study in revenge pushed past sense.
11078-what-dress-makes-of-us:
Dorothy Quigley wrote this 1897 book on dress and its effect on how people are seen, gathering articles first printed in the New York Sun and New York Journal. Quigley opens with caricature in clothes: a short round coat exaggerating a stout man into an old jug, a bonnet giving a saintly matron a tipsy air.

An Oxford divine in a soft round hat and long frock coat, mistaken for a New England spinster, shows how dress can undo dignity. Quigley argues that everyone laughs at neighbours' errors while missing their own. Illustrations by Annie Blakeslee picture the follies described. The book amuses while teaching taste, proportion, and the social power of what we wear.
11263-the-adventures-of-a-special-corres:
Jules Verne's Claudius Bombarnac sends a special correspondent of the Twentieth Century newspaper from Tiflis to Uzun Ada, then across Asia on the Grand Transasiatic railway toward Peking. Ordered to interview remarkable people and report even trivial incidents by letter or telegram, Bombarnac collects fellow travelers, accidents, and intrigues along the route. The journey crosses Transcaucasia, the Caspian, and Central Asia.

Verne builds the novel from railway timetables, geography, and character sketches, with humor in Bombarnac's professional eagerness. The book belongs to his later geographical romances, less famous than his voyages under the sea or to the moon. It still rewards readers who enjoy travel fiction grounded in real routes.
11275-the-anti-slavery-examiner-omnibus:
This omnibus gathers the whole run of the Anti-Slavery Examiner, the American Anti-Slavery Society's tract series from 1836 onward. Early numbers defend free speech and appeal to Southern Christian women, argue the Bible against slavery, and debate Congress's power in the District of Columbia. Later numbers add James Williams's slave narrative, emancipation in the West Indies, and the thousand-witness testimony of American Slavery As It Is.

Read as one volume, the series traces abolitionist strategy from moral appeal to documented indictment. Its editors reprinted revised and enlarged editions as arguments developed. For historians, the omnibus is the most convenient single source for the Society's printed campaign in the years before the Civil War.
1131-coriolanus:
Caius Martius, Rome's great soldier, wins the name Coriolanus for his valor, then loses the city by scorning its common people. William Shakespeare's tragedy follows his rise to consul, his banishment for pride, and his march on Rome with its enemy, stopped only by his mother's plea.

The play pits patrician honor against plebeian hunger, and neither side comes off clean. Coriolanus is brave, blunt, and fatally unable to bend. His end, murdered by his new allies, closes a cold study of pride and politics. The play draws readers who like Shakespeare's Roman mind at its hardest.
11580-the-teaching-of-jesus:
George Jackson's 1903 study, dedicated to his children Dora, Kenneth, Basil, and Arnold, sets out what Jesus taught, chapter by chapter, each headed by a Gospel text. An opening chapter presents him as a prophet mighty in word and a teacher come from God.

Later chapters take up God, Jesus himself, his death as a ransom for many, the Holy Spirit, the kingdom of God, and man. Jackson stresses contrast: Christ's teaching on righteousness is set against the ideals his hearers already held, revised and corrected by the words, it was said of old, but I say unto you.
11672-a-short-history-of-women-s-rights-:
Eugene A. Hecker traces women's rights from Augustus to his own day, with special care for England and the United States. Roman law opens the book, from guardianship under the early empire to a time when equality of the sexes was recognised in marriage, property, and divorce.

Later chapters cover the early Christian church, St. Paul and St. Peter on women, and the church fathers' mingled contempt and admiration. English suffrage closes the survey, with a constitutional union for peaceful methods and a militant union for coercive ones. The book is a second edition, revised with additions.
12081-lives-of-girls-who-became-famous:
Sarah K. Bolton's 1914 book Lives of Girls Who Became Famous, companion to her Poor Boys Who Became Famous and Social Studies in England, collects biographies of women who rose to distinction. Epigraphs frame the project: Lowell's line that earth's noblest thing is a woman perfected, and Madame de Staël's counsel to sow good services, since sweet remembrances will grow from them.

Bolton dedicates the volume to her aunt, Mrs. Martha W. Miller, whose culture and kindness she counts among the blessings of her life. The lives that follow, written for young readers, present famous women as examples of work, character, and perseverance, in the improving biography tradition of the period.
12809-quiet-talks-about-jesus:
S. D. Gordon's Quiet Talks about Jesus walks readers through Christ's purpose, person, and great experiences in plain devotional chapters. The Jordan, the wilderness temptation, the transfiguration, Gethsemane, Calvary, resurrection, and ascension mark the path, with study notes to close. Gordon's voice is gentle and pastoral throughout.

A mid-book passage on the last week shows Jesus as the calm master figure while leaders scurry like headless hens, with Lazarus also marked for death. The book aims to draw readers closer to Jesus as a living person. It remains a popular example of early twentieth-century devotional writing.
12978-in-search-of-gravestones-old-and-c:
W. T. Vincent, president of the Woolwich District Antiquarian Society, published In Search of Gravestones Old and Curious in 1896, with one hundred and two illustrations. Chapters trace the evolution of gravestones, artistic and professional stones, tramps through Kent, Irish and Scottish stones, stones abroad, and the regulation and preservation of stones. An early sample at Higham fronts the book.

Tramp notes record Wanstead's stone for William Swan, dead in 1715 aged sixteen, and Walthamstow's Jane Redfern of 1734, with skulls, ivy sprays, oak branches, and mourning figures. Vincent reads stones as folk art and local history. The book delights antiquaries and churchyard wanderers.
13181-the-boy-with-the-u-s-census:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler's 1911 boys' book, with thirty-eight illustrations mostly from government bureaus, follows Hamilton Day, a boy who works with the United States Census. It is dedicated to Hamilton Day, a friend of the author's son Roger. Chapters run from a blood feud in old Kentucky to a lost race, a rifle factory, and census heroes of the frozen north.

Hamilton watches rifle parts timed by asbestos clocks in furnace doors, learning how machines beat hand work for speed. Later he meets a learned tramp who knows Aristophanes and Juvenal, yet cannot run a business like a Greek fruit peddler. The book mixes adventure with civic lessons, showing how counting a nation touches farms, cities, mines, and migrant camps.
13289-the-certainty-of-a-future-life-in-:
Edited by L. P. Gratacap and published by Brentano's in 1903, The Certainty of a Future Life in Mars presents itself as the posthumous papers of Bradford Torrey Dodd. Dodd died at Christ Church, New Zealand, in January 1895, after illness blamed on exposure while receiving messages. The editor explains how the papers reached his hands, in a preface full of wonder.

Dodd's papers claim Mars draws earth folk to itself when the two planets near, their airs mingling so travelers suffer no loss of breath. On Mars, twin moons light canals a mile wide, with tilled ground, trees, villages, and hills beyond. The book is an early science-fiction vision, part spiritualism, part astronomy, and wholly earnest in its marvels.
13717-ted-strong-s-motor-car-or-fast-and:
Edward C. Taylor sent his cowboy hero Ted Strong into the motor age in this 1915 story. Ted and his Moon Valley Ranch friends argue about a pig, then face faster trouble. A motor car brings chases, breakdowns, and comic danger to ranch life. Bud Morgan, Carl Schwartz, and the rest trade jokes in broad Western speech.

Taylor keeps the plot simple: rivals, rescues, and races, with loyalty holding the crew together. The car itself is a character, admired and cursed in turn. The story first appeared in a cheap Western story library for young readers. Its humour and pace suit boys' adventure fiction of the period. It also marks the moment when motors reached the fictional West.
13830-the-wreck-of-the-hesperus:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's ballad The Wreck of the Hesperus tells of a schooner lost in a winter gale. An illustrated 1889 edition adds an introduction on Norman's Woe, a rocky headland between Gloucester and Magnolia, Massachusetts. Longfellow chose the spot as background, giving it lasting fame. The actual wreck lay nearer Gloucester, the note admits.

In the poem, wind rises from the north-east, snow hisses in brine, and billows froth like yeast. The storm smites the vessel in its strength, and the crew perishes. The ballad's steady rhythm made it a schoolroom favourite. It remains Longfellow's best-known sea poem. The short volume suits readers meeting the poem for the first time.
14107-the-lost-stradivarius:
J. Meade Falkner's 1895 ghost story follows a young Oxford man haunted by a violin with a dark past. A lost Stradivarius, tied to a dead player, draws its new owner toward music he cannot resist and visions he cannot explain. Letters and memories frame the tale, including a stormy night when a figure rises from a wicker chair and a proposal to Constance falters in terror.

Travel widens the dread. A later passage explores sea caves near the shore, where a guide begs the narrator not to enter the fifth, unlit cell. Panic seizes him on the threshold, and the pair flee to sunlight while the maid warns that the Cells of Isis are haunted. Falkner, scholar and industrialist alike, writes with restraint. Horror grows from suggestion rather than gore, and the violin stays a symbol of beauty bought at a fearful price.
14185-edward-macdowell-a-great-american-:
John F. Porte's 1922 life of Edward MacDowell presents him as a great American tone poet, with portrait and musical examples. Massenet praises MacDowell's sincerity, poetry, and exquisite harmonies, while Grieg calls him ideally endowed. Porte draws on MacDowell's Columbia lectures, where birds soaring suggest spirit and angels gain wings, while serpents seem sinister by contrast.

Piano pieces receive close, candid criticism. Forest Stillness opens in deep, mysterious stillness but grows dull and burdensome, lacking later genius. Play of the Nymphs shines technically yet spins out too long, while Rêverie stays tuneful and German-romantic. The Sonata Eroica, inspired by Arthurian legend, earns highest praise for beauty and noble dignity, though the Tragica sonata outweighs it in power. Porte writes for listeners ready to study, not merely admire.
14395-septimus:
William J. Locke wrote Septimus, a novel first printed in 1908, about a dreamer and his cure. Septimus holds a faith in a remedy that friends call a quack ointment. Zora Middlemist tests that faith, asking if he would give up his cure to keep her respect. He answers that he would give up all he owns, save the faith itself. Locke writes with humor and warmth about odd, kind people.

A second thread follows Sypher, a manager whose firm shrinks week by week. Tables once filled with girls stand empty, clerks dwindle, and orders slacken. His man Shuttleworth tiptoes in with gloom, till Sypher rebukes his dismal face. The novel pairs Septimus the dreamer with Sypher the man of business. Both face a world that changes under them, and both cling to what they trust. Locke's charm lies in that gentle contrast.
14529-the-old-english-physiologus:
Albert Stanburrough Cook edited this Yale Studies volume of 1921, giving the Old English Physiologus in text with prose translation, plus a verse translation by James Hall Pitman. The Physiologus is an early medieval bestiary in verse.

The panther leads the beasts: crowds of heroes and animals flock to its sweet perfume, as the poem compares Christ's grace to that scent, while the dragon alone is bound in torment. Cook's parallel sections let readers compare Old English with modern renderings. The book is a scholarly treasure for students of early English poetry and animal lore.
1454-maitre-cornelius:
Balzac's historical tale opens in a fifteenth-century church at Tours, where a miserly moneylender named Maitre Cornelius guards a hoard behind locked doors. A young nobleman in love, a stolen treasure, and a king's court in the background drive a plot of greed, fear, and a strange kind of justice.

Cornelius sleeps among his gold and wakes to find it less, and suspicion falls in turn on servants, lovers, and thieves. The tale blends Gothic gloom with Balzac's eye for money's power. It is a compact mystery of old France, where wealth itself becomes a prison for its keeper.
14646-christopher-and-columbus:
Christopher and Columbus, by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden, was published by Doubleday, Page in Garden City, New York, in 1919. The heroines are really named Anna-Rose and Anna-Felicitas, but they rename themselves for the voyage.

Orphaned and feeling like aliens, the twins sail second class from Liverpool on the liner St. Luke, watching the Mersey slip past into mist and facing days of grey, wet sea. In America they meet Mr. Twist, accept toffee, sip clam broth, and travel on by train with comic awkwardness. The novel is a warm, funny tale of two girls finding a home.
14959-the-hymns-of-prudentius:
R. Martin Pope translates the hymns of Prudentius, the Cathemerinon or hymns for the Christian's day, newly into English verse and published by Dent in 1905. A hymn at cock crow and a morning hymn open the set, in Latin and English side by side.

Prudentius, writing near the end of his life, asks what useful work he has done in so long a span. He recalls boyhood under the rod, a toga that taught him to speak falsely, and later wantonness and luxury he now regrets. His hymns turn the hours of the day into prayer, from waking to night. Pope's version keeps the Latin close, giving English readers a classic of early Christian poetry.
15044-a-reversible-santa-claus:
Meredith Nicholson's 1917 Christmas book, illustrated by Florence H. Minard and published by Houghton Mifflin, is titled A Reversible Santa Claus. An illustration shows a question put to a reader: do you mind telling me just why you read that newspaper, in a scene that sets the book's comic tone.

Nicholson, author of The Proof of the Pudding, The Poet, Otherwise Phyllis and A Hoosier Chronicle, writes a holiday tale that can be read two ways, like a reversible coat. Santa Claus himself becomes a figure who can turn, surprise and be seen from another side. The book is light seasonal fiction, written for Christmas giving and for readers who like a familiar figure made new.
1507-titus-andronicus:
Shakespeare's earliest tragedy, set in Rome, follows Titus Andronicus, a general whose triumph turns to ruin when he sacrifices a Gothic prince's son. Tamora, queen of the Goths, marries the emperor and plots revenge with her lover Aaron, and Titus's children suffer mutilation, murder, and madness in turn.

The play's violence is famous, even notorious, but its poetry and its sense of a state rotting from within give it weight. A final banquet of revenge closes the horror. Titus Andronicus is a brutal, gripping start to Shakespeare's tragic career, not for the faint of heart.
15336-the-life-of-columbus:
This life of Columbus follows the admiral from his early voyages to his later years, with a glossary to aid readers through Spanish terms. Entries explain adelantado as governor or commander, applied to Bartholomew Columbus, and cacique as a Native title, with weights like the arroba defined. Page headers and long paragraphs were adjusted for this edition.

The narrative stresses discovery, hardship, and the costs of conquest, in a straightforward popular style. Maps and images in other editions add context. Readers seeking a readable, older life of Columbus will find the book clear, if dated in its judgments.
1535-coriolanus:
Shakespeare's Roman tragedy follows Caius Martius Coriolanus, a warrior of immense pride who wins his name at Corioles and loses Rome by contempt for its people. Denied the consulship for refusing to flatter the crowd, he is banished and joins his old enemy Aufidius to march on Rome.

Only his mother Volumnia, his wife, and his child can turn him back, and his mercy costs him his life among the Volscians. The play's politics are fierce and its hero is unbending. Coriolanus is Shakespeare's most Roman tragedy, a study of pride, class, and the price of honour.
15355-nautilus:
Laura E. Richards published this children's story in Boston in 1895, with pictures. It opens on a river wharf, where a boy named John watches the tide carry logs and drift past mossy piers. The chapters that follow take him aboard a boat called the Nautilus, among sailors, a skipper, and a cast of coastal folk.

Mystery, a captive, a night alarm, and family quarrels give the plot its turns, and the later chapters move toward a choice John must make and a final sailing. Richards writes for young readers in plain, lively scenes, with the river and the boat always near at hand. The book's charm lies in that seaside world: work on the water, loyal friends, and a boy learning to hold his own.
15369-old-scores-and-new-readings-discus:
John Runciman's 1901 music book, Old Scores and New Readings, discusses music and certain musicians from Byrd to Tchaikovsky. Chapters treat Byrd's Mass, Purcell as a last great musician, Bach's Matthew and John Passions, Handel, Haydn's Creation, and Mozart's Don Giovanni and Requiem. Fidelio, Schubert, and Weber follow.

Wagner takes many chapters, from Flying Dutchman to Parsifal and Bayreuth in 1897, with notes on Brahms, Dvořák, and Lamoureux's orchestra. Runciman writes as a critic with strong views. Music lovers will find the book opinionated, learned, and lively on the classics. Critics and players alike will enjoy his strong, clear judgments.
1545-mucedorus:
A Most Pleasant Comedy of Mucedorus, an anonymous Elizabethan play, follows Mucedorus, king's son of Valencia, who disguises himself as a shepherd to win Amadine, king's daughter of Aragon. Through forests, a bear, and a camp of the King of Aragon, the lovers face rivals, a clown, and a king's anger.

The play, once added to Shakespeare's works, is a romantic comedy of disguise and pastoral adventure, with a prologue and induction of its own. Its charm is old-fashioned and its plot is cheerful. Mucedorus is a pleasant relic of the popular stage, and a footnote to the Shakespeare canon.
1572-timaeus:
Plato's Timaeus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, is the most obscure and, to modern readers, the most forbidding of Plato's works, yet it had the greatest influence over ancient and medieval thought. Timaeus tells how a divine craftsman ordered the cosmos from chaos, shaping the world soul, the elements, and the human body.

The dialogue ranges over astronomy, medicine, and the fate of the soul, with Atlantis mentioned as a tale within the tale. Its myths are dense but its vision is grand. The Timaeus is essential reading for the history of science, cosmology, and Platonic philosophy.
1598-euthydemus:
Plato's Euthydemus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, may look like an elaborate jest, but it has a serious purpose, and may claim to be the oldest treatise on logic. Two brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, dazzle a young listener with fallacies, while Socrates gently exposes the tricks and defends true argument.

The dialogue shows how misunderstandings arise at the first efforts of speculation, and why logic was born to untangle them. Its humour is sharp and its lessons are lasting. The Euthydemus is a witty, demanding introduction to fallacy, argument, and the Socratic art.
1616-cratylus:
Plato's Cratylus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, has always perplexed students of Plato. In fancy, humour, style, and metaphysical originality it ranks with his best. Yet its motive is uncertain: Socrates and his friends debate whether names are natural and true, or merely agreed by custom.

Through puns, etymologies, and jokes that run for pages, the dialogue asks how words hook onto things, and whether a name can be right or wrong. Its playfulness hides serious questions. The Cratylus is a fascinating, funny work on language, and a key text for the philosophy of naming.
16217-prince-fortunatus:
William Black's Prince Fortunatus, published by Harper in New York in 1905 with illustrations, blends theater and Highland romance. Contents open with a rehearsal, the great god Pan, Nina, and country and town. Wars and rumors follow, then Strathaivron and the twelfth of August. A phantom stag, a globe of goldfish, and a magnanimous rival appear next. A stricken deer, an awakening, a crisis, entrapment, a den of lions, and a reunion carry the plot.

Black, author of A Princess of Thule and Macleod of Dare, writes warm, scenic fiction of Scotland and society. One illustration shows a heroine dashing her engagement ring to the floor before her lover. Readers who like Victorian romance with Highland color will enjoy this generous novel.
1636-phaedrus:
Plato's Phaedrus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, is closely connected with the Symposium, and together the two dialogues hold Plato's whole philosophy of love. By a river outside Athens, Socrates and Phaedrus discuss speeches on love, and Socrates gives his great myth of the soul as a charioteer with two horses.

The dialogue moves from rhetoric to the soul's wings, from writing to memory, and ends with a prayer. Its beauty is famous. The Phaedrus is essential Plato, a work on love, language, and the soul that has shaped Western thought for two thousand years.
16581-the-life-of-jesus:
Ernest Renan's Life of Jesus, in the Modern Library edition with an introduction by John Haynes Holmes, treats Jesus as a figure of history. Renan dedicates the book to his sister Henriette, who died at Byblus in 1861. She read and copied each page as he wrote at Ghazir, with sea, villages, and mountains at their feet.

Chapters move from Jesus' place in world history through infancy, education, John the Baptist, and the growth of his ideas. Renan writes with poetic grace and critical freedom, a mix that made the book famous and fought over. Readers of religious history will find a landmark work, beautiful and bold.
1682-menexenus:
Plato's Menexenus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, presents a funeral oration that Socrates claims to have learned from Aspasia, the companion of Pericles. The speech praises Athens and its dead with grand rhetoric, while Socrates' frame gently mocks the art of patriotic praise itself.

An appendix on genuine and spurious works frames the text, as with the Lesser Hippias. The dialogue is short and ironic. It is a witty Platonic jeu d'esprit, best read after the great funeral oration of Pericles, which it both honours and parodies. The speech praises Athens and its fallen soldiers.
16956-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-pla:
Laura Lee Hope's 1916 story sends Bunny Brown and his sister Sue home to stage a circus of their own. Pets, dolls, a calf, a rooster, and a strange boy named Ben all feed the plan, and practice turns into a real show with hoops, tents, and wild-animal acts. The siblings' dog Splash, lost and found along the way, adds worry to the fun.

A storm, a fall, and a brave act by Bunny keep the tale moving between laughs. The book is made for young readers who like pets, play, and small mishaps solved by pluck. Its simple chapters and clear pictures make it an easy, cheerful entry in the long Bunny Brown series.
17148-cessions-of-land-by-indian-tribes-:
C. C. Royce's short Bureau of Ethnology paper, from the First Annual Report for 1879 to 1880, studies land cessions by Native tribes to the United States, shown by Indiana cases. A map of Indiana fronts the text. Royce opens on the peculiar ties between the government and tribes within its limits, and on white growth pressing for more land.

The paper lists cessions, dates, and terms in compact, official prose, with Indiana as a clear example. It suits historians of Native land, treaties, and the Midwest. Short as it is, the work gives a precise, source-based view of how tribal land passed, tract by tract, into United States hands.
1726-theaetetus:
A boy good at mathematics sits down with Socrates, and the two of them try, three times over, to say what knowledge is. The young mathematician Theaetetus, with Socrates as midwife, works through each answer and watches it fail.

The dialogue is famous for its discussion of doxa, the Greek word for seeming or opinion, and for its honesty about ending without a settled definition. Readers meet Plato at his most searching. The book pairs naturally with the Parmenides: both show a philosopher willing to leave a question open rather than close it with a slogan.
1744-philebus:
Pleasure or wisdom — which one makes a life good. Socrates puts the question to Protarchus after Philebus himself refuses to defend his own side. Socrates argues with Protarchus about the good life: is it pleasure, as Philebus holds, or wisdom and knowledge, as Socrates maintains.

The talk sorts pleasures into kinds, weighs true pleasures against false ones, and ends by mixing reason with the better pleasures rather than choosing one side outright. Readers who come from the Phaedo or Republic will notice the shift: less poetry, more sorting. A Plato testing how far argument alone can carry a question about happiness.
17933-songs-of-angus-and-more-songs-of-a:
Violet Jacob joined two small books of Scots verse into this volume, first printed in 1915 and reissued by John Murray in 1919. Jacob, also known for her novel Flemington, wrote in the Scots tongue of Angus, her home shire in the north-east of Scotland.

Poems sing of Tam in the kirk, the Howe of the Mearns, the long road, the water-hen, the blind shepherd, and the wild geese. The verse is full of place names, farm folk, and old Jacobite feeling. Readers who love Scots speech and country life will find these songs warm, sad, and true, like talk heard on a brae at dusk.
18435-good-things-to-eat-as-suggested-by:
Rufus Estes, formerly of the Pullman Company private car service and then chef of subsidiary companies of United States Steel in Chicago, published this cookbook himself in Chicago in 1911. Good Things to Eat as Suggested by Rufus offers practical recipes for meats, game, fowl, fish, puddings, pastries, and more. Estes signs the book with his own hand on the front matter.

A sketch of his life opens the volume. Estes was born in Murray County, Tennessee, in 1857, enslaved, and named for his master D. J. Estes. At five he carried water, drove cows, minded calves, and gathered chips, and after the war his mother moved the family to Nashville. Readers get a chef's book with a life behind it: plain, tested recipes from a Black cook who rose from slavery to the kitchens of industry.
1898-albert-savarus:
In a drawing-room under the Restoration where the Archbishop of Besançon was sometimes seen, a lawyer named Albert Savarus lodges with the Wattevilles and loves their daughter. Albert Savarus, a lawyer of secret ambition, boards with the Wattevilles and loves their daughter, while his past waits to undo him.

The tale follows Savarus through provincial society, bargains for rooms, and payments in advance, as his hopes rise and fall. Balzac writes the story as a study of ambition deferred. Its sadness comes from a man of talent who does everything right and still loses, because a single old secret will not stay buried.
19027-the-revolt-on-venus:
Carey Rockwell wrote this 1954 Tom Corbett space cadet tale, with Willy Ley as technical adviser. Tom and his unit train at Space Academy in the year 2353, where only a few of each year's thousand boys can hope to become officers. The Solar Guard patrols the lanes between planets.

Tom, Roger, and Astro land their ship Polaris at the Academy port, then face revolt on Venus, where colonists and power seekers clash. Rocket blasts, ship drills, and cadet loyalty drive the action. Young readers get a fast space tale of duty, friendship, and order among the planets.
19052-stories-that-words-tell-us:
Elizabeth O'Neill wrote this 1918 book on what English words reveal about history. She shows how names of places, people, trades, and wars live on in daily speech, and how new words arrive with new things. Chapters range from British history to London street names and Bible words.

Calico takes its name from Calicut, coffee and magazine come through Arab trade, and chocolate, tomato, canoe, and hammock arrive from the Americas by way of Spain. Each word carries a small voyage in it. Readers get a lively word history, full of stories hidden in plain speech.
19077-salads-sandwiches-and-chafing-dish:
Janet McKenzie Hill, editor of a Boston cooking magazine, wrote this cookbook on salads, sandwiches, and chafing-dish cooking. The 1909 edition adds new recipes to her 1899 original and pairs the text with pictures of dishes set for tea and light meals. Its aim is food that is fresh, neat, and fit for guests.

Hill explains dressings of oil, acid, and spice, the need for tender fresh produce, and how a salad can suit any meal. Recipes then cover meats, fish, eggs, nuts, fruit, and cheese in many forms. Cooks get a practical guide to light fare, written with care for taste, looks, and good digestion.
19775-vaughan-s-vegetable-cook-book-4th-:
Vaughan's Vegetable Cook Book, in its fourth edition, teaches cooking and using vegetables. Its guidance runs from soil to table. One passage covers forcing heads of leafy crops under manure-warmed soil. Fresh manure twelve inches thick, it advises, warms the bed slightly. That warmth hastens the making of the head. Vaughan's was a Chicago seed house serving home gardeners.

Cookbooks from seed firms doubled as garden manuals. Recipes sold seeds, and growing notes sold recipes. A fourth edition proves steady demand for both. The book preserves period varieties and period tastes together. Kitchen historians can trace how vegetables were raised and served. Few sources tie the garden bed to the dinner plate so directly.
19819-milton-s-comus:
John Milton wrote Comus, a masque, in 1634, when he was twenty-five. This edition, prepared by William Bell, adds an introduction and notes. Bell quotes Walter Bagehot's high estimate of the poem. Bagehot doubted any similar poem shows so well the mind's dignity. He found its sentiments tedious and its story uninteresting, yet praised it anyway. That tension shapes Bell's school edition.

Comus defends chastity and temperance in enchanted-wood scenes. A school edition must make its poetry teachable. Notes explain myth, language, and Milton's life. Bagehot's mixed verdict models honest criticism for students. The masque's music and moral argument still reward slow reading. Bell's volume shows Victorian schools keeping Milton central.
20181-a-defective-santa-claus:
A Defective Santa Claus, from 1904, is a Christmas tale told in lively dialect verse. Uncle Sid clucks, leans back laughing, and waves the sleigh away. He yells that the old horse ought to wear bells by now. Pa yells back that bells can wait till Santa comes this way.

Such verse tales ran in papers and gift books each December. Dialect spelling gives the jokes their rural, Hoosier-style flavor and bounce. Family, snow, and a flawed Santa drive the fun along. Readers get a short, warm dose of old Christmas humor in rhyme.
20732-the-carmina-of-caius-valerius-catu:
Catullus, a Roman poet of the first century before Christ, wrote short, fierce, and tender poems called the Carmina. The notes here grew in an odd way, drafted at a hotel table between courses. A Latin text sat open while talk went on around the writer.

Readers get love poems, insults, jokes, and grief in quick turns. Catullus can sound sweet in one line and brutal in the next. His voice feels startlingly modern across two thousand years. This edition pairs the poems with lively notes that show a reader working through the Latin line by line, with real delight.
20981-tristram-of-blent-an-episode-in-th:
A club man who once quit the Bar for letters fills Tristram of Blent's opening talk. He edits, not writes, by his own cheerful account of his trade. Anthony Hope sets this 1900 tale in an ancient house's long story.

Imposture, inheritance, and a fine old place drive Hope's polished plot. The true heir and a bold stand-in circle the Tristram name and lands. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, writes with speed and sheen. This tale shows his lighter hand at work on English soil, with secrets in every portrait-hung room.
2139-alvira-the-heroine-of-vesuvius:
Rev. A. J. O'Reilly retells a sensational Italian tale of Alvira, heroine of Vesuvius, drawn from traditions of a past generation. Sin, repentance, and chivalry fill a narrative the editor calls both interesting and instructive. O'Reilly, a priest and writer, retold the tale from Italian tradition for English readers.

O'Reilly warns that the old code of manners has given way to a prudish age, yet he presents the thrilling record in full. The book reads as a Victorian Catholic romance, with saints, sinners, and a volcano at its heart. Vesuvius, looming over Naples, gives the heroine's story its fire and its danger.
2156-china-and-the-manchus:
Herbert A. Giles traces China under the Manchus, from the Nu-chens and Kitans through the fall of the Mings to the last emperors and Sun Yat-sen. Chapters follow Shun Chih, K'ang Hsi, Ch'ien Lung, and their successors. Giles wrote China and the Manchus in 1912, as the Qing dynasty fell.

Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge, writes a clear dynastic history with maps and illustrations. The book serves as a compact introduction to Qing China, from conquest to revolution. Sun Yat-sen, who closes the book, led the republic that replaced two centuries of Manchu rule.
21858-the-daughters-of-danaus:
Marriage and a woman's right to her own growth are fought over in Mona Caird's The Daughters of Danaus, first published in 1894. The tale opens in a garret ballroom in an old keep, where dancers move to a reel in the moonlight. Celtic music sets nerves athrill even in the low-key scene. Caird's Scotland is wild, old, and full of pressure on its women.

An appendix prints Caird's own essay asking whether marriage hinders a woman's self-development. She had already scandalized Victorian readers by calling marriage a failure in print. The novel gives her argument flesh and landscape. It stands as one of the boldest feminist novels of the 1890s, still startling in its plain refusal of women's lot.
21909-a-military-genius:
Anna Ella Carroll of Maryland is called the great unrecognized member of Lincoln's Cabinet in this 1891 life by Sarah Ellen Blackwell. Blackwell compiled the book from family records and congressional documents. She had hoped Carroll herself would oversee the statements, but the family decided otherwise. The claim at the book's heart is bold: that Carroll, a woman, supplied key military thinking for the Union cause.

Carroll moved in Maryland politics and wrote pamphlets for the Union when her state wavered. Blackwell argues her plans reached Lincoln's war councils without public credit. The book was sold at the Woman's Journal office and suffrage rooms. It is at once a biography and a brief for women's uncounted public work, argued from papers her subject's family kept.
22-roget-s-thesaurus:
Writers hunting the exact word need a map of ideas, not just an alphabet list. Peter Mark Roget's Thesaurus groups English words and phrases by meaning. This edition derives from the 1911 printing, with over a thousand added words.

Six broad classes branch into sections on abstract relations, space, matter, mind, will, and feeling. Each entry links synonyms and near-synonyms for composition. The book admits gaps, especially in modern and technical terms. Even so, it remains the classic tool for finding the word that fits. Later editors kept Roget's idea classes while adding modern words the 1911 text lacked.
22004-the-genius:
Margaret Potter's novel The Genius came out in 1906, after her books Istar of Babylon and The House of De Mailly. The action opens on New Year's night in 1840, in the Russian town of Klin. Snow, church bells, and the old calendar set the scene. From there the tale follows a gifted young Russian as he grows up under the Czar's rule.

Chapters carry him through the Corps of Cadets, first love, and the Moscow Conservatoire. Music becomes the centre of his life, yet the secret police, the Third Section, watch men like him closely. Potter mixes court balls, camp life, and student folly with a darker strain of fate. The result is a big, earnest story of talent tested by power.
22270-bloom-of-cactus:
Robert Ames Bennet published Bloom of Cactus in 1919, a western novel of the Arizona desert. Its frontispiece shows Lennon raising his rifle to fire a parting shot over fleeing riders' heads. Lennon lingers on a ridge to enjoy the glorious view while his burro, uninterested in scenery, plods down the far trail. The desert light, not the animal, holds the man.

Bennet peoples the cactus country with prospectors, raiders, and a girl worth the title's bloom. Gunplay and desert craft move the plot in the pulp-western manner. Bennet wrote many such tales of the border country. This one keeps his formula: a hard land, a cool hero, and romance flowering where nothing should grow.
22521-the-young-acrobat-of-the-great-nor:
The Young Acrobat of the Great North American Circus promises big-top adventure. Its circus bills itself as an unparalleled show of many attractions. Never, the puff claims, has it embraced a greater variety.

World-famous acrobats headline the bill in large numbers. Clowns, bareback riders, and rope walkers fill out the ring. Trapeze artists and star performers complete the human cast. A colossal menagerie adds elephants, tigers, and lions. Leopards and other wild animals appear in great variety too. Behind that glitter stands the young acrobat of the title. His story takes readers inside circus life. Period boys read such books with sawdust in their dreams.
2259-coriolanus:
Caius Martius, Rome's greatest soldier, earns the name Coriolanus for capturing Corioli, then fails utterly as a politician. Shakespeare's tragedy pits the proud warrior against a hungry populace and scheming tribunes, until his contempt for the people drives him into exile and alliance with his enemy Aufidius. His mother Volumnia, who made him, must unmake his revenge.

The play's politics feel startlingly modern: grain riots, class anger, and a hero who cannot flatter. Coriolanus dies at the hands of those he joined, betrayed by pride on every side. It is Shakespeare's most Roman tragedy, stern and unsparing.
2260-titus-andronicus:
Titus Andronicus, a Roman general returned from war, sets off a spiral of revenge when he sacrifices a Gothic prince's son. Shakespeare's earliest tragedy is famously gory: hands are cut off, tongues cut out, and a pie baked from two villains crowns the final banquet. Aaron the Moor schemes through it all with chilling delight.

Beneath the blood, the play stages Rome's decay and the failure of law when emperors are weak. Its horrors shocked later ages, but modern stages find real power in its stark emotions. Readers should expect a brutal, early Shakespeare at full stretch.
22875-circus:
A fall starts the trouble in Circus, a story told in the first person. The narrator broke no bones but was shaken up and left limping. The fall happened near the highway to the George Washington Bridge. From there he tried to flag down a ride, and his troubles found their road.

The circus of the title waits ahead of that roadside opening, with its own world of performers and risk. The telling stays plain and close, like a man recounting the strangest stretch of his life. Injury, travel, and the show business of big tops and small towns mix in the pages. Readers who like offbeat American storytelling will find a curious, grounded little narrative here.
22955-the-mistakes-of-jesus:
Bold questions drive The Mistakes of Jesus, a work of religious criticism dated 1932. Suppose a critic declares that Jesus lacked the highest intelligence. How, the book asks, can the critic be sure of his own judgment? How do you know your appraisal is right, lest you be found to fight against God? The author takes that challenge head-on rather than dodging it.

Page by page, the text examines sayings and actions of Jesus and judges them by reason and ethics. Believers of its day found the book shocking, and it was printed for a freethought readership that prized plain speaking. Its value now is historical as much as argumentative. It shows how far public criticism of scripture had come by the early twentieth century.
24055-the-sayings-of-confucius:
Leonard A. Lyall translated this collection of the sayings of Confucius, the Chinese teacher whose talks with his disciples shaped thought in China for centuries. Published by Longmans, Green and Co., it gathers the teachings into twenty books, with notes from the translator where a passage needs plain explanation.

The sayings cover how a person should learn, behave toward family and rulers, and take part in public life. Confucius returns again and again to duty, honesty, respect for elders, and the self-control a good ruler needs. Readers meet a teacher who valued character over rank, and who taught by short answers, questions, and examples from daily life.
24146-a-commentary-on-herodotus: W. W. How, fellow and tutor of Merton College, and J. Wells, warden of Wadham College from 1913 to 1927, wrote this commentary on Herodotus, with an introduction and appendixes. The text file hosted here is only a place-taker note, since the many Greek and other Eastern language lines made a plain text version too hard for the volunteer to attempt. The full work was supplied instead as .doc and .pdf files, so readers should seek those formats for the commentary itself.
24368-my-beloved-poilus:
These home letters come from a young American woman whose father was a retired general of the United States Army. She gave her trained services to wounded soldiers in France at an army ambulance, and succored distress wherever she met it. Her friends published them without her knowledge, solely to raise money for her work, begun August 4, 1914. Every dollar from sales, less printing and express costs, goes to the fund. Barnes and Company of St. John, New Brunswick, published the book in 1917, priced at one dollar.

Its preface recalls Florence Nightingale's work in Scutari's hospital wards in 1854, and how far its effects have reached. Hundreds of thousands of brave women now follow her example, giving themselves to wounded, sick, and dying soldiers in countless hospital wards. The book's first edition dates to March 15, 1917, the second to April 15, 1917. Readers get a war nurse's letters, sent home from France.
24430-nights-with-uncle-remus:
Joel Chandler Harris wrote these nights with Uncle Remus, with pictures by Milo Winter, published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in Boston and New York in October 1917. Its copyrights run from 1851 and 1853 through 1909 and 1911 to 1917. The publishers call it a story-book dearly loved by children, and an important contribution to Afro-American folk-lore, long carrying a learned introduction of great interest to students.

That introduction, rather forbidding to youthful readers, is omitted in this new edition, prepared for children and pictured in colors, while the stories and their setting stay intact. Contents run from Mr. Fox and Miss Goose and Fox catches Mr. Horse through Brer Rabbit and the little girl to Brer Fox copies Brer Rabbit and Brer Rabbit's astonishing prank. Brer Rabbit secures a mansion, Mr. Lion hunts for Mr. Man, and the story of the pigs follow. Readers get Uncle Remus tales for children.
24784-the-royal-pawn-of-venice-a-romance:
Mrs. Lawrence Turnbull published this historical romance in 1911, set in the second half of the 1400s. Its central figure is Caterina Cornaro, Queen of Cyprus, caught between Venice and her own island kingdom. Venice, hungry for Cyprus with its forests, mines, and rich trade, treats the young queen as a piece in its game.

Turnbull fills the court scenes with luxury and scheming, and sets against them a stern priest, Father Johannes, who sees a wide gulf between rich rulers and the suffering poor. The novel follows Caterina through nights of strain and choice as Venice closes in. Readers get a lush, old-style romance built on a real queen and a real island prize.
25086-the-delegate-from-venus:
Henry Slesar's Delegate from Venus is a short science-fiction story set in Washington, where reporters wait to see what an envoy from Venus looks like. Young correspondent Jerry Bridges, warned by his editor to keep his decorum, senses a larger story behind a flurry of couriers and chases it anyway.

When the delegate finally speaks, the message is a stark warning. Humanity may compete for minds and ideas, but if its rivalries turn to violent war with modern weapons, Venus will destroy Earth rather than let the contagion spread. Slesar turns a Cold War fear into a sharp fable about restraint.
25224-the-happiness-of-heaven-by-a-fathe:
The Happiness of Heaven, by F. J. Boudreaux, a Father of the Society of Jesus, was published in Baltimore in 1872 with Jesuit approbations dated 1870. Its text is a Catholic meditation on the life promised to the blessed, grounded in the words, Come, ye blessed of my Father.

Chapters treat the Beatific Vision, in which the intellect is glorified and thirst for knowledge is satisfied. A second element is perfect love, which sight of God as He is must produce in the soul. Boudreaux addresses rich and poor alike, urging readers to look past passing joys toward lasting glory.
25468-faustus:
This 1864 prose romance, translated from the German, tells the life, death, and doom of Faustus. The translator defends his strange scenes of vice and crime as beacons, meant to warn the ignorant from shoals where they might wreck. He insists the work as a whole is strictly moral: neither a priest burning a victim at an auto-da-fe nor a Calvinist hounding innocent pleasures earns praise.

Faustus travels with the Devil, whose spirits banquet him, and visits a prince-bishop so corpulent that fat seems to have overwhelmed his soul. The bishop lives only while eating, and his table, crowned by a calf's head, outdoes even the Devil's feasts. W. Kent and Company published the romance in London, from a translator who leaves his name off the title page.
25896-tommy-trot-s-visit-to-santa-claus:
Thomas Nelson Page tells how Tommy Trot, a boy set on staying awake till midnight, wins a visit to Santa Claus. Printed by Scribner's in 1908 with pictures in color by Victor C. Anderson, the book follows Tommy past great ice doors into a hall of ice, clear as glass yet warm and dry. Every kind of Christmas thing Tommy ever saw, and a myriad more he never dreamed of, lies packed and stacked on both sides.

Little workers toss the gifts about and shout look out in glee, as Tommy walks among them wide awake and full of wonder. Page dedicates the book to the greatest lover of children he ever knew and to the children she loves best. The tale is a gentle Christmas dream, told for reading aloud and made bright by Anderson's color plates.
26071-religion-and-lust-or-the-psychical:
James Weir Jr.'s monograph argues a psychical link between religious emotion and sexual desire, studied from what he calls a physio-psychical standpoint. In this third edition, revised with added notes, he claims early Slavonic peoples nearly all venerated the generative principle. Its rites, he claims, left a lasting mark on every people that held them.

Weir draws on sleep, dreams, hypnosis, trance, and ecstasy, reading them as moments when upper consciousness subsides and a deeper stratum rises. References to Newbold and Westermarck's History of Human Marriage support his survey of belief and rite. The essay presents its theory as scientific work, built on observation and cited evidence rather than on doctrine.
26087-paul-the-courageous:
Mabel Quiller-Couch's story follows Paul Anketell in Slewbury, a large, handsome country town on a steep hill that offers boys almost nothing. There is no river, no sea, and no mountains, only walks, flower-picking, tree-climbing, and whittling. Paul feels the lack keenly.

Chapters move from disappointment through rising hopes and the reward of over-confidence to a rescue, a troublesome pair of boots, a midnight search, and a test of bravery. After an escapade, Paul must clean his boots before morning or be betrayed, limping on a tight bandage while his mother reads beside him. Stella's adventure and Paul's confession close the tale.
26542-on-the-affinities-of-leptarctus-pr:
J. L. Wortman wrote this short 1894 paper for the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History. It examines a fossil jaw from the Loup Fork deposits of Nebraska. Leidy had first named the animal Leptarctus primus from a single tooth. A museum expedition had since found more material, including a lower jaw from a young animal. Wortman provisionally assigned that jaw to the same species.

Wortman compares the jaw tooth by tooth with the raccoon, the kinkajou, and Bassaricyon. He notes its deeper jaw, straighter lower edge, heavier chin, and extra cusps on the premolars. He concludes that Leptarctus shows transitional characters between typical members of the raccoon family and the more unusual kinkajou. Specialists still cite the paper as an early study of that fossil group.
26700-saronia-a-romance-of-ancient-ephes:
Richard Short published this romance of ancient Ephesus with Elliot Stock at London in 1900. It opens in the agora at sunrise. The river Cayster joins the blue Aegean, and Samos lies like a purple vision upon the sea. Boats of quaint form and gorgeous colouring glide toward Ephesus, chief of Ionia and home of the goddess. Marble pillars of the Temple of Diana shine like a brilliant star.

Ephesus wakes to temples, theatre, and daily toil. Its wealth of art and gold is envied by conquerors. Its odeum, theatre, villas, hills, and groves make one of the loveliest cities. Markets sell fruits, flowers, perfumes, bread, fish, and wine, with offerings for the temples. Chapters run from the messenger of Eros and the curse of Hecate through the priestess of Diana and the festival of Artemis. The grove of Hecate, the doomed city, and the crown of life follow.
26798-the-genus-pinus:
George Russell Shaw wrote this monograph of the pine genus as publication number 5 of the Arnold Arboretum, printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge in 1914. Part one sets out the characters of the genus, from cotyledon and primary leaf through bud, branchlet, cone, wood, and bark. Plates show leaf sections, cones, and seeds. Shaw notes that cotyledon number varies from 4 to 15 and, since any given number suits so many species, counts for nothing as a mark.

Part two classifies the species into two sections, Haploxylon and Diploxylon, with subsections and groups running from the Cembrae and Strobi to the Australes and Macrocarpae. Each species entry gives its published names and dates, from Linnaeus onward, with a short account of shoots, leaves, and cones. The volume closes with an index, and thirty-nine plates carry the visual evidence.
27019-my-shipmate-columbus:
Stephen Wilder's My Shipmate Columbus starts in a history class, where Danny Jones doubts that Columbus was quite the bold skipper of the history books. His professor presses him: if he knows better history, is it not his duty to tell it?

Danny has no time machine, or so he thinks, until a machine of a lifetime's use carries him back to the first crossing itself. The story lets a modern schoolboy test the taught version against the voyage as lived, asking how much of history we take on faith and what an eyewitness would really see.
27251-some-say-neighbours-in-cyrus:
Laura E. Richards's Some Say, Neighbours in Cyrus, copyright 1896 and in its twelfth thousand, opens on village gossip: some say Rose Ellen will marry him before the year's out. Her sister wed a minister, and her father served as a deacon, so some think she holds a master-key to the Kingdom.

Others say the minister is so wrapped up in his garden truck he cannot tell a girl from a gooseberry bush. Mrs. Mellen, gazing at neighbours' windows on an elegant night, soothes the minister's fears of harpies' tales, in Richards's gentle comedy of small-town talk.
27349-personal-friendships-of-jesus:
J. R. Miller, author of Silent Times and Making the Most of Life, published this devotional study with Thomas Y. Crowell in New York in 1897. Miller starts from a simple claim, quoted from George MacDonald, that life's business is understanding the Lord Christ, and that no mirror shows a man's heart as his friendships do.

Chapters take up the humanheartedness of Jesus, his mother, his forerunner, his conditions of friendship, his choosing of friends, and the beloved disciple. Miller calls the chapters suggestive rather than exhaustive, and hopes they make close personal friendship with Jesus plainer for hungry readers. The book is gentle, direct, and meant for daily reading.
28030-reluctant-genius:
O. H. Leslie's Reluctant Genius is a short science-fiction tale about two beings sent to watch a young green planet. Buos and Laloi, airy creatures who drift like wind, must observe the world below without meddling in it. Laloi loves the flowers, grass, and warm light, while Buos insists on duty and rules.

Their quarrel grows sharper as they learn their own dying world may need help from these people, who are still far from the knowledge that could save it. The tale asks whether watchers should stay apart or step in. It is a brief, odd, and gentle story about duty, delight, and first contact.
28125-dear-santa-claus:
Dear Santa Claus, published in Chicago in 1901 by W. B. Conkey, is a picture book of holiday stories and verse for boys and girls. Its best-known piece retells The Night Before Christmas, with stockings hung by the chimney, eight tiny reindeer, and St. Nicholas himself on the roof. Handsome pictures run through the volume.

Other stories and poems keep the same Christmas mood: gifts, snow, family, and wonder at the year's turning. The language is simple and meant for reading aloud on winter evenings. The book offers a charming sample of how American children met Santa Claus at the start of the twentieth century.
28299-the-orbis-pictus:
John Amos Comenius wrote the Orbis Pictus, here in an 1887 Syracuse edition, as the first children's picture book, in the words of the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Comenius, once invited to head Harvard College, pairs Latin and English in small blocks, with pictures of the world: trades, animals, plants, and human life. C. W. Bardeen published the volume.

The e-text unpacks old ligatures and astrological symbols, noting that Dutch generally means German in the original. Cotton Mather's Magnalia praises brave old Comenius. The book offers a landmark in education: learning through pictures, in two tongues, for children.
28507-the-mind-of-jesus:
John R. Macduff's The Mind of Jesus, published in New York in 1860, follows his earlier volume on the words of Jesus with a study of character. Macduff argues that Jesus must first be known as Saviour, and then studied as example, since his doing and dying lie at the centre of a sinner's hope.

The book invites readers to gaze on Christ feature by feature, as the apostle's word consider literally means gaze, until study becomes companionship and likeness. Macduff presents Jesus as the true angel standing in the sun, projecting no shadow, and as the man Christ Jesus, no shadowy model. The volume is a classic of Victorian devotional writing.
28547-the-words-of-jesus:
The Words of Jesus, published by Stanford and Delisser of New York in 1858 from the last London edition, gathers sayings for daily devotion. Its author, known for The Morning and Night Watches and The Faithful Promiser, selects words especially for the weary, calling them healing leaves from the Tree of Life. Each portion pairs a motto-verse with meditation for a day of the month.

The first day offers the gracious invitation, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, from Matthew chapter 11, verse 28. Eighteen hundred years after the words were spoken, the book says, they still come fresh. Readers get a pocket companion for morning duties and nightly rest.
2856-moon-of-israel-a-tale-of-the-exodus:
H. Rider Haggard retold the Exodus story in Moon of Israel, centering it on the Egyptian court and a Hebrew girl named Merapi. The scribe Ana comes to Tanis, and the chapters follow a broken cup, a court betrothal, the prophecy of plagues, and the crowning of rival kings. Haggard suggests in his author's note that the Pharaoh of the Exodus was not Meneptah, son of Rameses the Great.

The novel mixes romance and adventure, as Prince Seti protects Merapi from her vengeful betrothed Laban while Egypt slides toward disaster. The Red Nile, the night of fear, and the flight from Memphis drive the later chapters. It reads as a romantic retelling of the biblical tale, shaped by Haggard's taste for courts, prophecy, and fate.
29181-foundling-on-venus:
John and Dorothy de Courcy wrote this short science fiction story about colonized Venus. The magazine's introduction calls Venus the system's most wretched planet, inhabited by poor excuses for human beings. Its north continent, unlike Gaul, is divided into four parts, and its dank, stinging, caustic air swallows men's lives.

Among the colonists walks a being unlike the others, who talks like them but is different, and fears discovery. The foundling at the story's center cannot be more than three years old, yet holds a secret that could bring joy to many unhappy people. Readers get a brief, bleak Venus tale about a hidden child and hope in a bitter, fought-over land.
29240-be-it-ever-thus:
Robert Moore Williams wrote this science fiction story about conquest and liberty. The magazine's introduction says men have always fought and died for life and liberty, and will go on doing so until time ends. Williams tells just such a situation, one that could forecast the chilling future of readers' children.

On a conquered planet, natives look so like their conquerors that no one can tell them apart, save for how differently they think. Graduation Day brings seniors from the Star Institute of Advanced Science through the Museum of the Conquered, past remnants of the race that once ruled. Readers get a thoughtful invasion tale about identity, memory, and a fight that never quite ends.
29510-an-essay-on-the-beautiful-from-the:
Thomas Taylor translated this essay on the beautiful from the Greek of Plotinus, printed in London in 1917 by John M. Watkins. Plotinus asks what makes bodies fair to sight, sounds lovely to the ear, and virtue lovely to the mind. Beauty, he says, lives not only in sight but in skillful words, consonant sounds, and, higher still, in studies, offices, actions, and habits of soul.

The essay climbs from sense to soul, seeking a beauty above all these: a source that makes fair things fair. Taylor's plain rendering keeps the argument close and readable. Students of ancient thought, art, and the philosophy of beauty will find a short classic that still shapes how we ask what beauty is.
29737-the-leper-in-england-with-some-acc:
Robert Charles Hope built this short work from notes for a lecture given at Christ Church Schoolroom, Scarborough, on March 5, 1891. He makes no claim for originality. He draws on Sir James Y. Simpson, Sir Risdon Bennett, and Dr. Greenhill, among others, and the book was printed at Scarborough by request.

Hope treats the leprosy of Scripture, then the leprosy of the Middle Ages. He follows with lazar houses, the status of lepers, and a summary. Appendix notes and a list of English lazar houses close the book. It is a compact, antiquarian account of how England housed, ruled, and regarded its lepers in old times.
29912-the-social-principles-of-jesus:
Walter Rauschenbusch, professor of church history at Rochester Theological Seminary, wrote The Social Principles of Jesus for the College Voluntary Study Courses, fourth year, part one. The Woman's Press of New York printed it in 1917, under a 1916 copyright held by the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations. The book was written under the direction of the Sunday School Council's sub-committee and the Council of North American Student Movements, speaking for twenty-nine communions.

Spread over four years, the series offers the smallest course of voluntary study covering North American problems, foreign missions, and the Bible. Its books are planned for student classes in Sunday School and campus groups, not for the academic curriculum. Part one treats the axiomatic social convictions of Jesus, opening with the value of life. Rauschenbusch writes plainly for student readers, joining gospel teaching to the social questions of his day.
3037-the-age-of-big-business-a-chronicle:
Burton Hendrick wrote The Age of Big Business, a chronicle of the captains of industry, for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters cover industrial America at the Civil War's end and the first great trust. The epic of steel, the telephone as America's most poetical achievement, public utilities, agricultural machinery, and the democratization of the automobile follow. Andrew Carnegie dominates the steel chapters, choosing Captain Bill Jones, new to steel, as first manager of his works.

Jones became America's greatest practical genius in making steel, and Carnegie suggested his own epitaph as the man who knew how to gather men cleverer than himself. The book gives a vivid history of industrial empire building, admiring and critical by turns.
30563-the-evolution-of-the-country-commu:
Warren H. Wilson writes The Evolution of the Country Community, a study in religious sociology, copyrighted in 1912 and published by the Pilgrim Press in Boston, New York, and Chicago. Dedicated to Miss Anna B. Taft, who found rural leadership in service on neglected New England town borders, the book traces country life in stages.

Chapters move from the pioneer and the land farmer to the exploiter, the husbandman, and exceptional communities. Wilson studies how churches, schools, and neighbors shape rural towns as farming changes. The volume serves ministers, teachers, and reformers who want a clear, grounded account of country community life.
30734-mushrooms-of-america-edible-and-po:
Edited by Julius A. Palmer Jr. and published by L. Prang and Company of Boston in 1885, this book of charts aims at popular use, not at students of botanical science. Its general directions say technical terms are avoided as far as possible, and that mushroom and toadstool are loose names, both applied to any fleshy fungus. The charts are meant to help ordinary readers tell one kind from another.

Palmer's key warning is that no general test can tell a poisonous mushroom from an edible one. Each species, he says, has its own marks in look, quality, or place of growth, and knowing the species is the only safe guide. Modern readers must treat its advice with care, since later science has changed much mushroom lore, but the book remains a fine example of Victorian popular natural history.
31319-ball-s-bluff-an-episode-and-its-co:
Charles Lawrence Peirson's 1913 monograph, privately printed at Salem and written for the Military Historical Society of Massachusetts, gives an eyewitness account of Ball's Bluff. Peirson, then first lieutenant and adjutant of the Twentieth Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry under Colonel William Raymond Lee, with Major Paul J. Revere, left Boston in the autumn of 1861 for active service.

The regiment, a few weeks in service and stationed first at Washington, called with Lee on Generals Scott and McClellan. Its men, never having heard a hostile bullet, were no more soldiers than militia until battle taught them. Peirson presents the episode and its consequences for his comrades, filling a gap he found in the society's records.
3148-a-village-stradivarius:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells this story around a prized violin in a village. The tale first appeared in her collection The Village Watchtower, and this 1904 Gay and Bird edition gives it a volume of its own. An Emerson verse heads the opening page, urging readers to drop doleful problems and court the sunny brook.

The Stradivarius stands for rare craft come down to plain hands. Wiggin, best known for Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes village life with warmth and humor. A rare violin in plain hands proves worth what neighbors make of it: talk, kindness, and vanity in equal measure.
31824-the-genius:
Theodore Dreiser's novel The Genius was published in 1915 by John Lane Company. It opens with a wedding question put to Eugene Witla, and then returns to his beginnings in Alexandria, Illinois, between 1884 and 1889. The town then had near ten thousand people, one street-car line, two railroads, an opera house where no opera was ever performed, and four newspapers.

From that small-city setting, the novel follows an artist's growth, loves, and ambitions in a changing America. Readers get a long, frank Dreiser novel about talent, marriage, and the price of pursuing art, rooted in the manners and streets of the American Midwest.
31855-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the alphabetical range from Cockaigne to Columbus. Its transcriber's notes point to articles on Alicia Cockburn, whose ballad Robert Chambers links to a commercial disaster among Selkirkshire lairds. They also point to Charles Abbot, Lord Colchester, who gained the chancellor's medal for Latin verse at Oxford.

Its longer articles include a discussion of the compass, from a magnetized needle floated on cork in a bowl of water to the Turkish compass of eight points. Readers get another slice of the great eleventh-edition encyclopedia, where a single volume can carry a reader from a Scottish ballad to the history of navigation.
31996-is-there-a-santa-claus:
Jacob A. Riis's Is There a Santa Claus was published by Macmillan with copyright in 1904 and reprinted in 1912 and 1922. It answers a question from a six-year-old boy on the western frontier, who wrote to an editor asking whether there is a Santa Claus, since his papa says not. The editor passed the letter to Riis just as Riis was going on a journey, with Christmas at the door.

Riis wonders whether he was chosen because his own boyhood home lay toward the white north, where little boys ride in sleds behind reindeer. Another reason may be that as a young lad he knew Hans Christian Andersen and spoke his tongue. Readers get a warm Christmas essay, part memoir and part answer, from the famous reformer and storyteller.
32207-a-mixture-of-genius:
Arnold Castle's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in June 1958, opens at Stevenson Airport, where a sleek transcontinental airliner settles onto a maze of runways. Its tagline asks who, but the imaginative young, shall inherit the stars. Senator Vance Duran unhooks his seat belt, reaches for his briefcase, and steps into a crowded aisle of strangers, having spent an hour on several hundred pages of legislation and reports.

Duran chairs the Committee on Extraterrestrial Development, and his papers concern that committee's business. Ahead of him lie reporters, local political pleaders, dinner at the Governor's, and whatever unexpected event follows. Readers get a political science-fiction story, where a senator's routine trip meets the imaginative young who may decide who inherits the stars.
32393-toby-tyler-or-ten-weeks-with-a-cir:
James Otis's boys' classic follows Toby Tyler, a small boy first met haggling over peanuts at a circus booth. With only a penny in hand, Toby counts six small nuts, cracks the largest, and asks the vendor about swapping a bad one. The man, amused, tosses him two more nuts and asks his name; Toby answers, adding that Uncle Dan'l also calls him by it.

From that meeting the story follows Toby through ten weeks with the circus, a world of tents, performers, animals, and hard work behind the show. Readers see circus life from a child's eye: wonder at the acts, hunger, homesickness, and the slow learning of a trade. The book remains a vivid, plain-spoken picture of travelling show life in an earlier America.
32406-the-city-curious:
Jean de Bosschère's fantasy, retold in English by F. Tennyson Jesse and published in New York and London in 1920, follows Smaly and his wife Redy in search of three little girls. In chapter one the pair are bewitched so their noses turn into beaks, Smaly eats a door latch, Redy eats a hinge, and Redy's fingers weep tears. They meet a confectioner who resembles a kangaroo, and Smaly perches on a paw of the kangaroo-like confectioner.

Later the little people meet the inhabitants of a peculiar country, including sugar horses and other sweet, strange folk, in a city built on curiosity itself. Bosschère illustrated the book himself, and a frontispiece shows Fritilla and the red flying-fish. The story suits readers who enjoy nonsense, wordplay, and dreamlike journeys in the manner of classic children's fantasy.
32486-the-legion-of-lazarus:
Edmond Hamilton's tale, printed in Imagination in April 1956, opens in a small room with a window looking on space and the huge red circle of Mars. Expulsion from an airlock into deep space is the legal method of execution in this future, yet it is also the only way to qualify for the Legion of Lazarus. The condemned wait alone, thinking, before a walk down a corridor to the airlock room with men who go with them but not all the way.

Outside lie naked men on a barren plain, white as ivory, hair loose across their faces, some seeming to smile as Mars watches them forever. Hamilton asks what dying means when death itself may not be the end. The story pairs a stark execution ritual with a strange, timeless afterlife among the sleepers of space.
32544-the-golden-amazons-of-venus:
John Murray Reynolds's The Golden Amazons of Venus, printed in Planet Stories in winter 1939, sends Commander Gerry Norton on a second attempt to reach Venus from Earth. Aboard the Viking at New York's municipal airport, Norton and Steve Brent check instruments while crowds gather. Pilot Olga Stark joins a crew facing a planet still without communication from Earth.

On Venus, Norton stands against Lansa, lord of the Scaly Ones, who seeks the fair city of Larr and the rich, shadowless lands of the Amazons. Reynolds mixes space flight, court intrigue, and battle, as knowledge Norton carries makes him a target for a conqueror's plans.
32607-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, volume eight, slice four, covers Diameter to Dinarchus. Its articles run from Diameter, Diamond, and the affair of the Diamond Necklace through Diana, Diary, Dickens, Diet, Differential Equation, and Diffraction of Light.

Entries also treat places such as Dieppe and Dijon, people such as Diane de Poitiers and Porfirio Diaz, and subjects from digestive organs to digitalis. The slice shows the Britannica's range at a glance, packing arts, sciences, literature, and general information into one alphabetical span. Side notes in the original serve as paragraph titles, and characters such as macrons and the partial-derivative symbol carry special marks in this transcription.
3277-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part seven of Artemus Ward's complete works gathers the miscellaneous pieces. The cruise of the Polly Ann and Ward's own autobiography lead the contents, with a serenade and O'Bourcy's Arrah-na-Pogue. Ward among the Fenians and Ward in Washington follow, with scenes outside the fair grounds and a piece called The Wife.

A juvenile composition on the elephant, a poem by the same hand, and east side theatricals keep the variety going. A soliloquy of a low thief, the negro question, and Ward on health show the humorist on public themes. Brigham Young's wives and a Mormon bill of fare close a set that proves Ward could make any subject, sacred or silly, serve a joke.
32861-the-genius:
Con Pederson asks what becomes of genius when machines forbid mankind to change, in a story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of May 1954. Sethos, a great artist of his world, walks through West Park to a party at Matya's hillhouse. Ela, beautiful with startling gold hair, meets him there, and the sculptor Andian boasts of building North Square.

Old Paton, a greensman developing a perfect Lyocanthia, welcomes Sethos among the woodcutters. The party's smoke, terraced hillside, and contoured glass facade frame a world that has stopped moving. The mechanoids explain their single structural law: they must preserve man exactly as he existed when they were created, and cannot allow him to change or expand. Sethos, perhaps the most celebrated man of his age and planet, learns that other worlds exist, and that the grass is always greener there.
32901-the-merchants-of-venus:
A. H. Phelps Jr.'s story, from Galaxy Science Fiction in March 1954, follows Rod Workham, personnel director for a Venus settlement project that is falling apart. Resignations pour in with every mail flight, thirty at a time, and his superiors demand answers by telephone. The pioneers he recruited are quitting a world that was never built for comfort.

Phelps treats the settlement less as a wonder than as a hard, ugly job of building. The tale's note compares a pioneer movement to a building whose foundation is never made for beauty, and Workham must hold that foundation together while men walk away. It is a dry, sharp story about labor, morale, and the gap between grand plans for a new planet and the people asked to live them.
32933-the-daughters-of-a-genius:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel opens at Chedworth Manor, where the master finds his wife frowning over a letter that brings bad news after a holiday. Stephen Charrington writes that Edgar is dead, a fortnight gone, his funeral already held. The letter also brings unknown cousins into the household's orbit, and the daughters of a genius must reckon with a family changed by death.

Vaizey follows the young women as they face money, marriage, and the shadow of a father's talent, which opens doors and also sets expectations they did not choose. The novel is a domestic story with a sharp eye for manners, money, and the small cruelties of family life. Its strength lies in its heroines, who learn to judge their inheritance for themselves rather than live inside it.
32965-mothering-on-perilous:
Lucy Furman's Mothering on Perilous, published by Macmillan in 1913 from pieces copyrighted in 1910 and 1911, tells stories of a woman's work among mountain children in a remote settlement. Its chapter headings, given as quotations, catch the flavor at once. The headings include boys wild after the first snow and a child giving another a whipping in the stable lot. Nine little pigs follow a woman out of the tall weeds, and a voice cries to make for the spruce pines in a hurry.

Furman writes in mountain dialect and with warm humor, letting feuds, churchgoing, schoolyard fights, and small kindnesses build a picture of a community.
