The mothering of the title is practical and tireless, meeting children where they live. The book belongs to the settlement literature of its day, and it still reads as a vivid, affectionate portrait of mountain life and the women who held its families together.
33420-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
G. A. Chadwick's volume in The Expositor's Bible series expounds the Book of Exodus, for readers who want the text opened with care. Chadwick, Dean of Armagh, works through Exodus chapter by chapter, noting its story of bondage, deliverance, and law, and drawing out its teaching for faith and life. The volume follows the series' plan of blending scholarship with practical counsel.

The book suits preachers, teachers, and serious lay readers, with a clear, reverent tone and notes that help modern readers follow an ancient text. Its Greek and Hebrew terms are transliterated for those without the languages. For Bible students, it remains a useful, readable guide to Exodus, from Egypt to Sinai.
33594-eneas-africanus:
Harry Stillwell Edwards tells the story of Eneas, an elderly Black man whose disappearance during the Civil War became a Southern legend. The book frames its tale with an 1872 advertisement from the Atlanta Constitution. In it Major George E. Tommey seeks a family servant who vanished in 1864 between a Floyd County stock farm and the family home in Jefferson County, along with prized family silver. The silver includes a long-kept bride's cup.

Edwards presents Eneas as a talkative, wandering figure welcomed from household to household as he travels the postwar South. The author's preface asks whether the story is true and answers that everybody says it is. Modern readers will approach the tale as a period piece, valuable for its folklore frame and for what it reveals about how white Southerners remembered slavery and the war.
33666-a-captured-santa-claus:
Thomas Nelson Page sets a Civil War Christmas story at Holly Hill, an old rambling homestead in Virginia on a high hill above wide fields and far woods. From Bob, a veteran barely out of boyhood, down to Evelyn, brown-eyed and golden-haired, every child hangs up a stocking. Santa Claus's visit is the event of the year. The children go to bed on Christmas Eve full of thrills and little squeakings.

Eight chapters follow Major Stafford home, his search for Christmas presents, the boys' lessons in war, a spy, Santa Claus passing the lines, Bob securing a uniform, and finally Santa Claus surrendering. Page blends holiday sentiment with wartime adventure, as a father's love crosses battle lines. The story suits readers who enjoy old-fashioned Christmas tales with a historical setting.
33730-lycanthropus: C. Edgar Bolen's short poem Lycanthropus, published in Weird Tales in August-September 1936, pictures a night transformation in twelve vivid lines. Jellied darkness oozes from the hills to fill a valley floor, torn clouds stand lightning-limned like a hellish door, and old gods break loose upon the world. The speaker feels blood-lust rise, his body shrink, and his hairless hide turn to a furry coat. He slips through the opened door, raises his head, and howls, only to hear an answering howl from the plain.
33766-history-of-phosphorus:
This Smithsonian paper traces the history of phosphorus as Paper 40 of United States National Museum Bulletin 240. That bulletin is a series of papers on science and technology published by the Smithsonian Press in Washington in 1966. The bulletin gathers work from the Museum of History and Technology, presenting new findings in anthropology, biology, history, geology, and technology. Front material, introduction, and relevant index entries are included in each single-paper volume.

The phosphorus paper follows the element from its discovery and early alchemical associations through its uses in matches, fertilizers, and industry, and its place in the history of chemistry. Scholars and general readers interested in the material history of science will find a careful, museum-grade account of how a strange, glowing substance became an everyday chemical and an industrial staple.
34004-yolanda-of-cyprus:
Cale Young Rice wrote this verse drama of Cyprus, published in New York in March 1908. The play is set in the sixteenth century on the island of Cyprus, near Famagouste. It centers on Renier Lusignan, a descendant of the Lusignan kings, his wife Berengere, and their son Amaury, commander under the Venetians. Yolanda, Berengere's ward, is betrothed to Amaury.

A baron of Paphos, a Venetian lady, a priest, and castle folk fill a hall mixing Gothic and Saracenic styles. Love, honor, and Venetian power braid through the acts. The play offers a romantic, old-world drama of Cyprus under foreign rule.
34122-roman-society-from-nero-to-marcus-:
Samuel Dill, professor of Greek at Queen's College, Belfast, wrote this study of Roman society from Nero to Marcus Aurelius, published in London in 1925 by Macmillan. A first edition appeared in 1904, a second in 1905, with reprints to 1925. Book one opens with the aristocracy under the terror, and the light Seneca throws on moral life in Nero's reign.

Dill weighs Seneca's pessimism, his picture of greed and luxury, his ideal of the principate in De Clementia, and Nero's ambition to be an artist. Tacitus, as historian and moral judge, closes the opening argument. The book remains a classic study of Roman character under empire.
37-the-1990-united-states-census:
The 1990 count of the United States put the national population near 248.7 million. This census file opens with the four regions and their states, then gives population figures for the nation, regions, and states. A November 1991 release date marks the tables.

State and regional totals let readers compare growth across the Northeast, South, Midwest, and West. The file serves as a compact reference for the census year. Planners, students, and historians use it to anchor later change. It captures America just before a decade of rapid growth. Later censuses built on these tables as the nation kept growing.
4021-dear-brutus:
J. M. Barrie's play asks what happens when people get a second chance at the lives they might have lived. On Midsummer Eve, a strange host invites guests into a wood where each may meet the self they could have been, had one choice gone the other way.

A chivalrous man named John Purdie speaks out rather than hide behind subterfuge, lifting a scene that might have turned mid-Victorian into plain, brave talk. Barrie mixes whimsy, regret, and wit, letting each guest face a road not taken. The play suits readers who like fantasy with a moral edge, and a stage full of second chances.
4209-at-the-mercy-of-tiberius:
Augusta Evans Wilson's novel At the Mercy of Tiberius opens in antebellum days, when states' rights stood as a sacred faith and a precious palladium. State pride blossomed under southern skies, and state coffers overflowed with abundance.

When a new penitentiary site was needed, the health and central place of one town commended it so strongly that the spacious structure rose within its limits. Wilson builds a long southern romance around law, prison, and fate. Readers who enjoy vast Victorian novels of the South will find a sweeping, earnest tale.
4271-a-modern-telemachus:
Charlotte M. Yonge took the idea for this tale from The Mariners' Chronicle. That early book held true sea adventures, and she stresses that its most unlikely events are actual fact. The story follows the family of the Comte de Bourke. He was an Irish Jacobite naturalized in France.

The year is 1719, when war among Spain, England, France, and Austria scattered families across Europe. The count, moved from Spain's embassy to Sweden's, sends for his wife and elder children. They must join him at a Spanish port, and the young travelers face a voyage full of hazards. Yonge turns a footnote of history into adventure for young readers.
4323-the-heart-cry-of-jesus:
Byron J. Rees wrote this devotional book on the prayer of Jesus in the Gospel of John, taking its chapters from that prayer's themes. The contents move from a word in the prayer and some errors about it, through those for whom Christ prayed, to Christian unity, fearlessness, responsiveness, soul-rest, and prayerfulness.

Rees, author of Christlikeness and other Holiness writings, addresses a growing demand for full-salvation literature in his day. His introduction links the book to the Holiness movement's publishing work. Readers seeking a devotional reading of Christ's prayer, chapter by chapter, will find it earnest, plain, and practical.
4617-woman-s-trials-or-tales-and-sketche:
T. S. Arthur published Woman's Trials, or Tales and Sketches from the Life Around Us, at Philadelphia in 1851. His preface says the stories aim to create sympathy and true consideration for woman in the various life-trials she must pass through, in her own sex as well as in ours. People, he argues, are too engrossed in their own wants, trials, and sufferings to give others the thought true humanity should inspire.

Fiction, therefore, must remind readers of their duty, by presenting moving pictures from the world of life around us, in which we see the effect of our actions on others. Arthur's tales dwell on the tried and tempted, the suffering and oppressed, the grief-stricken and the mourner. Readers get a set of earnest mid-century sketches, written to soften hearts toward women in hardship, and to teach sympathy as a daily practice.
519-a-kidnapped-santa-claus:
L. Frank Baum tells how the Daemons of the mountain caves plot against Santa in this short Christmas tale. Santa lives in the Laughing Valley, happy among ryls, knooks, pixies, and fairies who make his toys. The Daemons of Selfishness, Envy, Hatred, and Malice hate him for making children glad.

Baum writes with bright, simple humor as the Daemons seize Santa on Christmas Eve, and his helpers rally to free him. The tale ends, as it must, with gifts delivered and spite undone. Young readers will enjoy a brisk fable where joy proves stronger than spite.
520-the-life-and-adventures-of-santa-cla:
L. Frank Baum tells how Claus became Santa in this fantasy, from forest child to Christmas saint. Raised in the Forest of Burzee by fairies, knooks, and ryls, Claus leaves the woods for the Laughing Valley, where he makes toys for children. A great battle between good and evil, reindeer journeys, and first stockings follow.

Baum divides the tale into youth, manhood, and old age, ending with the mantle of immortality. His Santa is kind, plain, and wholly devoted to children's joy. The book charms as a warm origin myth, where a mortal man earns, by love, a place beyond time.
5260-a-duet-with-an-occasional-chorus:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Duet, published in 1899, tells the story of a young married couple in the form of a musical duet. An occasional chorus of friends and family joins them. Its movements run from the overture and two solos through keeping up appearances, the home-coming, laying a course, confessions, trouble, a rescue, and the last note of the duet.

Doyle, better known for Sherlock Holmes, writes here a tender domestic novel about the voyage of marriage, with rocks and sandbanks along the way. The book offers a gentle, old-fashioned romance, notable for its warmth and for its picture of middle-class married life at the century's end.
5608-trial-of-the-witnesses-of-the-resur:
Thomas Sherlock wrote The Trial of the Witnesses of the Resurrection of Jesus, first published about 1729, as a legal defense of the resurrection accounts. It answers objections raised by Thomas Woolston in his Sixth Discourse on the Saviour's Miracles, along with objections published in other books. Sherlock frames the question as a trial, with witnesses examined as in a court.

The book opens among gentlemen of the Inns of Court, well known to one another and free to speak their minds on any subject arising in conversation. Their talk turns to evidence, testimony, and credibility. Readers get an eighteenth-century work of Christian apologetics, arguing faith in the language of law.
6068-the-pony-rider-boys-in-montana-or-t:
Frank Gee Patchin sends the Pony Rider Boys to Montana, opening at Forsythe station, where the trainman calls the stop and Tad Butler asks if this is where they get off. Professor Zepplin confirms it, Stacy Brown sees no town, and Ned Rector calls it a one-sided town across the tracks, telling Chunky to use his eyes more and his tongue less.

The four boys, sun-burned, clear-eyed, and springy, step down in regulation cowboy suits worn by long service. A mystery of an old custom house awaits them in Montana. Patchin keeps the pace quick, with teasing, train travel, and frontier work framing the boys' latest quest.
6122-tobogganing-on-parnassus:
Franklin P. Adams dedicates Tobogganing on Parnassus to Bert Leston Taylor, guide, philosopher, but friend, and opens by hoping his vagrant verses make one heart glad or bring a single smile. If he has eased one heart of pain or made one throb or thrill, his labor has not been in vain.

His publishers, he jokes, would not rejoice at so modest an aim, and he would feel a little disappointed himself. Contents promise Us Poets, Rubber-Stamp Humour, the Simple Stuff, Carpe Diem, Horace the Wise, Catullus the kisser, and verses on money, jealousy, and advice. Adams toboggans through classic poets with light wit.
6375-quaint-gleanings-from-ancient-poetr:
Edmund Goldsmid gathers curious poetical compositions of the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries, from manuscripts and rare printed originals. He collected them over several years in out of the way corners, public and private libraries, dusty bookstalls, and auction rooms, with pencillings on flyleaves among his finds. The contents run from Beauties Fort and a bonny lass's eye to Anthony Munday on John Fox's captivity and a letter from the Duke of Monmouth to the king.

An epitaph on Dundee, the robber robbed, a shepherd's mournful fate, and verses to a friend follow. A panegyric upon Oates, patriots, justice in masquerade, a brawny bishop's lament, and a poor blind boy come next. A ballad on the fleet, an imitation of Horace, and an epitaph on Dr. Johnson close the run. Goldsmid's book is an antiquary's cabinet, odd, learned, and full of voices from three centuries.
6387-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Suetonius, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester, gives Augustus as the second life of the twelve Caesars. The Octavii were of first distinction in Velitrae, where a street named Octavian and an altar to one Octavius recalled a general. Attacked while sacrificing to Mars, he snatched half raw entrails from the fire, offered them, marched out, and returned victorious. A law grew from the act, Suetonius says.

Augustus, D. Octavius Caesar, rules his household as strictly as his empire. He sets daughters and granddaughters to domestic work and even spinning, and makes them speak and act openly before the family for a diary. He rebukes a handsome young visitor to his daughter at Baiae for lack of modesty, and teaches grandsons reading and swimming himself. The life mixes anecdote and statecraft, showing an emperor as father, censor, and keeper of Roman manners.
6388-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Regilli, a Sabine town, gives Rome the patrician Claudii. They moved to the city soon after its building with a great body of dependants, under Titus Tatius, joint king with Romulus. On better authority, they came under Atta Claudius, admitted to patrician rank six years after the Tarquins' expulsion. Lands beyond the Anio rewarded their following, and the family rose to power and dignity unmatched by its plebeian namesakes.

Tiberius Nero Caesar, their heir, rules with a punctilious regard for forms, dismissing attendants at his door when indisposed and letting decrees pass without complaint even when they cross his opinion. A praetor elect gains leave to depart as legate at large, though Tiberius thinks magistrates should stay to receive honours in person. Suetonius writes a reserved emperor, learned, suspicious, and bound by law's letter while bending its spirit.
6390-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Livia, married to Augustus while pregnant, bore Drusus within three months, father of Claudius Caesar, first named Decimus, then Nero, with gossip that his father in law begot him in adultery. A verse ran everywhere: nine months for common births the fates decree, but for the great, reduce the term to three. Drusus, as quaestor and praetor, commanded in Rhaetian and German wars, first of all Roman generals in those lands, Suetonius notes.

Claudius himself completes public works few but useful: an aqueduct begun by Caius, an emissary draining the Fucine lake, and the harbour of Ostia. Augustus had refused the Marsians' pleas, and Caesar had often intended the harbour. He also rules that parents of four children gain honours still in force. Suetonius writes an unlikely emperor, mocked for weakness, who built, administered, and endured where cleverer men fell.
6394-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Very different accounts are given of the Vitellian family's origin, Suetonius admits, some ancient and noble, others recent, obscure, and mean. He inclines to think flatterers and detractors shaped these stories after Vitellius became emperor, unless the family's fortunes varied before. A memoir by Quintus Eulogius to a Vitellius, quaestor to Augustus, claims descent from Faunus, king of aborigines, and Vitellia, worshipped as a goddess, with a reign from early times.

Vitellius himself, short of money, pawns a pearl from his mother's earring to pay road expenses, and eludes creditors from Sineussa and Formia, whose taxes he had taken, by threatening false accusation. He sues a clamorous freedman for a debt, pretending the man kicked him, and holds the action until paid. Suetonius writes an emperor of appetite and debt, whose origin, like his reign, wavers between fable and farce.
6396-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Titus, sharing his father's name, was the darling and delight of mankind, Suetonius says, by natural genius, address, or good fortune that conciliated all favour. The praise was hard won, for before becoming emperor, and even under his father, he lay under public odium and censure. Born on December 30, in the year of Caius's death, near the Septizonium, he lived in a mean house and a very small, dark room still shown to the curious. He was educated in the palace circle.

As emperor, Titus meets disaster with a father's affection, not a prince's formality alone. Fire burns for three nights, plague rages as scarcely ever known, and Campania suffers losses. He repairs them by lot chosen commissioners of consular rank, comforting by proclamation and relieving to his utmost power. Suetonius writes a brief reign where popularity, once lost, was regained by conduct in calamity.
6438-fables-for-the-frivolous:
Guy Wetmore Carryl offers Fables for the Frivolous in 1898, with apologies to La Fontaine and pictures by Peter Newell. The contents pair grand adjectives with humble beasts. Ambitious fox meets unapproachable grapes, persevering tortoise meets pretentious hare, patrician peacocks meet overweening jay, arrogant frog meets superior bull, and domineering eagle meets inventive bratling. Many first appeared in Harper's periodicals, Life, and Munsey's.

Carryl's verse turns each fable sideways, as a bumpkin musing on a pumpkin wishes pumpkins grew on trees, having learned a creed iconoclastic by rote. Whatever was not, must be right, he reasons, and whatever was, was wrong. The book is light satire in fable dress, where moral tags arrive with a wink. Impecunious cricket, frugal ant, pampered lapdog, and misguided ass all get their turn.
6493-mediaeval-lore-from-bartholomew-ang:
Robert Steele gathers Mediaeval Lore from Bartholomew Anglicus, with a preface by William Morris, offering curious examples of Middle Ages literature. Not long ago, Morris writes, the Middle Ages were supposed an unaccountable phenomenon thrust between classical and modern civilisation. It seemed a period without growth or meaning, beginning with Rome's decay and ending suddenly at the Reformation. Its society was called lawless, its ethics hypocrisy, its art gloomy fanaticism, its literature mere form.

Steele answers with extracts written with no aim but utilising knowledge common to all, true statements, not romances inventing situations and suiting manners to them. Little statements crop up everywhere, a few words in most cases, giving information of mediaeval life in context. The book shows the Middle Ages thinking, not merely dreaming: philosophers on Mount Olympus on its title page, and everyday lore within.
6810-christopher-columbus:
Mildred Stapley tells Columbus for young readers in the True Stories of Great Americans series. She opens with Lowell's verse on a man in Genoa. He said no to Europe's wise men curled in snail shells. Chapters run from Columbus befriended by royalty and his youth to lands in the west, a sojourn in Madeira, a season of waiting, and Isabella's decision. Off at last, land, natives, triumph, and a second voyage follow.

Later chapters cover new isles, a sea of troubles, a third voyage, a return in disgrace, and public sympathy. Stapley writes with a hero's tale in plain prose. Christopher Columbus is a clear, old-style life for children, vivid in its sense of daring.
6920-thoughts-of-marcus-aurelius:
The Thoughts of the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus appear here in Long's translation, edited by Edwin Ginn for school use. The preface defends giving children a book that some might deem fit only for grown minds. Its rule in choosing school reading, the editors say, is to seek the best of all ages for grown people, not a milk and water diet for dear children.

Young readers, they argue, like to be treated as little men and women able to prize a good thing. The Thoughts themselves offer short counsels on duty, death, nature, and the mind's own rule, in eleven books. A biographical sketch and a study of his philosophy frame the text, with a general index to guide the reader.
7478-toby-tyler-or-ten-weeks-with-a-circ:
James Otis's classic boys' book opens at a circus booth, where a very small boy with big staring eyes bargains over peanuts. Wouldn't the vendor give more than six peanuts for a cent? The boy counts his six nuts, each suddenly small in his hand, cracks the largest, and tastes a deep shade of disappointment. That small scene is the doorway into Toby's story.

Toby Tyler runs away to join the circus. The book follows his ten weeks with it: the work, the wonders, the homesickness, and the education of a boy who learns what show life really costs. Otis writes plainly and kindly, without hiding the hard parts. Generations of American children have met the circus through Toby, and the book still earns its place as a classic.
7528-the-roman-pronunciation-of-latin-wh:
Frances E. Lord, writing from Wellesley College in Boston, published this guide in 1894 with Ginn and Company. Its question is in its title: why do we use the Roman pronunciation of Latin, and how do we use it? The book answers in two parts, beginning with the sounds of the letters, and argues the case for pronouncing Latin as the Romans themselves pronounced it.

The guide was made for teachers and students who had learned Latin by eye and now wanted it by ear. A transcriber's note in this edition explains its markings for short and long vowels, so readers without special type can follow. Lord's little book helped a generation of American classicists hear Cicero and Virgil as living speech rather than silent print.
7540-quotes-and-images-from-christopher-:
This volume is not Filson Young's life of Columbus itself, but a companion to it: a collection of quotations and images drawn from Young Christopher Columbus. The reader is told how to use it: copy a short segment of any quotation into a search, open the eBook below, and find the full context. It is a browser's book, made for dipping and following up.

The quotations show Young's Columbus from many sides: a man standing on the sea-shore, Amerigo Vespucci, peoples going naked and unashamed, and the old belief that the Spaniards came from heaven. Other entries touch Bede's eighth-century proof of the earth's roundness, attempts to glorify Columbus socially, and biography that obscures truth with legends. Together they sketch an explorer half history, half myth.
789-the-gathering-of-brother-hilarius:
Michael Fairless wrote this romance of the Black Death, about Hilarius, a monk with an artist's eyes. Through the book runs the road of life, the white highway Hilarius watched from the monastery gate. The tale follows him from blind eyes in the forest to cities of gold, and to a dying little maid whose speechless witness teaches him sorrow and love.

Fairless calls it a romance of the Image of God, in which the Divine Face is unveiled for Hilarius amid plague and loss. The prose is gentle and devout, like The Roadmender by the same author. The book rewards readers who like medieval tales of faith, where a monk's journey becomes a picture of every life.
7959-the-reign-of-tiberius-out-of-the-fi:
Tacitus wrote the Annals in the early second century as a history of Rome under its first emperors, and this volume gives the first six books, covering the reign of Tiberius. Thomas Gordon's English translation is edited here by Arthur Galton. The same volume adds two shorter works by Tacitus: his account of Germany, describing its peoples and customs, and his life of Agricola, the general who campaigned in Britain.

Tiberius, who followed Augustus, ruled through conspiracy, treason trials, and the growing power of his minister Sejanus, and Tacitus tells that story with cold, sceptical brilliance. The Germany essay and the Agricola life widen the view to Rome's frontiers. Together the three texts offer one of the sharpest surviving portraits of imperial power, and of the peoples who lived beyond it.
8002-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Exodus, the second book of the Bible, tells how Israel escaped slavery in Egypt. Moses, drawn from the Nile as a baby and called at the burning bush, confronts Pharaoh with ten plagues. Leads the people through the Red Sea, and receives the law at Mount Sinai. The second half describes the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary where God would dwell among his people, built to exact pattern.

The Exodus became the founding story of Israel and a lasting symbol of liberation, quoted by enslaved peoples and reformers ever since. Its laws, from the Ten Commandments to the rules of the camp, shaped Western ideas of justice. In the King James Version, the narrative moves from terror to triumph, and its phrases, let my people go, remain among the best known in English.
8003-the-bible-king-james-version-book-3:
Leviticus, the third book of the Bible, stands at the centre of the laws given to Israel after the Exodus. Spoken to Moses from the tabernacle, its chapters set out offerings of herd and flock. The duties of Aaron and his sons as priests, rules for purity, the Day of Atonement, and the feasts and holy days. The book's name comes from Levi, the tribe set apart for priestly service.

Readers often find Leviticus dense, but its pattern is clear: a holy people must worship in holy ways. Its sacrifices, washings, and festivals shaped Jewish and Christian thinking about atonement and clean living for centuries. In the King James Version, its measured, repeated language gives the laws a solemn rhythm that has made the book both daunting and strangely moving.
8229-the-world-english-bible-web-exodus:
Exodus, in the World English Bible, begins with the names of Israel's sons who came into Egypt with Jacob, seventy souls in all, Joseph already there. Joseph died, and all his generation, but Israel grew exceedingly mighty and filled the land, until a new king arose who did not know Joseph. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Moses, the plagues, the Red Sea, Sinai, and the tabernacle.

The modern version tells the founding liberation story in plain prose, so its laws and wonders read steadily. Exodus here keeps its two halves in balance: escape from slavery and the giving of the law. For readers meeting the Bible's second book fresh, this rendering offers its drama and its commandments without archaic distance.
8230-the-world-english-bible-web-levitic:
Leviticus, in the World English Bible, presents the priestly laws in modern English, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward. Yahweh calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and sets out offerings of livestock from herd and flock. Burnt offerings without blemish, the laying on of hands, and the sprinkling of blood by Aaron's sons, the priests. Later chapters add purity laws, the Day of Atonement, and the feasts.

The modern rendering keeps the book's careful, repeated patterns, which can feel dense, but also makes its logic clearer: a holy people worships in holy ways. Readers who found the King James version daunting may find this version easier to follow. Leviticus remains the Bible's handbook of sacrifice and holiness, now in plain contemporary prose.
859-polly-of-the-circus:
Margaret Mayo wrote this tale of Polly, a young circus girl found in the women's dressing tent while the band of the Great American Circus plays. Polly sits wistful, chin in hand, amid the chatter and bright disarray of show life, a girl caught between the sawdust ring and a quieter world beyond it.

Mayo follows Polly through the circus world, its kindness and its risks, toward a choice about where she belongs. The tale, dedicated to her kleine Mutter, is warm and theatrical, with the colour of the big top in every scene. It charmed stage and screen audiences, and it still reads as a tender circus romance.
8714-four-plays-of-aeschylus:
E. D. A. Morshead translates four plays of Aeschylus into English verse in this volume: The Suppliant Maidens, The Persians, The Seven Against Thebes, and Prometheus Bound. The dedication, addressed from out of the grave of time, mourns shattered Greek urns and Athenian crowns, while the marble dead speak farewell from their tombs. A frontispiece shows Hera and Prometheus from a red-figure vase in the British Museum.

The plays themselves span suppliant women seeking asylum, Persia's defeat at Salamis told from the Persian side, brothers killing brothers before Thebes, and Prometheus chained for giving fire to humans. Together they show Aeschylus as poet of fate, law, and suffering on a grand scale. Morshead's verse keeps the choruses singing, and the volume serves as a strong first Aeschylus for readers who know only the Oresteia.
8844-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, bondservant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes in Weymouth's Titus for building up the faith of God's people and spreading full knowledge of religious truth. In hope of the life of the ages promised by God, who never breaks his word, before time began. At the appointed time, God made his message known through preaching entrusted to Paul by God's command. The letter goes to Titus, Paul's own true child in their common faith, with grace and peace.

Paul left Titus in Crete, he says, to set right what remains and appoint elders in every town. The letter that follows gives qualifications, warnings against false teachers, and counsel for old and young, slaves and masters. Weymouth's modern speech keeps the short letter brisk and practical. Readers get a compact pastoral handbook, and a glimpse of the early Church organizing itself island by island.
937-poems-patriotic-religious-miscellane:
Abram J. Ryan, known as Father Ryan, the poet-priest of the Confederacy, gathers poems under three heads: patriotic, religious, and miscellaneous. His verses gave voice to Southern feeling after the Civil War. Ryan, called the poet-priest of the South, wrote verses that Southern readers memorised.

Ryan writes of lost causes, faith, and home with earnest feeling, and his poems were widely reprinted in his day. The collection suits readers of American Civil War poetry and of Catholic devotional verse. His Conquered Banner, among his most famous poems, mourned the lost Confederate cause.
9464-bohemian-san-francisco-its-restaura:
Clarence E. Edwords wrote Bohemian San Francisco in 1914, a book on the city's famed restaurants and their best recipes. Edwords toasts old Bohemia, where good food, good talk, and carefree hours ruled the night. He dedicates the book to his wife, his best Bohemian comrade, and praises a city where liberty never meant license. The book mixes town lore with the elegant art of dining.

Pages recall famed eating houses, their hosts, their dishes, and the nights that made them legend. Recipes let a home cook taste the town's best tables. A reader gets a fond, pre-quake-era portrait of San Francisco at table, and a cookbook steeped in the city's gay, generous spirit.
9793-josephus:
Norman Bentwich wrote Josephus in 1914, a life and study of Flavius Josephus, for the Jewish Publication Society of America. Chapters trace Jews and Romans, Josephus's life to Jotapata's fall, and his life after surrender. His works, the Jewish Wars, and his Bible writings follow, with post-biblical history and an apology for Judaism. A bibliography and index close the book.

Bentwich opens by binding Josephus's life to the Jews' struggle against Rome. His study weighs a historian caught between peoples. A reader gets a clear, scholarly Josephus, fit for grasping a writer who chronicled his nation's ruin.
985-father-sergius:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this tale of Father Sergius, once a handsome prince and officer of the Cuirassier Life Guards in Petersburg in the 1840s. Predicted to become aide-de-camp to Emperor Nicholas I, he leaves the service, breaks his engagement to a beautiful maid of honour, and becomes a monk and hermit.

Sergius seeks holiness in solitude, yet pride and temptation follow him to his cell, and his fame as a holy man becomes its own snare. Tolstoy tells the fall and the slow finding of true humility with stark power. The tale is a masterwork of his late period, on faith, pride, and grace.
9901-grace-harlowe-s-return-to-overton-c:
Jessie Graham Flower's school story, copyrighted in 1915, brings Grace Harlowe back to Overton College after her schoolgirl years. Grace and her friends return to the quiet town in midsummer, where a welcome guest and an unexpected caller soon stir up campus life.

Later chapters follow a secret session, new friendships, and the girls' busy work for college causes. Flower writes for young readers in a friendly, earnest tone, with loyalty and teamwork as the prizes. Fans of the earlier Overton books will find the same circle, a little older and still close.
9970-the-dramatic-values-in-plautus:
Wilton Wallace Blancké, a Philadelphia Latin teacher, wrote this 1918 doctoral thesis on the Roman comic playwright Plautus. The first part reviews earlier criticism and the evidence for how Plautus's plays were acted on the Roman stage.

Later parts weigh what makes his comedies work as theatre: plot, character, and the actor's craft, rather than merely as texts to read. Blancké writes for students of Latin drama, with care for evidence and argument. Readers interested in ancient theatre get a scholarly study of why Plautus still plays well after two thousand years.
a-duet-with-an-occasional-chorus:
A. Conan Doyle's A Duet, with an Occasional Chorus appeared from Grant Richards in London in 1899, transcribed here from that edition. A letter to Maude Crosse frames the fiction as her private log, given by the author in January 1899. Two-oared boats putting out on the ocean stand for young married couples. The Overture is told in letters.

Frank Crosse and Maude Selby write their way from engagement at Woking and St. Albans to marriage. Chapters named like music — Two Solos, Keeping Up Appearances, The Trio — track the first years. Money trouble, a thundercloud, and danger test the duet. Doyle wrote the novel between Holmes stories, and his affection for ordinary happiness fills it. The chorus is the voice of friends and family around the pair. It remains his most personal fiction, a marriage manual disguised as a love story.
a-kidnapped-santa-claus:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Christmas story about the kidnapping of Santa Claus. It begins in the Laughing Valley, where Santa's castle stands and his helpers — ryls, knooks, pixies, and fairies — make toys all year. Next to the valley rise the caves of the Daemons: Selfishness, Envy, Hatred, and Malice, one in each cavern, with worse things rumored beyond.

The Daemons hate Santa precisely because he makes children happy, and they plot to stop his Christmas ride. Their capture of him leaves his helpers to deliver the toys in his place, scrambling through the night. Baum, the creator of Oz, gives the tale a moral machinery of temptations and repentance. It is a compact, darker companion to his better-known Christmas writings about Santa's life.
a-modern-telemachus:
Charlotte M. Yonge's A Modern Telemachus, reprinted here by Macmillan in 1889 from the 1886 first edition, takes its idea from Scott's Mariners' Chronicle. The Comte de Bourke was real: an Irish Jacobite naturalized in France, married to the Marquis de Varennes's daughter, and in high favor with Marshal Berwick. In 1719, with Spain and England at war, his family's voyage ends in wreck on a hostile shore. Yonge's preface insists that all that is most improbable in the tale is actual fact. The modern Telemachus is the young Arthur, thrust into adventures his tutor must survive beside him.

Inside, shipwreck, captivity among the Moors, and escapes test the boy as the Odyssey tested Telemachus, with a faithful mentor in the Mentor role. Yonge writes history's underside: Jacobite exiles, Spanish wars, and children carried through both. Readers get her historical fiction in compact form, a true story stranger than its romance dress.
a-reversible-santa-claus: Meredith Nicholson tells a Christmas story in this illustrated volume, published in Boston and New York in 1917 with pictures by Florence Minard. Its figures include Mary, Humpy, and the Hopper, whose grin earns grudging admiration, and a prowler whose faint click at a hedge marks his approach. A note read aloud, questioned at the frontispiece, sets the seasonal mystery turning.
a-short-history-of-women-s-rights-from-t: Eugene Arthur Hecker traces the rights of women from the days of Augustus to his own time, with special attention to England and the United States. The volume is a second edition, revised with additions. The opening chapter treats Roman law from 27 BC to 527 AD, when women passed from perpetual guardianship toward equality under the Empire, holding property, suing in law, and inheriting. A second chapter turns to women and the early Christian church, its apostles and fathers.
a-village-stradivarius:
Kate Douglas Wiggin first printed her tale in The Village Watch Tower, and this 1904 Gay and Bird edition presents it on its own. It opens with a music lesson: a boy named Davy is told to find page three hundred and seventeen of the old instruction book and begin at the top. His teacher is the village music master, a man with one great treasure.

That treasure is a violin. He believes, or hopes, it to be a true Stradivarius. Around it gather the village, a love story, and a question of what the instrument is really worth. Wiggin writes rural New England with warmth and a light hand. The tale runs short and sweet, built on music and kindness.
albert-savarus:
Honoré de Balzac sets his novel in Besançon, in Ellen Marriage's translation, among the drawing rooms of the Restoration. The great house there belongs to the Baronne de Watteville, a proud heiress of the old Rupt family. Her young daughter watches the town's brilliant new lawyer, Albert Savarus, with growing fascination.

Savarus is able, ambitious, and silent about his past. The novel slowly uncovers the Italian love affair that shaped him and the vow that binds him still. Balzac builds the tale on letters, gossip, and political ambition in a provincial city. The ending, quiet and ironic, ranks among his most perfectly judged finishes.
alvira-the-heroine-of-vesuvius:
The Reverend A. J. O'Reilly presents his narrative as one culled from the traditions of a past generation, under the heading The Penitent Saints. His introduction admits the tale is sensational and defends printing records of sin and repentance against the false literature of the day. The scene opens in Paris a hundred and fifty years before his time.

Chapters move through a usurer, a mixed marriage, secret societies, flight, and tragedy in the mountains, with a funeral in the snow along the way. Alvira's story turns on sin, suffering, and repentance in the Catholic moral tradition. Vesuvius looms over the Italian parts of the tale. The book is old-fashioned melodrama with a preacher's purpose.
anti-federalist-papers-brutus:
The Brutus essays, sixteen in all, ran in New York papers across 1787 and 1788 against ratifying the Constitution. Brutus is thought to be Robert Yates, a New York judge and delegate who left the Philadelphia convention. The essays are the weightiest work of the Anti-Federalist side.

Brutus warns that a vast republic cannot stay free, and that the new federal courts and tax powers would crush the states. He predicts the Senate, the presidency, and the judiciary would drift into an aristocracy. The Bill of Rights owes much to pressure from Brutus and his allies. His losing side still frames American debates on federal power.
at-the-mercy-of-tiberius:
Augusta Evans Wilson's novel At the Mercy of Tiberius opens with a dying mother begging her daughter for one act of humility. Beryl refuses to beg her rich grandfather for help. Her pride, she answers, is for her mother, not herself. The mother dies with the reproach spoken. Beryl is left poor and alone, a grandfather's door shut against her. Evans Wilson, the Alabama author of St. Elmo and Beulah, builds her heroine's trials in the grand melodramatic manner.

General Darrington is then robbed and brutally murdered, and suspicion falls on Beryl. The district solicitor has no doubt of her guilt, and her trial becomes the town's sensation. Readers get the full Evans Wilson design: faith and pride tested by poverty, scandal, and a courtroom.
bohemian-san-francisco-its-restaurants-a:
Clarence E Edwords published Bohemian San Francisco in 1914, a guide to the city's restaurants and their most famous recipes. Edwords calls eating an art and cooking a science in his city. His toast is to the ever-living now, and he dedicates the whole to his wife.

Famous dining rooms pass in review, from grand hotels to dingy spots run by chefs with royal medals. Edwords tells how dishes were born and gives the recipes that made houses known. Italian, French, and Spanish kitchens all get their due, with tales of lean days and kind landladies. Room lore, prices, and habits of the old crowd fill the gaps. The result is both a cookbook and a memoir of a pleasure-loving city before it changed.
britannica-1911-aarhus:
Aarhus receives a port entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Danish seaport on Jutland's east coast is the kingdom's chief Jutland port and second town, with 51,814 folk in 1901. A bishop's see and amt capital, it draws railways from all parts.

Farm goods go out and coal and iron come in through a good, safe harbour. The thirteenth-century cathedral, much restored, stands as Denmark's largest church, with an art and antiquities museum near by. Low, fertile, well-wooded land frames the town. South-west lies lake country on the Gudenaa, Jutland's largest river, rising to the Himmelbjerg. Silkeborg's fine setting ends the tour. The see itself dates at least from 951, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-abacus:
Abacus receives an entry in three trades in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In architecture the word names the top slab of a column capital, which spreads the load of architrave or arch. Greek Doric keeps it a plain square, while Corinthian work moulds and cants it.

Counting gives the word a second life: the Roman board with beads on rods, units to millions, fives on short bars. China's swan-pan works the same way with balls on bamboo. School boards with beads on wires descend from both. Logic takes the word last, for Jevons's and Venn's machines that sort term pairs on slips. One Greek word for a slab ends up serving builders, counters, and logicians alike.
britannica-1911-ablatitious: Ablatitious is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry gives the word, from Latin ablatus, taken away, as meaning reducing or withdrawing. Astronomy takes it as its own term. A force that steps between moon and earth and lessens gravitation's pull is called ablatitious, the entry states. A force that raises that pull is called addititious by the same rule. One tight contrast fixes the pair of terms.
britannica-1911-acanthus:
Acanthus is a genus of plants in the order Acanthaceae, native to southern Europe and the warmer parts of Asia and Africa. Best known is Acanthus mollis, called brankursine or bear's breech, common around the Mediterranean with large, deeply cut, shining leaves. Acanthus spinosus takes its name from spiny leaves, and several species make bold garden plants with flower spikes two or three feet high.

Decoration gives the genus its wider fame. Greek craftsmen first copied the acanthus leaf in metal, then carved it in stone, and later styles of architecture kept it as a basic ornament. Two leaf types guided that tradition, the spiny form favoured by Greeks and the softer mollis form preferred by Romans.
britannica-1911-acarus: Acarus is a genus of arachnids, the group that includes mites and ticks, and this entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is a single identifying sentence. The name comes from a Greek word meaning a mite. The genus is represented, the entry says, by the cheese mite and other related forms. The entry gives the name, its Greek root, and its best-known member, and stops there — a one-line identification, not an account of the animals themselves.
britannica-1911-acastus:
Acastus, in Greek legend, was the son of Pelias, king of Iolcus in Thessaly, and a great friend of Jason. He sailed on the Argonautic expedition and joined the Calydonian boar-hunt, two of the famous shared adventures of Greek heroes. After his father's death he held splendid funeral games in his honour, celebrated by artists and poets such as Stesichorus.

Marriage brought his ruin. His wife Astydameia fell in love with Peleus, who had taken refuge at Iolcus, and when he refused her she accused him falsely. Acastus hid Peleus's famous sword and left him asleep on Mount Pelion, but Peleus recovered the sword, returned, and slew both Acastus and Astydameia.
britannica-1911-accius-lucius:
Lucius Accius was a Roman tragic poet, son of a freedman, born at Pisaurum in Umbria in 170 B.C. He lived to a great age, since Cicero remembered conversing with him on literary matters. Horace and Cicero both rate his reputation highly. About seven hundred lines survive from some fifty plays, most of them free translations from Greek originals.

Favourite subjects were the legends of the Trojan war and the house of Pelops, though Roman history supplied his Brutus and Decius. Accius also wrote verse treatises on the history of poetry and dramatic art, works on agriculture, and an Annales. He introduced innovations in spelling and grammar as well, and the fragments show vigorous language and a lively power of description.
britannica-1911-accursius-franciscus:
Franciscus Accursius (1182-1260) was an Italian jurist born at Florence, a pupil of Azo who taught law with great success at Bologna. His life's work was a rescue operation. Comments on the Roman Code, Institutes, and Digests lay scattered among many writers, breeding obscurity and contradiction, and Accursius undertook to arrange them into one body.

Resulting compilation is the Glossa ordinaria, usually called the Great Gloss. Written in barbarous Latin, it still had more method than any predecessor, and lawyers of his age called him the idol of jurisconsults. Later ages judged him lower, granting his skill in disentangling laws but blaming his weak history for absurdities. His son taught law at Oxford at Edward I's invitation.
britannica-1911-acephalous:
Acephalous means headless, whether literally or in a figurative sense, leaderless. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the word through several sciences. In prosody and grammar it describes a verse or sentence whose beginning is wanting. In botany it describes ovaries that do not end in a stigma, the part that receives pollen.

Zoology gives the word its heaviest work. Molluscs divide into cephalous kinds, with an organized head bearing brain and senses, and acephalous kinds without one. The Acephala, also called Lamellibranchiata, are the familiar bivalve shellfish, clams and mussels among them. Laennec also gave the name acephalocyst to the hydatid, the larval stage of a tapeworm.
britannica-1911-achelous:
Achelous, now called the Aspropotamo or white river, is the largest river in Greece at about one hundred and thirty miles. Rising in Mount Pindus, it divides Aetolia from Acarnania and reaches the Ionian Sea. In its lower course it winds through fertile, marshy plains, and its water carries fine mud that builds banks and has formed the Echinades islands at its mouth.

Myth shares the entry with geography. Homer couples Achelous with Ocean as chief of rivers, and the name became that of the typical river-god. A familiar legend tells of the god's contest with Heracles for the hand of Deianira. Other Greek rivers also bore the same name.
britannica-1911-achiacharus:
Achiacharus is a name in the book of Tobit, one of the books of the Apocrypha, where he appears as Tobit's nephew and an official at the court of Esarhaddon at Nineveh. The 1911 Britannica entry connects that figure to a much wider eastern legend. Versions in Rumanian, Slavonic, Armenian, Arabic, and Syriac tell of a sage called Ahikar, and scholars identified the two as the same man.

Resemblances spread further. Traces of the legend have been claimed in the New Testament, and its likeness to the Life of Aesop is called striking. Strabo mentions an eastern sage Achaicarus. The entry concludes that the legend was undoubtedly oriental in origin, though how its versions relate can scarcely now be recovered.
britannica-1911-achilles-tatius:
Achilles Tatius of Alexandria was a Greek writer of about A.D. 450. He wrote the love romance called the Adventures of Leucippe and Cleitophon. One late source says he became a Christian and a bishop. The entry warns that no proof supports that claim. The critic Photius praised his clear, brief style. Photius also blamed his lapses into indecency.

Judgement of the romance is mixed. Many events in it are hard to believe. Only the heroine wins much sympathy. Yet its descriptive passages are called the best part of the work. Many surviving copies attest its fame. Other books on word origins and the sphere bear his name too. Their authorship is doubtful, the entry says.
britannica-1911-acinus:
Acinus is the Latin word for a berry. Science borrowed it for anything built like one. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the term through botany first. There it names compound fruits like the blackberry. The raspberry is such a fruit too. Each is made of many small berries clustered together. The term then applies to each small berry itself. It also applies to grapestones.

Anatomy took the word by analogy. Glands are built of small lobules. These are clusters of tiny sacs. They group like berries on a stem. Such granules or lobules are called acini. Readers meeting the term in medicine should picture that cluster. Many small round parts make one working whole.
britannica-1911-acontius:
Acontius, in Greek legend, was a beautiful youth of Ceos. His love story came from a lost poem by Callimachus. Ovid retells it in two of his Heroides. At the festival of Artemis at Delos, Acontius saw Cydippe. She was a well-born Athenian maiden. He fell in love at once. He wrote an oath on an apple. The words bound her to marry him. He threw the apple at her feet.

Trickery worked slowly. Cydippe picked the apple up. She read the words aloud without thinking. Reading them aloud made the oath binding. She still treated Acontius with contempt. Yet each betrothal ended in sudden illness. The Delphic oracle blamed the goddess's wrath. Her father then consented to the marriage.
britannica-1911-acorus-calamus:
Acorus calamus, called sweet-sedge or sweet-flag, is a plant of the arum order. It shares Britain's claim to that order with the cuckoo pint. A long root-stock creeps through mud. Tufts of flat, sword-like leaves rise from it. The leaves smell sweet and run three or four feet long. A stem much like a leaf bears the flower spike. The spike is blunt, tapering, and densely packed.

Spread came through gardens. The plant grows wild across Asia, Siberia, and North America. In England it lines ditches, ponds, and rivers. Botanist Clusius grew it at Vienna in 1574. His root came from Asia Minor. He shared it with other botanists. Gerard likely brought it to England about 1596. Its fragrant rhizome flavours beer and snuff.
britannica-1911-acro-helenius:
Helenius Acro was a Roman grammarian and commentator. He probably flourished late in the second century A.D. He wrote commentaries on the playwright Terence. A commentary on Persius may also be his. The 1911 Britannica entry is short and cautious. It separates the man from a famous false attribution. A set of notes on Horace circulates under his name. Those scholia were anonymous in the early manuscripts.

Scholars judge the Horace notes wrongly ascribed. Someone attached Acro's name in the fifteenth century. The notes themselves are not of great value. Editors Pauly and Hauthal printed them with other Horace scholia. Keller's edition of the older Horace scholia appeared in 1902 to 1904. Readers should not credit Acro with that commentary.
britannica-1911-acta-senatus:
Acta Senatus were the minutes of the Roman senate. They recorded its discussions and its decisions. Before Caesar, such minutes were kept only unofficially. They were published now and then, without authority. Caesar changed that in his first consulship. He ordered the proceedings recorded and issued authoritatively. His aim was to tear away a veil of mystery. That mystery gave the senate unreal importance, he thought.

Augustus kept the recording but banned publication. A young senator, styled ab actis senatus, drew the minutes up. Imperial archives and public libraries stored them. Examining them needed the city prefect's special permission. The entry shows secrecy returning after Caesar. Openness had been a weapon in his politics. His successor preferred the archives closed.
britannica-1911-adam-scotus:
Adam Scotus flourished about 1180 as a theological writer. Some called him Adam Anglicus or Anglo-Scotus. He was born in southern Scotland early in the twelfth century. About 1150 he became a Premonstratensian canon. St Andrews housed his order's house in Scotland. Twenty years later he rose higher still. He became abbot and bishop of Candida Casa. That see is Whithorn in Galloway.

Writing won him a European reputation. His works are of mystico-ascetic type. One gives an account of his order. Another collects his festival sermons for the year. A third work teaches the disciple's instruction. Older writers ascribed that Soliloquia to Adam of St Victor. The entry corrects that attribution here. His reputation rested on devotion, not disputation.
britannica-1911-agoracritus:
Agoracritus was a sculptor of Phidias's age. He came from Paros and worked at Athens. Tradition calls him Phidias's favourite pupil. His most noted work stood at Rhamnus. It was a statue of Nemesis, goddess of retribution. Some writers attributed that statue to Phidias himself. Part of its head survives today. The British Museum holds that portion now. Fragments of its pedestal reliefs survive as well. Athens's museum keeps those pedestal fragments.

Attribution uncertainty is the entry's quiet lesson. A master's favourite pupil invites confusion of hands. Ancient fame attached the work to the greater name. Modern museums divide the surviving pieces between two cities. Readers get a sculptor known by one statue. That statue's authorship has never been certain.
britannica-1911-agricola-gnaeus-julius:
Gnaeus Julius Agricola (A.D. 37-93) was a Roman statesman and general. He was born at Forum Julii in Gaul. Caligula had executed his father, Julius Graecinus. His mother Julia Procilla raised him at Massilia. Army service began under Suetonius Paulinus in Britain. Quaestor, tribune, and praetor followed at Rome. Vespasian's cause won his prompt support in 69. Command of the Twentieth Legion in Britain followed. Governorship of Aquitania came after that.

Britain made his name as governor. He held the post seven years, unusually long. Ordovices and Anglesey fell to his arms first. He fortified the Clyde-Forth line against Caledonians. At the Graupian hill he defeated Galgacus decisively. Domitian's envy recalled him to Rome. Tacitus, his son-in-law, wrote his Life as panegyric.
britannica-1911-agricola-rodolphus:
Rodolphus Agricola (1443-1485) was a Dutch scholar. Roelof Huysmann was his proper name. He was born at Baflo near Groningen in 1443. Louvain graduated him as master of arts. Paris hosted him for some time afterward. In 1476 he went to Ferrara in Italy. Theodorus Gaza lectured on Greek there. Pavia and Rome completed his Italian tour.

Influence, more than books, made him great. About 1479 he returned to the Netherlands. Groningen made him its syndic soon after. Johann von Dalberg invited him to Heidelberg in 1482. Three years of lectures on Greek and Latin followed. His teaching promoted learning across Germany powerfully. Erasmus praised him in the next generation. His De inventione dialectica attacked scholastic philosophy. That attack anticipated the coming intellectual revolution.
britannica-1911-agrippa-marcus-vipsanius:
Agrippa, Marcus Vipsanius, the Roman statesman and general of 63 to 12 B.C., is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Of humble origin, he was the same age as Octavian, the future Augustus, and studied beside him at Apollonia. News of Julius Caesar's murder in 44 B.C. reached them there, and on Agrippa's advice Octavian set out for Rome at once.

Agrippa fought in the war that ended with Perusia's capture, quelled a rising in Gaul, and crossed the Rhine against German raids. Made consul in 37 B.C., he built Octavian a safe fleet harbour by cutting through the land between Lake Lucrinus and the sea, joining Lake Avernus behind it. Later years brought friction at court, where jealousy around Marcellus and Livia drove him into a governorship of Syria that was almost an honourable exile.
britannica-1911-agrippa-von-nettesheim-h:
Agrippa von Nettesheim, Henry Cornelius, the German writer, soldier, and physician of 1486 to 1535, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Common report also called him a magician. Born at Cologne into a family long serving the house of Habsburg, he learned eight languages, studied at Cologne, and spent time in France. Young, he entered the German king Maximilian's service on a bold venture in Catalonia.

Soldiering and secretarial work could not hold him, and he turned to theosophy and magic. Lecturing at Dole on Reuchlin's work on the wonder-working word brought heresy charges from the monk John Catilinet. Later he became archivist and historian to the emperor Charles V under Margaret of Savoy. Her death in 1530 weakened his standing, his writings stirred old enemies, and he suffered a short imprisonment.
britannica-1911-ahasuerus:
Ahasuerus, a royal Persian or Median name in the Bible, is examined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name appears in three Old Testament books and once in the Apocrypha. In every case, the entry warns, identifying the actual king behind the name is a matter of dispute. The article works through the candidates text by text.

Daniel calls Ahasuerus the father of Darius the Mede, whose own identity is one of ancient history's hardest questions. In Ezra, Babylonian tablet forms of the name lead modern scholars to identify Ahasuerus with Xerxes, who reigned from 485 to 465 B.C. Esther's Persian king bears the same name, though the Greek version renders it Artaxerxes throughout. Tobit adds a further notice linking Ahasuerus with the taking of Nineveh.
britannica-1911-ahenobarbus:
Ahenobarbus, meaning brazen-bearded, names a plebeian Roman family covered in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family belonged to the gens Domitia, one of Rome's great clans. Its members were marked out by red beards and red hair, which gave the branch its name. The entry then picks out the members worth individual notice.

Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, tribune in 104 B.C., carried the lex Domitia, a law making the people elect priests of the higher colleges instead of filling posts by co-optation. He became chief priest, consul, and censor, often quarrelling with his colleague Crassus. His son Lucius backed Pompey, surrendered to Caesar at Corfinium, was pardoned, resisted again at Marseilles, and died fleeing after Pharsalus, where he had commanded a wing.
britannica-1911-ailanthus:
Ailanthus, a genus of trees, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name, more correctly ailantus, comes from an Amboyna word said to mean Tree of the Gods, or Tree of Heaven. The trees belong to the natural order Simarubaceae. The best known kind, Ailanthus glandulosa, is also called Chinese sumach or tree of heaven.

Handsome and quick-growing, it spreads wide branches and large compound leaves rather like an ash's. Its small greenish flowers grow in branched clusters, and the male flowers smell disgusting, the entry warns. The winged fruits carry a seed in the middle of each long wing. A native of China and Japan, the tree reached England in 1751 and became a park favourite. A silk moth feeds on its leaves and yields silk cheaper and tougher than mulberry silk, though less fine and glossy.
britannica-1911-albertus-magnus:
Albertus Magnus, called Albert of Cologne (about 1206–1280), taught in town after town across Germany before Paris crowned his rise. Born to the noble Bollstadt house at Lauingen in Suabia, he was schooled most at Padua, where the works of Aristotle reached him. He joined the Dominican order in 1223 and read theology under its rule at Bologna and in other places.

Picked as lecturer at Cologne, he taught through Germany, then took his doctorate at Paris in 1245 and taught there to great acclaim. As head of his province from 1254 he shielded the Dominicans from attack by Paris university and fought the views of Averroes, the Arabian thinker. The pope made him bishop of Regensburg in 1260. His chief works on faith are a three-volume gloss on Peter Lombard's Sentences and a two-volume Summa Theologiae. His grasp of nature's science was wide for his age.
britannica-1911-alberus-erasmus:
Alberus, Erasmus, a German humanist, reformer, and poet who lived from about 1500 to 1553, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Sprendlingen near Frankfort-on-Main, the son of a schoolmaster, he was oddly neglected in his early schooling. He reached Wittenberg university in 1518 and studied theology there. Luther and Melanchthon both noticed him.

Alberus became one of Luther's most active helpers, nearly alone in that party at wielding literary satire against Roman Catholics. His 1542 prose satire, with a preface by Luther, ridiculed the Franciscan order through an adaptation of Bartolommeo Albizzi's book. His Buch von der Tugend und Weisheit of 1550 gathered forty-nine fables on Church and State. The entry calls his satire incisive but scholarly, lacking the fierce popular directness of the Catholic satirist Thomas Murner. Several of his hymns survived in church use.
britannica-1911-alcaeus:
Alcaeus sang in the Aeolic dialect on themes that ran from gods to war to love. A Greek lyric poet from Mytilene in Lesbos, he flourished near 600 B.C. and was an older man of Sappho's time. His city tore itself with feuds, and his life was bound up in them. Born into a noble house, he took his class's side against the tyrants then rising in Mytilene.

That choice cost him his home for a spell of exile. In time, men say, he made peace with Pittacus, the ruler set up by the people's party, and came back to Lesbos. His hymns honoured the gods. Other songs dealt with war and public life, burned with love of freedom and hate of tyrants, or spoke of love. The canon made at Alexandria ranked him second of the nine lyric poets. Plenty of pieces survive, and Horace copied him closely.
britannica-1911-ampelius-lucius:
Universal history, squeezed into fifty short chapters, is the Liber Memorialis of Lucius Ampelius. Written for a certain Macrinus, it runs from the earliest times to Trajan's reign. Its dedication gives the aim plainly: the reader wants to know everything, so the notes set out what the universe holds and what mankind has done. Pupils seem meant to learn it by heart.

Ampelius himself may have been a tutor or schoolmaster, though nothing sure is known of his date; guesses scatter over three centuries. Opening chapters treat the heavens, lands, and myths, then turn to history, chiefly of the republic. That later part is judged untrustworthy and the text often corrupt, yet one chapter alone keeps an ancient mention of the famed Pergamum altar sculptures.
britannica-1911-angelus:
Three times a day the Angelus bell rings, near six in the morning, at noon, and near six in the evening, and Catholics answer with prayer. Some English country churches still sound that bell, where it has often been taken for a leftover of the curfew. Who began the practice is disputed: some name Pope Urban II, others John XXII, while Louis XI of France gets credit for the thrice-daily round, ordered in 1472.

The Angelus is a Roman Catholic devotion recalling the Annunciation, the angel's announcement to Mary. Its name comes from its first Latin words, Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariae. Three short texts telling the mystery are spoken as versicle and response, with the Hail, Mary worked in between them.
britannica-1911-angerstein-john-julius: John Julius Angerstein (1735–1822) was a London merchant and patron of the fine arts. Born at St Petersburg, he settled in London about 1749. His lasting fame rests on his collection of paintings, about forty works described as among the most exquisite specimens of the art. On his death the British government purchased the collection, and it formed the nucleus, the founding core, of the National Gallery in London.
britannica-1911-arcadius:
Other hands ruled for Arcadius. The prefect Rufinus guided him first, until troops killed Rufinus late in 395. The eunuch Eutropius then held sway until his death in 399. His wife Eudoxia, a Frank's daughter, bent him strongly to her will before she died in 404, and in the reign's last year the prefect Anthemius propped the throne up.

Arcadius (378–408) was a Roman emperor, elder son of Theodosius the Great, who made him Augustus in 383. On his father's death in 395 he took the east; his brother Honorius took the west. Both were weak men who, in Gibbon's phrase, slept on their thrones and left rule to others. Danger pressed in: Goths under Alaric ravaged Greece in 395 and 396, the Gothic general Gainas rose in revolt in 399 and 400, and two court parties split the capital.
britannica-1911-arcesilaus:
Arcesilaus (316–241 B.C.) was a Greek philosopher. He founded the New, or Middle, Academy. Pitane in Aeolis was his birthplace. Autolycus the mathematician trained him first. Athens then drew him for study. Theophrastus and Crantor taught him there. Crantor led him to join the Academy. He later succeeded Crates as school head. Diogenes Laërtius claims drink killed him.

Other testimony discredits that story, though. Cleanthes contradicts it directly. His own precepts contradict it too. Athenians respected him much in life. His doctrines survive only through others' writings. Cicero and Sextus Empiricus preserve them. He attacked the Stoic criterion of truth. Strong conviction proves nothing, he argued. Contradictory convictions feel equally strong. Sense data are uncertain throughout. Reason's conclusions share that uncertainty. Probability must therefore suffice for action. That probability doctrine guides his practical teaching.
britannica-1911-archelaus-of-miletus:
Archelaus of Miletus was a Greek philosopher. He lived in the fifth century B.C. Athens was probably his birthplace. Diogenes Laërtius says Miletus instead. Anaxagoras was his teacher and master. Ion of Chios calls him Socrates's teacher. Some scholars doubt that connection, though. They see an attempt to link Socrates to Ionia. Gomperz upholds the story against them.

His cosmology followed Anaxagoras generally. He returned to earlier Ionian ideas partly. Primitive Matter was identical with air for him. Mind was mingled with that air. Dualism was thus avoided in his system. Thickening and thinning of air produced everything. Cold and warmth arose that way. Water and fire arose that way too. Earth formed from mud of fire and water. Humanity sprang from that mud initially. Moral and artistic faculties distinguish man from animals. No fragments of his writing remain.
britannica-1911-archermus:
Archermus was a Chian sculptor of the sixth century B.C. He worked in that century's middle decades. His father Micciades was also a sculptor. His sons Bupalus and Athenis sculpted too. The family used their native island's fine marble. Their school excelled in draped female figures. A scholiast on Aristophanes credits Archermus specially. He was first to give Victory wings, reportedly. Love also received wings from him first.

A Delos discovery seemed to confirm that claim. A basis signed by Micciades and Archermus emerged. A winged female figure in rapid motion stood nearby. Scholars naturally connected them as his Victory. Further investigation discredited that connection, though. The basis seems rather to have supported a sphinx. The entry thus records a tantalising near-proof. Greek archaic sculpture's development is its context.
britannica-1911-archestratus:
Archestratus was a Greek poet of Syracuse or Gela. He flourished about 330 B.C. He travelled extensively in search of delicacies. Foreign tables were his research field. He embodied results in a humorous poem. Hedypatheia was that poem's Greek title. Ennius later translated it freely into Latin. His version was called Heduphagetica. About 300 lines survive today.

Athenaeus preserves those surviving lines. Archestratus parodies the old gnomic poets' style. Critics call him the Hesiod of gluttons. Others call him their Theognis instead. Fish receive his chief attention in detail. Varieties, seasons, and sources all matter to him. The poem is a gastronomical catalogue in verse. Ribbeck edited the fragments in 1877. Brandt and Schmid added later scholarship. The entry captures classical food writing's high point.
britannica-1911-archias-aulus-licinius:
Aulus Licinius Archias was a Greek poet born at Antioch in Syria in 120 B.C. By 102 his fame was firm, most of all as a maker of verses on the spot. He came to Rome that year. His chief patron was Lucullus, whose family name he took. In 93 he went to Sicily with his patron. There the town of Heracleia made him a citizen. By law that grant in time gave him the rights of Rome as well.

In 61 a man named Gratius charged that Archias held those rights by fraud. Cicero spoke for him and won the case. That speech, the Pro Archia, tells us most of what we know of the poet. At the time of the trial he was at work on a poem about Cicero's own year as consul. Thirty-five short poems bear his name in the Greek Anthology.
britannica-1911-autocephalous: Autocephalous is a church term meaning of independent headship. It comes from two Greek words: autos, meaning self, and kephalē, meaning head. The term describes certain church officials and organisations that govern themselves. They answer to no higher church authority above them. The entry is a brief dictionary-style definition, giving the Greek origin and the kind of ecclesiastical independence the word names.
britannica-1911-autolycus:
Cattle theft brought Autolycus his one defeat. Sisyphus, missing beasts and suspecting him, burnt his own name into their hoofs, a mark no power could alter. Visiting Autolycus, he knew his cattle at once. The tale then turns sharp: on that same visit, Sisyphus is said to have lain with Anticleia, making Odysseus his son in truth, not Laertes', whom she later wed.

Autolycus belongs to Greek myth as a son of Hermes, living at the foot of Mount Parnassus. His daughter Anticleia was Odysseus's mother. Whatever his hands touched could change its shape. The thread running through the tale is plain: Hermes, god of theft and guile, stands behind Autolycus, Sisyphus, and Odysseus alike. Autolycus is also said to have taught Heracles to wrestle.
britannica-1911-auxentius:
Auxentius of Cappadocia was an Arian churchman of some note. He was at his height about the year 370. When the emperor Constantine put out the bishops who stood for the old creed, Auxentius was set in the seat of Dionysius at Milan. Men came to see him as the great foe of the Nicene faith in the west. His name stood out so far that a church council named him in its act of blame in 369. Damasus, bishop of Rome, called that council at the urging of Athanasius.

When a sound-creed emperor, Valentinian, took the throne, Auxentius was left in peace in his see. His teaching was still fought in public. Hilary of Poitiers led that attack. The chief source for the man's life and views is Hilary's book against him. The short piece sends the reader to the life of Arius for the creed at stake.
britannica-1911-aventinus:
Aventinus (1477-1534) was the name taken by Johann Turmair, author of the Annals of Bavaria, from the Latin name of Abensberg, his birthplace. After study at Ingolstadt, Vienna, Cracow, and Paris, he became tutor in 1509 to two sons of Duke Albert of Bavaria-Munich.

Encouraged by Duke William IV, he wrote the Annales Boiorum in seven books, joining Bavarian history to general history down to 1460, then made a German version, the Bayersche Chronik. His care with sources foreshadowed modern scientific history, and he has been called the Bavarian Herodotus. Though he never openly joined the reformers, sympathy for them and dislike of monks brought him prison in 1528, before friends won his release.
britannica-1911-avernus:
Avernus is a lake of Campania, Italy, about twelve miles north of Baiae, filling an old volcanic crater nearly two miles around. It lies 32 feet above the sea, runs 213 feet deep, and has no natural outlet. Dense forests once ringed it.

Legend made the lake an entrance to the underworld, used by Odysseus and Aeneas, and home of the Cimmerii; its Greek name was explained as a place no bird could cross. Agrippa turned it into a naval harbour in 37 B.C., cutting canals and a long tunnel toward Cumae. Remains by the lake include great baths known as the Temple of Apollo and a rock-cut passage called the Sibyl's Grotto.
britannica-1911-avianus:
Avianus was a Latin writer of fables, placed by some critics in the age of the Antonines and by others as late as the 6th century A.D. He seems to have lived at Rome and to have been a heathen. Forty-two fables carry his name, dedicated to a Theodosius praised warmly for his learning.

Nearly all the tales appear in Babrius, though Avianus worked from a rough Latin prose version rather than the Greek original. His language and metre are mostly correct, with faults chiefly in the pentameter. The fables became a popular school-book, drawing introductions, morals, and paraphrases, including the Novus Avianus of Alexander Neckam. Caxton printed an English version at Westminster in 1483.
britannica-1911-avienus-rufius-festus:
Avienus, Rufius Festus, was a Roman aristocrat and poet from Vulsinii in Etruria who flourished in the second half of the 4th century A.D. He was probably proconsul of Africa in 366 and of Achaia in 372. A pagan, he stood firmly by the old religion.

His verse work rests on Greek models: he translated Aratus on the stars and paraphrased Dionysius as a Description of the Earth's Lands, both in hexameters. He also described the coasts of the Mediterranean, Caspian, and Black Seas in iambic verse, though only a fragment of the first book survives. His summaries of Livy and the Aeneid in the same metre are lost, but minor poems under his name remain in anthologies.
britannica-1911-azotus:
Azotus is the name Greek and Roman writers gave to Ashdod, an ancient city of Palestine, now a small village called Esdud in the district of Acre. It stood three miles inland from the Mediterranean on the great military road between Syria and Egypt, midway between Joppa and Gaza.

As one of the five chief Philistine cities and seat of the god Dagon's worship, Ashdod kept a stubborn independence against Israel down to Maccabean times. Assyrians took it in 711 B.C., yet it later held off Egypt's king Psammetichus for twenty-nine years. Rome's Gabinius rebuilt it from Jewish war ruins, and Augustus gave it to Herod's sister Salome. Its one New Testament mention is in Acts, and a Saracen khan is its chief relic.
britannica-1911-balbus:
Balbus, meaning stammerer, was a name borne by several Roman families. The 1911 Britannica entry lists men of the Acilii Balbi who reached the consulship. It also names a supporter of Pompey later pardoned by Caesar. Another entry figure is Marcus Atius Balbus, whose daughter Atia was the mother of Augustus.

Most space goes to the two Cornelii Balbi, uncle and nephew from Gades in Spain. The elder won Roman citizenship from Pompey for service against Sertorius, helped bring about the First Triumvirate, and served Caesar as chief engineer. In 56 B.C. enemies challenged his citizenship in court, and Cicero, Pompey, and Crassus spoke for him before he was cleared.
britannica-1911-balduinus-jacobus:
Jacobus Balduinus was an Italian jurist of the 13th century, born at Bologna and said to be of noble family. He studied under Azo, a famed teacher of law. In time he taught men who became noted in their turn, among them Odofredus and Hostiensis.

His fame as a professor of civil law at Bologna led Genoa to elect him podestà, its chief magistrate, and to trust him with reforming the laws of the republic. Balduinus died at Bologna in 1225. The 1911 Britannica entry credits him with treatises on legal procedure, described as the earliest works of their kind.
britannica-1911-baldus-de-ubaldis-petrus:
Petrus Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1406) was an Italian jurist born at Perugia. He studied civil law under Bartolus and took his doctor's degree at only seventeen. He then taught law at Bologna for three years before gaining a chair at Perugia, where he stayed thirty-three years.

Baldus later taught at Pisa, Florence, Padua, and Pavia, when those schools rivalled Bologna.
