The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his work in public life and his legal opinions, printed in five volumes, as the base of his fame. Among his pupils was Pierre Roger de Beaufort, later Pope Gregory XI. His commentary on the Liber Feudorum counts among his best works.
britannica-1911-barnett-samuel-augustus:
Samuel Augustus Barnett (born 1844) was an English clergyman and social reformer, born at Bristol on 8 February 1844, son of an iron manufacturer. After Wadham College, Oxford, and a visit to the United States, he was ordained and in 1872 became vicar of St Jude's, Whitechapel, in London's east end. In 1873 he married Henrietta Rowland, a fellow worker with Octavia Hill.

The Barnetts worked hard for their poor parish: evening schools for adults, music and wholesome entertainment, and seats on the guardians' board and school committees. Barnett fought outdoor relief, handouts given outside the workhouse, as a cause of pauperism, while bettering relief inside and drawing the charities together. The 1911 Britannica entry follows Arnold Toynbee's visits to Whitechapel from 1875.
britannica-1911-bartolus:
Bartolus (1314–1357), an Italian jurist from Sassoferrato in the duchy of Urbino, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the most famous master of his school of law teachers. He studied civil law at Perugia and Bologna and took his doctorate in 1334. Before teaching, he gained courtroom experience as an assessor, a legal adviser to judges, at Todi and Pisa, experience that later gave his lectures their practical edge.

Perugia made Bartolus's name. Appointed to its chair of civil law in 1343, he raised the school to Bologna's level. The entry credits him not with inventing the dialectical method, which earlier teachers had abused, but with using it well and reviving clear explanation of the legal texts. His treatises on procedure and on evidence are called valuable, and his Commentary on Justinian's Code was in some countries treated as equal in authority to the Code itself.
britannica-1911-bassus-aufidius:
Aufidius Bassus was a Roman historian who lived in the reign of Tiberius, as recorded in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His history probably began with the civil wars or with the death of Caesar. The elder Pliny took up the work where Bassus left it. By his own account he carried the story down to the end of Nero's reign. Together the two histories span the empire's first century.

Praise and a warning survive together. Bassus's Bellum Germanicum, his account of the German war, is commended in the sources, though it may have been a separate work or only a section of the general history. Seneca spoke highly of Bassus as a historian. Yet the fragments in Seneca's Suasoriae, on the death of Cicero, are marked by an affected style. Quintilian and Tacitus are cited at the end as further witnesses to his standing.
britannica-1911-bassus-caesius:
Caesius Bassus was a Roman lyric poet who lived in the reign of Nero, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the intimate friend of Persius, who dedicated his sixth satire to him, and after Persius's death Bassus edited his friend's works. He is said to have died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, which buried Pompeii. The entry reports that end as tradition, not certain fact.

Praise for Bassus ran very high. Quintilian said that, Horace excepted, he was the only lyric poet worth reading. Bassus is also identified as author of De Metris, on poetic metres. Large fragments survive, probably from a shortened edition. The work seems first to have been written in verse and later recast in prose as a teaching book. A scanty Ars Caesii Bassi circulating under his name is judged not his, being borrowed from the genuine treatise.
britannica-1911-bassus-cassianus:
Cassianus Bassus, called Scholasticus, meaning the lawyer, was one of the geoponici, the writers on farming, in the account given by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived at the end of the sixth or the beginning of the seventh century AD. From earlier writers he compiled a collection of agricultural literature known as the Geoponica. An unknown editor later revised the collection. It was published around 950, under Constantine Porphyrogenitus, to whom the work has sometimes been wrongly ascribed.

Scope is the entry's main point. The Geoponica carries a full list of the authorities Bassus drew upon, so readers can see the chain of older farming writers behind him. Its subjects treated include agriculture in general, and then birds, bees, horses, cattle, sheep, dogs, and fishes in turn. Editions by Needham, Niclas, and Beckh are listed, with studies of the text's tangled transmission from late antiquity into the Byzantine world.
britannica-1911-bassus-saleius:
Saleius Bassus was a Roman epic poet in the reign of Vespasian, and a fellow poet of Valerius Flaccus. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on him rests on what writers of his own time said. Quintilian gave him a strong poetic gift. Julius Secundus, a speaker in the Dialogus of Tacitus, called him a perfect poet and a most famed bard, and the entry quotes that praise.

Poverty and loss close the account. Bassus fell into poverty, but Vespasian made him a gift of 500,000 sesterces, a large sum of money to help a poet the court prized. Yet none of his work has come down to us at all. The Laus Pisonis, a poem in praise of Piso that some writers gave to him, is now thought to be the work of Titus Calpurnius Siculus. Bassus lives on only in the praise of men who had read him.
britannica-1911-bathybius:
Bathybius, from Greek words for deep and life, is the name of a sea substance that turned out not to be alive, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a slimy material thought to lie in great masses on the deep ocean floor. Men of science took it for raw protoplasm, the living stuff of cells, in simple form. About 1868 Huxley named it Bathybius haeckelii and treated it as an organism, a first step of life in the sea.

Tests on a famed voyage killed the claim. Work linked with the Challenger expedition showed what the slime in fact was. It was an artificial product, a soft fall of gypsum thrown down from sea-water by the alcohol used to store samples. Most biologists then gave up the idea that it was alive, and Huxley gave it up too. It stands as a record of a scientific error.
britannica-1911-battus:
Battus is named in legend as the founder of the Greek colony of Cyrene in Libya, about 630 BC, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greeks who went with him came, like him, from the island of Thera, and were in part of Minyan stock.  In the Cyrenaean tale in Herodotus, Battus, who had a fault in his speech, asked the oracle at Delphi for help and was told to found a colony in Libya.

Name and kings fill the rest. Some linked Battus to a Greek word for stammering, from his speech fault. Herodotus says instead that Battus was the Libyan word for king, and that the name was given only after he reached Libya. Pindar calls the founder by his true name, Aristoteles. Four kings named Battus, taking turns with four named Arcesilaus, then ruled in Cyrene. Their line held power till about 450 BC.
britannica-1911-belisarius:
Belisarius (about 505–565) ranks among the most famous generals of the later Roman empire. He was born in a district called Germania, on the borders of Thrace and Macedonia, and served as a youth in Justinian’s bodyguard. Justinian soon made him commander of the Eastern army, where he beat the Persians in 530.

After crushing the Nika revolt at Constantinople in 532, Belisarius took the Vandal kingdom in Africa with only 15,000 men, capturing Carthage and King Gelimer. Honours followed: the consulship and medals struck in his name. The entry also follows his later Italian wars and closes by dismissing the tale of Belisarius ending as a blind beggar as fiction.
britannica-1911-benedict-sir-julius:
Sir Julius Benedict (1804–1885) was a composer born at Stuttgart, son of a Jewish banker. He learned composition from Hummel at Weimar and from Weber at Dresden, who treated him like a son for three years. Weber presented him to Beethoven at Vienna in 1823, the year he took a theatre post there.

Benedict worked at Naples, where his first operas met small success, then settled in London in 1835 for the rest of his life. He conducted English opera at Drury Lane, led Mendelssohn’s Elijah for Jenny Lind’s first oratorio appearance, and ran festival concerts for decades. Knighted in 1871, he also wrote a life of Weber before dying in London in 1885.
britannica-1911-benedictus:
Benedictus is the hymn of Zacharias, found in the first chapter of Luke’s Gospel, named from the first word of its Latin form. Christians have used it in worship since at least the ninth century. It came into the Anglican morning prayer from the Roman service of matin-lauds.

The Prayer-Book of 1549 allowed no substitute: the Benedictus was to be said through the whole year. In 1552 the Jubilate was added as an option, and wording of 1662 limits when it may take the Benedictus’s place. The name also belongs to a part of the Roman Mass that begins Benedictus qui venit, “blessed is he that cometh.”
britannica-1911-berengarius:
Berengarius, or Berengar (died 1088), was a medieval theologian born at Tours early in the eleventh century. He was schooled at Chartres under the famous Fulbert, yet showed great independence of judgment from his youth. As head of Tours’ cathedral school he drew pupils from all over France and spread the new logic-driven study of theology.

Made archdeacon of Angers before 1040, Berengar then examined the received teaching on the eucharist for himself. He concluded that transubstantiation, the doctrine that the bread becomes Christ’s body in substance, ran against reason, scripture and the fathers. The quarrel that followed fills the rest of the entry, told largely through the works written to refute him, since his own survive only in fragments.
britannica-1911-bering-vitus:
Vitus Bering (1680–1741) was a Danish navigator born at Horsens who entered the Russian navy in 1703. Peter the Great’s far-reaching plan to map Asia’s north coast set his life’s course. In 1725 he travelled overland to Okhotsk, crossed to Kamchatka and built the ship Gabriel, pushing north in 1728 until no land showed north or east.

A greater expedition followed. From his new settlement of Petropavlovsk in 1740, Bering sailed in 1741 with the St Peter and St Paul toward America and sighted Alaska’s south coast. Storms split the ships, scurvy struck him down, and his vessel was wrecked on the island that now bears his name. Bering died there on 19 December 1741; Cook later proved his observations true.
britannica-1911-bessus:
Bessus was satrap, or provincial governor, of Bactria and Sogdiana under Darius III of Persia. At Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BC he led the troops of his satrapy. When Alexander chased the fleeing Persian king east in 330, Bessus joined the plot against Darius. The conspirators deposed the king and soon killed him. Bessus then claimed the throne himself, taking the royal name Artaxerxes.

This short 1911 Britannica entry follows his bid to rally the eastern provinces against the Macedonian conqueror. Treachery delivered him as a prisoner in the summer of 329. Alexander sent him to Ecbatana, where he was condemned to death. Before the execution his nose and ears were cut off. The entry notes that Darius I had punished usurpers the same way, as the Behistun inscription records.
britannica-1911-bibulus:
Bibulus was a surname in the Roman family, or gens, Calpurnia. The best-known bearer was Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, consul with Julius Caesar in 59 BC. The aristocratic party backed him against Caesar's ally Lucceius. Bribery was used freely, with even Cato's approval, to win his election. In office he proved no match for his colleague. Caesar's agrarian law for Campania lands met his resistance in vain.

The mob manhandled Bibulus when he opposed the law in public. He shut himself in his house for eight months of his consulship. From home he issued edicts against Caesar that only drew mob attacks. Rome joked that the consuls that year were Julius and Caesar. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to Syria as proconsul for Pompey. His wife Porcia, Cato's daughter, later married Brutus.
britannica-1911-binchois-egidius: Egidius Binchois (died 1460) was a musical composer of the early 15th century. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single sentence. It gives only three facts about him. He was evidently named after his birthplace, Binche, near Mons. He worked as a composer in the early 1400s. Theorists of his time and later ranked him very high. They placed him second only to Dunstable and Dufay. No works, posts, or birth year are recorded.
britannica-1911-boletus:
Boletus is a group of fungi known by a thick cap on a central stem, with soft flesh and a sponge of fine tubes under the cap. Those tubes stand upright, pack tight, and peel away easily from the flesh. All the kinds grow on the ground, in woods or under trees, in early autumn.

Caps run brown, red, or yellow, and the pores range from pure white through brown, red, yellow, and green. A few kinds are poisonous, while several are good to eat. The prize of the table is Boletus edulis, with a brown cap and white pores that turn green with age, sold across Europe as ceps. Forty-nine British kinds are counted in all.
britannica-1911-bonar-horatius:
Horatius Bonar (1808–1889) was a Scottish Presbyterian minister best loved as a hymn writer. Born in Edinburgh and schooled there, he did mission work at Leith, became parish minister of Kelso in 1837, and at the Disruption of 1843 joined the new Free Church. From 1866 he served the Chalmers memorial church in Edinburgh.

He took a doctorate from Aberdeen in 1853 and was moderator of his church's general assembly in 1883. Bonar wrote much religious prose and edited several journals, among them the Christian Treasury and the Quarterly Journal of Prophecy. His fame rests on three series of Hymns of Faith and Hope (1857–1866). Nearly every hymnal since, the entry says, keeps a score of his hymns, such as I heard the voice of Jesus say.
britannica-1911-bonchamps-charles-melchi:
Charles Melchior Artus, marquis de Bonchamps (about 1760–1793), was a leader of the royalist rising in the Vendée. Born at Jouverteil in Anjou, he first soldiered in the American War of Independence and came home a captain of grenadiers. Loyal to the monarchy, he quit his command at the Revolution and retired to his château at St Florent.

In spring 1793 the Vendée insurgents chose him as a leader, and his counsel is credited with much of the peasants' early success. He fought at Bressuire, Thouars, and Fontenay, where he was wounded. Quarrels among the chiefs weakened the cause, and at Cholet in October 1793 the Vendéans were beaten and Bonchamps mortally hurt. His last act, the entry says, was to pardon 5000 republican prisoners his men had sworn to kill.
britannica-1911-bond-sir-edward-augustus:
Sir Edward Augustus Bond (1815–1898) was an English librarian who rebuilt the manuscript department of the British Museum. Born at Hanwell, a schoolmaster's son, he went to Merchant Taylors' school and joined the public record office in 1832. In 1838 he moved to the museum's manuscript department under Sir Frederick Madden.

He rose step by step: Egerton librarian in 1852, assistant keeper in 1856, keeper in 1867, and principal librarian in 1878. His classified catalogue of manuscripts and faster, surer publishing are called lasting gains. The new White Wing for prints, drawings, manuscripts, and newspapers rose under him, and the Stowe manuscripts were bought. With Sir E. Maunde Thompson he founded the Palaeographical Society and made the study of handwriting an exact science.
britannica-1911-bonifacius:
Bonifacius (died 432) was the Roman governor of Africa blamed for calling the Vandals into the province. The story says he acted in revenge on Placidia, who ruled for her son Valentinian III in 428–429. Procopius lays the invitation on his rival Aëtius instead, and the earliest sources blame a minister named Felix for slandering Bonifacius.

Guilty or not, he soon turned on the Vandals and bravely defended Hippo against them. In 432 he came back to Italy, was taken into Placidia's favour, and was made master of the soldiery. Aëtius resented the rise, the two met, perhaps in single combat, and Bonifacius won yet took a wound that killed him three months later. The entry calls the whole history obscure and points readers to Freeman and Gibbon.
britannica-1911-bonus:
Bonus is a money word used with a smile, the entry says, a playful use of the Latin bonus for a good thing. In company finance it means an extra sum paid to shareholders on top of the ordinary dividend. Such payments usually come from profits piled up over years, or from the gains of one special deal.

Insurance firms use the word in a second sense. There it is the extra amount added to a policy's value when pooled profits or surplus are shared out among policy holders in fair shares. In the widest sense, a bonus is any payment or reward given over and above what was owed and promised. The whole entry is a compact note on these three uses.
britannica-1911-borel-petrus:
Petrus Borel (1809–1859), in full Pierre Joseph Borel d'Hauterive, was a French writer of the wild Romantic school. Born at Lyons, the son of a man ruined for royalist resistance to the Convention, he was trained in Paris as an architect. He soon quit building to become one of the loudest partisans of Romanticism.

His fierce feelings filled volume after volume: Rhapsodies (1832) in verse, the tales Champavert (1833), and Madame Putiphar (1839). The books never freed him from poverty. Through Gautier's and Madame de Girardin's kindness he gained a small civil service post. He died at Mostaganem in Algeria in 1859, and the entry points readers to Clarétie's study, Petrus Borel, le Lycanthrope.
britannica-1911-brachylogus:
Brachylogus is the name, given in the 1500s, to a short systematic account of Roman law. Its age was long disputed. Some writers placed it under Justinian. Others called it a fake of the 1500s. The earliest surviving edition came out at Lyons in 1549. The title Brachylogus totius Juris Civilis first appears at Lyons in 1553.

The entry argues for a date in the 1100s. The book quotes a Lombard law of Louis le Débonnaire, so it cannot be older than his reign. Its style and reasoning far outclass the law writers of the 900s and 1000s. Its method shows no mark of the Bologna gloss writers. Any later work would bear that mark. Savigny's researches on its history are pointed to at the close.
britannica-1911-briareus:
Briareus, also called Aegaeon, stands in Greek myth as one of the three hundred-armed, fifty-headed giants known as the Hecatoncheires, brother to Cottus and Gyges. Homer gives him two names: Aegaeon among men, Briareus among the gods. He was a son of Poseidon, or in other tellings of Uranus, and of Gaea, the earth.

Tales about the brothers clash with each other. In the best known one, Zeus calls them to help against the Titans, who are beaten and shut in Tartarus with the three set as guards at its gates. Other tales make Briareus an attacker of Olympus buried under Mount Aetna, or a sea giant who ruled fabled Aegaea in Euboea, fought Poseidon and invented warships. The entry closes by asking what force of nature such beings stand for, naming quakes and the many-moving sea.
britannica-1911-briggs-charles-augustus:
Charles Augustus Briggs (born 1841) was an American Hebrew scholar and theologian born in New York City on 15 January 1841. He studied at the University of Virginia from 1857 to 1860, graduated from Union Theological Seminary in 1863 and studied further at Berlin. Pastor of the Presbyterian church at Roselle, New Jersey, from 1869 to 1874, he then taught Hebrew at Union for many years.

From 1874 to 1891 he held the Hebrew chair, then Biblical theology until 1904, when he moved to theological encyclopaedia and symbolics. He edited the Presbyterian Review from 1880 to 1890. In 1892 the New York presbytery tried him for heresy over his inaugural address and acquitted him. The charges, set out in detail, claim he taught that reason and the church rival scripture as fountains of divine truth, that errors may stand in the original text. That Moses did not write the Pentateuch.
britannica-1911-britannicus:
Britannicus was the son of the Roman emperor Claudius by his third wife Messallina, born probably in the year 41. He was first called Claudius Tiberius Germanicus and took the name Britannicus from the senate in honour of the conquest in Britain made near the time of his birth. Until 48 he stood as heir presumptive to the throne.

His mother's execution that year changed everything. Agrippina, Claudius's new wife, persuaded the weak emperor to adopt her own son Lucius Domitius, the later Nero, pushing Britannicus aside. After Nero took power, Agrippina played on his fears until he had the young prince poisoned at a banquet in the year 55. The emperor Titus later set up a golden statue of him, and Racine made him the subject of a tragedy, a fate the entry closes by recording.
britannica-1911-brownson-orestes-augustu:
Orestes Augustus Brownson is traced in this biographical entry through a restless religious pilgrimage, though the hosted file begins mid-article, with his church changes rather than his birth. He became a Presbyterian in 1822, served as a Universalist minister from 1826 to 1831 while editing that church's chief journal, preached independently at Ithaca in 1831. Turned Unitarian minister in 1832.

In 1836 he organised in Boston the Society for Christian Union and Progress, serving as its pastor seven years. In 1844 he became a Roman Catholic and remained one, though the orthodoxy of his writings was once laid before Cardinal Franzelin by the pope. His philosophy followed Comte briefly, then Victor Cousin, and is summed as a modified intuitionalism, while his social reform schemes moved from Robert Owen's influence toward Catholicism. Brownson's Quarterly Review, begun in 1844 in Boston and after 1855 in New York, carried his views until its suspension in 1864.
britannica-1911-brutus:
Brutus was a surname borne by several Romans of the Junian gens. This 1911 Britannica article first explains the word itself. It began as an adjective meaning heavy or stupid. It is kin to the Greek barys and to the English “brute.”

The longest treatment goes to Lucius Junius Brutus. He was one of the first two consuls, in 509 B.C. He helped expel the Tarquin kings after the outrage on Lucretia. He condemned his own sons for plotting to restore them. He died in single combat with Aruns, the deposed king's son. Later bearers include Decimus Junius Brutus, consul in 138 B.C. He won the name Gallaecus from victory in Spain. The jurist Marcus Junius Brutus helped found Roman civil law. The article closes with the famous Marcus. It weighs his character, his writings, and his letters to Cicero.
britannica-1911-bryennius-nicephorus:
Nicephorus Bryennius (1062–1137) was a Byzantine soldier and statesman. He was also a historian. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and work. He was born at Orestias, the modern Adrianople. He won the favour of the emperor Alexius I. He married the emperor's daughter Anna. He took the high titles of Caesar and Panhypersebastos.

Bryennius defended Constantinople against Godfrey of Bouillon in 1097. He made peace with Bohemund of Antioch in 1108. He helped defeat Malik-Shah in 1116. When Alexius died, his wife plotted to seize the throne. Bryennius refused to join the plot against John, the rightful heir. He joined John's Syrian campaign in 1137. Illness forced him home, and he died that year. He also wrote a history of the years 1057 to 1081. It drew on Psellus, Scylitza and Attaliota. The entry calls it a family chronicle, written to glorify the house of Comnenus.
britannica-1911-brzozowski-thaddeus:
Thaddeus Brzozowski (d. 1820) was the nineteenth general of the Jesuits. This 1911 Britannica entry covers his time in office. He succeeded Gabriel Gruber on 2 September 1805. In 1801 Pius VII had let the Jesuits re-form in north Russia. Brzozowski led the society during its wider restoration in Europe.

In 1812 he won a key concession. The Jesuit college of Polotsk was recognized as a university. In 1814 the pope restored the order across Europe. The pope gave Brzozowski full power to receive new members. Then Russia turned against the growing order. An edict expelled the Jesuits from St Petersburg in December 1815. Brzozowski asked leave to retire to Rome. The request was refused. He died on 5 February 1820. His chief interest is his place at the head of the restored society.
britannica-1911-bucephalus:
Bucephalus was the favourite horse of Alexander the Great. He was a Thracian horse. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives the few facts the sources support. The horse died in 326 B.C. He died either of wounds or of old age. The wounds were received at the battle on the Hydaspes.

Alexander marked the loss with a city. He built Bucephala on the river bank. The entry ties its site to a mound opposite the modern Jhelum. It cites Arrian as the chief authority for the story. It also cites Plutarch and Curtius for other tales. For the site, it points to Vincent Smith's Early History of India. The notice is brief, and it sticks to the horse, his death, and the town named for him.
britannica-1911-buchanan-claudius:
Claudius Buchanan (1766–1815) was an English divine who worked in India. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born at Cambuslang, near Glasgow. He studied at Glasgow and at Cambridge. He was ordained in 1795. He held a chaplaincy at Barrackpur from 1797 to 1799. He then became Calcutta chaplain. He also served as vice-principal of the college of Fort William.

In India, Buchanan pushed native education. He organized translations of the Scriptures in a planned way. His travels in the south and west added to knowledge of Indian life. He set them out in Christian Researches in Asia, in 1811. He returned to England in 1808. He stayed active in Indian church affairs. His book Colonial Ecclesiastical Establishment appeared in 1813. It helped settle a public controversy of that year. The result was the setting up of an Indian episcopate.
britannica-1911-bucyrus:
Bucyrus is a city in Ohio, in the United States. It is the county-seat of Crawford county. It stands on the Sandusky river, 62 miles north of Columbus. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its growth and trades. Its population was 5974 in 1890. It rose to 6560 in 1900 and 8122 in 1910. Three railway systems serve the city. Interurban electric lines serve it as well.

The city stands about 1000 feet above sea-level. Farm land and stock country surround it. Its works make machinery and structural steel. They also make furniture, ploughs and wagons. Heating apparatus and clay-working machines come from its shops. The Ohio Central railway keeps shops and a division terminal there. Settlers first came in 1817. The town was laid out in 1822. It became a village in 1830 and a city in 1885.
britannica-1911-calenus-quintus-fufius:
Quintus Fufius Calenus was a Roman general of Caesar's age. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in politics and war. As tribune of the people in 61 B.C., he acted for the defence. He helped win acquittal for the notorious Publius Clodius. Clodius stood charged with profaning the mysteries of Bona Dea. In 59 B.C. Calenus was praetor. He passed a law on how the voting orders voted in court.

Calenus then fought under Caesar in Gaul and Spain. In 48 B.C. Caesar sent him to fetch troops from Italy. Pirates under Bibulus caught most of his ships on the way. Calenus himself barely escaped the disaster. Caesar's influence made him consul in 47 B.C. After the dictator's murder, he joined Mark Antony. He commanded Antony's legions in north Italy. He died in 41 B.C., at the foot of the Alps.
britannica-1911-capricornus:
Capricornus, the Goat, is the tenth sign of the zodiac. It is also a constellation of the southern hemisphere. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its history and stars. The word joins two Latin roots, caper and cornu. They mean a goat and a horn. Its symbol is meant to show the goat's crooked horns. Eudoxus mentioned the constellation in the 4th century B.C. Aratus named it in the 3rd century B.C.

Ptolemy catalogued 28 stars in Capricornus. Tycho Brahe also listed 28, while Hevelius gave 29. The ancients pictured it as a mixed creature. Its front half was a goat, and its rear half a fish. Sometimes it was drawn simply as a goat. The entry singles out one member for the reader. Alpha Capricorni is a pair of stars, of the 3rd and 4th magnitudes. Each of those stars has a faint companion of the 9th magnitude.
britannica-1911-caracalla-marcus-aureliu:
Caracalla (186–217) was a Roman emperor. His full imperial name was Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his violent reign. He was born at Lugdunum, Lyons, on 4 April 186. His father was the emperor Septimius Severus. His birth name was Bassianus, and Caracalla was a nickname. It came from the long Gallic tunic he wore and spread in the army.

Severus died at York in 211, leaving two sons as joint rulers. Caracalla wanted the throne for himself alone. He had his brother Geta murdered in their mother's arms. Some 20,000 of Geta's suspected friends died with him. The jurist Papinian was among the victims. In 212 Caracalla gave Roman citizenship to all free men of the empire. The entry says revenue was his real motive. Citizen heirs paid an inheritance tax that others escaped. His spending and the soldiers' demands drained the treasury. Taxes and extortion of every kind made up the gap.
britannica-1911-caractacus:
Caractacus was a British chieftain who fought Rome. His name, strictly Caratacus, is a Latin form. It survives in the Welsh name Caradoc. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives what is known. He led the native resistance to the Roman invaders. That struggle ran from A.D. 48 to 51. He was captured at last and sent to Rome. Tacitus and Dio are the entry's sources for the story.

Two old camps on the Welsh border bear his name. They are both called Caer Caradoc today. The entry warns that the names are not ancient. Antiquaries invented them in later ages, it says. They are no true memorials of the Celtic hero. The notice is brief and cautious in tone. It gives the dates, the capture, and the sources. It refuses to build legend on the camp names.
britannica-1911-carausius-marcus-aureliu:
Carausius was a Roman usurper who ruled Britain alone. He held power from A.D. 286 to 293. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was a Menapian from Belgic Gaul, of humble birth. In his early days he had been a ship's pilot. He rose fast in the army. The emperor Maximian posted him at Boulogne. His task was to guard the Channel coasts. Frankish and Saxon pirates were the threat he faced.

At first Carausius fought the pirates with energy. Then came charges that he shared their plunder. The emperor sentenced him to death for the offence. Carausius crossed to Britain and proclaimed himself ruler. The legions joined him at once, and Franks enlisted too. Maximian's attempt to recover the island failed in a storm. In 292 Constantius took Boulogne back from him. Before the invasion of Britain could follow, Allectus murdered him.
britannica-1911-carinus-marcus-aurelius:
Carinus was a Roman emperor, reigning in A.D. 283–284. He was the elder son of the emperor Carus. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his short, dark reign. On his father's accession he governed the west of the empire. He fought with success against the German tribes. Then he left the Upper Rhine to his legates. He returned to Rome and gave himself to debauchery.

Carus died in the east, and the eastern army turned homeward. Numerianus, the younger son, was murdered at Chalcedon. The soldiers proclaimed Diocletian emperor in his place. Carinus marched east to meet the rival claimant. In Pannonia he crushed the usurper Julianus on the way. He won several engagements against Diocletian's army in Moesia. At the river Margus his troops were gaining the day. Then a tribune whose wife he had seduced assassinated him. The entry calls him one of the worst of the emperors.
britannica-1911-carpathus:
Carpathus is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an island in the Mediterranean about 30 miles south-west of Rhodes, called Scarpanto in Italian. The sea around it took its name from the island, the Carpathian Sea. In ancient and medieval times the island stayed closely tied to Rhodes. Noble families held it under Venetian rule, notably the Cornari from 1306 to 1540, when it passed at last into Turkish hands.

Distance from the main routes let Carpathus keep many old ways. The entry notes that its dress, customs, and dialect hold peculiarities long lost elsewhere, and that its speech resembles the dialects of Rhodes and Cyprus. Short as it is, the entry gives the island's place, its chain of rulers, and the reason its traditions survived. It closes with references to travel accounts and studies in Greek journals for readers who want the detail behind the summary.
britannica-1911-carrickfergus:
Carrickfergus is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport and watering-place of County Antrim, Ireland, on the northern shore of Belfast Lough. The town stretches about a mile along the lough, some nine and a half miles north-east of Belfast by rail, and its urban district held 4208 people in 1901. Its chief building is the castle, first built by John de Courci late in the twelfth century and much enlarged since.

The castle stands on a rock jutting into the sea and still serves as an arsenal with heavy guns. Its old keep rises 90 feet and survives in good repair. The town walls built under Sir Henry Sidney remain on the west and north, with the North Gate standing. The parish church of St Nicholas holds monuments of the Chichester family. Trade in farm produce, leather, and linen, with flax mills and bleach-works nearby, rounds out the account.
britannica-1911-carus-marcus-aurelius:
Marcus Aurelius Carus is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Roman emperor who reigned from A.D. 282 to 283. He was probably born at Narona in Illyria and educated at Rome. A senator who had filled civil and military posts, he was prefect of the praetorian guards under Probus. After Probus was murdered at Sirmium, the soldiers proclaimed Carus emperor, though some suspected his own hand in the killing.

Carus never returned to Rome, but simply announced his accession to the senate. He gave the title of Caesar to his sons Carinus and Numerianus, left Carinus over the west, and marched east against Persia. After beating the Quadi and Sarmatians on the Danube, he conquered Mesopotamia and pushed past the Tigris. Then, after a violent storm, he was found dead. The entry lists disease, lightning, and murder by his own soldiers among the reported causes.
britannica-1911-cauliculus: Cauliculus is a single sentence 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term of classical architecture. From the Latin caulis, a stalk, the word names the stalks in a Corinthian capital. The entry counts eight of them. Each stalk bears two leaves, and from these stalks rise the helices, the spiral scrolls of the capital. The scrolls in turn support the abacus, the slab that crowns the capital.
britannica-1911-cavallo-tiberius:
Tiberius Cavallo (1749–1809) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Anglo Italian electrician and natural philosopher born at Naples, where his father was a physician. He came to England in 1771 meaning to follow a mercantile career. He soon turned to scientific work instead. He made several clever improvements in scientific instruments. The entry judges his mind as imitative and critical rather than creative.

His books cover much of physics. They include A Complete Treatise on Electricity in 1777 and a treatise on air and other elastic fluids in 1781. He wrote on aerostation, on magnetism, and on medical electricity. His Elements of Natural and Experimental Philosophy appeared in 1803. A late work treated the medical properties of factitious air in 1798. He died in London on 21 December 1809. The entry reads as a catalogue of a busy, wide ranging writer on the physical science of his day.
britannica-1911-celsus:
Celsus is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a second century opponent of Christianity, dated to about A.D. 178. He is known mainly through his book The True Word. That work survives because Origen published it in 248, some seventy years after it was written, in order to answer it. Origen quotes, paraphrases, and refers to the arguments in turn. By that method about three quarters of the text survives in verbatim form. Only about a tenth is really lost.

The entry sets the scene of 248. Rome was marking its thousandth year, and the church stood against the worship of Caesar. It then rehearses Celsus's attack. He repeats Jewish taunts: Jesus was born in adultery and raised on the wisdom of Egypt. His poverty and wretched end disprove his claims. The resurrection was revealed only to his own followers. Celsus also mocks the Jews as nearly as foolish as their Christian foes.
britannica-1911-censorinus:
Censorinus is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Roman grammarian and miscellaneous writer of the third century A.D. His work De Accentibus is lost. His treatise De Die Natali survives. He wrote it in 238 as a birthday gift for his patron, Quintus Caerellius. Its contents range widely. They cover the natural history of man, the influence of the stars, music, religious rites, and astronomy.

The second part of the book treats chronology and mathematics. It has been of great service in fixing the main epochs of ancient history. The entry praises the style as clear and concise, though somewhat rhetorical. The Latin is good for its period. His chief sources were Varro and Suetonius. Some scholars hold that the whole work adapts Suetonius's lost Pratum. The entry also warns that fragments on astronomy and music, often printed with the book, are not his.
britannica-1911-census:
Census is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the periodic counting of people. The word comes from the Latin censere, to estimate or assess. In modern times the count is limited to population, and at times to industry and farming. In older times it reached property of all kinds, for the purpose of assessment. Counts of this kind are very ancient.

The entry opens its survey in the Bible. At the Exodus, Israel counted all males of twenty years and upward for war. The Levites were counted apart, from the age of thirty. David's census under Joab covered the fighting men only. The entry notes that its dire results were quoted against such inquiries into the eighteenth century. Registers survived the Babylonian captivity. Persia fixed tribute by provincial resources. China had an ancient count tied to revenue and military duty. Egypt, under Amasis, registered each person's occupation every year.
britannica-1911-centaurus:
Centaurus is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a constellation of the southern hemisphere, named the Centaur. Eudoxus mentioned it in the fourth century B.C., and Aratus in the third. Ptolemy catalogued thirty seven stars in it. Its star Alpha Centauri is a splendid binary. Its two components are of the first magnitude. They revolve in a period of eighty one years. Its parallax of 0.75 seconds makes it the nearest star to the earth.

The entry also singles out Omega Centauri. It calls it the finest globular star cluster in the heavens. About 6000 stars crowd into a space some twenty minutes across. About 125 variable stars in it had been examined. A new star, Nova Centauri, closes the account. Mrs Fleming discovered it in 1895, in photographs taken at Harvard. The short entry works as a guide to the constellation's chief sights as astronomy then knew them.
britannica-1911-civilis-claudius:
Civilis, Claudius, more correctly Julius, was the leader of the Batavian revolt against Rome in A.D. 69 to 70. Twice imprisoned on a charge of rebellion, he narrowly escaped execution before the rising. After Nero's death he took up arms under pretence of siding with Vespasian and induced his countrymen to rebel. Heavy conscription and the oppression of provincial governors drove the Batavians, though exempt from tribute, toward revolt.

Neighbouring German tribes, above all the Frisians, joined at once, and Roman garrisons by the Rhine were driven out with 24 ships captured. Two legions were defeated and surrounded at Castra Vetera, and Batavian veteran cohorts joined their countrymen. Revolt spread into Gaul, where commanders Classicus and Tutor took the Roman forces over. The prophetess Velleda predicted Civilis's complete success and the fall of the Roman Empire, but disputes among the tribes broke cooperation apart.
britannica-1911-cleobulus:
Cleobulus was one of the Seven Sages of Greece, a native and tyrant of Lindus in Rhodes, in the entry's opening account. Strength and a handsome person distinguished him, along with wise sayings. The acuteness of his riddles and the beauty of his lyric poetry are praised in the same breath. Diogenes Laertius quotes a letter where Cleobulus invites Solon to take refuge with him against Peisistratus, which would place him alive in 560 B.C.

Advanced views on female education are said to have been held by Cleobulus, a notable point in the short record. His daughter Cleobuline was herself wise, and her riddles were not less famous than his own in the telling. That pairing of father and daughter in riddle craft closes the facts offered. Mullach's Fragmenta Philosophorum Graecorum is named as the source collection for readers who want the sayings themselves.
britannica-1911-cletus:
Cletus was formerly regarded as the name of one of the early successors of Saint Peter in the see of Rome. According to Epiphanius and Rufinus he was instead said to share the direction of the Roman Church with Linus during Peter's own lifetime. Those two traditions frame the whole notice here. No acts, dates or writings of Cletus are offered beyond that question of identity and office.

Identification settles the matter for the entry, which states the conclusion without doubt. Cletus has been identified beyond doubt with Anencletus, and readers are sent to that headword for the substance. A reference to Père Colombier, in the Revue des questions historiques of April 1876, supports the finding. Name, rival traditions and a settled identification make up all the facts this very short entry contains.
britannica-1911-cluentius-habitus-aulus:
Cluentius Habitus, Aulus, of Larinum in Samnium, was the hero of a Roman cause célèbre centred on poison and a bribed jury. In 74 B.C. he accused his stepfather Oppianicus of an attempt to poison him, for his property would have fallen to his mother Sassia. Oppianicus was condemned and died in exile, but suspicion fell on the verdict. A juryman was known to have received a large sum for distribution among his colleagues.

Degradation of Cluentius and several jurymen followed, and in 66 B.C. Sassia had him charged with poisoning the elder Oppianicus. Cicero defended him in the extant speech Pro Cluentio, and Cluentius was acquitted of the charge. Cicero afterwards boasted openly that he had thrown dust in the eyes of the jury. The speech is considered one of his best, though only its small final portion deals with the specific charge.
britannica-1911-cocculus-indicus:
Cocculus Indicus is the commercial name for the dried fruits of Anamirta Cocculus, a large climbing shrub of the natural order Menispermaceae, native to India. The fruit contains a bitter poisonous principle, picrotoxin, at the heart of its uses and its dangers. That principle is used in small doses, the entry says, to control the night sweats of phthisis. Dose is the line between remedy and poison in the account given here.

Formerly the fruit was known as Levant nut and Levant shell in the trade names of Europe. Those names came from its route to market rather than from its home ground. It was brought to Europe by way of the Levant, though the shrub itself is native to India. Commercial name, plant, poisonous principle, medical use and old trade names make up the whole of this brief drug notice.
britannica-1911-cohn-ferdinand-julius:
Ferdinand Julius Cohn (1828–1898) was a German botanist born at Breslau on 24 January 1828. He studied at Breslau and Berlin. In 1859 he became a junior professor of botany at Breslau, and full professor in 1871. The entry notes that his Jewish origin made his career a hard one. He worked beside Pringsheim, Goeppert and Ehrenberg, among others.

Skill with the microscope drove his fame. He improved the tool and used it to probe cell walls and plant cell growth. He found the fine hairs on zoospores and traced their motion. He showed that plant protoplasm and animal sarcode were one and the same stuff of life. Later work turned to the smallest forms of life in water and blood. It led toward the study of bacteria. He died at Breslau on 25 June 1898.
britannica-1911-coxe-henry-octavius:
Henry Octavius Coxe (1811–1881) was an English librarian and scholar born at Bucklebury in Berkshire on 20 September 1811. He was schooled at Westminster and at Worcester College, Oxford. On taking his degree in 1833 he began work in the manuscript department of the British Museum. In 1838 he became sub-librarian of the Bodleian at Oxford. In 1860 he rose to head librarian there.

He held that head post until his death in 1881. Skill in old handwriting won him a state mission in 1857. He was sent to inspect the libraries in the monasteries of the Levant. He found valuable manuscripts on that trip. The monks were too wise to part with their treasures, though. One gain of the trip was his exposure of a forgery by Constantine Simonides. Under his hand the Bodleian catalogue grew past 720 volumes. He also edited a five-volume chronicle of Roger de Wendover.
britannica-1911-cratinus:
Cratinus (about 520–423 before Christ) was an Athenian comic poet. He stands as chief voice of the old comedy and founder of its political kind. Hardly anything is known of his life as a man. Only fragments of his works have come down to us. The views of his peers, above all Aristophanes, give a good sense of their cast.

Direct and vigorous political satire marks his plays above all else. One burlesque stands apart from that rule. His Odysseus piece mocks the tale of Odysseus in the cave of Polyphemus. It was most likely written while a law barred all political matter from the stage. His plays also lack the parabasis and chorus found in his peers. Persius calls him the bold, and with cause. Pericles at his height felt his attacks in full. The Panoptae lashed the sophists and the all-knowing thinkers of the day.
britannica-1911-cratippus:
Cratippus (flourished about 375 before Christ) was a Greek historian known from three or four mentions in ancient books. His weight rests on a point of debate among scholars. Several of them, Blass among the names, hold him to be the author of a history fragment found by Grenfell and Hunt. That fragment came out in the Oxyrhynchus Papyri, in its fifth volume.

A passage in Plutarch backs a fair guess on his life. He was an Athenian writer who falls in date between Thucydides and Xenophon. His work took up the tale where Thucydides stopped, in 410 before Christ. It ran down to the battle of Cnidus in 394. The fragments of his work stand in Müller's collection of Greek historians. The entry points to Theopompus for the full list of sources. Three or four ancient mentions form a thin base, and the entry grants the ID as inference, not proof.
britannica-1911-critolaus:
Critolaus was a Greek philosopher born at Phaselis in the second century before Christ. He studied under Aristo of Ceos and rose to lead the Peripatetic school. His fame as orator, scholar, and moralist carried that lead. He lived to eighty-two and died probably before 111 before Christ. In most points he stayed loyal to the older Peripatetic teaching.

Critolaus held pleasure to be an evil and taught that the soul consists of aether. Life's end, for him, was the full perfection of natural life, goods of soul, body, and fortune all counted. Yet goods of the soul far outweighed the rest in his scale. He defended the eternity of the world against the Stoics. In 156 to 155 before Christ he went to Rome with Carneades and Diogenes to protest the fine of 500 talents laid on Athens for the sack of Oropus. Their lectures in Rome alarmed Cato.
britannica-1911-crocus:
Crocus is a botanical genus of the order Iridaceae with about seventy species. Its kinds are native to Europe, North Africa, and temperate Asia, and thrive most in the dry country of the south-east. The plants rest through the hot, dry season as a short, thick stem called a corm under the soil. Stored food in the corm feeds the new shoots when growth returns. Fresh corms form each season and multiply the plant.

Garden crocuses come mostly from C. vernus, C. versicolor, and the yellow Dutch crocus, C. aureus. The entry gives planting depth, soil needs, and the rule to lift and replant crowded corms every five or six years. Named garden varieties are listed by colour, purple, striped, white, and yellow. Long lists then sort species by flowering season. Spring, autumn, and winter bloomers each receive their own roster for growers who collect hardy bulbs.
britannica-1911-croesus:
Croesus was the last king of Lydia, of the Mermnad line, reigning from 560 to 546 before Christ. He succeeded his father Alyattes after a war with his half-brother. He completed the conquest of Ionia, taking Ephesus and Miletus, and pushed his empire to the Halys. His wealth from trade became proverbial among the Greeks. Part of it bought alliances with Greek states whose fleets could aid his army.

When Cyrus overthrew the Median empire, Croesus joined Nabonidos of Babylon in a league against Persia. Swift Persian moves and the treachery of Eurybatus broke the league, and Croesus fell back on Sardis. Cyrus stormed the city and took him. The entry weighs rival tales of his fate, from a pyre lit by his own hand to rescue by Apollo in Herodotus. In Ctesias's version he joined Cyrus's court and governed Barene in Media.
britannica-1911-cronje-piet-arnoldus:
Piet Arnoldus Cronje (born about 1840) was a Boer general born in the Transvaal. In the first Boer War of 1881 he held the rank of commandant. He commanded at the siege of the British garrison at Potchefstroom, which held out until after the general armistice. He held office through the years to 1899 and forced the surrender of the Jameson raiders at Doornkop in 1896.

In the war of 1899 Cronje commanded in the west and began the siege of Kimberley. He fought Methuen's advance at Belmont, Graspan, and Modder River without success. At Magersfontein in December 1899 he beat back a general attack and checked the British advance for two months. In February 1900 Roberts outmanoeuvred him, relieved Kimberley, and surrounded him near Paardeberg. After stubborn resistance Cronje surrendered with the remnant of his army on 27 February 1900. He was held at St Helena until the peace.
britannica-1911-crypto-porticus:
A crypto-porticus is a concealed or covered passage, an architectural term from Greek and Latin words for hidden and porch. Such passages run generally underground. Yet they are lighted and aired from the open air above. The best-known example lies beneath the palaces of the Caesars in Rome. Passages of this kind served great houses as hidden links between their rooms.

At Hadrian's villa the crypto-porticus formed the chief private link between the several buildings. That single example carries the entry's point about use. A covered way could move people and goods out of sight while staying dry and cool. The definition, the Roman example, and the villa example complete the short entry. No other kinds, dates, or lands are named in it. The term belongs to the study of Roman building.
britannica-1911-cryptobranchus:
Cryptobranchus is a genus of wholly aquatic, lung-breathing tailed amphibians of the family Amphiumidae. Its build is heavy and flat, with a porous, warty skin and a frilled fold along each side. The limbs are short and stout, with four short fingers and five short toes. The eyes are minute and lack lids. A strong row of teeth crosses the palate.

Three species are known to the entry. One is the giant salamander of Japan, also found in China, and a fossil kin from Oeningen joins it. Both grow past five feet, the largest tailed amphibians known. The third is the hellbender of North America, reaching eighteen inches. Eggs are laid in rosary-like strings, in deep holes in the water. In Japan the female coils round a clump of eggs, while reports from Amsterdam tell of the male guarding a far larger batch.
britannica-1911-damasus:
Damasus is the name of two popes, and the entry gives the far greater space to the first. Damasus I held the papacy from 366 to 384. As a deacon he had shifted sides in the quarrel over the exiled Liberius and the anti-pope Felix. When Liberius died, one party named Damasus and another set up the deacon Ursinus against him. Riots followed, and one fight left 137 dead in a basilica.

The prefect of Rome backed Damasus, and Ursinus and his leaders were driven from Italy. Lawsuits and riots still dogged the new pope. Damasus courted the Roman great ladies and fed the cult of the martyrs. He hunted out martyrs' tombs and dressed them with marbles and verses of his own making. He died on 11 December 384. Damasus II, born Poppo, bishop of Brixen, held the papacy only from 17 July to 9 August 1048.
britannica-1911-danaus:
Danaus, in Greek legend, was a son of Belus, king of Egypt, and twin-brother of Aegyptus. Born at Chemmis in Egypt, he was driven out by his brother and fled with his fifty daughters to Argos. Argos was the home of his ancestress Io. There he became king and taught the people to dig wells. Then the fifty sons of Aegyptus arrived and claimed his daughters in marriage.

Danaus consented, but gave each daughter a knife to slay her husband on the wedding night. All obeyed except Hypermnestra, who spared Lynceus and was acquitted at her trial. For their crime the Danaïdes were doomed to fill a bottomless vessel with water for ever. The entry reads that punishment as a transferred rite, and the murders as a figure for the summer drying of the streams of Argolis.
britannica-1911-dares-phrygius:
Dares Phrygius appears in Homer's Iliad as a Trojan priest of Hephaestus. He was said to have written an account of the destruction of Troy and to have lived before Homer himself. A Latin work claiming to be a translation of that account, the De excidio Trojae historia, was much read in the middle ages. It passed under the name of Cornelius Nepos, who is made to dedicate it to Sallust.

The language of the Latin is very corrupt, and the entry dates the work much later than Nepos, probably to the fifth century. Whether it shortens a larger Latin work or adapts a Greek original stays doubtful. With the similar work of Dictys Cretensis it formed the chief source for medieval accounts of the Trojan legend.
britannica-1911-darius:
Darius, in Persian Darayavaush, is the name of three Persian kings, and the article treats each reign in turn. Darius the Great, son of Hystaspes, tells his own story in the Behistun inscription, and the article trusts that account over the legends in Herodotus. With six noble Persians he killed the usurper Gaumata in October 521, then crushed revolts across the empire by 519.

The article follows his Scythian war, the expedition beaten at Marathon in 490, and his death in the year after the Egyptian revolt of 486. Darius II, called Nothos, leaned on his wife Parysatis and ordered war on Athens through his satraps. Darius III, raised by the eunuch Bagoas, lost to Alexander at Issus and Arbela and was killed by Bessus in July 330.
britannica-1911-demaratus:
Demaratus was a king of Sparta of the Eurypontid line who succeeded his father Ariston. He is known chiefly for blocking his fellow king Cleomenes, first over making Isagoras tyrant in Athens and then over punishing Aegina for medizing. Cleomenes struck back by backing Leotychides, a relative and personal enemy, who claimed Demaratus was not Ariston's son but Agetus's. A Delphic oracle, swayed by Cleomenes' bribes, ruled for Leotychides in 491 B.C.

Demaratus soon fled to Darius, who gave him Pergamum, Teuthrania and Halisarna, where his descendants still ruled in the early fourth century. He went with Xerxes on the expedition to Greece. The entry doubts the famous stories of the warnings and advice he gave the king.
britannica-1911-democritus:
Democritus, probably the greatest of the Greek physical philosophers, was a native of Abdera in Thrace. Tradition, nearly all we have for his life, makes him born about 470 or 460 B.C., an older contemporary of Socrates. A large inheritance let him travel widely in the East, and he settled seven years in Egypt studying its mathematics and physics. He came home poor, and one tale says his townsmen voted him 500 talents and a public funeral.

Diogenes Laertius counts seventy-two works, praised for a purity of style rivalling Plato's. Bacon restored his true place after centuries in which the shallow label of the laughing philosopher hid his worth. The article then sets out his atoms and cosmology, taken in part from Leucippus.
britannica-1911-dolabella-publius-cornel:
Publius Cornelius Dolabella was a Roman general and the son-in-law of Cicero, born about 70 B.C. He was by far the most important of the Dolabellae, a family of the patrician gens Cornelia. In the civil wars he first sided with Pompey, then went over to Caesar and fought at Pharsalus. As tribune he proposed cancelling all debts, a bill his colleagues resisted until it stirred serious disorder in Rome.

Caesar took him off to the African and Spanish campaigns, and on Caesar's death Dolabella seized the consulship promised him. Antony then bought him with Syria and the Parthian command, and his march east was marked by plunder and the murder of Trebonius. Declared a public enemy, he was besieged by Cassius at Laodicea and had a soldier kill him in 43. The article calls him a profligate and a spendthrift throughout.
britannica-1911-emmaus:
Emmaus is the name of two places in Palestine, and the entry treats them in turn. The first is a village named by Luke, with no hint of direction, as 60 stadia from Jerusalem, though some manuscripts read 160 stadia. Its placing is, the entry says, mere guesswork. Six candidate sites are listed, with their distances, and el-Kubeibeh or ’Urtas is judged the most likely.

The second place is Emmaus-Nicopolis, now ’Amwās, a town on the maritime plain. It mattered in the Maccabaean and Jewish wars. Near it Judas Maccabaeus defeated Gorgias in 164 B.C., and Vespasian set a fortified camp there in A.D. 69. The town was later rebuilt and named Nicopolis, and became an episcopal see. It was also noted for a healing spring. The entry thus pairs a lost Gospel village, which scholars still hunt, with a documented town of war and bishops.
britannica-1911-ephesus:
Ephesus was an ancient Ionian city on the west coast of Asia Minor. It stood on the lower slopes of the hills Coressus and Prion, above a fertile plain near the mouth of the river Caÿster. Its temple and precinct of Artemis stood in the plain about a mile away, and to that shrine the town owed much of its fame. The site always commanded great trade.

Greek writers give the earliest people of Ephesus as Amazons, Leleges, Carians, and Pelasgi. By tradition Androclus, son of the Athenian king Codrus, landed there with Ionian colonists in the 11th century B.C., and Greek Ephesus dates from his conquest. The city's goddess was Artemis, kin to the old Asiatic nature goddess of nearby Ortygia. Twice in 700 to 500 B.C. the goddess was said to have saved the city, once from the Cimmerians and once when Croesus besieged it.
britannica-1911-epicharmus:
Epicharmus (about 540–450 B.C.) was a Greek comic poet born in the island of Cos. Early in life he went to Megara in Sicily, and after its destruction by Gelo in 484 he moved to Syracuse. He died at ninety, or, by a statement in Lucian, at ninety-seven.

Epicharmus was the chief voice of the Sicilian or Dorian comedy, and 35 titles of his works survive, with a few fragments. In a city of tyrants, attacks on the rulers, as on the Athenian stage, would have been dangerous. His comedies are therefore of two safe kinds. Some are mythological travesties, like Busiris, where Heracles appears as a greedy glutton, and the Marriage of Hebe, with its long list of dainties. Others are character comedies drawn from classes of the people, the sailor, the prophet, the boor, and the parasite.
britannica-1911-epidaurus:
Epidaurus is the name of two ancient cities of southern Greece, and the entry treats them in turn, with a third place in Illyricum named at the end. The first, Epidaurus the Holy, was a sea city on the east coast of Argolis. It stood on a small rocky point with a natural harbour on the north and an open bay on the south. 

Nearness to Athens and the Saronic gulf, trade gains, and the fame of its temple of Asclepius made it a place of weight. The entry traces its peoples in turn: a Carian colony, Ionians, and then Dorians of Argos under Deiphontes. Rule passed from kings to an oligarchy of 180 men from set families, and the city stayed a close ally of Sparta.
britannica-1911-epirus:
Epirus, or Epeirus, was an ancient district of northern Greece running along the Ionian Sea from the Acroceraunian promontory in the north to the Ambracian gulf in the south. Its name meant “mainland,” and was first applied to the whole coast down to the Corinthian Gulf, against the islands offshore. The land is all mountainous, above all toward the east, where the great rivers of north-western Greece, the Achelous, Arachthus, and Aous, rise in the Pindus chain.

The country never grew corn enough for its people, but it was famed, as almost to the present day, for its cattle and horses. Remote from the centres of Greek thought, and held half barbarian, Epirus still weighed on early Greece through the oracle of Dodona. In historic times its part was mostly passive, though Greek states planted colonies on its coast, Ambracia among the earliest and strongest.
britannica-1911-eridanus:
Eridanus, or Fluvius, “the river,” is in astronomy a constellation of the southern hemisphere, named by Eudoxus in the 4th century B.C. and by Aratus in the 3rd. Ptolemy catalogued 34 stars in it. The entry is a short star notice. It centres on two stars whose stories run against each other, one fading and one in swift motion.

Theta Eridani, a fine double star, is now of the third magnitude. Omicron 2 Eridani, numbered 40 by Flamsteed, was found by Herschel in 1783 to be a triple group. A close pair, turning in 180 years, is tied to a brighter star 82 seconds of arc away. The group has an unusually swift proper motion, about 4 seconds of arc a year. Eridanus was also the ancient name of the river Po.
britannica-1911-erigena-johannes-scotus:
Erigena, Johannes Scotus (about 800 to about 877), was a medieval philosopher and theologian whose real name was Johannes Scotus, or John the Scot. The entry warns that the full name Johannes Scotus Erigena has not been traced earlier than Ussher and Gale. His birth date and birthplace are both unsure. The name Scotus, in the usage of the time, points to Irish origin, and Prudentius of Troyes states plainly that he was Irish.

Of Erigena's early life nothing is known, and tales of travel in Greece, Italy, and Gaul are judged legend, likely confused with another John. His works, though, show a sound knowledge of Greek, rare in his age. Roger Bacon, scolding the ignorance of Greek among the great schoolmen, expressly excepts Erigena. His translations of Dionysius the Areopagite and of Maximus, and his ease with Neoplatonist writers, prove the point.
britannica-1911-ermoldus-nigellus:
Ermoldus Nigellus, or Ermold the Black, was a monk of Aquitaine who went with King Pippin, son of the emperor Louis I, on a campaign into Brittany in 824. He was later banished from Pippin's court on a charge of stirring the king against his father. At Strassburg he sought to win back the emperor's favour by writing a poem on Louis's life and deeds. About 830 he gained his recall.

Ermoldus was a cultured man with a knowledge of the Latin poets. His poem In honorem Hludovici imperatoris runs to four books and covers Louis's life and exploits from 781 to 826. The entry grants it some historical value. He also wrote two poems in imitation of Ovid, addressed to Pippin. The entry points readers to studies of the worth of his poems as history.
britannica-1911-ernest-augustus:
Ernest Augustus (1771–1851), king of Hanover and duke of Cumberland, was the fifth son of the English king George III, born at Kew on 5 June 1771. He studied at Göttingen and entered the Hanoverian army. As a cavalry leader in the war with France from 1793 he won a name for bravery. He lost the sight of one eye at Tournai in May 1794.

Back in England, Ernest was made lieutenant-general in 1799 and duke of Cumberland and Teviotdale the same year. A stanch Tory, he fought all reform and all relief for Roman Catholics, and held great sway with his brother the prince regent. The entry closes with his death at Herrenhausen on 18 November 1851, noting that, for all his hard rule, his Hanover subjects mourned him as a father of the land.
britannica-1911-eucalyptus:
Eucalyptus is a large genus of trees of the order Myrtaceae, native, with few exceptions, to Australia and Tasmania. Australians call them gum-trees or stringy-bark trees, from their gummy products and fibrous bark. Leaf remains show several species already present in Eocene times. The leathery leaves hang slanting or upright and carry glands of fragrant volatile oil. The petals join into a cap that drops as the flower opens.

Some species rank among the tallest trees known. E. amygdalina reaches 480 feet, taller than the Californian big-tree. E. globulus, the blue gum of Victoria and Tasmania, attains 375 feet. Since 1854 it has been planted across southern Europe, Algeria, Egypt, California and India. Its fame for clearing malaria is credited here to root drainage, not to the leaves. The timber list runs from karri and jarrah to ironbark, and the bark serves paper-making and tanning.
britannica-1911-faunus:
Faunus was an old Italian rural god, the giver of fruitfulness to fields and cattle. His name may come from favere, kindly, or from fari, to speak. He was akin to Inuus and Lupercus. Faunus also revealed the future through strange sounds in woods, or through visions given to men who slept in his precincts on the skins of sacrificed lambs. In that role he was called Fatuus, with a wife or daughter, Fatua, beside him.

Under Greek influence Faunus was identified with Pan, and many Fauni were imagined: goat-footed forest goblins who tormented sleepers with nightmares. In poetic tradition he was an old king of Latium, son of Picus and father of Latinus, who taught farming and cattle-breeding. His Faunalia festivals fell on 13 February and 5 December, with goat sacrifices and offerings of wine and milk.
britannica-1911-favorinus:
Favorinus, a Greek sophist and philosopher of the second century after Christ, flourished under Hadrian. A Gaul born at Arelate, modern Arles, he travelled from youth through Greece, Italy and the East. His wide knowledge and strong oratory raised him to eminence in Athens and Rome alike. He lived on close terms with Plutarch, Herodes Atticus, Fronto, Aulus Gellius and Hadrian himself, while his great rival was Polemon of Smyrna.

Silenced once by Hadrian in argument, Favorinus remarked that it was foolish to dispute logic with the master of thirty legions. Of his many works only fragments survive, kept by Gellius, Diogenes Laertius and others, unless one speech credited to his tutor Dio Chrysostom is his. As a philosopher he belonged to the sceptical school. His Pyrrhonean Tropes, in ten books, argued that Pyrrho's methods could serve men pleading in the law courts.
britannica-1911-felix-antonius:
Antonius Felix was Roman procurator of Judaea from A.D. 52 to 60, in succession to Ventidius Cumanus. A freedman, most likely of the empress Antonia, he persuaded Drusilla, wife of Azizus of Emesa, to leave her husband and live with him as his wife. His cruelty, loose living and openness to bribes fed a great rise in crime across Judaea during his rule, the entry says.

Felix used the Sicarii, or Dagger-men, against the Zealots and contrived through them the murder of the high-priest Jonathan. Feuds and unrest marked his government, and he put them down harshly. The apostle Paul, seized at Jerusalem, was sent to him at Caesarea and held in custody for two years. Back in Rome, Felix was accused over killings and plunder at Caesarea, but his brother Pallas's influence with Nero saved him from punishment.
britannica-1911-flamininus-titus-quincti:
Titus Quinctius Flamininus (about 228-174 B.C.) was a Roman general and statesman. He began public life as a military tribune under Marcellus, the conqueror of Syracuse. Quaestor in 199, he leapt over the offices of aedile and praetor to win the consulship the next year. The entry presents him as a leader of a rising school: men of Greek culture and wide imperial aims, set against the narrow patriotism summed up in Cato.

His charm, polish, knowledge of men and fluent Greek fitted him to speak for Rome in the East. Macedonia and the war with Philip V were given to him after two years of Roman failure. He turned an unassailable position to drive the Macedonians from the Aous valley and made himself near master of Macedonia. In Greece the Achaean League deserted Philip's cause and Sparta's tyrant Nabis came over to him, as the entry follows his campaign onward.
britannica-1911-flaminius-gaius:
Gaius Flaminius was a Roman statesman and general of plebeian family. As tribune in 232 B.C., against the senate's strong opposition and his own father's, he carried a law sharing out the ager Gallicus Picenus, new land south of Ariminum, among the plebeians. As praetor in 227 he governed Sicily so well that its people kept a lasting gratitude. As consul in 223 he crossed the Po against the Insubrian Gauls.

After an early check forced him to terms, Flaminius, reinforced by the Cenomani, won a clear victory on the banks of the Addua. The senate's recall he ignored, and his triumph came only when popular clamour overbore its decree. As censor in 220 he confined freedmen to the four city tribes. Two great works carry his name: the Circus Flaminius on the Campus Martius, built for the plebeians, and the road that the entry goes on to describe.
britannica-1911-focus:
Focus is Latin for hearth or fireplace. In science it names a point at which converging rays meet, or toward which they are directed. Where rays only seem to come from such a point, it is called a virtual focus. The entry sends readers to the articles on the microscope, the telescope and the lens for working detail.

In geometry, focus names certain special points tied to curves, and the entry points to the articles on geometry, conic sections and perspective. The hosted text is a genuine short article of a few lines. It gives the Latin sense, the optical sense, the virtual focus, and the geometric use, and nothing further.
britannica-1911-fraser-sir-william-augus:
Sir William Augustus Fraser (1826-1898), English politician, author, and collector, was born on 10 February 1826. His father, the third baronet, had served on Wellington staff at Waterloo. Educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, the son joined the 1st Life Guards in 1847 and retired as a captain five years later to seek a seat in parliament.

His election path was rough. Returned for Barnstaple in 1852, he lost the seat when the vote was voided for bribery. He won it again in 1857, and later sat for Ludlow and for Kidderminster. A familiar Carlton Club figure, he stored up anecdotes of Wellington, Disraeli, and Napoleon III. His books include Words on Wellington and Disraeli and his Day, and his library sold for some 20,000 pounds after his death in 1898.
britannica-1911-freeman-edward-augustus:
Edward Augustus Freeman (1823-1892), English historian, was born at Harborne in Staffordshire on 2 August 1823. Orphaned in infancy and raised by a grandmother, he won a scholarship at Trinity College, Oxford, took a fellowship in 1845, and in 1860 settled at Somerleaze near Wells. Church architecture drew him early, and his History of Architecture appeared in 1849.

His fame rests on the History of the Norman Conquest, issued from 1867 to 1876, marked by full research and exact care. Freeman taught two lessons: that history is one whole, not split between ancient and modern, and that students must weigh the original authorities for themselves. He wrote for the Saturday Review until 1878, followed Gladstone, and backed Home Rule in 1886. His saying that history is past politics sums up a range centred on Greek, Roman, and early English political life.
britannica-1911-fresenius-karl-remigius:
Karl Remigius Fresenius (1818-1897), German chemist, was born at Frankfort-on-Main on 28 December 1818. After time in a pharmacy he entered Bonn in 1840, moved to Giessen as assistant in Liebig laboratory, and became assistant professor in 1843. In 1845 he took the chair of chemistry, physics, and technology at the Wiesbaden Agricultural Institution.

Three years later he became first director of the chemical laboratory he had persuaded the Nassau government to found at Wiesbaden, and under him it kept growing. His name rests on analytical chemistry: his textbooks on qualitative analysis (1841) and quantitative analysis (1846) became standard works for their fullness and exact care. In 1862 he founded the Zeitschrift für analytische Chemie and edited it until his sudden death at Wiesbaden in June 1897. The hosted file also holds the neighbouring Frescobaldi and Fresnel entries.
britannica-1911-frischlin-philipp-nikode:
Philipp Nikodemus Frischlin (1547-1590), German scholar and poet, was born at Balingen in Württemberg on 22 September 1547, son of the parish minister. At Tübingen he took the chair of poetry and history in 1568. His comedy Rebecca, read before the emperor Maximilian II at Regensburg in 1575, won him the laureateship, and in 1577 he was made a count palatine.

Unguarded speech and a reckless life drove him from Tübingen in 1582 to a school post at Laibach. Back at the university, he faced a criminal charge, fled to Frankfort in 1587, and taught at Brunswick. Libellous letters written from Mainz brought his arrest in March 1590. Held in the fortress of Hohenurach, he was killed by a fall on the night of 29 November 1590 while trying to climb down from his cell window. His Latin verse, comedies, and notes on Virgil once held real standing.
britannica-1911-frontinus-sextus-julius:
Sextus Julius Frontinus (about AD 40-103) was a Roman soldier and author. City praetor in 70, he was sent to Britain five years later to succeed Petilius Cerealis as governor. He subdued the Silures and held the other native tribes in check until Agricola replaced him in 78. In 97 he became superintendent of the aqueducts at Rome, a post given only to men of the highest standing.

His chief work, De aquis urbis Romae in two books, gives the history and layout of the water supply of Rome. It also sets out the laws for its use and upkeep. A treatise on military science is lost. His Strategematicon collects examples of stratagems from Greek and Roman history for the use of officers. Its fourth book, stressing discipline and the morals of war, is judged the work of another hand.
britannica-1911-fronto-marcus-cornelius:
Marcus Cornelius Fronto (about AD 100-170), Roman grammarian, speaker, and advocate, was born of an Italian family at Cirta in Numidia. He came to Rome under Hadrian and won such fame at the bar that he was ranked second only to Cicero. Wealth followed, with grand buildings and the famous gardens of Maecenas among his purchases.

Antoninus Pius made him tutor to his adopted sons Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and in 143 he held the consulship for two months. His followers, the Frontoniani, aimed to restore the plain purity of old Latin against Greek sophistic fashion, prizing Ennius, Plautus, and Sallust above the Augustan writers. Until 1815 only two grammar works passed under his name, one wrongly. Then Angelo Mai found a palimpsest at Milan holding Fronto letters to his royal pupils, printed at Rome in 1823. The entry judges the letters below his reputation, though rich in extracts from lost authors.
britannica-1911-furst-julius:
Fürst, Julius (1805–1873), a German Orientalist of Jewish parentage, was born at Zerkowo in Posen on the 12th of May 1805. He studied philosophy and philology at Berlin and oriental literature at Posen, Breslau and Halle. In 1857 he took a lectureship at Leipzig, and in 1864 he rose to a professorship there, which he held until his death at Leipzig on the 9th of February 1873.

His writings include a treatise on the Aramaic idioms in 1835 and a Hebrew and Chaldaic concordance of the Old Testament, issued between 1837 and 1840. He also published a Hebrew and Chaldaic dictionary in 1851. He edited the Bibliotheca Judaica from 1849 to 1863 and the journal Der Orient from 1840 to 1851.
britannica-1911-gabinius-aulus:
Gabinius, Aulus, was a Roman statesman and general of the late republic and a supporter of Pompey. As tribune in 67 B.C. he carried the Lex Gabinia, which gave Pompey the command against the pirates, with control of the sea and the coasts for fifty miles inland. Consul in 58, he helped Clodius bring about the exile of Cicero. As proconsul of Syria from 57 he reinstated Hyrcanus as high priest at Jerusalem, quelled revolts and rebuilt several towns.

Sent by Pompey without the senate's consent, Gabinius restored Ptolemy Auletes in Egypt, while Syria fell to robbers behind him. Tried on his return, he was acquitted of treason but convicted of extortion over Ptolemy's payment of 10,000 talents, and he went into exile with his property confiscated. Caesar recalled him in 49 B.C., and after Pharsalus he was sent to Illyricum, where he died of illness at Salonae in 48 or early 47.
britannica-1911-gale-theophilus:
Gale, Theophilus (1628–1678), an English nonconformist divine, was born at Kingsteignton in Devonshire, where his father was vicar. He entered Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1647, became fellow and tutor in 1650, and in 1657 was appointed preacher at Winchester cathedral. In 1662 he refused the Act of Uniformity and was ejected. He then tutored the sons of Lord Wharton, accompanying them to the Protestant college of Caen, and returned to England in 1665.

His later years were spent in London as assistant to John Rowe, the Independent minister in Holborn, whom he succeeded in 1677, dying the next year.
