Domnus Apostolicus, or Apostolic Lord, is a title given to the pope, most used between the sixth and eleventh centuries. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the pope is called apostolic because he holds an apostolic see, one founded by an apostle, as were Ephesus, Philippi, and Corinth. Rome, the only apostolic church of the West, made apostolic see mean simply the Roman see.

In Gaul, though, the phrase stretched as early as the fifth century to cover any bishop's see, on the ground that bishops succeed the apostles. By the sixth century it was in general use, and Merovingian kings wrote to bishops as lords most worthy of the apostolic see. The entry closes by noting that domnus marks a human ruler, set against Dominus, the divine Lord.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-echinus:
Echinus, a titular see of Thessaly in Greece, stood on the Gulf of Lamia's northern shore. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names its forms, Echinos and Echinous, and finds it today as the small village of Akkhinos, five hundred souls in the district of Phalara. On the conical hill above the village stand remains of the old walls.

Quakes ruined and rebuilt the city many times, notably in 426 before Christ and in 551 after. Philip the Second of Macedon left it to the Malians, Philip the Fifth took it from the Aetolians, and Justinian fortified it. Its see, named in bishop lists to the twelfth or thirteenth century, answered to Larissa, with three bishops known, Theodore, Peter, and Aristotle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edesius-and-f:
Probably brothers, Edesius and Frumentius were fourth-century Tyrian Greeks who carried Christianity into Abyssinia. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how, still boys, they sailed with their uncle Metropius toward Abyssinia. At a Red Sea harbor their ship put in, and local people massacred the crew. Only the two boys were spared, taken as slaves to Axum's king about 316.

The boys soon won the king's favor and rose to trust, gaining freedom before his death. The widowed queen then kept them at court to school the young prince Erazanes and to help rule the kingdom in his minority. Frumentius, later saint and first bishop of Axum, is styled the Apostle of Abyssinia, dying about 383.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emile-paul-co:
Emile-Paul-Constant-Ange Le Camus was a French preacher, scholar of Scripture, and Bishop of La Rochelle and Saintes, born at Paraza in 1839 and dead near Castelnaudary in 1906. He studied at Carcassonne and Saint-Sulpice in Paris, took a doctorate in theology at Rome in 1861, and was ordained at Carcassonne in December 1862. His preaching gifts soon showed, and in 1867 he gave the Lenten sermons at Avignon.

He served as assistant director of the Dominican school at Soreze, then founded and headed the school of Saint Francis de Sales at Castelnaudary until 1887. From then on he gave himself to the New Testament, travelling to the Holy Land from 1888 to study its places. Named Bishop of La Rochelle and Saintes in April 1901 and consecrated that July, he kept writing on Scripture. His Life of Our Lord Jesus Christ, in three volumes, was translated into English, German, and Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmaus:
Emmaus was a titular see in Palaestina Prima, suffragan of Caesarea, first named in 166 or 165 before Christ, when Judas Maccabeus beat the army of Gorgias there. Soon after, the Syrian general Bacchides fortified and garrisoned it. In the year 4, during the revolt of Athrongius, its people fled, yet Varus destroyed the city. It rose again, and Josephus and Pliny rank it among the toparchies, of the land.

Vespasian seized it at the start of his Jewish campaign, quartered a legion nearby, and named it Nicopolis, the name Christian writers use. A spring where Christ was said to have washed his feet, famed for healing all diseases, was closed by Julian the Apostate. Four Greek bishops are known from the fourth to the sixth century. Today Amwas, eighteen miles from Jerusalem on the Jaffa road, keeps ruins of a fourth- or fifth-century basilica repaired by Crusaders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephesus:
Ephesus was a titular archiepiscopal see in Asia Minor, said to have been founded in the eleventh century before Christ by Androcles, son of King Codrus. Its coinage goes back to 700 before Christ, when money was struck. After Lydia, Persia, and Alexander's Syrian successors, it passed after Magnesia in 199 before Christ to Pergamum. Its last king, Attalus III, left his kingdom to Rome in 133 before Christ.

There Mithradates in 88 before Christ signed the order to kill all Romans in Asia, a massacre of a hundred thousand. Four years later Sulla slaughtered the rebellion's leaders at Ephesus. From 27 before Christ to after 297, Ephesus was capital of the proconsular province of Asia and a trading city. Its glory was the temple of Artemis, a marvel of the world four hundred feet long on a hundred and twenty-eight pillars. It was burned by Herostratus in 356 before Christ and rebuilt by Dinocrates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphanius:
Epiphanius Scholasticus, or the Philologist, turned Greek works into Latin in the middle of the sixth century. He worked when Latin readers wanted Greek books in their own tongue, and he gave them just that. For Cassiodorus he prepared the Historia Tripartita, drawn from Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret. He also turned into Latin the notes of Didymus on the seven Catholic Epistles.

Another of his works was the Codex Encyclicus, a list of Eastern bishops who backed Chalcedon, drawn up in 458 by order of Emperor Leo I, to which Epiphanius made additions. He also turned into Latin Didymus on Proverbs, and Epiphanius of Salamis on the Song of Songs, though these works are lost or still undiscovered. Julicher places him with Dionysius Exiguus and other workers who met the Latins' need for Greek books of faith in Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-oec:
An episcopal oeconomus is the steward charged with a diocese's temporal goods, from Greek words for house and distributing. The office began in the Eastern Church and reaches back to the fourth century: a law of Honorius and Arcadius in 398 speaks of it as already widespread. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 ordered an oeconomus in every diocese, to manage church property under the bishop's authority.

In the East the office has lasted to the present day in the Greek Church. The growth of church property after the Edict of Milan in 313, and the press of episcopal duties, made such a steward very useful. In the West the oeconomus appears in Spain at Seville in 619, in Sardinia, and perhaps in Sicily, late in the sixth century. Western bishops more often relied on a confidential aide, the vicedominus, who ranked next to the bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-to-di:
The Epistle to Diognetus is a little apology for Christianity, cited by no ancient or medieval writer, and kept in a single manuscript lost at Strasbourg in 1870. Its author is unknown, its date lies anywhere between the Apostles and Constantine, and it was plainly written during a severe persecution. The manuscript ascribed it to Justin Martyr, but Justin could not have written with its restrained eloquence and clearness.

Diognetus, a well-disposed pagan, asks what the Christians' religion is. Idol worship is ridiculed, and Jewish sacrifices give no pleasure to the one God. Christians are no nation or sect, but are spread through the world, not of the world yet citizens of heaven, and in a famous image, the soul of the world. God sent his Child to save man after man had learned his own weakness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-to-t:
The Epistles to Timothy and Titus, called the Pastorals, open with their addressees, two of Paul's most beloved and trusted disciples, whom he took on many journeys. Timothy appears across Acts and the epistles, and Titus across Corinthians, Galatians, and Second Timothy. Timothy is regarded by some as the angel of the church of Ephesus, and the ancient Roman martyrology says he died Bishop of Ephesus.

One life says that during the Neronian persecution John arrived at Ephesus, where he lived with Timothy until exiled to Patmos under Domitian. Timothy, unmarried, stayed Bishop of Ephesus until, past eighty, pagans beat him mortally. Tradition says Titus stayed after Paul's death as Archbishop of Crete and died there past ninety. The rest of the article takes up authenticity, attacked by German and other writers since the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erycius-putea:
Erycius Puteanus, also called Errijck de Put, was born at Venloo in Dutch Limbourg on 4 November 1574 and died at Louvain on 17 September 1646. This Belgian humanist and philologist studied at Dordrecht and Cologne, taking his Master of Arts degree there on 28 February 1595. Italy drew him in 1597, and he lived among its learned men, above all Cardinal Federigo Borromeo. Borromeo secured his appointment as professor of Latin at Milan's Palatine School, a post he held from 1600 to 1606.

Louvain then offered him the chair Lipsius had left vacant. For forty years he taught with éclat at the Collège des Trois-Langues, and princes loaded him with favours. From 1603 onward he also served as historiographer to King Philip IV for the Milanese, alongside other appointments. Those posts were often ill-paid, because war had drained the treasury.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-le-ca:
Etienne Le Camus was a French cardinal, born at Paris in 1632 and dead at Grenoble in 1707. Through his father Nicolas, a state councillor, he was attached young to the court as the king's almoner, and enjoyed Bossuet's friendship. The Sorbonne made him doctor of theology at eighteen. Consorting with Benserade, Vivonne, and Bussy drew Mazarin's severity, and he was exiled to Meaux for a while.

Colbert secured his recall, and in 1665 he withdrew to La Trappe with de Rancé, exchanging levity for an asceticism that drew him to Port-Royal. Ingold's publication of his letters shows Jansenism was for Le Camus more personal sympathy and spiritual discipline than doctrine. Unwillingly made Bishop of Grenoble in 1671, he reformed diocesan abuses with near-excessive zeal. In the régale affair he acted as intermediary between Rome and Versailles, showing courage before Louis XIV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-europus:
Europus was an ancient city on the Euphrates, now a titular see of the province of Euphratensis, suffragan to Hierapolis. Its first name was Thapsacus, an Aramean word for ford, and it was a key trading post at the northern edge of Solomon's kingdom. The younger Cyrus and Alexander the Great both forded the river at this point. The Macedonians renamed it Amphipolis, and it finally took the name Europus, under which Ptolemy, Pliny, and other geographers list it.

Only two of its bishops are known, one Greek bishop in 451 and one Jacobite bishop between 793 and 817. Justinian built a fortress there. When the city fell is unknown, but its ruins stand at Djerabis, a worn-down form of Europus, along the Euphrates some twenty-five kilometers south of Biredjik.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euthalius:
Euthalius served as an Alexandrine deacon, later Bishop of Sulca who lived toward the middle of the fifth century. He is chiefly known for his work on the text of the New Testament, above all as author of the Euthalian Sections. Early copies of the New Testament had no chapters or verses, and often no spaces between words. Following Ammonius of Alexandria, who had divided the Gospels into sections, Euthalius extended a like system to the other New Testament books except the Apocalypse.

He also framed divisions for the lessons read in public worship, fifty-seven sections in all, fifty-three for the Sundays of the year and four for great feasts. He carried further the division of the text into short verses, each a complete sense or a single breath. His sections, noted by copyists across the Greek Church, now help scholars date manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eutychius:
Eutychius, born Said ibn Batriq at Fustat in 876, was the Melchite Patriarch of Alexandria and author of a history of the world. He first studied medicine and history and practiced medicine for a time. He then entered a monastery and became patriarch in 933, taking the name Eutychius. As the Orthodox patriarch, his reign passed mostly in strife with the Monophysite Copts, the great majority of Egyptian Christians, and with his Coptic rival.

His works, in Arabic and kept only in part, cover medicine, theology, and history. Best known is Nazm al-Gawahir, the Chaplet of Pearls, a chronicle from Adam to 938 meant as a short universal history. The book won fame in the seventeenth century when John Selden printed part of it to argue that early Alexandria made no distinction between bishops and priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evagrius:
Evagrius, born about 345 at Ibora on the Black Sea, ranks among the foremost ascetical writers of the fourth century. Taught by Saint Gregory Nazianzen, he was ordained reader by Saint Basil the Great and deacon by Saint Gregory of Nyssa, whom he followed to the Second Council of Constantinople in 381. After a time as archdeacon in the capital under Patriarch Nectarius, he left the city for its spiritual dangers, passed through Jerusalem, and settled in the Nitrian Desert under the younger Macarius.

There he lived as a hermit from 383, turned down the bishopric Theophilus of Alexandria offered, and won fame for his holy life and writings. Saint Jerome charged him with Origenist errors and called him a forerunner of Pelagius, and later general councils condemned him with Origen. Named here are his works on the active life, on monastic matters, and on the eight evil thoughts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evodius:
Evodius was the first Bishop of Antioch after Saint Peter, predecessor of the famed Ignatius. Eusebius writes that Evodius having been set over the Antiochians, Ignatius flourished at that time, in the age of Clement of Rome and Trajan. Harnack showed that Eusebius drew on a list of Antioch's bishops without dates, taken from the Chronography Julius Africanus published in 221, and had to match them roughly with the popes. Jerome's translation of Eusebius places Evodius ordained first Bishop of Antioch in the fourth year of Claudius, the year 44.

No witness names Evodius before Africanus, but Origen, his contemporary, confirms the order by calling Ignatius second bishop after Peter. We may be sure he is real and truly Ignatius's predecessor, yet when he was ordained and when he died are quite uncertain, and no early witness makes him a martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exul-hibernic:
Exul Hibernicus labels an Irish stranger on the Continent in Charlemagne's time. He wrote Latin poems, several addressed to the emperor himself. He is sometimes identified with Dungal. The label exul, or exile, was one Irish wanderers on the Continent often took.

His poems show more than a poet. They show a grammarian and a dialectician as well, and a teacher, probably in the palace school. Most interesting are his verses on a ninth-century teacher's stance toward pupils. His poem in meter on the seven liberal arts gives twelve lines to each branch in turn. Each part sets out the branch's origin, scope, and use. Like Theodulf of Orléans, the lines may have matched a set of pictures of the seven arts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felicissimus:
Felicissimus was a deacon of Carthage who led a short-lived but dangerous schism in the third century. Chosen by the presbyter Novatus, he headed opponents of Bishop Cyprian. The quarrel turned on readmitting Christians who had lapsed during the Decian persecution. Cyprian's strict policy toward the lapsed fuelled the revolt.

Cyprian excommunicated Felicissimus for blocking the alms commission he sent from exile. After Cyprian's return in 251, a synod of bishops, priests, and deacons reaffirmed the sentence. Felicissimus appealed to another council, but his demand failed. His followers drifted away, and the schism soon disappeared.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-filliuc:
Felix Filliucius was an Italian humanist, philosopher, and theologian of note. Born at Siena about 1525, he studied philosophy at Padua. He served Cardinal Del Monte, later Pope Julius III, for a time. Famed as orator and poet, he knew Greek widely and read it with ease.

In 1551 he left court life and entered the Dominicans at Florence. There he took the cloister name Alexus for his later works and translations. He translated Aristotle and Demosthenes into Italian with skill. At Trent he spoke in Latin and rendered the Council's Roman Catechism into Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-firmicus-mate:
Firmicus Maternus was a Christian author of the fourth century, known only from one work. His De errore profanarum religionum survives in a single tenth-century manuscript. Addressed to the emperors Constantius II and Constans I, it was likely written during their joint reign. The work argues, from philosophy and history, that Christianity surpasses pagan superstition and licence.

Its first part surveys Greek and Eastern religions from earlier sources, with less original value. Its later part sets out the mysteries of Eleusis, Isis, and Mithra in detail, seemingly from experience. The emperors are urged to stamp out this network of superstition as a sacred duty. Some identify the author with Julius Firmicus Maternus Siculus, writer of a work on astrology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-claud:
Flavius Claudius Jovianus was Roman emperor for less than a year, in 363 and 364. The army proclaimed him after Julian the Apostate died on campaign against Persia. A Christian born in Pannonia, he promised religious toleration and won Christian joy at his rise. He lacked a soldier's spirit and accepted Shapur's harsh peace terms to save the army.

Four satrapies east of the Tigris, with Nisibis and Singara, were given up against the people's wishes. Rome's sway over Armenia and the Euphrates lands was broken at a stroke. He restored the Church's privileges, recalled Athanasius from exile, and proclaimed freedom of worship. He died suddenly at Dadastana in February 364, suffocated by coal gas, or possibly murdered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-honor:
Flavius Honorius ruled the Western Roman Empire from 395 until his death in 423. Eleven years old at his accession, he stood under the general Stilicho. Stilicho twice saved Italy from Alaric's Visigoths, at Pollentia in 402 and Verona in 403. The court then took refuge at Ravenna, safe in its marshes, which became the western capital.

Honorius had Stilicho put to death on suspicion of treason, leaving Italy open to Alaric. Alaric sacked Rome for three days in August 410, sparing lives and treating churches with respect. The general Constantius later won back the provinces and became co-ruler in 420. Honorius died in August 423, and Valentinian III took the purple after a brief usurpation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-josep:
Flavius Josephus was a Jewish historian born at Jerusalem in 37 and dead about 101. Of priestly stock, he tried the Essenes, Pharisees, and Sadducees in his youth. He joined the revolt of 66 and commanded in Galilee until his capture at Jotapata in 67. Freed by Vespasian, he watched the fall of Jerusalem and lived on at Rome as a writer.

His Jewish War, in seven books, drew on his own notes, Vespasian's memoirs, and Agrippa's letters. His Jewish Antiquities, in twenty books, runs from Creation to the revolt of 66. The later books are our only source for many events, with dates and documents otherwise lost. He wrote in elegant Greek to free educated Gentiles from prejudice against Judaism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-juliu:
Flavius Julius Constantius ruled the Roman Empire from 337 to 361, after his father's death. Son of Constantine the Great, he became sole ruler in 353 after his brothers and Magnentius died. His wars with Persia went badly, and in 353 he ordered heathen temples closed under pain of death. Won over to Arianism, he persecuted orthodox bishops and used violence against the synods.

Athanasius above all drew his hatred; Liberius, Hosius, and Hilary were exiled for resistance. At Milan in 355 he burst into the synod with drawn sword to force the decrees he wanted. He backed now the Anomoeans, now the Semi-Arians, bent only on destroying Catholic doctrine. He died of illness in 361, campaigning against his nephew Julian, newly baptized by an Arian bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-marce:
Flavius Marcellinus was a high official at the court of Emperor Honorius, trusted for good sense. In 411 Honorius sent him to Africa to judge the great Catholic-Donatist conference. He ran the talks with patience and fairness, and decided in favour of the Catholics. New imperial decrees against the Donatists followed his sentence.

Augustine wrote him letters and dedicated books to him, including the first books of the City of God. Jerome also wrote to him, and he and Augustine grew close over shared religious questions. In 413 Marinus jailed him as a supposed backer of Heraclianus, on false Donatist charges. Despite Augustine's plea, he was beheaded on 12 September 413 and is honoured as a martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-rusti:
Flavius Rusticius Helpidius is the name of several Latin writers, hard to tell apart. A reviser signing Domnulus worked on manuscripts of Pomponius Mela and Julius Paris. Sidonius knew a Domnulus, ex-quaestor and poet at Arles under Majorian in 457 to 461. The two Domnuli are likely one man, count of the consistory and ex-quaestor in Sidonius.

Another Helpidius, deacon and physician of Theodoric, died about 533 and is plainly distinct. The former quaestor left twenty-four tristichs on scenes from both Testaments. Sixteen scenes pair off as type and fulfilment, likely as texts for church decoration. A short poem of 140 hexameters on Christ's miracles, in a mystical tone, also bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florus:
Florus was a deacon of Lyons and a famed theologian of the Frankish realm in the ninth century. First heard of in a letter of 827 to 830, he already enjoyed fame beyond Lyons. He defended church freedom against Modoin of Autun after Agobard fell in 835. He lamented the realm's divisions in his Querela de divisione Imperii.

He wrote on the Mass, on electing bishops, and against Amalarius on the liturgy. On predestination he taught twofold predestination with human free will intact. He answered John Scotus Eriugena in 852 and completed Bede's Martyrology with additions. After 852 nothing more is known of him; he likely died about 860.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortunatus:
Venantius Fortunatus was a Christian poet of the sixth century, born between 530 and 540 in upper Italy between Ceneda and Treviso and educated at Ravenna. His early verse celebrated a church dedication there. In 565 he left Ravenna, crossed the Alps, and travelled through southern Germany to the Moselle, praising bishops and churches at Mainz, Cologne, Trier, and Metz along the way. At Metz he wrote for the wedding of King Sigebert and Brunhild in 566.

From Paris he went to Tours, drawn by St. Martin, whose intercession he believed had cured his eyes. Then he went to Poitiers, where St. Radegunde and her monastery shaped the rest of his life. He settled there as friend to Radegunde and Abbess Agnes, writing poems and letters that mirror sixth-century Gaul, its courts, churches, and friendships, until Radegunde's death in 587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-acc:
Francesco Accursius is the name of two Italian lawyers, father and son, whom history often confuses. The elder, born at Florence in 1182 and dead at Bologna in 1260. He took up law late, taught at Bologna, and compiled a gloss, or commentary, covering the whole body of Roman law that outranked every work then in existence. Weak in the classics but masterly in law, he was called the jurisconsults' idol.

His son Francesco, born at Bologna in 1225 and dead in 1293, was known more for tact than for wisdom. Edward I of England, coming back from the Holy Land, brought him to England, and he returned to Bologna in 1282 to practise law until his death. His two sons and a daughter also studied and practised law, and Dante places the younger Francesco in Hell. Father and son share a tomb at Bologna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-briti:
Francis Britius was a Capuchin orientalist, a scholar of eastern languages, from Rennes in Brittany, whose dates of birth and death are unknown. He spent his early religious life in mission work in the Levant, the eastern Mediterranean lands, devoting himself with special zeal to Oriental languages. His skill soon drew the notice of his superiors, who called him to Rome to work for the Congregation of the Propaganda, the church's missionary department, translating important works into Arabic.

His first great fruit was an Arabic abridgement of Baronius's church annals, continued by Sponde to 1646, published at Rome in three quarto volumes in 1653, 1655, and 1671. He also had much to do with an Arabic Bible giving the Vulgate text in parallel columns, published at Rome in 1671. Both works are now exceedingly rare, since nearly the whole editions were sent east for mission use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-sylvi:
Francis Sylvius, born at Braine-le-Comte in Hainault in 1581 and dead at Douai on 22 February 1649. He was a theologian of the University of Douai whose quiet life was given to study and teaching. Remarkable from youth for love of study and piety, he studied humanities at Mons, philosophy at Louvain, and theology at Douai. He taught philosophy at the royal college while still a student. On 9 November 1610 he became doctor of theology with the highest honours.

When no chair stood vacant, a professor resigned in his favour. On the death of Estius, the great light of Douai, in 1613, Sylvius succeeded him and later directed the episcopal seminary where he had studied. His complete works, published at Antwerp in 1698 in six folio volumes, praise his learning, conciseness, and penetration as a disciple of Augustine and interpreter of Thomas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franciscus-qu:
Franciscus Quaresmius, born at Lodi in Lombardy on 4 April 1583 and dead at Milan on 25 October 1650. He was a Franciscan writer and Orientalist whose work in the Holy Land won him fame among historians and biblical scholars. Son of the noble Alberto Quaresmi and Laura Papa, he joined the Franciscan Observantines at Mantua young and taught philosophy, theology, and canon law. He rose to guardian, custos, minister of his province, and in 1645 to 1648 definitor and procurator general of the order.

On 3 March 1616 he went to Jerusalem, serving as Guardian and Vice-Commissary Apostolic of Aleppo, then Superior and Commissary Apostolic of the East. He was twice imprisoned by the Turks. Between 1616 and 1626 he wrote his classic Elucidatio Terrae Sanctae, a monumental contribution to Holy Land history, geography, and archaeology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franciscus-so:
Franciscus Sonnius, whose real name was Van de Velde, was born at Zon in Brabant on 12 August 1506 and died at Antwerp on 30 June 1576. He was a theologian and first Bishop of Antwerp. He took his later name from his birthplace, studied at Bois-le-Duc and Louvain, tried medicine, then theology, taking his licentiate in 1536 and doctorate in 1539. After parish work at Meerbeek and Louvain he became professor of theology at Louvain in 1544 and attended the Council of Trent in 1546, 1547, and 1551.

 Philip II sent him to Rome to treat with Paul IV over new dioceses in the Netherlands and separating Belgian monasteries from German ones, where heresy spread fast. His success won him the bishopric of Bois-le-Duc in 1566, consecrated in 1568, and in 1569 he became first Bishop of Antwerp, founding a church court and visiting every parish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-loui:
Francois-Louis Blosius, also called de Blois, was a Benedictine abbot and spiritual writer born at Donstienne near Liege in 1506 and dead at Liessies in 1566. His parents were nobles of Hainault, his father Sieur of Jumigny, and Francois served as page to Archduke Charles, afterwards Emperor Charles V, before entering Liessies Abbey at only fourteen. Still a novice he was sent to Louvain University, recalled in 1527 as coadjutor to Abbot Gilles Gippus, and confirmed by a bull of Paul III. In 1530 he succeeded as thirty-fourth abbot, ordained and blessed the same year.

 War soon threatened. Francis I invaded Flanders in 1537, Liessies on the frontier grew unsafe, and Blosius proposed moving to the priory of Ath inland. But most monks, opposing reform, stayed or left for laxer houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-k:
Franz Xaver Kraus, born at Trier on 18 September 1840 and died at San Remo on 28 December 1901, was a German church and art historian of brilliant, versatile talent. Schooled at Trier, he studied theology there from 1858 to 1860 and spent 1860 to 1862 in France as tutor in distinguished families. He finished theology in 1862 to 1864 and was ordained by Suffragan Bishop Eberhard on 23 March 1864.

In spring 1872 he became extraordinary professor of Christian art history at Strasburg. In autumn 1878 he succeeded Alzog as ordinary professor of church history at Freiburg, becoming grand-ducal privy councillor in 1890, university pro-rector in 1890 to 1891. He was curator of Baden's religious antiquities and member of its historical commission from 1883. His histories of Christian art, his editions, and his liberal Catholic stance in the reform Catholicism of his age made him a central, contested figure. He is honoured in lives by Hauviller, Grauert, and Kunstle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fredegarius:
Fredegarius is not a real author but a name invented in the sixteenth century for the unknown writer of a seventh-century Frankish chronicle. Claude Fauchet first used the name in 1599, admitting it came from ignorance of who truly wrote the work. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains how modern scholars took the compilation apart and found three hands in it.

A Burgundian epitomized Gregory of Tours down to 584 and added extracts from earlier writers, forming the largest but least original share. A second Burgundian wrote fresh history to 642, valued because it alone covers those years. A third, a partisan of the palace mayor Grimoald, carried the tale to 658. Together they form the only continuous account of Frankish history from 591 to 658.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frejus:
Fréjus, a diocese in southern France covering the whole department of Var, carries a history stretching back to Roman times. Suppressed under the Concordat of 1801, it was restored in 1817 and set on firm footing in 1823. Its bishop later also bore the title of Toulon, joining two ancient sees in one diocese.

The entry names bishops from Leontius in the fifth century through Riculfus, who rebuilt after Saracen raids, to Jacques d'Euse, who later became Pope John XXII. It also treats Toulon apart, weighing a legend about its founding against the first bishops known to history. The island monastery of Lérins, sold in 1859, still lends the diocese several honored saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-sta:
Friedrich Staphylus, a theologian born at Osnabrück in 1512, moved from Luther's circle to the defense of the old Church. Left without parents when young, he came under an uncle's care and studied at Cracow and Padua. He took his master's at Wittenberg in 1541 and tutored for a count on Melanchthon's word. In 1546 Duke Albert made him professor of theology at the new Königsberg school.

Quarrels with Gnapheus and Osiander, and the drift of Protestant teaching, pushed Staphylus toward church tradition and Church rule. He joined the Catholic Church at Breslau late in 1552. He faced Melanchthon himself at the Worms disputation of 1557. In a 1558 book he hit out at the splits among Luther's heirs. In 1560 he took the teaching chair at Ingolstadt and drafted reform counsels for Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fulgentius-fe:
Fulgentius Ferrandus, a deacon of Carthage in the early sixth century, stood among the fiercest defenders of orthodoxy in the West. He likely followed his master Fulgentius of Ruspe into exile in Sardinia under the Arian Vandal king Thrasamund. After the exiles returned in 523, Ferrandus, though only a deacon, became a voice whom bishops consulted on hard questions of doctrine.

His writings defended the Trinity against Arians and treated Christ's two natures, baptism, and the Eucharist. He also summed up early councils in 232 canons on the life of clergy and conduct toward Jews, pagans, and heretics, and he set seven rules for Christian soldiers. When Justinian condemned the Three Chapters, Ferrandus urged refusal, and the African bishops broke with Pope Vigilius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gallienus:
Gallienus, Roman emperor from his father Valerian's capture until his murder in 268, ruled an empire coming apart. Born about 218, he took the western half in 255 while Valerian held the east. Indolent and pleasure-loving, he bribed Frankish chiefs to guard the Rhine, beat the Alemanni at Milan, and barred senators from army and provinces, erasing the old split of imperial and senatorial lands.

Persecution of Christians broke out in 257 on charges of shirking defense, and Cyprian of Carthage, Sixtus II, and Lawrence died in 258. When Valerian fell to Persia in 260, Gallienus freed Christian worship and leaned on Odenathus of Palmyra in the east. Generals rose as rival emperors across the provinces, the so-called Thirty Tyrants, and his own officers cut him down during the siege of Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudiosus:
Gaudiosus, bishop of Tarazona in Spain, died about 540, and almost all we know of him comes from his own grave. His father Guntha served as sword-bearer to Visigothic King Theodoric. The boy was schooled by Saint Victorianus, abbot near Burgos, who trained him for the Church. Around 530 he became bishop of Tarazona, and nothing more of his acts survives.

After death he was honored as a saint and buried in Saint Martin's church by his old monastery. When his remains were moved in 1573, a parchment life was found in the grave, the sole written record besides Tarazona's breviary lessons. It dates his death to October 29, though the church keeps his feast on November 3. His relics now rest in Tarazona Cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gelasius-of-c:
Gelasius of Cyzicus, a church writer of Bithynia around 475, compiled the Acts of the Council of Nicaea. Son of a priest of Cyzicus, he wrote against the Eutychians to show that the Nicene Fathers never taught one-nature doctrine. Beyond his preface, nothing of his life is known. His Syntagma, long scorned as a sorry compilation, has lately won respect.

The work runs to three books: Constantine's life to 323, the council's history in thirty-six chapters, and fragments of a third book found whole by Cardinal Mai at Milan. Turner traced long passages to Rufinus, and Löschcke's source study, through Eusebius, Socrates, and Theodoret, restored Gelasius among serious historians. It even revived the idea of an official Nicene record behind his texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genesius:
Genesius names three saints of the early and medieval Church, each honored on a different ground. Genesius of Rome, a comedian martyred under Diocletian, mocked baptism on stage before the emperor, then declared himself Christian in earnest and was tortured and beheaded. Actors and musicians claim him as patron, and he is invoked against epilepsy.

Genesius of Arles, a notary martyred under Maximian, threw down his tablets rather than copy a persecution decree, fled, and was caught and killed, winning baptism in his own blood. Notaries honor him, and sufferers call on him against chilblains. A third Genesius, bishop of Clermont who died in 662, founded a hospital and the abbey of Manlieu, fled to Rome fearing for his soul, and returned at his flock's plea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gentian-herve:
Gentian Hervetus, a French theologian born near Orléans in 1499, spent his life translating Greek Fathers and fighting Calvinists. Schooled at Orléans, he tutored in Paris, followed an English pupil to England and Rome, and lived in Cardinal Pole's household turning Greek texts into Latin. Later he served Cardinal Cervini, the future Marcellus II, as secretary.

Hervetus spoke at Trent in 1546 against secret marriages, was ordained only in 1556 at fifty-seven, and became vicar-general of Noyon and a canon of Reims. As pastor he preached with success against Calvinists and wrote many pamphlets against them. He returned to Trent in 1562 with Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, and his history of that council appeared at Reims in 1564.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-hamart:
George Hamartolus, a monk at Constantinople under Michael III, wrote a chronicle that matters most for his own ninth century. Hamartolus is not his name but his self-styled epithet, George the Sinner, taken from his work's title, A Compendious Chronicle from Various Chroniclers and Interpreters. Krumbacher prefers Georgios Monachos. Nothing is known of him beyond what his book reveals.

Four books run from Adam to Alexander, through Old Testament history, from Caesar to Constantine, and down to 842. Only the near-contemporary portion counts as history; the rest shows Byzantine monkish ideas, with pious reflections, long extracts from Greek Fathers, and fierce hatred of the just-ended Iconoclast storm. Later hands carried the tale to 948, and Slav and Georgian translations spread it. It remains valuable for the years just before Photius's schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgius-sync:
Georgius Syncellus, a Byzantine chronicler who died after 810, wrote one of the Middle Ages' great date-ordered works. A monk for many years in Palestine, he came to Constantinople under Patriarch Tarasius, who reigned from 784 to 806. There he filled the post of syncellus, the patriarch's private aide and the capital's second churchman. On his patron's death he retired from court life and wrote his chronicle.

His Extract runs the world's history from Creation to Diocletian's death in 316, arranged strictly by year. Long tables of dates make it, in Krumbacher's phrase, a great historical list with notes. He labored hardest over Bible history, Christ's dating, and comparing Septuagint manuscripts, drawing later years from Eusebius. His friend Theophanes continued the work, and Anastasius's Latin Historia Tripartita of 873 to 875 spread his dating westward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gindarus:
Gindarus was a titular see of Syria Prima in the Patriarchate of Antioch, now Djenderis on the Afrin river near Aleppo. Ancient geographers place it in Cyrrhestica or the region of Seleucia, and Strabo calls it a celebrated haunt of brigands. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a small, short-lived bishopric known from a single bishop.

That bishop was Peter, who attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and the Council of Antioch in 341. The see appears in neither the sixth-century nor the tenth-century lists of Antioch. Later geographers omit the town. Under Theodosius the Great it was only a small fortified village, and by Justinian's day it kept a periodeutes, a visiting priest, rather than a bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gondulphus:
Gondulphus, or Gundulfus, is the name of three saints, one Bishop of Tongres, one Bishop of Metz, and one Gondulphus of Berry. Little is known of any of the three, and the medieval documents give only a slight idea of each. A Catholic Encyclopedia article gives the fullest account of the Metz bishop.

Gondulphus of Metz, whose feast falls on 6 September, succeeded Angilram, who died probably in 791. His consecration is dated 28 December 816, and the old Metz catalogue says he held the see six years, eight months, and seven days, dying on 6 September 823. He was buried at Gorze, where his relics are still honored on his feast day, with no special patronage recorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-baeti:
Gregory Baeticus was Bishop of Elvira in Baetica, Spain, from which he took his surname, who died about 392. First met as bishop in 375, he defended the Nicene creed after Hosius of Cordova had assented at Sirmium to a second Sirmian formulation in 357. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an ardent opponent of Arianism.

He stood for the Nicene creed at the Council of Rimini and refused communion with the Arian bishops Ursacius and Valens. With Lucifer of Cagliari he held that no advances could be made to bishops or priests ever tainted with Arian heresy. On Lucifer's death in 370 or 371 he became head of the Luciferian party in Spain, though its progress was not considerable. Jerome says he wrote treatises in simple, ordinary language into a ripe old age, including an excellent De Fide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-fil:
French cardinal Guillaume Fillastre, born at La Suze in 1348, was canonist, humanist, and map lover at the heart of the Western Schism's ending. After teaching law at Reims he backed Benedict XIII, then joined the Pisa council of 1409. He became cardinal in 1411 and Archbishop of Aix in 1413, and at Constance pressed first for the rival claimants to abdicate.

His Constance diary, found by Heinrich Finke and published in full in 1889, is the leading source for the council's voting fights, its deposed popes, and its conclave. At Constance he also copied Ptolemy's geography and sent a walrus-skin world map to Reims in 1418. He later added an eleventh map of Europe preserving Claudius Clavus's first chart of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Greenland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-halicarnassus:
Caria's Halicarnassus, a colony from Troezen and one of six towns in the Dorian Hexapolis, stood on the Ceramic Gulf as the largest and strongest town in Caria. Forts guarded it around a famous harbour. Persian-appointed tyrants held it loyal to Persia while taking up Greek speech and arts. Queen Artemisia sailed with Xerxes to Salamis.

A second Artemisia built the Mausoleum for her husband Mausolus, part of which now stands in the British Museum. Alexander later captured and burned the town, which never regained its prosperity. Herodotus and Dionysius were born there, bishops appear in its records to the twelfth century, and modern Bodrum counts 6,000 people, most of them Muslims with a Greek minority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Münster reformer Heinrich von Ahaus, natural son of the Lord of Ahaus, born in 1371, carried the Brethren of the Common Life into Germany. Joining the Brethren at Deventer about 1396 and learning their spirit from Florentius Radewyns, he returned to Münster and founded a house there in 1400. He endowed it from family wealth and settled it on his Springbrunnen estate in 1429.

Houses at Cologne in 1416, Wesel in 1435. Osnabrück followed, with sisters' communities at five more towns, all amid steady opposition from priests and laymen. At Constance he helped clear the Brethren of Dominican charges. In 1428 he joined the Münster and Cologne houses in a union confirmed by papal decree after his death in 1439, leaving a mark on clergy training, schooling, and popular devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heliogabalus:
Roman emperor Heliogabalus, born Varius Avitus Bassianus of a Syrian family, ruled from 218 to 222 after a boyhood priesthood gave him his name. Grandnephew of Julia Domna, he was priest of the sun god Elagabal at Emesa when soldiers, told he was Caracalla's son, proclaimed the fifteen-year-old emperor in May 218. Macrinus's troops deserted to him east of Antioch.

In Rome he lived as an oriental despot. He wedded his black meteoric stone idol to the moon goddess Astarte and made its priest Rome's pontifex maximus, to the confusion of pagan worship and the contrast of steady Christians. His grandmother forced him to adopt his cousin Alexander as Caesar, repeated attempts to kill the boy failed, and soldiers murdered Heliogabalus with his mother in March 222.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-spondan:
Henri Spondanus, born at Mauléon in 1568, first trained at a Calvinist college and worked as a jurist before reading Bellarmine led him into the Catholic Church in 1595. Ordained at Rome in 1606, he served as reviser of briefs for the Penitentiaria and became Bishop of Pamiers in 1625. There he worked to keep Catholicism alive in his diocese and win converts. Ill health forced his resignation in 1639, and he retired to Toulouse, where he died in 1643.

His lasting work lay in church history rather than in pastoral office alone. Spondanus condensed the annals of Baronius into an epitome, wrote a sacred history running from creation to redemption, and carried the Baronian annals forward from 1197 to 1622. An earlier study of sacred cemeteries also survives from 1596, showing a scholar who moved between antiquarian detail and the long sweep of ecclesiastical chronicle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henricus-cani:
Henricus Canisius, a canonist and historian from Nijmegen and nephew of Saint Peter Canisius, taught canon law at Ingolstadt from 1590 until his death in 1610. His legal writings include a summa of canon law, academic lectures, a commentary on the third book of the Decretals, and a treatise on betrothal and marriage. They were later gathered into a complete edition at Louvain and Cologne. He also edited early chronicles and a work of Paul the Deacon for the first time.

Canisius is best remembered for Antiquae Lectiones, six volumes of medieval source material issued between 1601 and 1604, with a seventh supplementary volume in 1608. The collection lacked systematic order and mixed valuable documents with minor matter, so Basnage later recast and sifted it as the Thesaurus Monumentorum. Even in that revised form, the enterprise shows a scholar gathering the raw materials of medieval history for others to use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hephaestus:
Hephaestus was a titular see of Augustamnica Prima, listed by Hierocles and George of Cyprus among the thirteen towns of that province and suffragan to Pelusium. Lequien names only two of its bishops: John, who took part in the Councils of Ephesus in 431 and 449, and Peter, who attended the Council of Constantinople in 459.

Hephaestus's native name and its site are both unknown, a frank admission that marks this short entry. It survives as a record of a vanished Egyptian see, known through geographers, conciliar lists, and a Coptic allusion published by Rougé. No remains or local tradition fix the town on the map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-contr:
Hermann Contractus, also called Hermann of Reichenau, was an eleventh-century monk who could not move without help from birth yet became one of the great scholars of his age. Born in Swabia in 1013 to a noble family, he was placed at seven with Abbot Berno on the island of Reichenau, where he took monastic vows in 1043. His learning ranged across theology, mathematics, astronomy, music, and Latin, Greek, and Arabic.

Students came from far off to learn from him, drawn by both his knowledge and his kind character. His chief work is a world chronicle running from the birth of Christ to his own day. It is the earliest such medieval chronicle still extant, built from many sources with care for accuracy. He also wrote on music, astronomy, and poetry, and the entry sets out why later ages kept his name alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-rolfu:
Hermann Rolfus was a German Catholic educationist, born at Freiburg in 1821 and dead at Buhl in 1896. Ordained priest in 1844, he served a string of parishes in southern Germany and took a doctorate in theology from Freiburg in 1867. His working life joined parish ministry with a steady push for better Catholic schooling and teaching.

With Adolf Pfister he edited a four-volume encyclopedia of education on Catholic principles, issued from 1863 to 1866, with a fifth supplementary volume by Rolfus alone in 1884. He also ran a Catholic school weekly paper with Pfister and wrote guides to faith, morals, and world history. Teachers and school planners find here a practical reformer rather than a theorist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-thrya:
Hermann Thyraeus was a German Jesuit of the Counter-Reformation, born at Neuss on the Rhine in 1532 and dead at Mainz in 1591. He studied at Cologne and at the Collegium Germanicum in Rome, joined the Society of Jesus in 1556, and taught theology at Ingolstadt and Trier. He later served as rector at Trier, provincial of the Jesuit Rhine province, and rector at Mainz until his death.

Thyraeus worked to strengthen the Catholic cause in Germany through teaching, preaching, and writing. His annotated Confessio Augustana appeared at Dillingen in 1567, and his sermons drew crowds said to reach four thousand at Trier. A book on religious liberty long ascribed to him was most likely written by his younger brother Peter. Readers meet a trusted adviser to the Rhine archbishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hieronymus-ba:
Hieronymus Balbus, also called Accellini, was a Gurk bishop in Carinthia, and a humanist, poet, and diplomatist, born at Venice about 1450 and dead there probably in 1535. A pupil of Pomponius Laetus, founder of the Roman Academy, he offended many in youth by a quarrelsome manner and a loose life. Later years ranked him among his day's most accomplished men.

Balbus taught at Paris from 1485 until quarrels forced him out in 1491, then lectured at Vienna at the invitation of Emperor Maximilian I on poetry, classics, and jurisprudence. He moved on to Prague in 1498 after fresh clashes with colleagues, though at Vienna he had joined the Danube Society and befriended its founder, Conrad Celtes. The entry follows a brilliant, combative scholar across the universities of Renaissance Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hieronymus-fa:
Hieronymus Fabricius, surnamed ab Aquapendente, was a distinguished Italian anatomist and surgeon, born at Acquapendente in 1537 and dead at Padua in 1619. He takes his surname from his birthplace to set him apart from the German surgeon Fabricius Hildanus. English medical writers know him above all as Harvey's teacher, whom Harvey fully credited with finding the vein valves.

Some vein valves had been seen before, even in ancient times. But Fabricius grasped that they formed a system, and that insight mattered greatly for Harvey's own finding of blood circulation. A favourite pupil of Fallopius at Padua, he succeeded his master at twenty-five and held the chairs of anatomy and surgery for nearly half a century. Venice built him a great anatomical theatre at Padua and made him a Knight of St. Mark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierotheus:
Hierotheus is the teacher whom Pseudo-Dionysius praises in his writings as guide and master after St. Paul, and this entry argues that no such historical person ever existed. All attempts to find a real Hierotheus outside those writings fail, the entry says. The author wove fictitious figures of the apostolic age into his narrative on purpose to mislead.

We must therefore turn to three passages in On the Divine Names. There Dionysius calls Hierotheus a gifted teacher for mature minds, rich in sublime knowledge of divine things from mystical insight and contemplation. His teaching was terse, concise, and full of deep meaning, and his hearers could hardly follow it. Readers meet a literary portrait, not a recoverable life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-himerius:
Himerius was archbishop of Tarragona in Spain in 385, the first archbishop of that province known by name after St. Fructuosus, martyred in 259. Nothing is known of his own acts, not even when his reign began or ended, and he played no recorded part in the Priscillian controversy of his time. He had sent questions to Pope Damasus, who died before they arrived.

Pope Siricius took up the questions and answered on 10 February 385, in what is the first known papal decretal. That letter forbids rebaptizing converts from Arianism. It orders baptism normally only at Easter and Pentecost, after forty days of prayer and fasting, and insists on swift baptism for infants and others in danger of death. Himerius was ordered to publish these enactments to the other churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hippo-diarrhy:
Hippo Diarrhytus, now Bizerta in northern Africa, was a titular see that began as a Tyrian colony. Its surname probably came from the canal running through the city. Agathocles captured and fortified it and opened a new harbour in the years 310 to 307 BC. Later it backed mercenaries against Carthage, then became a Roman colony early in the empire.

In 1535 Spain's protectorate first claimed it, but soon it cast that off, and French and Venetian fleets bombarded it in later centuries. Since the French occupation of 1882, Bizerta has been chief town of its district, famed for fortifications, trade, and fisheries. St. Restituta was born there, St. Augustine often preached in its basilicas, and six bishops from between 255 and 646 are known by name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hippo-regius:
Hippo Regius was a titular see of Numidia, now part of the residential see of Constantine in Algeria. A Tyrian colony on the bay's west coast, named for it, it earned the surname Regius as one of the places where Numidian kings resided. Roman colonia status came to it, and it prospered until the Vandals took it in AD 430. In the seventh century Arabs rebuilt the town.

About two miles away, Arabs founded Beleb-el-Anab in the eleventh century, later held by Spaniards and French and now called Bone or Bona. Seven bishops of Hippo are known, among them martyrs Theogenes and Fidentius, Leontius, Valerius, who ordained St. Augustine, and Augustine himself, bishop from 395 until his death in 430. A fine basilica to Augustine stands in the town today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-name-of-:
The Holy Name of Jesus is honoured not because power hides in its letters, but because the name recalls every blessing received through the Redeemer. At that name Christians uncover their heads and bend their knees, and Justinian's law book puts it at the head of all undertakings. Invoked with confidence, the name brings help in bodily needs, as Christ promised.

The apostles, in Jesus's name, gave strength to the lame and life to the dead, and the name consoles in spiritual trials. It reminds sinners of the prodigal son's father and the Good Samaritan, and recalls to the just the suffering Lamb of God. It also guards against Satan and his wiles. The entry traces the feast and devotion that grew around this reverence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospital-sist:
The Hospital Sisters of the Mercy of Jesus live under the Rule of St. Augustine, in an institute dependent on the pope through the bishop. Before the end of the thirteenth century, Hermit Sisters of St. Augustine served the Hôtel-Dieu of Dieppe in the diocese of Rouen. They formed a secular congregation, living on goods held in common and on alms under constitutions drawn up for their use.

Besides serving the Hôtel-Dieu, they helped the sick poor across the city. An unbroken chain of credible traditions links those early hospitallers to the Institute of the Mercy of Jesus. Its constitution sets two classes. Lay sisters do manual tasks, skip the Divine Office, and do not nurse. Choir sisters recite the Office in common, nurse the sick daily, and take the night watch in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-and-leo-:
Hugh and Leo Etherianus were Tuscan brothers employed at the court of Constantinople under Emperor Manuel I, who reigned from 1143 to 1180. Their name appears in many spellings. Leo matters little: his brother notes he translated imperial letters, evidently serving as interpreter for Latin correspondence. Hugh, though holding no court office, was a very learned theologian.

Hugh often debated the questions dividing Orthodox and Catholics. From those disputes he wrote a three-book work on the heresies Greeks charged to Latins, defending the Filioque, the doctrine that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. Composed in Latin and Greek, it was the first exhaustive scientific defence of the Filioque. He sent copies to the Orthodox patriarch of Antioch and to Pope Alexander III, whose letter of thanks survives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inscription-o:
A second-century Greek tomb text opens a window onto an early bishop and his travels. Abercius, bishop of Hieropolis in Phrygia, left his city about the middle of that century and visited Rome. On his way home he passed through Syria and Mesopotamia. He was welcomed with high honor in many places. Soon after his return he died, but first he wrote his own epitaph, full of what he had admired in Rome.

That epitaph, the entry argues, likely inspired the later Life of Abercius. Every detail in the Life can be traced to hints in the stone. The rest comes from stock material common to saints' legends. Scholars such as Tillemont and Pitra weighed its wording and its claim to be genuine. Readers get both the travel tale and a lesson in how legend grows from a short carved text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ipsus:
A vanished Phrygian city famous for one great battle is the subject of this short see entry. Ipsus was a titular see under Synnada. It won fame in 301 before Christ when Alexander's successors fought there. Antigonus was killed, and his kingdom was split among his rivals. As Ipsos or Hypsos the city appears in Hierocles, George of Cyprus, and most medieval church lists.

Le Quien names four bishops: Lucian at Chalcedon in 451, George at the Seventh Council in 787, and Photius and Thomas at Constantinople in 868 and 878. The city stood where roads to Byzantium and Sardis met, though its exact site was never found. Modern scholars place it at Ipsili-Hissar or at Tchai, 82 miles from Apamea, leaving the map as open as the history is sharp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irnerius:
Bologna jurist Irnerius, also called Garnerius, born about 1050 and dead about 1130, founded the School of Glossators and revived the study of Roman law. Barely past twenty he already taught grammar and rhetoric at Bologna, and at Countess Matilda of Tuscany's urging he turned to jurisprudence with Justinian's code as his guide. Law study had been much neglected in the empire, so he leaned heavily on private reading, with a likely spell at a Rome law school.

After a short spell teaching law in Rome he returned to Bologna. There he founded his new law school in 1084. Glossing became the method of a generation. Glossing means line-by-line comment on legal texts. Only in recent decades, the entry notes, has his influence drawn the attention it deserves. Readers meet the teacher who turned old codes into a living medieval science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-issus:
Battles, not bishops, made Issus famous, and this short see entry lists them in order. Alexander beat Darius there in 333 before Christ, Septimius Severus beat Pescennius Niger in 194, Heraclius beat Chosroes in 622. The Egyptian sultan Baybars beat the Armenian king Hetoum in August 1266. So many armies fought at Issus because nearby lay the Gates of Syria, the seashore defile leading from Cilicia into the Syrian east.

A titular see of Cilicia Prima under Tarsus, Issus oddly never appears in Antioch's church lists, to which Cilicia belonged. How it became a Latin titular see is unknown. Its ruins lie near Ayaz. The entry is a crossroads in miniature: one pass, four famous victories, and a church title with a missing paper trail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-baradae:
Jacob Baradaeus was a Syrian Monophysite bishop born at Tella around 500. He died in 578. His true name was Jacob bar Theophilus, son of a Tella priest. His nickname came from the coarse horse-cloth he usually wore. After a good education he became a monk at Pesilta monastery. He followed Severus, head of the Monophysites.

By the mid-sixth century Monophysitism was fading fast. Internal splits and Emperor Justinian's opposition weakened it. Severus died in 538, leaving the movement near collapse. Likely through Empress Theodora's influence, Baradaeus became bishop of Edessa in 543. From then on he devoted all his energy to defending Monophysitism. His tireless travel and ordinations breathed new life into the dying cause. The entry credits one bishop with saving a church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-hus:
Jan Hus, also spelled John, was born at Husinec in southern Bohemia in 1369. He died at Constance on 6 July 1415. At an early age he went to Prague, supporting himself by singing and serving in churches. His conduct was exemplary and his devotion to study remarkable. In 1393 he earned a bachelor's degree from Prague university, and a master's in 1396. He was ordained priest in 1400 and became university rector in 1402 to 1403.

About the same time he became preacher at the newly built Bethlehem Chapel. Hus strongly backed the Czechs, and hence the Realists, and was greatly influenced by Wyclif's writings. Though forty-five of Wyclif's propositions were condemned in 1403, Hus translated Wyclif's Trialogus into Czech and helped circulate it. From the pulpit he attacked the morals of clergy, bishops, and papacy. The entry follows a preacher whose reforming zeal led to Constance and the stake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jassus:
Jassus was an ancient town on the coast of Caria, in Asia Minor, whose bishop answered to the see of Aphrodisias. Settlers from Argos founded it, and people from Miletus rebuilt it after war with the native Carians. It stood on a small island at the head of a gulf, later joined to the mainland by a narrow strip of land.

Greek inscriptions found among its ruins help rebuild its home history, and its walls and fisheries were noted by ancient writers. Spartans took it during the Peloponnesian War, and Philip of Macedon seized it before Rome made him hand it back to Egypt's king. Four bishops are named between 421 and 878. By 1835 a visitor found white marble walls, theatres, and tombs standing in a deserted ruin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François Baltus, a French Jesuit theologian born at Metz in 1667 and dead at Reims in 1743. He joined the Society in 1682 and taught humanities, rhetoric, Scripture, Hebrew, and theology at Dijon, Pont-à-Mousson, and Strasbourg, where he also led the university.

Baltus served as general censor of books at Rome in 1717 and later led houses at Chalon, Dijon, Metz, and Châlons. His apologetic works answer Fontenelle on pagan oracles in defence of the Fathers, refute a charge of Platonism against them, judge pagan morals by their light. They prove Christianity from fulfilled prophecy in both Testaments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-louis-le:
Jean-Louis Lefebvre de Cheverus, first bishop of Boston, was born at Mayenne in 1768 and died at Bordeaux in 1836. Ordained before twenty-three, he served his uncle at Mayenne until refusal of the revolutionary oath cost him parish and nearly life. He fled in disguise to London.

Within three months Cheverus could teach in English, and within a year he had gathered a congregation. A letter from Matignon at Boston drew him across the Atlantic in 1796, and for twenty-seven years he served New England in every mission form. He lived among Indigenous peoples, walked long roads to scattered Catholics, and nursed the sick through two yellow fever outbreaks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joannes-bunde:
Joannes Bunderius, a Flemish Dominican theologian born at Ghent in 1482 and dead there in 1557. He joined the Dominicans about 1500, studied at Louvain, and returned to Ghent in 1517 to teach philosophy and theology for most of his life. He served three terms as prior of Ghent convent.

As general inquisitor for Tournai, Bunderius laboured tirelessly against Lutheran, Calvinist, and Mennonite errors, yet with prudence toward heretics. School training fitted him to defend Catholic doctrine and unmask false teaching, and as prior he federated Ghent's religious orders to guard faith and rights. His order honoured his preaching with the title Preacher General.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joannes-maxen:
Joannes Maxentius led the Scythian monks at Constantinople in 519 and 520. They pressed the formula that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, meant to shut out Nestorian and Monophysite error. The monks also sought condemnation of Faustus of Riez as tainted with Pelagianism, and met opposition on both fronts.

Maxentius appealed to papal legates at Constantinople without success, and some monks, though not he, carried the case to Pope Hormisdas at Rome. African bishops in Sardinian exile, through Fulgentius, warmly backed them, but Hormisdas in August 520 rebuked the monks and set Faustus aside from the Fathers. Maxentius answered that letter as a heretics' forgery, his last trace in history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-alexan:
Johann Alexander Brassicanus, a German humanist probably born at Cannstatt in 1500 and dead at Vienna in 1539, came from the Constance family Köll, Latinised Brassicanus. His father, a Württemberg humanist who taught at Urach and Tübingen and wrote a grammar in thirteen editions, schooled him to early maturity.

Brassicanus matriculated at Tübingen in 1514, took his arts master's in 1517, and was crowned poet and orator laureate in 1518 with a coat of arms from Maximilian. He lectured on Latin poets, edited Calpurnius and Nemesianus eclogues he had found, and kept the greatest humanists' praise. After Bebel's death drove him from Tübingen's reaction, he carried humanism to new posts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-cochla:
Johann Cochlaeus, properly Dobeneck, was a German humanist and Catholic controversialist born in 1479 and dead at Breslau in 1552. Named for the snail shell, cochlea, after his birthplace Wendelstein, he studied under Grienniger at Nuremberg, then at Cologne, Bologna, and Rome, taking a theology doctorate in 1517.

Ordained at Rome under the Oratory of Divine Love's sway, Cochlaeus turned to answer Luther, first with On Both Priesthoods in 1520 and tracts in quick succession. Meeting nuncio Aleander at Worms in 1521, he laboured tirelessly to reconcile Luther, then spent decades assailing Luther's chief theses. His early Latin schoolbooks on grammar and music show the humanist behind the controversialist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-crotus:
Johann Crotus, properly Johannes Jäger, called Venator, hunter, and in Greek form Crotus, archer, was a German humanist born at Dornheim about 1480 and dead probably at Halle about 1539. From his birthplace came Rubianus, and he is best known as Crotus Rubianus.

At Erfurt, then German humanism's centre, Crotus took his bachelor's in 1500 and master's in 1508, moving under Mutianus and Hutten. He went from scholastic defender to humanist partisan and fierce foe of old learning. He led Hutten from Fulda monastery in 1505 and headed Fulda's school in 1510. About 1515 he wrote the sharpest Letters of Obscure Men, venomous satires on scholasticism and monks that still sting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-ludwig:
Johann Ludwig Brassicanus, younger brother of Johann Alexander, was born at Tübingen in 1509 and died at Vienna in 1549. He followed his brother to Vienna in 1524 and won like distinction as philologist and jurist, serving Herberstein and Oláh before taking the title court historiographer of the Roman king.

After studying law at Heidelberg from 1532, Ludwig taught Greek briefly at Vienna and Padua, where he took a law doctorate in 1536. He became Vienna professor of the Institutes in 1537 and later of canon law. Ferdinand called him to council, he was twice university rector and four times dean, and in 1544 provincial superintendent, though he seldom published beyond a few legal addresses and treatises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-pistor:
Johann Pistorius the Younger was a German controversialist and historian who changed confessions twice before entering the Catholic Church. Born at Nidda in Hesse in 1546, son of a Protestant superintendent, he studied theology, law, and medicine. His schools were Marburg and Wittenberg. He took a medical doctorate and served as court physician to the Margrave of Baden-Durlach.

From Lutheranism he moved to Calvinism, carrying a margrave with him, then grew dissatisfied and became Catholic in 1588. He arranged the religious disputations of Baden in 1589 and Emmendingen in 1590, at which the court preacher and the margrave himself converted. Ordained priest in 1591, he later served as vicar-general of Constance, imperial councillor, and confessor to Emperor Rudolph II. He wrote sharp, learned tracts against Protestantism, above all his Anatomia Lutheri.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-mosc:
Johannes Moschus was a monk and writer of the early seventh century whose Spiritual Meadow remains a vivid window on Eastern monastic life. Born about 550, probably at Damascus, and surnamed the Abstemious, he lived with monks near Jerusalem, hermits in the Jordan valley, and the New Laura of St. Sabas, then traveled with Sophronius, later Patriarch of Jerusalem, through Egypt, Sinai, Antioch, Cyprus, and Rome, where he died in 619.

His Leimon, or Spiritual Meadow, retells his meetings with great ascetics and the edifying stories they told him. The book shows little critical judgment and teems with miracles and visions, yet it gives clear insight into monastic practice, religious ceremony, and the heresies threatening the Eastern Church. First edited in 1624 and again in 1681, it was translated into Latin and Italian, and Moschus also joined Sophronius in writing a life of John the Almoner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-beccus:
John Beccus was the Patriarch of Constantinople who changed from opponent to champion of reunion with Rome. Born early in the thirteenth century at Constantinople, he rose to chartophylax and won the esteem of Patriarch Arsenius. He gained the confidence of Emperor Michael Palaeologus, who used him on delicate negotiations. At first he called the Latins heretics and opposed the emperor's reunion plan, and his defiance earned him imprisonment.

In enforced retirement he studied the points of difference. He found, in Athanasius, Cyril, Maximus, and other Fathers, that Greek and Latin teaching substantially agreed. The Latins said the Holy Ghost proceeds from Father and Son; the Greeks preferred from the Father through the Son. Convinced, he backed the union proclaimed at Lyons in 1274 and at Constantinople, and held those convictions to the end despite the opposition they stirred.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-capreolu:
John Capreolus, called the Prince of Thomists, was a Dominican defender of St. Thomas Aquinas in the early fifteenth century. Born about 1380 in the diocese of Rodez in France, he was assigned by his order's general chapter at Poitiers in 1407 to lecture on the Sentences at Paris, beginning in 1408. He took his degrees at the Sorbonne in 1411 and 1415.

His celebrated commentary on Aquinas, finished in four parts between 1409 and 1433, calmly expounds Thomas's teaching. It defends that teaching against Scotus, Henry of Ghent, Ockham, Durandus, and other nominalists, drawing on Aristotle and Averroes with copious citation. His scrupulous fidelity earned him the title Soul of St. Thomas. The manuscripts once narrowly escaped fire, saved by a lay brother, and the work, published at Venice from 1483, stands among the enduring achievements of scholasticism's golden age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-ephes:
John of Ephesus, also called John of Asia, was a very famous Syriac historian, the earliest of them. Born at Amida about 505, he was ordained deacon in 529 and fled his Monophysite doctrine to Palestine and then to Constantinople. There he found a friend in Jacob Baradaeus and a protector in Justinian, who set him over Constantinople's Monophysite community and sent him to convert the heathens of Asia.

Consecrated Bishop of Ephesus by Baradaeus, he won the titles Teacher of the Heathens and Idol-breaker for hunting secret idolatry in 546. After Justinian's death his fortunes fell: the persecution of 571 brought imprisonment and banishment, and he resigned his missions to Deuterius. His Ecclesiastical History from Julius Caesar to 585 survives only in part, with excerpts in the British Museum and possibly whole in the chronicle of Denys of Tell-Mahre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-parvus:
John Parvus, called Jehan Petit, was a French theologian of the University of Paris whose defense of tyrannicide made him notorious. Born in Normandy about 1360, he was no friar despite historians' claims, but owed his education to the Duke of Burgundy's pension. Master of arts by 1385, he wrote poems including a Complaint of the Church in 1394 and a defense of the Immaculate Conception in 1388.

Licentiate in theology in 1400 and doctor before 1403, he joined Charles VI's embassy of April 1407 urging Benedict XIII and Gregory XII to give up their claims and end the schism. The embassy had just returned fruitless when, on 23 November 1407, the Duke of Orleans was murdered by assassins paid by John the Fearless of Burgundy. Parvus's subsequent justification of that murder, defending the duke who had funded his education, gave him a lasting and dark notoriety in history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-paul-naz:
John Paul Nazarius was an Italian Dominican theologian famed for his learning and eloquence in controversy. Born at Cremona in 1556, he entered the Dominicans young, noted for spirituality and love of study, and probably studied at Bologna. He taught with great success in his order's Italian schools.

In 1592 Clement VIII sent him with the nuncio to Prague to combat heresy, where he spent three years teaching, lecturing, preaching, and defending the faith. Back in Italy he became regent of studies at Milan. In 1597 the pope set him to defend the Mass against Calvinist preachers in a public disputation at Chiavenna, which he won so triumphantly that his services were sought everywhere. Milan chose him ambassador to Philip III in 1620, and he closed his life teaching and writing at Bologna until 1645.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-scholast:
John Scholasticus, or John III of Constantinople, was the lawyer-patriarch who made the first important systematic collection of church canons. Born at Sirimis near Antioch, he practiced law before ordination, became a priest of the Antiochene patriarchate, and served as legate at Constantinople under Justinian. When Eutychius was deposed in 565, John succeeded him and died in 577.

Between 540 and 560 he compiled his Collection of Canons, called by Pope Nicholas I the Harmony of Canons. It arranges 377 canons under fifty titles by subject, the first attempt to gather canons from the Fathers' letters alongside synodal decrees. As patriarch he enlarged it to sixty titles and added eighty-seven chapters from Justinian's Novels. Later hands added more, until the whole grew into the Nomocanon of Photius, the foundation of Eastern canon law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-slotanus:
John Slotanus was a Dominican polemicist who defended the faith at Cologne against the reformers. Born at Geffen in Brabant, he joined the Dominicans at Cologne about 1525 and preached and wrote ably against heretics for many years. He taught sacred letters there, and became doctor of theology in 1554 and prior of his convent.

As prior he served as censor of the faith and papal inquisitor for the Cologne archdiocese and the Rhine country. He clashed with the learned Justus Velsius, expelled from Cologne in 1556 for heretical teaching. Velsius's vehement writings against the Cologne theologians moved Slotanus to answer with works discussing nearly every heretical doctrine of the age with admirable skill. They included his Disputations against Heretics of 1558, his book on retaining orthodox faith of 1560, and his 1559 work on converting barbarous nations, testifying to the missionary zeal of his time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-trithemi:
John Trithemius was a famous Benedictine scholar and abbot whose library made Sponheim a center of learning. Born at Trittenheim on the Moselle in 1462, he suffered harsh treatment from a selfish stepfather and grew up ignorant until fifteen. He then learned reading, writing, and Latin with remarkable speed. Fleeing home, he reached Wurzburg and studied under the humanist Wimpheling until 1482.

A January journey homeward brought him by chance to Sponheim in a snowstorm. At the prior's invitation he stayed, took the habit, and made his vows that same year. Though the youngest monk and not yet ordained, he was elected abbot at twenty-two. With youthful vigor he repaired the neglected monastery's material needs and restored its discipline by his own example in observance and tireless study. He built a rich collection of books in every branch of knowledge before his death at Wurzburg in 1516.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jovianus:
Jovianus was a fourth-century monk who opposed Christian asceticism and was condemned as a heretic in 390. Almost all we know of him comes from St. Jerome's two-book reply, Adversus Jovinianum, written in 393 after his friend Pammachius sent Jerome the condemned writings.

Jovianus taught that virginity is no better than marriage, fasting no better than eating with a right heart, and that all sins are equal, with one grade of punishment and reward hereafter. He also denied Mary's perpetual virginity. Synods at Rome under Pope Siricius and at Milan under Ambrose condemned him, and nothing is known of his later life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-bautista:
Juan Bautista Villalpandus was a Spanish Jesuit famed for his commentary on Ezekiel and its Temple plates. Born at Cordova in 1552, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1575 and died in 1608. He finished the Ezekiel commentary begun by Jerome Prado, publishing it at Rome from 1596 to 1604 in three volumes.

The third volume pictures Jerusalem and the Temple in rich classical dress, with porphyry courts, Parian marble, and golden vessels. Praised by some as a masterpiece, the vision now looks too classical and too splendid for the real sanctuary. Villalpandus also wrongly claimed a Pauline commentary for Remigius of Reims rather than Remigius of Auxerre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judas-machabe:
Judas Machabeus was the Jewish guerrilla leader who freed the Temple from Syrian rule. Third son of the priest Mattathias, he took command of the revolt in 167 BC and led it until 161. His surname likely comes from a Syriac word for hammer, marking his crushing blows, like Charles Martel's.

Judas routed Apollonius, Seron at Beth-horon, and the generals Gorgias, Nicanor, and Lysias, then cleansed and rededicated the profaned Temple in a feast of eight days, the origin of the annual feast. He also sent envoys to Rome seeking protection for the young revolt. The entry praises his tactics, daring, and trust in God's help.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-africa:
Julius Africanus was the father of Christian chronography, the dating of sacred history. Born about 160, a Libyan by name and perhaps of Roman descent, he knew Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. He served as a soldier and wrote as a Christian after studying at Alexandria's catechetical school. Little of his life is certain, and little of his work survives.
