His Chronicle in five books ran from Creation, dated by him to 5499 BC, to AD 221. He led the restoration of Emmaus as Nicopolis under Alexander Severus and knew Abgar VIII of Edessa as a holy man. Through Eusebius he shaped all later Greek chroniclers and Church historians. He died about 237, or after 240 by some accounts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justus-baroni:
Justus Baronius Calvinus was a German convert and apologist who took his second name from gratitude to a cardinal. Born of Calvinist parents at Kanthen about 1570, he studied theology at Heidelberg. Reading the Fathers drew him toward Catholicism and finally to Rome, where Cardinals Bellarmin and Baronius and Pope Clement VIII received him kindly. Bellarmin's writings strengthened his conviction, and he added Baronius to his own name.

Back in Germany he became a Catholic in 1601 and a staunch defender of Catholic truth. His Apologia of 1601 sets out his reasons for converting. A second work, published in 1602, appeals to the Fathers in support of Catholic truth. Together the two books form his whole case: personal reasons first, then the witness of the early Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justus-lipsiu:
Justus Lipsius, or Josse Lips, was a Netherlandish philologist and humanist whose editions shaped Latin scholarship. Born at Overyssche in 1547, he studied at Ath and at the Jesuit College in Cologne, where he wished to become a novice in 1562. His father recalled him instead and sent him to Louvain to study law and letters. At the Collegium Trilingue he threw himself into correcting Latin texts, publishing three books of Variae Lectiones in 1569.

Cardinal Granvelle made him his Latin secretary at Rome in 1569, and his Tacitus of 1574 first separated the Annals from the History. Though he lacked the chief manuscripts, he added over 450 corrections that later editors accepted. After teaching at Louvain, Jena, and Cologne, he held a chair at Leyden from 1578 to 1591. His shifts of confession followed the masters of the moment wherever he taught.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juvencus:
Juvencus was a fourth-century Christian Latin poet, a Spaniard of good birth, a priest under Constantine. Almost all we know of him comes from St. Jerome, dating his poem to about 330. Evangeliorum libri retells Christ's life in dactylic hexameters, following Matthew closely, borrowing the infancy story from Luke. His task was to turn Gospel prose into easy verse in the Latin poets' manner, above all Virgil's.

The result is correct, well-built verse with little color or movement; its originality is coined words and elegant synonyms. God becomes the Thunderer, the Father the Begetter, the Holy Ghost the Breath, and the Devil slyness itself. His prologue sets the glories of the true faith against the lying tales of Homer and Virgil. The four books match the four Evangelists, and his reading of the Magi's gifts proved enormously influential: incense for God, gold for the King, myrrh for the Man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knights-of-co:
The Knights of Columbus is a fraternal and charitable society of Catholic men, founded at New Haven, Connecticut, on 2 February 1882 and incorporated under Connecticut law on 29 March 1882. Father Michael McGivney led the founders, who also included Father P. P. Lawlor and laymen James Mullen, Cornelius Driscoll, and others.

Its aims were practical Catholic living, Catholic education and charity, and insurance aid for families of dead members. The first council, San Salvador No. 1, opened at New Haven on 15 May 1882. Councils spread through Connecticut, then to Westerly, Rhode Island, in April 1885, the first step beyond the home state. Government by a Supreme Council gave way to a Board of Government in 1886, State Councils in 1892, and a National Council in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lampsacus:
Lampsacus was a titular see of the Hellespont, suffragan of Cyzicus, set in Mysia at the strait's entrance, opposite Callipolis. Once called Pityussa, it was colonized by Phocaea and Miletus in a region settled by Bebryces from Thrace.

Its story runs through Persian rule in the Ionian revolt and a gift of its wine-famed territory to Themistocles. It allied with Athens after Mycale in 479 before Christ, then was recaptured after the Sicilian disaster. Later it defended itself against Antiochus and allied with Rome, voting Rome a golden crown. Gold and silver staters survive, a Lysippus lion went to Rome, and natives included the historian Charon, the orator Anaximenes, and Metrodorus, Epicurus's disciple.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamus:
Lamus, at the mouth of the river Lamus dividing rough Cilicia from Cilicia proper, was a titular see of Isauria, suffragan of Seleucia. Strabo and Ptolemy both mention the village, and the whole district bore the name Lametis.

Today it is the poor village of Adana, with an aqueduct's remains and a fortress. In 945 the Byzantine general John Courcouas made peace with the Arabs there. Emperor Manuel Comnenus seized the fortress, and Armenians retook it after he left. Bishops include Nounechios of Charadrus, who also held Lamus in 458, and Eustathius, present at Nicaea's second council in 787.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lanspergius:
Lanspergius, or John Justus of Landsberg (1489-1539), was a Carthusian monk and ascetical writer. He was born at Landsberg in Bavaria to a family named Gerecht, of which Justus is the Latin form. After philosophy at Cologne he entered the Charterhouse of St. Barbara at twenty in 1509.

Novice-master in 1520, he became prior of Cantave near Juliers in 1530. He preached at Duke William's court and confessed the duke's mother. Ill health and overwork sent him back to Cologne in 1534 as sub-prior until death. No polemicist, he wrote paraphrases and homilies on the liturgical Epistles and Gospels. He added sermons, meditations on Christ's life and Passion, and treatises on the spiritual life, nearly all in Latin. His tender theme was God's love calling for man's love, above all through the Sacred Heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurentius-su:
Laurentius Surius (1522-1578) was a hagiologist of Lubeck, brought into the Church, Canisius says, from heresy by Peter Canisius himself. After Frankfort and Cologne universities, he spent most of his life in Cologne's Carthusian house, which Lanspergius persuaded him to enter in 1542. He lived there in piety, strict observance, and scholarship, esteemed by St. Pius V.

He worked chiefly in church history and saints' lives. He translated Tauler, Suso, Ruysbroeck, Gropper, and others into Latin. He answered Sleidanus with a short commentary on world events from 1500 to 1564. His council collection ran to four volumes in 1567. Greatest of all stands his lives of the saints, De probatis Sanctorum historiis. Six volumes appeared at Cologne from 1570 to 1577, with a seventh added after his death. New editions followed at Cologne in 1618 and Turin in 1875 to 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lazarus:
Lazarus, from Hebrew Eleazar, God has helped, names two New Testament figures: the beggar of Christ's parable and the brother of Martha and Mary of Bethany. The parable, found only in Luke 16, stages two scenes: life here and life hereafter.

Here the rich man feasts daily in purple and fine linen while the sore-covered beggar at his gate longs for fallen crumbs and gets none but dogs' company. Hereafter the banquet reverses: Lazarus rests in honour on Abraham's bosom while the rich man, now outcast, begs a drop of water in vain. Catholic readers take it as parable teaching wise use of opportunity: Lazarus is rewarded for virtuous acceptance of poverty, not poverty itself, and the rich man punished for vicious neglect, not wealth. The Bethany Lazarus, Jesus's friend, rose from the dead at his sisters' plea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lebedus:
Lebedus was a titular see of Asia Minor, suffragan of Ephesus, on the coast ninety stadia east of Cape Myonnesus and 120 west of Colophon. Pausanias says Carians lived there when Ionians arrived under Andraemon, son of Codrus, while Strabo credits Andropompus and an older name, Artis.

Commerce made it flourish, mineral springs made it famous, but Lysimachus nearly destroyed it by moving its people to Ephesus. Under Rome it revived as the meeting place of all Ionia's actors, with festivals for Dionysus. Its scant remains lie near Hypsili Hissar in the Smyrna vilayet. As a bishopric it appears in the Notitiae until the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Only three bishops are known. Cyriacus attended the Robber Council of 449, Julian Chalcedon in 451, and Theophanes or Thomas Nicaea in 787.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-allatius:
Leo Allatius, or Alacci (1586-1669), was a learned seventeenth-century Greek, born on Chios. He was schooled at Rome's Greek college from 1600 and later helped Chios's Latin bishop after three years in Lucania. In 1616 he took a medicine doctorate from the Sapienza, became a Vatican Library scriptor, and briefly taught rhetoric at the Greek college.

Gregory XV dispatched him to Germany in 1622 to fetch Heidelberg's Palatinate library, Maximilian's gift for war subsidies, a task he finished despite great difficulties. Gregory's death in 1623 cost him his chief patron. Yet churchmen's support kept his Palatinate manuscript research alive. Alexander VII made him Vatican Library custodian in 1661 until death. His great work, De Ecclesiae Occidentalis atque Orientalis perpetua consensione of 1648, stresses the Churches' agreements and softens their differences toward reunion. He corresponded with Europe's foremost scholars. He left some 150 manuscript volumes and over 1,000 letters to Rome's Oratorians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-diaconus:
Leo Diaconus was a Byzantine historian, born at Kaloe under Mount Tmolos in Ionia about 950, his death year unknown. Studying young at Constantinople, he was ordained deacon, as his name says. He marched in Basil II's 986 war against the Bulgars, stood at Triaditza's siege, where the imperial army lost, and barely escaped alive.

After 992 he began at Constantinople a ten-book history of the empire from 959 to 975. It covers Romanus II, Nicephorus Phocas, and John Zimisces, but he apparently died before finishing it. It tells the Arab wars winning back Cilicia, Cyprus, Antioch, and northern Syria, the Bulgarian war of 969, and the southern Russians' defeat in 971. For Nicephorus and John he is the sole source, the only contemporary historian. He wrote from his own eyes and eyewitnesses, though critics call his style affected, dull, and pedantic, stuffed with odd Latin words and artificial synonyms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-lessi:
Leonard Lessius, or Leys (1554-1623), was a Flemish Jesuit theologian, born at Brecht in Antwerp province. His farming parents died when he was six. In 1568 he entered Arras college at Louvain. He studied classics and philosophy and took his doctorate in philosophy at seventeen. He learned Greek later, yet mastered it well enough to turn refectory reading into Greek in his head.

He entered the Society of Jesus in 1572 and taught philosophy at Douai until 1581. He studied theology in Rome under Suarez. From 1585 he held the theology chair at Louvain for fifteen years. Urged by superiors, he published his lectures. Twice sent to Rome for general congregations, in 1608 and 1615, he was sought in vain by Bellarmine for the Sacred Penitentiary. Consulted widely, he corresponded with the doctors of his day. At the end he longed for prayer and contemplation. His remains lie in the Jesuit church choir at Louvain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leontius-byza:
Leontius Byzantinus was a theologian of the sixth century whose life and works have been disputed. Bellarmine and Labbe put him before the fifth general council at Constantinople in 553. Miraeus assigned him to Gregory the Great's time. Others matched him to a seventh-century bishop of Salamis or an Origenist Leontius. Fabricius held that no clear view of the man or his writings was possible at his time.

In an undisputed work, Contra Nestorian et Eutychian, he says that in youth he belonged to the Nestorian sect but holy men converted him. Other works call him a monk of Jerusalem. Friedrich Loofs's study, accepted by later scholars, makes him the monk who came with Scythians to Rome in 519. There he pressed Pope Hormisdas to authorize the suspect formula One of the Trinity suffered. Loofs puts his birth at Constantinople about 485, of a family related to the imperial general Vitalian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leviticus: Leviticus is the third book of the Pentateuch. Its name comes from its subject: the priests' and Levites' offices, ministries, rites, and ceremonies. It sets out the duties and worship practices of those who served at the sanctuary, covering how sacrifices, purifications, and sacred observances were to be carried out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liber-septimu:
Three canonical collections of different legal weight bear the title Liber Septimus. The first is the Clementinae, so named by medieval canonists and once by John XXII in 1321. Clement V promulgated it at Monteaux near Carpentras on 21 March 1314 and sent it to Orleans and Paris. His death on 20 April raised doubts, so John XXII by Quoniam nulla of 25 October 1317 issued it again unchanged.

The second is Pierre Mathieu's 1690 collection, a private set of canons in Gregory IX's order, holding decretals from Sixtus IV to Sixtus V. It was wholly private and without scientific value, though some Corpus editions print it as an appendix. The third, officially Decretales Clementis VIII, owes the name to Cardinal Pinelli, prefect of Sixtus V's code congregation. It was meant to fill the codification gap since the Clementinae of 1317, after Gregory XIII about 1580 named cardinals and Sixtus V set up the congregation in 1587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucas-holsten:
Lucas Holstenius was a German philologist, born at Hamburg in 1596 and dead at Rome in 1661. Schooled at Hamburg and Leyden under Vossius and Heinsius, he travelled Italy and Sicily with Cluver in 1618 and caught a taste for geography.

After England and Paris, where he turned Catholic through reading the Greek Fathers, he reached Rome in 1627. He served Cardinal Barberini as librarian, then Innocent X as head of the Vatican Library. Popes sent him on honoured missions, to Warsaw, to receive Queen Christina's abjuration, and to win converts. His grand plans, editions of Neoplatonists and Fathers, filled notebooks more than books, yet editors long mined his notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucius-caecil:
Lactantius was a fourth-century Christian apologist, African by birth despite a name that misled some into calling him an Italian from Fermo. Pupil of Arnobius at Sicca, he taught rhetoric at home, then at Nicomedia at Diocletian's call.

Conversion likely followed his move east, and Diocletian's edict of 303 cost him his chair, leaving him so poor he sometimes lacked bread. Writing kept him alive through persecution, until Constantine's friendship made the aged scholar tutor in Latin to Prince Crispus. He followed his pupil to Trier, where he spent his last years, polished in style rather than deep, yet called the Christian Cicero.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucius-perpet:
Marius Maximus was a Roman historian of about 165 to 230, known only through quotations in the Historia Augusta and inscriptions. Identified with a prefect of the same name, he served in the army, won praetorian rank, campaigned in Gaul, Belgium, Germany, and Syria, and held high administrative posts.

Consul first after 197 under Septimius Severus, prefect under Macrinus in 217, and consul again in 223 under Alexander Severus, he governed Asia and Africa as proconsul. He then wrote emperors' lives from Nerva to Elagabalus, continuing Suetonius in a senate-friendly, diffuse, document-rich manner. Senators admired and read the lives, though the early books survive only in fragments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucius-vitell:
Vitellius was proclaimed Roman emperor by the Rhine soldiers at Cologne in the civil war year of 69, and died at Rome on 21 December of that year. Galba had given him the Lower Rhine army, judging a man devoted to the table too soft to conspire.

After Galba's death and Otho's failure, the German legions raised Vitellius, and his legates Caecina and Valens marched on Italy, beating Otho at Bedriacum. Vitellius entered Rome with 60,000 unruly troops, while Vespasian rose in the East. Caecina's treachery opened the way to a second defeat at Cremona, and Vespasian's men took Rome, killing Vitellius after he had abdicated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lupus:
Lupus, called Servatus Lupus or Loup, was Abbot of Ferrieres and a famed Benedictine writer, born near Sens about 805 and dead about 862. He took the name Servatus for a miraculous escape from illness or battle, studied at Ferrieres under Aldric and at Fulda under Rabanus Maurus, and befriended Einhard.

Esteemed by Empress Judith and Charles the Bald, he became abbot in 840, fought and was captured in war in 844, reformed Burgundian monasteries, and sat at councils from Verneuil to Soissons. In the predestination debate he held a twofold foreordination: God foreknows sins and foreordains their punishment, without predestining any to damnation. His 132 letters remain a treasure of ninth-century letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macarius:
Macarius is the name of two famous fourth-century Nitrian monks, not to be confused. Macarius the Alexandrian, called ho politikos for his city birth or polished manners, died about 405. He burned to outdo every ascetic feat he heard of. He fasted seven years without cooked food in Lent and lay six months in a marsh under African gnats.

Macarius the Egyptian, the Elder, born about 300 and dead in 390, was a disciple of Anthony and founder of a Scetic desert community. Ordained ten years after leaving the world at thirty, he drew thousands to a semi-eremitical life. Cells stood close together, worship fell only on Saturdays and Sundays, elders served as guides rather than rulers, and mutual help was the bond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magnus-felix-:
Magnus Felix Ennodius was a rhetorician and bishop of Pavia. He was probably born at Arles in 474 and died at Pavia in 521. Schooled at Pavia, he was betrothed while young. He then chose the priesthood, while his fiancee entered a convent. Whether they ever married is unclear.

After his patron Epiphanius died in 496, he took minor orders at Milan. His uncle Laurentius was bishop of that city. Soon he became a deacon and a teacher. In 498 two popes were chosen at once, Symmachus and Laurentius. King Theodoric called the Synodus Palmaris at Rome in 501. Ennodius served there as secretary to Laurentius of Milan. His writings mix occasional poems, church inscriptions, a defence of the 502 synod, an autobiography, a praise of Theodoric, and lives of Epiphanius and Antonius of Lerins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magydus:
Magydus was a small titular see of Pamphylia Secunda, under the metropolitan of Perga. It lay on the coast between Attaleia and Perga. Ancient geographers mention it now and then. Its name appears on many coins of the imperial age. Yet it left no great history behind.

Its site was probably Laara in the Konia region. Ruins of a small man-made harbour survive there. The see appears in lists of bishoprics down to the twelfth or thirteenth century. Five bishops stand on record. Aphrodisius attended Nicaea in 325. Macedo attended Chalcedon in 451. Conon and Platon attended councils at Constantinople. Marinus attended Nicaea in 787.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malchus:
Malchus was the Jewish servant whose ear Peter cut off at the arrest of Jesus. His name is Greek for Malluch, meaning counsellor. All four Evangelists tell the incident. Only John names the servant and the disciple. Only Luke notes the healing of the wound.

Judas led soldiers and servants sent by the high priests and Pharisees to seize Jesus. As the arrest began, Peter lashed out with his sword, severing the servant's right ear. Malchus must have stood in front and shown special zeal, or Peter would hardly have singled him out. Christ healed the wound at once and taught a lesson of peace. Later that night a kinsman of Malchus drew Peter's second denial. John's naming of the servant may hint that the writer himself was the disciple acquainted with the high priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mallus:
Mallus was a titular see of Cilicia Prima, under Tarsus. Legend says the seers Amphilochus and Mopsus, sons of Apollo, founded it. It stood at the mouth of the Pyramus, on a hill facing Magarsus, its port. Today the place is Kara Tash in the Adana region, and the district took its name, Mallotis, from the town.

Alexander built a bridge there and freed it from taxes. It joined Tarsus against Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who had given both cities to his concubine Antiochis. Many coins survive, some of the third century reading Mallus Colonia. Ancient writers mention it often, and medieval Arab, Armenian, and Italian writers too. It vanished with the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia. Six bishops stand on record, from Bematius at Antioch in 377 to Chrysippus at Chalcedon in 451, though Le Quien confuses it with a Pisidian namesake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marbodius:
Marbodius was Bishop of Rennes, a church writer and hymn writer, born about 1035 at Angers and dead there on 11 September 1123. He learned at Angers under Rainaldus, a pupil of Fulbert of Chartres. After teaching at Angers cathedral school, Bishop Eusebius Bruno set him over the city's schools in 1067. He later became archdeacon, and Urban II made him bishop in 1096.

His youth held many excesses, but his life as bishop was blameless. He attended the Council of Tours in 1104. In 1109 Bishop Rainaldus of Martigne left him to run Angers during a journey to Rome. At eighty-eight he resigned and withdrew to St Aubin's Benedictine house at Angers, where he soon died. His works, first printed at Rennes in 1524 and enlarged by Beaugendre in 1708, hold saints' lives, letters, and finely written hymns, with a French hymn translation by Ropartz in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus:
Marcus is the name of three leading Gnostics, kept distinct in this entry. First is the founder of the Marcosians, an elder contemporary of Irenaeus, who about 175 addresses him as still living. A pupil of Valentinus in aeon lore, he taught first in Asia Minor and perhaps later in the West. Irenaeus and Hippolytus tell of his immoral acts and juggling tricks, colouring cup contents and swelling their volume.

Second is a defender of Marcionism in Adamantius's Dialogue on Right Faith in God, beside Megethius. His dualism runs harder than Marcion's, with the demiurge as sheer evil, and he saves neither body nor soul, only spirit, leaning toward Apelles. Third is a Manichaean Gnostic from Memphis who carried dualist teaching into Spain about the mid-fourth century. His hearers Agape and Elpidius taught Priscillian, and Saragossa condemned Elpidius with him, though Elpidius escaped Priscillian's death in 385.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus-aureli:
Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman Emperor from A.D. 161 to 180, born at Rome on 26 April 121 and dead on 17 March 180. His father died while he was a boy, and his grandfather Annius Verus adopted him.

His accession ended the great Pax Romana that had made the Antonine age Rome's happiest era. War broke out in the East in 161 and ran to 166, and his co-emperor Lucius Verus died in 169, leaving Marcus to fight alone. The Thundering Legion incident of 174, during the Quadi war, drew both pagan and Christian witnesses. His last years brought the usurper Avidius Cassius and the grim knowledge that Commodus would follow him. A fine Stoic and one of heathen antiquity's best men, he still went further than predecessors against Christians. Under plague, famine, and war, crowds blamed Christians for heaven's anger, so Christian blood flowed freely.

Marcus Aurelius Probus was Roman Emperor from 276 to 282, raised by the army in Syria after Tacitus. He was born at Sirmium in Illyria of humble stock, and won soldiers' trust by courage and skill in eastern campaigns.

As emperor he made senate ratification binding on imperial edicts and gave the senate back its right to name governors of senatorial provinces. Wars with Germans filled his reign. He drove Alamanni across the Rhine, made nine German kings tributary, and settled sixteen thousand German warriors in Roman legions. Peace returned to Rhaetia, Illyria, and Moesia in 278, and his generals beat Franks on the lower Rhine. In peace he set soldiers to temples, bridges, canals, and vineyards, above all in Gaul, Pannonia, and Moesia. Resentful troops proclaimed Carus in Rhaetia, and Probus was killed near his birthplace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus-diadoc:
Marcus Diadochus was an obscure fourth-century writer known only by his name. It heads a Sermon against the Arians, found by Wetsten in a Basle codex of St Athanasius. Wetsten printed it at the end of his edition of Origen's On Prayer in 1694. Another version, lent by Galliciollus to Galland, appeared in the Veterum Patrum Bibliotheca and stands in the Greek Patrology, columns 1149 to 1166.

The sermon quotes and explains familiar texts, from John 1:1 and Hebrews 1:3 to Psalm 109 and John 14, and answers puzzles from Mark 13 and Matthew 20. A wholly different man is Diadochus, Bishop of Photike in Epirus in the fifth century. He wrote a Sermon on the Ascension and a hundred Chapters on Spiritual Perfection, praised by Victor of Vita. The two are often confused, as in Migne, but the sermon writer and the bishop of Photike must be kept apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marianus-scot:
Marianus Scotus names two Irish scholars of the eleventh century, both of whom spent most of their lives in Germany. The chronicler, Irish-named Maelbrigte, Servant of Brigid, was born in Ireland in 1028 and died at Mainz in 1082. He became a monk in 1052, took the name Marianus, and moved through Cologne, Fulda, Paderborn, and Wurzburg, where he was ordained in 1059.

As a hermit at Fulda, then at Mainz from 1070 at Archbishop Siegfried's order, he wrote the Universal Chronicle, a year-by-year world history from Christ's era to 1082. His dating system, claiming Dionysius Exiguus set Christ's birth twenty-two years too late, won little support, though he printed both systems. The abbot, Marianus of Ratisbon, left Ireland in 1067 for Rome and settled in Germany. He founded St Peter's at Ratisbon and won fame as a scribe of Scripture. His Paul's Epistles codex of 1078 survives at Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marius-aventi:
Marius Aventicus was Bishop of Avenches in Switzerland and a chronicler, born about 530 near Autun and dead at Lausanne in 594. Little of his life is known beyond his tomb inscription at St Thyrsius in Lausanne. It tells of a distinguished, rich, likely Roman family and an early embrace of church life.

He became Bishop of Avenches in 574, attended the Council of Macon in 585, and soon moved his see to Lausanne as Avenches declined. He won praise as an ideal bishop, a skilled goldsmith who made sacred vessels with his own hands, a protector of the poor, a man of prayer, and an eager scholar. After death Lausanne honoured him as a saint, feasted on 9 or 12 February, and St Thyrsius church took his name. His chronicle, continuing Prosper Tiro from 455 to 581 in dry annals, remains prized for Burgundian and Frankish history, above all the later sixth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-corv:
Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary from 1458 to his death at Vienna in 1490, was born at Kolozsvar in 1440. He was the son of the soldier Janos Hunyady. Schooled in the humanities under Gregor Sanocki and shaped by Bishop Johann Vitez, he lost his brother Ladislaus to execution after a court plot. He endured arrest and exile at Prague, and was proclaimed king at Buda on 23 January 1458.

Shaking off his uncle's regency, he fought Emperor Frederick III over the crown until a 1462 pact settled the claim. He then married, warred, and ruled as a Renaissance prince. The entry follows his campaigns, marriages, and court, and points readers to his letters and to studies of his son Joannes Corvinus and Queen Beatrice. It sketches a ruler who joined soldiering, learning, and statecraft in one restless reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maxentius:
Maxentius, Roman emperor from 306 to 312, was the son of Maximianus Herculius and son-in-law of Galerius. After his father's abdication he lived at Rome as a private citizen. When Galerius imposed Diocletian's new poll and land taxes on Rome and Italy, senators and praetorians, fearing for their privileges, chose Maxentius rival emperor on 28 October 306. He then called his father from Campania to share the purple.

Severus, Augustus of the West, marched to expel him, but much of his army deserted to Maximian, and Severus surrendered, only to be imprisoned and forced to suicide as Galerius approached. Maximian then allied with Constantine through the marriage of his daughter Fausta. Galerius himself advanced on Rome yet could take neither the city nor its region, and the entry follows the tangled six-emperor struggle that ended with Maxentius's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximianus:
Maximianus, whose full name was Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus, surnamed Herculius, served as Diocletian's co-regent from 285. Diocletian adopted him to share the burden of rule, hoping the split would check mutiny, usurpers, and foreign attack. He gave him the name Herculius, recalling the mythic Hercules who aided Jupiter against the giants. A peasant's son from near Sirmium in Illyria, Maximianus had little schooling but was violent, brutal, and brave.

While Diocletian fought Persia in Asia, Maximianus crushed the Bagaudan revolt of peasants and slaves in Gaul and won the title Augustus on 1 April 286. Rule was divided in administration only; Diocletian's will stayed absolute. From Mainz, Maximianus fought Burgundians and other foes, and the entry traces his campaigns, his partnership with Diocletian, and the Tetrarchy's inner strains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mencius:
Mencius, the Latin form of Chinese Meng-tze, Meng the Sage, was a philosopher born in 371 or 372 B.C. A disciple of Confucius's grandson, he ranks next to the master as his wisdom's expounder. His Book of Mencius stands among the four Shuh, just after the King, or classics. Only a thin account of his life survives, and it so mirrors Confucius's story that its strict history may be doubted.

He is said to have lived to eighty-four. His father died while he was very young. His mother took charge of his training so well that the Chinese of every class have honoured her ever since as the pattern of the true mother. After schooling in Confucius's doctrine, Mencius served Prince Hsuan, quit when the prince spurned his counsel, wandered teaching from state to state, and at last aided Prince Hui with wise reforms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-caeru:
Michael Caerularius, Patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 to 1058 and author of the second and final schism of the Byzantine Church, died in 1058; his birth date is unknown. After the reconciliation that followed Photius's schism, an anti-Latin party at Constantinople gloried in Photius's work. They honoured him as Orthodoxy's defender, and waited for a chance to renew his quarrel. The only account of his conduct is that he belonged from the start to that party's extreme wing and meant to break with the pope once he could.

 He began public life by plotting with Constantine Monomachus, the future emperor, to depose Emperor Michael IV. Both plotters were banished, and in exile formed the friendship to which Caerularius owed his later rise. Known as dangerous, he was to be stopped by making him a monk. At first he refused; then his brother's suicide brought his conversion, and he willingly entered a monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-psell:
Michael Psellus, a Byzantine statesman, scholar, and author, was born apparently at Constantinople in 1018 and died probably in 1078. He studied in the schools, then learned law from John Xiphilinos, later patriarch. Psellus practised law, judged at Philadelphia, and under Michael V became imperial secretary. Under Constantine IX he grew influential in the state.

At that time he taught philosophy at Constantinople's new Academy, rousing church professors by preferring Plato to Aristotle. His teaching career ended when he became Secretary of State to Constantine IX. In 1054 he followed Xiphilinos to the Olympos monastery in Bithynia, taking the name Michael, but soon quarrelled with the monks and returned to the capital. He treated with the rebel Isaac Komnenos in 1057, switched allegiance when Isaac triumphed, drew the indictment against Patriarch Caerularius in 1059, and kept influence under Constantine X and Michael VII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-scotu:
Michael Scotus, a thirteenth-century mathematician, philosopher, and scholar, was born in Scotland about 1175. The claim that he was Irish fails, since in 1223, offered Cashel's archbishopric, he declined for ignorance of Irish. Whether Scotus means a Scot, or a man of the Scott clan, is unclear. Tradition says he studied at Durham's cathedral school, then at Oxford and Paris, where he was known as the mathematician.

He was certainly a cleric, likely studied theology too, and probably visited Bologna before reaching Sicily and Frederick II's court about 1200. At Palermo he joined the emperor's learned circle, some say as imperial tutor, though manuscripts usually call him astrologer to the Lord Emperor Frederick. In 1209 he went to Toledo, met distinguished Arab scholars, and wrote his Abbreviatio Avicennae, dated 1210, taking up astronomy and alchemy as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micrologus:
Micrologus, meaning a synopsis or short explanation, served in the Middle Ages as a synonym for manual. The best known of several works so called is the Micrologus de ecclesiasticis observationibus, an explanation of the liturgy of the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass and of the ecclesiastical year. It was first edited at Paris in 1510 and survives in a number of manuscripts.

The work, valuable both for the history and for the right understanding of the Mass liturgy and the church year, falls into three parts. The author first treats the Mass in its historical development, then the liturgy of the ember days, and finally the feasts and offices of the year. Its comprehensive scope made it a standard guide to medieval worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miletus:
Miletus, a titular see of Asia Minor and suffragan of Aphrodisias in Caria, stood on Caria's western coast near the Latmic Gulf. It lay at the mouth of the Maeander and the end of several great roads of Asia Minor. For a long period it ranked among the ancient world's most prosperous cities. First inhabited by the Leleges and called Lelegeis or Pityussa, it was rebuilt as Miletus by the Cretans.

Homer mentions it in the Iliad. Around the tenth century B.C., Ionian settlers took it over and raised it into a sea-trading power of the foremost order. From Miletus numerous colonies were founded along the Hellespont, the Propontis, and the Black Sea. In Christian times it became an episcopal see, and St. Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders took place there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionaries-:
The Missionaries of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, of Issoudun, are a congregation of priests and lay brothers. Their object is to promote knowledge and practice of devotion to the Heart of Jesus. That devotion rests on the revelations to Blessed Margaret Mary Alacoque, and the congregation offers personal reparation to the Divine Heart. Their motto is Ametur ubique terrarum Cor Jesu Sacratissimum, may the most Sacred Heart of Jesus be loved everywhere.

The society was founded at Issoudun in the Archdiocese of Bourges, France, by Abbe Jules Chevalier. Its origin is tied to the definition of the Immaculate Conception on 8 December 1854. Chevalier honoured the Virgin the next year with a shrine of Our Lady of the Sacred Heart. Since France's separation of Church and State, its headquarters stand at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionary-si:
The Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, with their general mother-house at Rome, were founded in 1880 by Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini, then still living. The institute aims to spread devotion to the Heart of Jesus through spiritual and corporal works of mercy. The sisters run homes for the aged and sick, orphanages, industrial schools, and sewing classes.

They visit hospitals and prisons and give religious instruction in their convents, which are open to women wishing to make retreats. The congregation spread rapidly in Europe and America. In 1899, at Leo XIII's suggestion, the sisters came to New York, where Cabrini's work among Italian immigrants made her the first United States citizen to be canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mocissus:
Mocissus, a titular metropolitan see of Cappadocia, was a fortified site in northwestern Cappadocia which Justinian made metropolis of Cappadocia Tertia when he divided that province into three parts. The emperor gave it the name Justinianopolis. Its past is wholly unknown, and Mocessus may be the truer spelling of its name.

The modern town of Kir-Sheir beyond doubt stands on the site of Mocissus, or Mocessus. Kir-Sheir is chief town of a sanjak in the vilayet of Angora, with 8,000 inhabitants, most of them Mussulmans. Near Kir-Sheir there are some important remains, including a church, testifying to the town's Christian past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-:
Saint Lucius, known as Saint Luzi, is a monastery at Chur in Switzerland. Its church rose over the grave of Saint Lucius and kept his relics until the sixteenth century. The church began as the cathedral itself. Saint Valentinian enlarged it in the early sixth century with a crypt that still stands. Later it passed briefly under the Benedictine abbey of Pfafer.

About 1140 it became a Premonstratensian abbey. Its abbot Theodore Schlegel defended the Catholic faith so vigorously during the Reformation schism that Protestants tortured and executed him in January 1529. The monks were driven out and the house stood empty for a century before its restoration in 1624. Stripped of its lands in 1802, it passed to the episcopal seminary in 1806, which still occupies the site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-gudenu:
Moritz Gudenus, born at Cassel on 11 April 1596 and dead at Treffurt in February 1680, was a German convert from the Protestant ministry to the Catholic faith. Descended from a Calvinist family that had moved from Utrecht to Hesse, he studied at Marburg. He served as deacon of the Reformed church there until a change of rulers replaced Calvinism with Lutheranism.

Refusing the Augsburg Confession cost him his post, and after serving at Abterode he became its pastor in 1625. Reading Bellarmine opened Catholic doctrine to him in a new light, and after careful study he and his family entered the Church in 1630 at considerable personal cost. He later served as high bailiff at Treffurt until his death, leaving a treatise on the Eucharist and letters on his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myndus:
Myndus was a titular see of Caria, suffragan to Stauropolis, a Greek colony from Troezen on the Carian coast. It lay a little northwest of Halicarnassus, on the northernmost of the three Dorian peninsulas. Though a seaport and fortified town, its course ran quietly. Its chief event was the repulse of an attack by Alexander the Great with Halicarnassus's help.

The episcopal lists mention it as late as the twelfth or thirteenth century, yet only four bishops are known. They were Archelaus at Ephesus in 431, Alphius at Chalcedon in 451, John at Constantinople in 680, and another John at Second Nicaea in 787. Today it is the little port of Gumushlu Liman in the vilayet of Smyrna, where a pier and other ruins remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nazianzus:
Nazianzus was a titular metropolitan see of Cappadocia Tertia, a small town whose history is completely unknown. It is the modern village of Nenizi east of Ak-Serai, in the vilayet of Koniah, but has sometimes been wrongly identified with Diocaesarea. At the start of the fourth century it was suffragan to Caesarea. Under Valens it joined Cappadocia Secunda, whose metropolis was Tyana.

Later it depended on Cappadocia Tertia and on Mocessus, and finally became a metropolitan see under Emperor Diogenes. In 1370 it was united to the metropolitan see of Caesarea. Up to 1200, fourteen of its bishops are known. Its name is inseparably linked with its illustrious doctor and poet-bishop, Saint Gregory, whose writings and career the entry sketches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nectarius:
Nectarius, Patriarch of Constantinople from 381 to 397, died on 27 September 397. He was the eleventh bishop of that city since Metrophanes, and may count as its first patriarch. He came from Tarsus, of a senatorial family, and was praetor at Constantinople during the Second General Council in 381.

When Saint Gregory Nazianzen resigned the see, the people called for Nectarius, and the council ratified the choice before August 381. Sozomen adds that Diodorus of Tarsus, seeing his visitor's fitness, persuaded Meletius of Antioch to add his name to the candidates. The emperor, to everyone's surprise, chose the still unbaptised Nectarius, consecrated in a neophyte's robe. Soon after, the council's famous third canon ranked Constantinople just after Rome. Nectarius's reign was uneventful, and Saint Gregory was not altogether pleased with it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicodemus:
Nicodemus, the Pharisee who visited Jesus by night in the Fourth Gospel, is treated here as a figure of cautious, growing belief. A member of the Sanhedrin and a man of means, he is called a teacher in Israel during that night talk about new birth.

Later he speaks up for fair hearing when the council moves against Jesus, and at the end he helps Joseph of Arimathea embalm and bury the body. The entry also weighs later legends about him and his name in apocryphal writings. The entry also notes his name in later apocryphal writings, including the so-called Acts of Pilate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-cope:
Astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, born at Toruń in 1473, moved the earth from the center of the cosmos and set modern astronomy in motion. Raised by his uncle, the prince-bishop of Ermland, after his father's early death, he studied at Kraków and Bologna, where he learned Greek and astronomy.

Made a canon of Frauenburg, Copernicus spent years weighing the motions of the planets and drafting the sun-centered scheme published as On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. The book reached print in the year of his death, 1543, and reshaped how later ages read the sky.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-germ:
Fifteenth-century mapmaker Nicolaus Germanus, often miscalled Donis, redrew Ptolemy's world for Renaissance readers. Nothing is known of his birth or death, but Duke Borso d'Este paid him handsomely in 1466 for a Cosmographia and a calendar of many years.

His Cosmographia, kept at Modena, pairs a Latin Ptolemy text with new maps. Breaking from Ptolemy's flat projection, Germanus spaced the parallels of latitude evenly, a method later known as the Donis projection, and his work shaped how Europe pictured the known world. Duke Borso also paid thirty gold florins for a calendar covering many years to come.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicosia-cypru:
Nicosia, capital of Cyprus, carries under one name the older sees of Ledra, Leucosia, and Leucopolis in this entry. Its bishop Triphyllius, praised by Jerome as the most eloquent of his age, appears under Constantine, and after the eighth century the city replaced Constantia as island metropolis.

Richard the Lionheart took Cyprus in 1191, the Templars massacred townspeople who resisted them, and Guy de Lusignan founded a dynasty of fifteen rulers. Nicosia then became a Latin metropolitan see, with Frankish churches and institutions shaping its medieval life. At the conquest of 1191 Nicosia already stood as the island capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nimbus:
The nimbus, the ring of light painted round holy heads in Christian art, began in nature before it became a symbol. Rings round sun and moon, light pillars, mountain mists that halo a walker's shadow, and dew that glows round a footprint all gave early peoples a ready image of dignity.

From Babylonian sky watchers through Greek and Roman art to Christian painting, the disc hardened into a sign. Plain rings marked saints, a cross-marked ring marked Christ, and rays or a triangle marked God the Father. The entry tracks that shift across pagan, Byzantine, and Western images.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nonnus:
Nonnus of Panopolis, an Egyptian poet around the year 400, is credited with two hexameter poems of opposite spirit. One, the Dionysiaca, retells the mysteries of Bacchus at vast length, while the other paraphrases the Fourth Gospel verse by verse.

If one author wrote both, Nonnus likely turned from paganism to Christianity between them, though rival claims name Apollinaris or Ammonius for the paraphrase. Surviving in 3,750 lines across twenty-one chapters, the paraphrase matters chiefly as evidence for the Gospel text its author used. The Aldine Press first issued the paraphrase in 1501.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oecolampadius:
Johannes Oecolampadius, born Heusegen at Weinsberg in 1482, organized the Reformation at Basel. Trained in law at Bologna, then theology and letters at Heidelberg, he learned Greek at Stuttgart, Hebrew at Tübingen, and joined Erasmus's circle as preacher at Basel cathedral in 1515.

Drawn to Luther and Melanchthon at Augsburg, he broke with Rome, debated Zwingli's allies on the Eucharist, and led Basel's church from 1525 until his death in 1531. His biblical commentaries and church order, the entry notes, set the pattern for Reformed Basel. He was made bachelor in 1515, licentiate in 1516, and doctor of theology in 1518.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olaus-magnus:
Swedish historian Olaus Magnus, born at Skeninge in 1490, mapped the north for Renaissance Europe from exile in Rome. Of the noble Store family and schooled in Germany from 1510, he became provost of Strängnäs and went to Rome in 1523 to confirm his brother John as archbishop of Uppsala.

Loyal to Catholicism, Olaus lost his property when Gustav Vasa seized church goods, followed John to Rome in 1537, and succeeded him as archbishop in name after 1544. Attending Trent from 1545, he wrote the great History of the Northern Peoples and a Carta Marina, and died in 1558.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olenus:
Olenus, a titular see suffragan to Patras, counted among Achaia’s twelve oldest cities on the Peirus near Dyme. Noted by 280 BC, its people soon withdrew to Peirai, Euryteiai, and Dyme, and Strabo, forty stadia from Dyme, found it in ruins.

Repeopled under Frankish Morea, it gained its first bishop from Honorius III in 1217, while its church had been run by Archdeacon John, chaplain of Villehardouin. A Latin diocese replaced the Greek see of Elos, and its bishops usually lived at Andravida. Eubel gives the long list of bishops of Olenus and Andravilla in his hierarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olympus:
Olympus, a titular see in Lycia, Asia Minor, stood among the chief cities of the Lycian league near a burning mountain. Servilius Isauricus captured it from the pirate Zenicetas and carried its stolen statues and treasure to Rome, and its ruins, theatre, temple, and porticoes, lie at Delik-Tash.

The town rose near Mount Olympus, or Phoenicus, whose constant fires ancients called Chimaera, a monster Bellerophon slew, though wiser writers knew it as natural flame. Bishop lists name Olympus under Myra until the thirteenth century, with Saint Methodius among four known bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ombus:
Ombus, a titular see suffragan to Ptolemais in Upper Egypt, began as a small Ptolemaic garrison on a high plateau guarding the lower Nile. Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, Juvenal, and Hierocles all note it, and it later became capital of the Ombitos nome, then of Egypt's southern province instead of Elephantine.

Thirty miles north of Syene, its history stays unknown beyond bishops Silvanus and Verres under Patriarch Theophilus and a seventh-century inscription. Its ruins at Kom Ombo once held a Ptolemaic temple, destroyed in 1893, on the site of a shrine from Thutmose III's age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orcistus:
Orcistus, a titular see in Galatia Secunda, appears only in Peutinger's Table, yet an inscription of 331 fixes its site at Alikel Yaila in the vilayet of Angora. Then a road station where four roads met in the Diocese of Asia, it must have belonged to Phrygia before joining Galatia Secunda around 386.

Its name comes from the Orei tribe on Phrygia's eastern plains. Only three bishops are known, Domnus and Longinus in 451 and Segermas in 692, but bishop lists name the see among Pessinus's suffragans until the thirteenth century. In 451 it stood in Galatia Secunda, probably from that province’s formation about 386.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oremus:
Oremus, Latin for let us pray, invites prayer before collects and other short prayers throughout the Roman rite. Eastern rites use it alone or with additions, most often let us pray to the Lord, and Duchesne thought Gallican collects likewise opened with the word.

Mozarabic use restricts it to two places, before the Agios and the Pater Noster. Rome says or sings it before every separate collect, postcommunion, offertory prayer, and introduction to the Lord's Prayer. Once, the entry argues, it summoned private prayer before any set collect followed. In the East it appears as a single cry, or as the command to pray.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orientius:
Orientius, a fifth-century Gallic poet in Latin, wrote the Commonitorium, an elegiac poem of 1,036 verses in two books mapping the road to heaven and its hindrances. Converted after a life of sin and plainly a seasoned pastor, he wrote while invaders ravaged Gaul.

Those marks point to Orientius, bishop of Auch, sent as a very old man by Theodoric I in 439 as envoy to Roman generals Aëtius and Litorius. Quoting Virgil, Ovid, and Catullus and perhaps echoing Prudentius, the poem survives in a single tenth-century manuscript with shorter pieces beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orlando-de-la:
Orlando de Lassus, born Roland de Lattre at Mons about 1520, became the most celebrated composer of the later Renaissance. Admitted as a choir soprano at eight and a half for his voice and talent, he was abducted three times. Twice returned home, he was finally allowed to follow Ferdinand de Gonzaga to Milan and Sicily.

After Naples and Rome, where he became choirmaster of Saint John Lateran while still young, Lassus settled at Munich's ducal court. His masses, motets, and chansons, above all the Penitential Psalms, made him the age's master of sacred polyphony until his death in 1594.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oropus:
Oropus was an ancient city in Asia Minor whose church rank drew notice from early lists of bishops. The entry treats it as a titular see, a former bishop's seat kept on the books after it stopped working, first linked with Anazarbus in Cilicia Secunda. Its real tie, the writer argues, ran instead to Seleucia in Isauria.

Greek bishop lists from the sixth and tenth centuries call the place Oropa or Oroba, while a Latin version gives the name Oropus. On that proof the entry names Oropus as Olba, a suffragan, or subordinate see, of Seleucia. With the province of Isauria it passed to the Patriarchate of Constantinople in the eighth century, and later lists under Leo the Wise and Constantine Porphyrogenitus still mention it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orsisius:
Orsisius was a fourth-century Egyptian monk who rose to lead the community founded by Pachomius on the island of Tabenna in the Nile. Chosen to succeed Pachomius at his death in 348, he stepped aside for Theodore. He took up the post of hegumen, or head of the monks, only after Theodore's death around 380. He did so on the advice of Athanasius.

Tradition credits Orsisius and Theodore with helping Pachomius frame his monastic rule. Gennadius records a book by Orsisius that taught the whole range of monastic discipline. It did so through short talks on the Old and New Testaments. Jerome turned that work, the Teaching on the Training of Monks, into Latin. A second piece printed after it, on six thoughts of the saints, probably belongs to a later writer of the same name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ortwin-gratiu:
Ortwin Gratius, born van Graes at Holtwick in Westphalia in 1475, was a humanist scholar who worked at Cologne. He died there on 22 May 1542. Raised in the house of an uncle at Deventer, he was taught by Alexander Hegius. He reached Cologne University in 1501, took his licentiate in 1505 and his master's degree in 1506, and taught arts from 1507.

Short pay drove him to work as adviser and corrector for the Quentell printing house. Many medieval and classical texts passed under his eye there, with his own introductions and rhymed dedications. A keen humanist at first, he fell out with younger scholars when he sided with Cologne theologians and Dominicans in the Reuchlin dispute. He also translated writings by the Jewish convert Pfefferkorn, and the entry follows the pamphlet war that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ottmar-luscin:
Ottmar Luscinius, born Nachtgall at Strasbourg in 1487 and dead at Freiburg in 1537, was an Alsatian humanist of wide learning. Taught at Strasbourg by Jacob Wimpfeling, he went to Paris in 1508 to study Latin and Greek. He then read canon law at Louvain, Padua, and Vienna, learning music at Vienna too. He travelled in Greece and Asia Minor, and came home to Strasbourg in 1514.

Back home he joined Wimpfeling and Sebastian Brant in literary circles, became organist at Saint Thomas in 1515, and taught in two schools. He spread love of Greek letters through manuals, example books, and an edition of Lucian with translation. His later works include a 1518 edition of a Pauline commentary. There he attacks Scholasticism and backs Bible study. They also include a 1524 exposition of the Psalms, and a harmony of the Gospels in Latin and German.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oxyrynchus:
Oxyrynchus was a titular archdiocese of Heptanomos in Egypt and capital of its district, the nineteenth nome of Upper Egypt. Its god was Set, embodied in a sacred Nile fish, the mormyrus, which gave the Greek name, while Egyptians called the town Pemdje. Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy all mention it. Its people took up Christianity early, and by the late fourth century, Rufinus says, it held neither pagan nor heretic.

Twelve churches stood there, and monks' huts outnumbered ordinary homes, with many convents round the city. In 1897, 1903, and later years, Grenfell and Hunt found papyri with fourteen sayings of Jesus from the first half of the second century, plus lost Gospel fragments and third-century Christian papers. A 312 letter from Peter the Martyr, Bishop of Alexandria, pictures the church then, and today the ruined town is called Behneseh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pacandus:
Pacandus is a titular see listed under the name Pacanden in the Roman Curia's official list as late as 1884. It was then suppressed, since it had never existed as a residential see. Its present titular is Leon Livinhac, superior general of the White Fathers.

The name Pacanden almost surely comes from the See of Acanda in Lycia. Its bishop Panaetius signed the Lycian bishops' letter to Emperor Leo in 458. Acanda appears in bishop lists from the seventh to the thirteenth century among the suffragans of Myra. Its exact site is unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pacificus:
Pacificus was a disciple of Saint Francis of Assisi, probably born near Ascoli in Italy in the later twelfth century and probably dead at Lens in France about 1234. Local writers name him as William of Lisciano. Before joining the Friars Minor he had served as court poet to Frederick II of Sicily.

About 1212, hearing Francis preach at San Severino, he saw in vision two bright swords crossed on the saint's breast. Deeply moved, he asked to join the order, and Francis gave him the name Pacificus. Sent to France in 1217, he is said to have founded the French province. He witnessed Francis's stigmata in 1226, and Gregory IX commended the Poor Clares of Siena to his care in 1227.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palladius:
Palladius, born in Galatia in 368 and probably dead before 431, wrote the Historia Lausiaca, a gallery of Egyptian monks. Long debate over whether its author, the biographer of John Chrysostom, and the Bishop of Helenopolis were one man has lately been settled in favour of one identity. A disciple of Evagrius of Pontus and admirer of Origen, he turned monk on the Mount of Olives at twenty.

After three years he travelled to Egypt for study of famed monks, and stayed nine years in the Nitrian desert among thousands of monks, hermits and communities alike. He met Didymus the Blind and Evagrius, and visited the Thebaid and Scete. On Evagrius's death in 399 he travelled home through Alexandria and Palestine, meeting Jerome at Bethlehem, and later served as bishop and exile in the Chrysostom troubles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paltus:
Paltus was a titular see and suffragan of Seleucia Pieria in Syria Prima, founded by a colony from Arvad or Aradus. Pliny and Ptolemy place it in Syria, and Strabo sets it near the river Badan. When Justinian formed the province of Theodorias, Paltus joined it. From the sixth century, by Anastasius's bishop list, it stood as an autocephalous archdiocese under Antioch, and in the tenth century it still lived, its bounds then known.

Le Quien names five of its bishops. Cymatius, friend of Saint Athanasius, and his successor Patricius lead the list. Severus follows in 381, and Sabbas sat at Chalcedon in 451. Last comes John, exiled by Monophysites and restored by Emperor Justin I in 518. Ruins of Paltus can be seen at Belde, south of the Nahr es-Sin, the ancient Badan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamelius:
Pamelius, born Jacques de Joigny de Pamele at Bruges on 13 May 1536 and dead at Mons on 19 September 1587, was a Belgian theologian and editor of rare texts. Schooled at the Cistercian abbey of Boneffe, he studied philosophy at Louvain and took his master of arts on 27 March 1553. Nine years of theology followed under Ruard Tapper and Josse Ravestein, with a Sorbonne course after his baccalaureate.

Made canon of Saint Donatian at Bruges in 1561 and priest probably in 1562, he hunted every Low Countries library for manuscripts and unprinted works. His first fruit, the Micrologus of 1565, comments on the Roman Ordo from the early twelfth century. Dean of Bruges Christianity from 1568 to 1571, he helped the 1571 Index expurgatorius and the Jesuit college at Bruges, and Calvinist hatred later drove him from the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panemotichus:
Panemotichus was a titular see of Pamphylia Secunda, suffragan of Perge, which struck coins in the Roman age. Bishop Faustus attended Nicaea in 325, when the city belonged to Isauria, and later it passed to Pamphylia Secunda. Cratinus may have attended Chalcedon in 451, Hierius put his name to the provincial letter for Leo the Wise, and Helladius sat at a Constantinople council in 536.

No other bishop is recorded, and the see never appears in the bishop lists. Hierocles names the city in the sixth century, and Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the tenth. Radet identifies it with ruins at Badem Aghatch, south of Ghirme, in the Koniah region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pantaenus:
Pantaenus headed the Catechetical School of Alexandria about 180 and was still alive in 193, with his death likely about 200, since Clement, his successor, left Alexandria about 203. Trained in Stoic philosophy, he travelled as a Christian missionary to India, probably South Arabia, and found Christians there holding Matthew's Gospel in Hebrew, received from Saint Bartholomew.

Eusebius reports all this as what was said, and quotes Clement calling Pantaenus his teacher in the Hypotyposes. In the Stromata Clement lists his teachers by nation, not name, ending with a Hebrew of Palestine, greater than the rest, whom he hunted out in hiding in Egypt. Eusebius takes this last teacher for Pantaenus, though a Palestinian Hebrew seems an odd Stoic. The entry weighs the case for and against that reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paphnutius:
Paphnutius, bishop of a city in the Upper Thebaid in the early fourth century, ranks among the most striking figures at Nicaea in 325. Under Maximinus from 308 to 313 he lost his right eye and suffered mutilation of his left knee for the faith, and was then condemned to the mines. At Nicaea Constantine honoured him greatly, and Socrates says the emperor often sent for the old confessor and kissed the socket of the torn eye.

Paphnutius played a leading, perhaps decisive, part in the council's debate on clerical celibacy. Most bishops leaned toward Elvira's rule barring married bishops, priests, and deacons from conjugal life. He begged them not to lay that burden on the clergy. He urged the old tradition: only men celibate at ordination must stay continent, and no man be parted from the wife he wed before orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paralus:
Paralus was a titular see, suffragan of Cabasa in Egypt Secunda, set at one of the Nile's seven mouths, Sebennys or Paralus. The see appears during Arab rule in the Coptic bishop list. Its bishop Athanasius attended Ephesus in 431, while Pasmeius sat at the Robber Council of Ephesus in 449 and at Chalcedon in 451.

Le Quien adds two further Jacobite bishops. The site is now Burlos or Burollos, its headland Ras Burlos, and the old Sebennys lake Baheret-Burlos. Beyond its bishops at Ephesus, the Robber Council, and Chalcedon, little more of the see is known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parnassus:
Parnassus was a titular see in Cappadocia Secunda, suffragan of Mocessus, set between Ancyra and Archelais, with another road leading to Nyssa. Once important, it appears in Polybius and the itineraries, and in Hierocles in the sixth century. Hamilton puts it at Kotch Hissar near Lake Tatta, Ramsay north-east of the lake on the Halys, near Tchikin Aghyl.

The see first answered to Caesarea, passed under Valens to Cappadocia Secunda, and about 536 became suffragan of Mocessus. Bishop lists carry it into the thirteenth century. Le Quien names nine bishops. They run from Pancratius at Philippopolis in 344 and Olympius at Constantinople in 381 to Stephanus at Nicaea in 787 and Theognostus at Constantinople in 869. The troubled Eustathius stands among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-the-deac:
Paul the Deacon, also called Paulus Diaconus, Casinensis, Levita, and Warnefridi, was a Lombard historian born at Friuli about 720 and dead on 13 April, probably 799. Of noble Lombard stock, he was likely schooled at King Ratchis's court at Pavia under Flavian the grammarian. In 763 he stood at Duke Arichis's Benevento court. After the Lombard kingdom's fall he became a Monte Cassino monk. In 782 he joined Charlemagne's suite, winning by elegy the release of a brother captured in the 776 Friuli rising.

Back at Monte Cassino after 787, he likely died there. His first work, done at Benevento for Duchess Adelperga, was the Roman History, amplifying Eutropius and continuing him independently in books eleven to sixteen down to Justinian. Now valueless, it was widely copied and consulted in the Middle Ages. At Metz Bishop Angilram's request he also wrote the history of Metz's bishops to 766.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-barbus:
Paulus Barbus was an Italian philosopher and theologian born at Soncino in Lombardy, whence the name Soncinas heading his books, and dead at Cremona on 4 August 1494. Entering the Dominicans as a mere youth, he studied philosophy and theology in their schools. He then taught both subjects to acclaim at Milan, Ferrara, and Bologna. At death he was prior of the Cremona convent.

Of extraordinary intellect, he voiced deep thought in eloquent speech and polished writing. He won esteem from learned contemporaries, notably Pico della Mirandola. Many of his writings were lost early. Works printed often include his Questions on Aristotle's Divine Wisdom, chief edition Lyons 1579, and his Divine Epitome on the Sentences disputed by John Capreolo, chief edition Pavia 1522. The place and date of his exposition on predicables and predicaments are unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-jovius:
Paulus Jovius, or Giovio, was a historian born at Como in Italy on 9 April 1483 and dead at Florence on 11 December 1552. After a Padua medical degree, Pope Leo X's princely largesse drew him to Rome. There he practised medicine but gave himself chiefly to history, above all his own age, gathering rich sources for a wide work on all Europe from Charles VIII's Italian expedition.

Reading the first part to the Holy Father won him knighthood and Rome University's rhetoric chair. Adrian VI made him a Como cathedral canon, and Clement VII named him Bishop of Nocera in 1528 to repay losses from Rome's capture. Under Paul III he sought transfer to Como, failed, gave up Nocera in 1543 from vexation, and moved to Como, then Florence in 1550. As his writings show, he was a child of his age, living for pleasure little in accord with Christian practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-orosiu:
Paulus Orosius was a historian and Christian apologist probably born at Bracara, now Braga in Portugal, between 380 and 390, with birth and death dates not precisely known. His first name is known only since the eighth century. Early consecrated to God's service, he was ordained and went to Africa in 413 or 414, leaving his homeland, by his own words, without will, need, or consent.

He repaired to Saint Augustine at Hippo to ask points of doctrine on the soul and its origin, attacked by Priscillianists. In 414 he prepared for Augustine a Commonitorium on Priscillianist and Origenist error, which Augustine answered. To learn more of soul and origin, he went with Augustine's warm letter to Saint Jerome in Palestine. Pelagius was then spreading false doctrine there, and Orosius aided Jerome and others against that heresy, facing in 415 Bishop John of Jerusalem, inclined to Origen and swayed by Pelagius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-venatu:
Paulus Venatus was a theologian of the Augustinian Hermits, born, by his order's chroniclers, at Udine about 1368 and dead at Venice on 15 June 1428. He professed at Saint Stephen's convent in Venice, whence the name Venetus. In 1390 he was reportedly sent to Oxford for theology, but returned to Italy and finished at Padua, lecturing there through the fifteenth century's first quarter.

His writings, apart from present worth, show wide knowledge and keen interest in his age's scientific questions. Besides lectures on the Sentences, sermons, and instructions, he wrote on the Virgin's Conception, on squaring the circle, on circles composing the world, and his Little and Great Logic. The last, also called Double Logic, served widely as a textbook through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. In 1427 Martin V called him to Rome to weigh charges against Saint Bernardine of Siena over the new devotion to the Holy Name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pednelissus:
Pednelissus, or Petnelissus, was a titular see in Pamphylia Secunda, suffragan of Perge. In ancient times the city belonged to Pisidia. Strabo, Ptolemy, Pliny, Stephanus of Byzantium, and sixth-century Hierocles in his Synecdemus mention it, Hierocles placing it in Pamphylia. It mattered for frequent wars with Selge, told by Polybius. Its coins show two forms of the name, while other documents often give badly corrupted forms.

The Notices of Bishoprics mention the see as late as the thirteenth century. Yet only two bishops are known: Heraclides, present at Constantinople's ecumenical council in 381, and Martinus, who signed the Pamphylian bishops' letter to Emperor Leo. The city's exact site is unknown and is matched to several places. The likeliest match is ruins south of Tchaudir and east of Kizil Keui in Pambouk Ova, cotton field, in Koniah province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-nunez-n:
Pedro Nunes, known in Latin as Nonius, was a Portuguese mathematician and astronomer whose work shaped navigation. Born at Alcácer do Sal in 1492, he studied at Lisbon and Salamanca and served as inspector of customs at Goa. He became royal cosmographer in 1529. From 1544 to 1562 he held a Coimbra professorship in higher mathematics, created for him.

His work crossed pure mathematics, astronomy, and seafaring. He found a way to get the highest common divisor of algebraic expressions. He treated the problem of minimum twilight anew and built an angle-measuring device of concentric circles that bears his name. He also mapped the loxodrome, the curving course a ship traces when it cuts every meridian at the same angle. His collected works appeared at Basle in 1592.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peregrinus:
Peregrinus was a shadowy bishop whose name guards a puzzle about the canons of Priscillian. Prefixed to Paul's epistles in many Spanish manuscripts, the canons carry an introduction headed by Peregrinus explaining that Priscillian, not Jerome, wrote them, and that the text given is expurgated. The prologue that follows shows none of Priscillian's own style, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry judges it rewritten by Peregrinus himself.

Other traces deepen the riddle. A Leon codex prays for Peregrinus, and Spanish manuscripts of Jerome append the words bidding the reader to remember Peregrinus. St. Vincent of Lérins also wrote as Peregrinus, but he was no bishop. Scholars have identified the Spanish bishop with Bachiarius, a monk accused of Priscillianism who loved to speak of his wanderings, though no proof shows he ever held a see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pergamus:
Pergamus was an ancient city on the Selinus whose fortunes rose with the Attalid kings. First a refuge town, then a prize of Xenophon's raid and Persian revenge, it stayed minor until Lysimachus seized it in 301 BC. His lieutenant Philetaerus enlarged it and made it capital of a new kingdom in 281. Under Eumenes II it reached its height, with a school of sculpture, a great marble altar, and a famous library.

Attalus III left the kingdom to Rome in 133 BC, and after Aristonicus failed to restore the monarchy it became the province of Asia. Parchment took its name from the city, and Galen was born there. The entry also notes its Christian traces: the martyr Antipas of Revelation, and Gaius, addressee of John's third letter, as its bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-person-gobeli:
Gobelinus Person was a Westphalian historian and monastic reformer of the Great Schism era. Born in 1358 near Paderborn, he studied theology and canon law in Italy. He became a clerk of the papal court and an official of the papal treasury under Urban VI, to whom he stayed loyal. When the Schism soured his post, he resigned, was ordained at Ancona in 1386, and went home.

Back in Westphalia he gained the pastorate of St. Pancratius at Paderborn and the ear of Bishop Wilhelm von Berg, who made him court chaplain. From that post he pushed reform of lax cloisters. He turned the near-empty nunnery at Böddeken over to Augustinian men, and tackled the Benedictine abbey of Abdinghof despite fierce resistance. His chronicle work made him a historian as well as a reformer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pessinus:
Pessinus was a Galatian city famed for the cult of Cybele under the name Agdistis. On the Sangarius below Mount Dindymus, it guarded a heaven-fallen stone that stood for the goddess, served by eunuch priests called Galli. The city passed through Assyrian, Lydian, Persian, and Pergamene hands, then became capital of the Tolistobogii, one of the Gallic tribes that founded Galatia around 278 BC.

Rome came early for the sacred stone, carrying it to the Palatine temple of Victory in 204 BC, yet the cult endured, and Julian the Apostate later made pilgrimage there. Under Rome the city faded, though after Constantine it ranked as metropolis of Galatia Secunda. Ten bishops are known, from Demetrius, defender of Chrysostom, to Nicholas at the rupture council of 1054. Its theatre and temple ruins lie at Bala Hissar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-corneli:
Peter Cornelius was a German painter of grand fresco cycles, born at Düsseldorf in 1783. Early imagination and nerve for large undertakings led him to illustrate Goethe's Faust, whose first sheets paid for his journey to Rome in 1811. There he joined the Nazarene painters, German artists seeking a new Christian art, and kept his independence while drawing Faust, Romeo and Juliet, and the Nibelungenlied.

Returning home, he directed the Düsseldorf academy, then Munich's from 1825 under the generous patronage of Louis I of Bavaria. Fifteen years of misunderstandings and rivals' envy drove him to Berlin, where Frederick William IV made him director of its academy until his death in 1867. His frescoes for kings and princes made him the monumental painter of German revival art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-mongus:
Peter Mongus, the Stammerer, was an intruded Monophysite patriarch of Alexandria who died in 490. Deacon to Timothy Ailuros, he shared the persecution of the Melchites after Chalcedon, and on Ailuros's death in 477 his party elected him. Emperor Zeno sentenced him to death, but he fled, and after years of claiming the see he returned when John Talaia quarrelled with Acacius and refused Zeno's Henoticon.

Backed by the emperor from 482, Mongus took the see, signed the Henoticon, and entered Acacius's diptychs, while Pope Felix defended Talaia's rights. He became his party's chief champion, held a synod condemning Chalcedon, and desecrated the tombs of his Melchite rivals. Rome cut him off again and again, and communion with him helped cause the Acacian schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-paludan:
Peter Paludanus was a Dominican theologian and Patriarch of Jerusalem, born in Savoy about 1275. He joined the order at Lyons and took his doctorate at Paris in 1314. He shunned honours to teach and write, save for study posts and two terms as definitor to the general chapter. John XXII sent him as legate to Flanders in 1318 to broker peace with France, a mission that failed and drew charges he easily cleared.

He also sat on the commission judging Peter Olivi's writings and wrote against John of Poilly's condemned errors. In 1329 the pope consecrated him Patriarch of Jerusalem and sent him to Egypt to bargain with the sultan for the Holy Land. The sultan would not move, and his grim report spurred a crusade that princely apathy let die. He returned to his Sentence commentaries and died at Paris in 1342.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-ramus:
Peter Ramus, or Pierre de la Ramée, was a French humanist and logician born at Cuth in Picardy in 1515. Orphaned young and poor, he still graduated Master of Arts at Paris in 1536, defending the thesis that all Aristotle's doctrines are false. That shot at the reigning philosophy set his life's course. His Animadversiones and Dialecticae Institutiones of 1543, in elegant humanist Latin, sharpened the fight.

Paris condemned the books, and a royal committee, after hearing him against Anthony of Govea, judged him rash, arrogant, and impudent, a verdict the king confirmed. Under Henry II and Cardinal Lorraine's protection he became royal lecturer at Navarre in 1547. In 1562 he turned Calvinist. Ten years later, in the St. Bartholomew massacre, his enemies singled him out and killed him with particular cruelty at Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petinessus:
Petinessus was a titular see in Galatia Secunda, a city named by Strabo, Ptolemy, Hierocles, and Stephanus of Byzantium. Strabo sets it in the salt desert west of Lake Tatta, between Lycaonia and Haimama. The episcopal lists count it among the suffragans of Pessinus, created by Theodosius between 386 and 395 and lasting into the thirteenth century.

Only one bishop is on record: Pius, present at Chalcedon in 451. The city's exact name and site shift from document to document and remain unknown. Ramsay places it near Piri Begli or a little east of that site. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry gathers the ancient witnesses and leaves the puzzle open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-alphon:
Petrus Alphonsus was a converted Spanish Jew and controversialist, born at Huesca in 1062 as Moses Sephardi. King Alfonso I of Aragon, whose court physician he became, stood sponsor at his baptism on St. Peter's day in 1106, and the convert took his name from saint and sponsor together. Former co-religionists charged his conversion to ignorance or base motives, and he answered them in print.

His Latin justification runs as twelve dialogues between a Jew and a Christian, first printed at Cologne in 1536 and often reissued. His second work, the Disciplina Clericalis, drew on Arabic sources and travelled widely in translation and manuscript, with a Paris edition in 1824 and a Berlin edition in 1827. Both texts, with biographical notices, stand in Migne's Patrologia, volume 157.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-bernar:
Petrus Bernardinus was a Florentine follower of Savonarola who set himself up as a prophet-pope, born about 1475. Of common folk and no higher schooling, he steeped himself in Savonarola's sermons and writings until he preached in Florence's squares and spread secret, revolutionary doctrines during and after the friar's life. The Church, he taught, must be renewed by the sword, and meanwhile no priest was worthy to hear confession.

About twenty Savonarolans formed a secret society and elected the twenty-five-year-old Peter pope, anointing followers with oil as the Holy Spirit's gift and praying in spirit at meetings without Mass. The archbishop had the council ban their gatherings. In 1502 they fled to Mirandola, where Count Gian Francesco sheltered them until his brothers took the town that August and the sectaries fell into their hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-de-nat:
Petrus de Natalibus was a Venetian bishop and hagiographer who died between 1400 and 1406. Nothing survives of his early life beyond his Venetian birth and his entry into the church as a canon of Equilio, now Jesolo. On 5 July 1370 he rose to the bishopric of that city, and nothing is recorded of his pastoral work. His last mention dates from 1400, and another bishop appears by 1406.

His fame rests on one book: the Legends of the Saints in twelve books, arranged by the church calendar and prized for its wide circulation. First printed at Vicenza in 1493, it ran through many editions, the eighth and last appearing at Venice in 1616. For two centuries it served readers seeking the saints' lives in a single ordered collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-diacon:
Petrus Diaconus was a name shared by four notable churchmen, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry disentangles them. The first was a Scythian monk who brought the Theopaschite question before Pope Hormisdas in 519 and wrote on incarnation and grace against Faustus of Riez.
