The second, a friend of Gregory the Great who died in 605 or 606, prompted the Dialogues by his questions.

The third, a Monte Cassino monk also called subdeacon, died about 960 after continuing Naples's episcopal history and writing saints' lives. The fourth, the twelfth-century Librarian of Monte Cassino, continued Leo of Ostia's chronicle from 1075 to 1138, kept the abbey archives, and wrote on its illustrious men and holy places. He also forged a Passion of St. Placidus under Gordian's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pez-bernhard-:
Bernhard and Hieronymus Pez were Austrian Benedictine writers on history at Melk Abbey, brothers in blood and in work. Bernhard, born at Ybbs in 1683, entered Melk in 1699, studied at Vienna, was ordained in 1708, and became librarian in 1713. Taking French Benedictine scholars as models, he and Hieronymus hunted old books through houses in Austria, Bavaria, and Swabia in 1715 and 1717.

Bernhard's Thesaurus anecdotorum novissimus of 1721 to 1729 gathered sources on Scripture, belief, and history in six folio volumes, and his Bibliotheca ascetica ran to twelve volumes. A planned Benedictine library for the whole order stalled, though he collected 709 titles. Hieronymus, born in 1685, became his brother's helper and then took charge of the library, publishing the three-volume Scriptores rerum Austriacarum, still prized by students of Austria's past. He died at Melk in 1762.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharbaetus:
Pharbaetus was a titular see in Lower Egypt, suffragan to Leontopolis in Augustamnica Secunda. Its name is simply the native Harbait with the Coptic article P prefixed, a form George of Cyprus renders as Karbeuthos. Herodotus, Strabo, and Pliny describe it as capital of its nome, and John of Nikiû tells how its clergy killed the Greek governor Theophilus under Emperor Phocas.

Two bishops are recorded: Arbetion at Nicaea in 325, and a Theodorus of 1086 who may have belonged to a second, western Pharbaetus that was also a Coptic see. Today the town is Horbeit, north of Zagazig in Sharqyeh province, with about 520 inhabitants. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry gathers its ancient notices and its bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharsalus:
Pharsalus was a Thessalian city famed for Caesar's victory over Pompey on 9 August 48 BC. First mentioned after the Persian War, it withstood an Athenian siege in 445 BC. It fell to Larissa's tyrant Midias in 395, bowed to Jason of Pherae, and passed to Antiochus of Syria in 191. Pliny knew it as a free city, and later it served as a Thessalian port, a Macedonian theme town, and an autocephalous archbishopric.

Raised to metropolitan rank by Andronicus II in 1300, it sank again to Larissa's suffragan, joined Phanarion, and was suppressed in 1900 for the sees of Phanarus and Thessaliotides. Turkey ceded it with Thessaly to Greece in 1881, and Greeks were defeated there again in 1897. Its 2,500 inhabitants then included nearly half Turks. Le Quien lists three of its Greek bishops, the first doubtful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philoxenus:
Philoxenus of Mabbogh was a Monophysite bishop and master of Syriac prose, born at Tahal in Persian Beth-Garmai in the fifth century's second quarter. He studied at Edessa under Bishop Ibas, joined the Monophysites, and became their most learned and courageous champion. In 485 Peter the Fuller made him Bishop of Hierapolis, or Mabbogh, and he attacked Chalcedon's decrees while defending Zeno's Henoticon.

Twice he visited Constantinople for his party, and in 512 he persuaded Emperor Anastasius to depose Flavian of Antioch for Severus. Anastasius's death in 518 reversed his triumph: the orthodox Justin I restored deposed bishops and banished Philoxenus with fifty-three fellow Monophysites. He went to Philippopolis in Thrace, then to Gangra, where he was murdered in 523. His Syriac version of Scripture, made by Polycarp under his direction, survives in fragments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-photinus:
Photinus was a fourth-century heretic and Bishop of Sirmium who died in 376. A Galatian and deacon to Marcellus of Ancyra, he took the important Pannonian see where Emperor Constantius often resided. Sirmium was more Latin than Greek, and Photinus knew both tongues. When the Eusebian court party condemned Marcellus at Antioch in 344 with its long macrostich creed, Photinus stood condemned beside him.

Milan's synod of 345 condemned Photinus but not Marcellus, and a later synod failed to depose him when the populace rose in his favour. He appealed to the emperor, who set judges before a great Sirmium synod in 351, where Basil of Ancyra disputed with him. Deposed there under twenty-seven anathemas, he likely regained his see under Julian, only for Valentinian to banish him. His teaching denied the Son's full divinity, reducing Christ to an inspired man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physiologus:
The Physiologus was an early Christian book of animal lore with allegorical readings, written in Greek at Alexandria, probably in the second century. Lion cubs born dead revive when the old lion breathes on them. The phoenix burns and rises on the third day, the unicorn is caught only in a virgin's lap, and the pelican revives its dead young with its own blood. Each beast becomes a type: lion and phoenix of Christ risen, unicorn of the Incarnation, pelican of salvation by the Cross.

Other allegories warn against the Devil's lures or commend virtues to imitate and vices to shun. Later ages ascribed the book to Epiphanius, Basil, or Peter of Alexandria, but Origen already cites it by title, and Clement and perhaps Justin knew it. Its allegorical method owes less to Origen than to the earlier Letter of Barnabas. The entry traces a book that shaped medieval bestiaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierius:
Pierius was an Alexandrian priest and teacher called Origen the Younger, who died at Rome after 309. Probably head of Alexandria's catechetical school with Achillas under Bishop Theonas, he won fame as an exegetical writer and preacher. Philip of Side, Photius, and others call him a martyr. Jerome insists he survived the Diocletian persecution and spent his remaining years at Rome, so martyr here means sufferer, not one put to death.

The Roman Martyrology keeps him on 4 November. His book held twelve treatises or sermons, some repeating errors ascribed to Origen, such as the Spirit's subordination to Father and Son and the soul's pre-existence. Known sermons treat Luke's Gospel, Easter and Hosea, the Mother of God, and a eulogy of his disciple Pamphilus. Only fragments survive, edited by Routh and Boor and translated by Salmond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pious-workers:
The Pious Workers of Saint Joseph Calasanctius are a congregation founded at Vienna in 1889 by Father Anton Maria Schwartz for charitable work, above all among working men. Priests and lay brothers together follow the rule of the Piarists with some changes. Their mother-house is the College of Mary Help of Christians at Vienna.

They teach Christian doctrine, run elementary and trade schools, and build homes for apprentices and workmen. They open oratories for prayer, form working-men's associations, and spread good literature. At Vienna they also took charge of a reformatory in 1904 and opened a public library. Their prayer book for working men had already reached five editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pityus:
Pityus was a large and wealthy Greek city on the northeastern shore of the Black Sea, later kept as a titular see, a bishopric in name only. It was destroyed before Pliny's time, then rebuilt and fortified by the Romans. It was seized by Scythians under Gallienus and demolished by the Byzantines to keep the Persian king Chosroes out.

By 535 it was more fortress than city, and its bishop Stratophilus had attended the Council of Nicaea in 325. After that the see vanishes from the lists. The entry also notes that Saint John Chrysostom died on the road toward Pityus while being led into exile, and places the site near Cape Pitsunda on the Gulf's eastern end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polybotus:
Polybotus is a titular see in Phrygia Salutaris, suffragan to Synnada, mentioned only in the sixth century by Hierocles. It is now Boulvadin, chief town of its district in the Brousse region, with 8,000 people, all Muslims, and ruins of no interest. Two bishops are recorded by Le Quien.

Strategius attended the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and Saint John, whose feast falls on 5 December, lived under Leo the Isaurian. At Nicaea in 787 the see was represented by the priest Gregory. The earliest Greek lists place it under Synnada, and it stayed attached to that metropolis as a titular see. From the ninth century until it ceased as a residential see, it belonged to Amorium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polycarpus: Polycarpus names an eight-book canon-law collection put together in Italy by Cardinal Gregorius. Its chief sources are Anselm's collections and the Anselmo Dedicata. Most writers set it near 1124, since it carries a decretal of Callistus II, who died in that year. Others argue for before 1120 or 1118, when Bishop Didacus, its dedicatee, died, and read the Callistus decretal as added later. The Ballerini printed its dedication letter and titles, Theiner its rubrics, and Mai passages from Book IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pomponius-lae:
Pomponius Laetus, humanist, was born in Calabria in 1425 and died at Rome in 1497. A bastard of the Sanseverino house of Naples, Princes of Salerno, he would not recognise them as connections, out of admiration for antiquity and the Roman Republic. Still a boy, he reached Rome and studied under Valla. His vineyard on the Quirinal was cultivated by the precepts of Varro and Columella, and he was regarded as a second Cato.

With Platina and Sabellicus he founded a semi-pagan academy whose members took Latin names and yearly celebrated the Palilia, Rome's foundation festival. Paul II, no friend to humanists, had Laetus seized and confined in Castel Sant'Angelo in 1468, where he was tortured with Platina and others. He defended himself, noting he had maintained the soul's immortality. On Sixtus IV's accession in 1471 he was released, and the academy continued.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontus:
Pontus was the ancient province on the northeastern coast of Asia Minor, a long narrow strip along the Black Sea's southern shore. Shut in by high wild mountains, it was fertile on the coast, inland, and on the plateaux. It yielded fruit, above all cherries, which Lucullus is said to have brought to Europe from Pontus in 72 B.C. It also yielded wine, grain, timber, honey, iron, and salt.

Greeks settled early on the coast and founded Trapezus, Cerasus, Side, Cotyora, and Amisus. Mithradates I took the royal title in 296 B.C., and his line, Persian by descent, embraced Greek culture until Mithradates VI the Great lost three wars against Rome. His kingdom fell in 63 B.C., and its western lands joined Bithynia in the double province of Bithynia and Pontus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-brothers:
The Poor Brothers of Saint Francis Seraphicus are a congregation of lay brothers of the Third Order of Saint Francis, founded for charitable work among orphan boys and poor youth. Their founder was Philip Hoever, born near Cologne in 1816 and a schoolmaster at Breidt and Aachen. At Christmas 1857, moved by Mother Frances Schervier, he dedicated himself with four others to abandoned men.

The brothers gained a home at Aachen in 1860 and Cardinal Geissel approved the congregation in January 1861. At Hoever's death in 1864 it counted twenty-six members. It spread to Berlin, to the United States from 1866, and, after the Kulturkampf drove it from Prussia in 1876, to Blyerheide in Holland. By 1907 it numbered 230 members, fifty in the United States, and Pius X approved its constitutions in 1910.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-corneliu:
Pope Saint Cornelius, martyr, reigned from 251 to 253, two years, three months, and ten days by the Liberian catalogue, a first-rate authority for the date. His predecessor Fabian had been killed by Decius on 20 January 250. When persecution slackened in March 251, sixteen bishops assembled at Rome and elected Cornelius, though against his will. His election came by God's judgment, the clergy's testimony, the people's vote, and the consent of aged priests.

Cyprian marvels at his fortitude in taking the chair while the tyrant threatened bishops with sword, cross, and stake. Weeks later the priest Novatian made himself antipope, convulsing the Christian world. Cyprian's adhesion won Cornelius Africa's hundred bishops. Dionysius of Alexandria won the East, and a Roman synod of sixty bishops backed him. Eusebius preserves his letters to Fabius of Antioch detailing Novatian's faults and listing Rome's clergy and fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-donus:
Pope Donus, or Domnus, son of a Roman called Mauricius, was consecrated Bishop of Rome on 2 November 676 and died on 11 April 678. Little is known of his life and acts. The Liber Pontificalis says he paved the atrium before Saint Peter's with great blocks of white marble. He restored Saint Euphemia's church on the Appian Way and repaired the basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

During his reign Reparatus, Archbishop of Ravenna, returned to Rome's obedience, ending the schism of Archbishop Maurus, who had aimed to make Ravenna autocephalous, self-governing. A colony of Nestorian monks was also found in a Syrian monastery at Rome, the Monasterium Boetianum. Donus dispersed them through the city's religious houses, giving their monastery to Roman monks. After a reign of one year, five months, and ten days he was buried in Saint Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-formosus:
Pope Formosus reigned from 891 to 896 in the era of strife for Italy after the Carolingian empire's break-up. Probably a native of Rome, he was born about 816; Vulgarius calls him an old man of eighty at death. Nicholas I named him Cardinal-Bishop of Porto in 864 and trusted his zeal and ability. Nicholas sent him with Bishop Paulus to Bulgaria in 866 to answer Prince Bogoris's questions.

Bogoris favoured Formosus so much that he begged Nicholas to make him Archbishop of Bulgaria. The canons forbade a bishop to leave his own see, and Formosus returned to Rome. Hadrian II refused a renewed petition, then sent him to France in 869 over Lothair and Theutberga, and to Trent in 872 over the succession. John VIII first trusted him, then, after Charles the Bald's coronation in 875, Formosus fell among the pope's political opponents and fled Rome in fear of punishment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-liberius:
Liberius was a Roman deacon. He was consecrated pope in May 352. Emperor Constantius then pressed bishops toward a watered-down Arianism. That teaching denied Christ's full divinity. Like his predecessor Julius, Liberius defended Athanasius. He made the decisions of Nicaea the test of sound belief. He sent legates to plead for a council.

His legates caved under pressure at Arles. The entry then follows his exile. It covers his later years. It examines a set of letters later judged forged. It closes by weighing modern verdicts on his pontificate. That reign was torn between imperial power and loyalty to Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-romanus:
Of Romanus very little is known with certainty. Even the dates of his birth, consecration, and death are unsure. Gallese near Civita Castellana was his birthplace, and Constantine his father. He rose to cardinal of St Peter ad Vincula, then to pope about August 897, and died four months later.

Vitalis, Patriarch of Grado, got the pallium from him, with a privilege for his church. He confirmed the Spanish bishops of Elna and Gerona in their sees' possessions. His coins bear Emperor Lambert's name with his own monogram and St Peter. The historian Frodoard praised his virtue in three verses. He may have been deposed by a Roman faction, since records say he was made a monk, a phrase that often meant deposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sabinian:
Sabinianus was born at Blera near Viterbo, son of Bonus. His birth date is unknown. Gregory I sent him as nuncio to Constantinople in 593. He proved not astute enough for Byzantium's rulers, and Gregory was disappointed. He returned to Rome in 597. Chosen to succeed Gregory, he waited months for imperial confirmation and was consecrated probably on 13 September 604.

Fear of the Lombards and famine shaped his pontificate. Once the Lombard danger passed, he opened the church granaries. He sold corn at one solidus for thirty pecks. Because he would not give it away free, later legends painted him as avaricious and had Gregory punish him. He is said to have restored secular clergy to posts Gregory had given monks. He died on 22 February 606 and was buried in St Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-eu:
Eutychianus succeeded Felix I and governed the church from January 275 to 7 December 283. No details of his pontificate are known. A rite for blessing field produce, ascribed to him by the Liber Pontificalis, surely belongs to a later age. The claim that he set rules for burying martyrs and buried many himself has slight support. After Aurelian's death the church knew a long break from persecution.

Eutychianus very likely died no martyr's death. Rome's fourth-century calendar counts him among bishops, not martyrs. His remains lay in the Callistus catacomb's papal chapel. When that crypt was found, fragments of his epitaph turned up, giving his name in Greek letters. His feast is kept on 8 December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-hi:
Hilarus, a Sardinian archdeacon, was chosen to succeed Leo I and probably consecrated on 19 November 461. Leo had sent him as legate to Ephesus's Robber Synod in 449. There he defended Roman rights and fought Flavian of Constantinople's condemnation. Dioscurus of Alexandria exposed him to violence, and he escaped only by flight. He later apologized to Empress Pulcheria for failing to deliver Leo's letter after the synod.

His pontificate matched his predecessor's vigour. Gaul's and Spain's church affairs claimed his care. Hermes had illegally seized the bishopric of Narbonne, and two Gallican prelates brought the case to Rome. A Roman synod on 19 November 462 judged it, and Hilarus upheld the primatial rights of Arles as Leo had defined them. He warned bishops to keep within their bounds and meet yearly under Arles. He died on 28 February 468.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-sy:
Symmachus was a Sardinian, son of Fortunatus, baptized at Rome and ordained deacon. After Anastasius II died, a majority of Roman clergy elected him at the Lateran on 22 November 498, and he was consecrated at once. The same day a minority friendly to Byzantium elected the archpriest Laurentius at Santa Maria Maggiore. Both sides agreed to accept the Gothic king Theodoric's ruling at Ravenna. Theodoric chose Symmachus, elected first and by the majority, and Laurentius submitted.

At a synod on 1 March 499 Symmachus gave Laurentius the diocese of Nocera. Later synods under him voided the prefect Basilius's 483 edict on church property and set new rules for its care and sale. Theodoric would not enforce them, and the opposition recalled Laurentius to Rome. For four years the rivals divided the city, Laurentius in the Lateran palace and Symmachus by St Peter's, quarrelling furiously. Symmachus died on 19 July 514.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-severinu:
Severinus was a Roman, son of Abienus. He was elected three days after his predecessor's death, and envoys went to Constantinople in October 638 for imperial confirmation. The emperor instead ordered him to sign the Ecthesis, a Monothelite profession of faith. Severinus refused. The exarch Isaac plundered the Lateran to force him, but in vain.

His envoys refused to sign heretical documents, behaved with tact, and finally won confirmation. After a vacancy past a year and seven months, Severinus won consecration seemingly on 28 May 640. At once he declared that Christ had two natures and therefore two wills and two natural operations. In his brief reign he raised old St Peter's apse. He died on 2 August 640 and was buried there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sisinniu:
Sisinnius was a Syrian, son of one John. He succeeded John VII and was probably consecrated on 15 January 708. His pontificate lasted about three weeks, ending with his death on 4 February 708. He was buried in St Peter's.

Gout crippled him so badly that he could not feed himself. Yet report calls him a man of strong character who thought for Rome's good. He ordered lime prepared to repair the city's walls. Even in three weeks he acted for the city's defence and for Corsica's church. Before he died he consecrated a bishop for Corsica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-adeod: Adeodatus reigned from 672 to 676, a monk of the Coelian Hill's St Erasmus. He worked to perfect monastic discipline and to repress the Monothelite heresy. Little else is known. Only letters to Canterbury's St Peter abbey and Tours' St Martin abbey survive. He is sometimes called Adeodatus II, since his predecessor Deusdedit is occasionally known as Adeodatus I.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anacl:
Anacletus followed St Peter as second successor. Whether he matches Cletus, also called Anencletus, has been endlessly debated. Irenaeus, Eusebius, Augustine, and Optatus use both names for one person. Tertullian omits him entirely. The order also differs: Irenaeus lists Linus, Anacletus, Clement, while Augustine and Optatus put Clement before Anacletus.

The Liberian list, the Carmen against Marcion, and the Liber Pontificalis treat Cletus and Anacletus as distinct. The Felician list even calls one Greek and the other Roman. Modern scholars split: Hergenröther, De Smedt, Döllinger, and Duchesne hold them identical, while Jungmann leaves the question open. Dates stay uncertain, though Anicetus reigned in 154, which fixes the early list's end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anice:
Anicetus succeeded Pius around 157 and reigned until about 168. Exact dates for this period cannot be verified. While he was pope, the aged Polycarp came to confer about the Paschal controversy. Easterners kept the feast on 14 Nisan whatever the weekday, while Rome always kept it on Sunday, with the Lord's death on Friday.

Neither persuaded the other, and the question stayed open, but charity did not break. Anicetus let Polycarp celebrate as Smyrna always had. Hegesippus, the first Christian historian, also visited Rome then, as did Marcion, Valentine, and others who troubled the church with strange teaching. Anicetus is said to have suffered martyrdom in 161, though the day varies between 16, 17, and 20 April.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anter:
Anterus reigned from 21 November 235 to 3 January 236, some forty days. Certainty ends there. He was buried in the papal crypt of St Calixtus's cemetery at Rome. The Liber Pontificalis says he was martyred for having notaries collect martyrs' Acts for the church archives. That tradition is old and respectable, yet scholars judge it insufficiently guaranteed by its sole voucher, compiled late.

De Rossi found his tomb site in 1854. Broken remnants of a Greek epitaph on the slab point to his origin and to Greek's prevalence in Rome's church then. A letter attributed to him by Pseudo-Isidore is treated separately in the scholarship. The entry weighs a short reign known almost entirely through one late source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-cletu:
Cletus is only another form of Anacletus, the second successor of St Peter. The Liberian Catalogue, a fourth-century list ending with Liberius, gives both names as if they were different people. That is an error from two forms of one name, one an abbreviation of the other. The catalogue's order runs Peter, Linus, Clement, Cletus, Anacletus. It is the only pre-sixth-century authority for splitting them.

The Carmen against Marcion depends on the Liberian list. The Hieronymian Martyrology mentions both names on different December days, but only inside pope lists, so neither day marks the man. Every other ancient list from the second to the fourth century gives Linus, Anencletus, Clement. Africa and the East held to that order, as does the Roman Canon, where Cletus is the form used. The entry concludes that the single-person succession is certainly right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-diony:
Dionysius was a presbyter of the Roman church under Stephen, and took part in the dispute over heretical baptism. Dionysius of Alexandria wrote him a letter calling him excellent and learned. After Sixtus II was martyred in August 258, persecution left the Roman see vacant for nearly a year. Dionysius was raised to the bishopric of Rome on 22 July 259.

Months later Gallienus issued an edict of toleration, ending persecution and giving the church legal standing. Rome regained its buildings, cemeteries, and properties, and Dionysius restored administration. Around 260, Alexandria's Dionysius wrote inexactly about the Logos against Sabellianism. Accused before Rome, the matter went to a synod Dionysius called around 260. He died on 26 or 27 December 268.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-eleut:
Eleutherius was pope from about 174 to 189. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a native of Nicopolis in Greece. Hegesippus records him as a deacon under Anicetus, and he evidently stayed deacon under Soter, whom he succeeded around 174. Under Marcus Aurelius, Christians suffered in parts of the empire, though persecution at Rome itself seems not to have been violent.

Under Commodus, Christians enjoyed practically unbroken peace, apart from Apollonius's martyrdom at Rome. The Montanist movement reached Rome and Gaul in the later second century, and its odd nature made a firm stand hard at first. During the Lyons persecution of 177, imprisoned confessors wrote to Eleutherius through Irenaeus, opposing Montanism yet pleading forbearance and unity. When Rome finally took its stand is not certainly known. A tale of a British king seeking instruction from Eleutherius is rejected by recent critics as improbable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-euseb:
Eusebius followed Marcellus in 309 or 310 for a short reign. The Liberian Catalogue allows only four months, from 18 April to 17 August. Details come from an epitaph Damasus ordered for his tomb, preserved in ancient transcripts. Fragments of the original and a sixth-century marble copy turned up through De Rossi in the Callistus catacombs' papal chapel.

The bitter quarrel over readmitting the lapsi, those who had lapsed under Diocletian, continued under Eusebius. Rome's settled line, from the Decian persecution, was that apostates should return only after proper penance, not be barred forever. A Roman faction under Heraclius opposed him, likely demanding immediate restoration. Damasus describes the clash in fierce terms: sedition, slaughter, war, discord, lawsuits. The entry follows the strife that marked his brief reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-evari:
Evaristus died about 107. The Liberian list calls him Aristus. Second-century lists used by Irenaeus and Hippolytus place him fourth after St Peter, right after Clement. Those lists give him eight years, about 98 or 99 to about 106 or 107. The earliest sources offer no authentic facts about him. Eusebius merely says he succeeded Clement in Rome's bishopric, an order already known from Irenaeus.

The Liber Pontificalis says he came from a Hellenic family and was son of a Bethlehem Jew. It credits him with assigning fixed churches, or tituli, to Roman priests and dividing the city into seven deaconries. That claim wrongly backdates a later Roman institution to his time. More trustworthy is its word that he was buried in the Vatican near Peter's tomb. His martyrdom is traditional, not proven. His feast falls on 26 October. Two decretals ascribed to him are forged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-hygin:
Hyginus reigned about 138 to 142, succeeding Telesphorus, who died in 138 or 139 by Eusebius's account. The chronology of these Roman bishops cannot be fixed exactly. The Liber Pontificalis calls Hyginus Greek by birth. Its claim that he had been a philosopher likely rests on his name's likeness to two Latin authors.

Irenaeus says the Gnostic Valentine reached Rome in Hyginus's time and stayed until Anicetus. Cerdo, another Gnostic and Marcion's predecessor, also lived at Rome then. He recanted and regained readmission, then fell back into heresy and was expelled. How many of these events belong to Hyginus's reign is unknown. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with organizing the hierarchy and clerical ranks, a claim with no historical value. Eusebius gives his reign four years. No ancient authority calls him a martyr. Peter's tomb neighbours his grave on the Vatican Hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-linus:
Linus reigned about 64 or 67 to 76 or 79. Every ancient Roman bishop list handed down by Irenaeus, Africanus, Hippolytus, and Eusebius, plus the Liberian list of 354, puts Linus directly after Peter. Those lists trace to a roll existing under Eleutherius, when Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies. Tertullian instead places Clement right after Peter, as Jerome later did, but Irenaeus's Roman list carries greater authority.

Irenaeus claims Linus is the man Paul mentions in 2 Timothy 4:21. His passage says Peter and Paul founded Rome's church and handed the bishop's office to Linus, whose successor was Anacletus. Whether that identification rests on an ancient source or on mere name likeness cannot be settled. The lists give Linus twelve years, or twelve years, four months, and twelve days by the Liberian list. Its dates, 56 to 67, are incorrect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-marce:
Marcellinus was elected on 30 June 296 and died in 304. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Projectus. The Liberian list confirms his dates, and the Liber Pontificalis accepts them. Nothing has come down about his acts in eight years. A deacon's epitaph in the Callistus Catacomb records new burial chambers built at his order before the Diocletian persecution.

After 303 the persecution threw Rome's church into confusion, and the Callistus Catacomb was confiscated with other meeting places. Christians blocked its galleries to shield martyrs' tombs. Marcellinus died in the persecution's second year, probably naturally. No trustworthy fourth- or fifth-century source calls him a martyr, and his name appears in neither martyrs' nor bishops' lists in the 354 Chronograph. Later tales of his lapse rest on forged acts and Donatist rumour. It is accepted that he never surrendered scriptures or offered incense to a god.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-silve:
Silverius reigned from 536 to 537. He was the son of Hormisdas, who had married before taking higher orders. He was a subdeacon at Rome when Agapetus died in the East on 22 April 536. Theodora, favouring the Monophysites, wanted the deacon Vigilius, then in the East, as pope. Theodatus, the Ostrogoth king, forestalled her, backing Silverius to block a Constantinople-linked pope.

Choosing a subdeacon as Rome's bishop was unusual, and clergy opposition flared until Theodatus suppressed it. After Silverius took office, probably on 8 June 536, all Roman priests signed consent to his elevation. Claims that he bought Theodatus's backing are baseless, born of the biographer's hostility to pope and Goths. His reign fell in a disordered age, and he became a victim of eastern court intrigue. The entry follows his fall from that intrigue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-simpl:
Simplicius reigned from 468 to 483 and died on 10 March 483. The Liber Pontificalis calls him son of Castinus, a citizen of Tivoli. He was elected after Hilarius died in 468, without difficulty. During his reign the Western Empire ended: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and took the title King of Italy. Though Arian, Odoacer treated the Catholic Church with respect and kept much of the old administration, so Rome felt little change.

Simplicius defended the church's independence against Byzantine Caesaropapism and Rome's authority in faith. Chalcedon's twenty-eighth canon gave Constantinople honours equal to Old Rome's, though primacy stayed with Rome, and Leo confirmed only the council's dogmatic decrees. Constantinople's patriarch still pushed upward, and Simplicius held Rome's line through the Monophysite controversy until his death in 483.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-siric:
Siricius was born about 334 and died on 26 November 399. A Roman, son of Tiburtius, he served as lector and then deacon under Liberius. After Damasus died he was unanimously elected in December 384 and probably consecrated on 17 December. Ursinus, Damasus's old rival, still pressed his claims, but Valentinian's letter of February 385 backed the election and praised the new bishop's piety.

At once Siricius asserted primacy over the universal church. Bishop Himerius of Tarragona had written Damasus with fifteen questions on baptism, penance, discipline, and clerical celibacy. Siricius answered on 10 February 385 with full consciousness of supreme authority. His letter is the oldest fully preserved papal decretal, though earlier popes had issued such edicts too. Like Damasus, he joined the Priscillian controversy, sharply condemning the bishops who dragged Priscillian before a secular court and got Maximus to execute him. He excommunicated Felix of Trier, who backed the accuser Ithacius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-teles:
Telesphorus was the seventh Roman bishop after the apostles and lived about 125 to 136. Irenaeus testifies that he suffered a glorious martyrdom. Eusebius puts his pontificate's start in Hadrian's twelfth year, 128 or 129, and his death in Antoninus Pius's first year, 138 or 139. Those statements need comparison with Lightfoot and Harnack on early Roman successions.

In Irenaeus's fragment to Victor on Easter, Telesphorus appears among Roman bishops who always kept Easter on Sunday. He did not break fellowship with communities that kept it differently. None of the later Liber Pontificalis and other authorities' claims about his liturgical decisions are genuine. Rome's martyrology keeps his feast on 5 January, while the Greek church keeps it on 22 February.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zephy:
Zephyrinus reigned from 198 to 217 and died on 20 December 217. After Victor died in 198, Zephyrinus was elected and consecrated. Hippolytus calls him a simple man without higher studies, given to practical church work rather than theology.

At once he called the confessor Callistus from Antium, where Victor had pensioned him, and set him over the cemetery on the Via Appia that Rome's community had newly acquired. That burial ground took Callistus's name, and Callistus became the pope's close adviser and a deacon. Under Septimius Severus, Christian fortunes worsened, and a 202 or 203 edict banned conversion on severe penalties. Nothing is known of its execution at Rome. Inside the church, disputes over the Trinity sharpened as Theodotus the Tanner's followers, already excommunicated, pressed their teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zosim:
Zosimus reigned from 417 to 418 and died on 27 December 418. After Innocent I died on 12 March 417, Zosimus succeeded him. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek, son of Abram, though its family details for this period are not always exact. Nothing is known of his life before elevation. He was consecrated on 18 March 417.

Patroclus of Arles attended his consecration and at once won his trust. Within days Zosimus gave Patroclus metropolitan rights over Viennensis and Narbonensis, plus a kind of vicariate over Gaul: no Gallic cleric might travel to Rome without Patroclus's certificate. Arles had replaced Trier as the prefect's seat in 400, and Patroclus used Constantine's backing to win supremacy. Zosimus also handled the Pelagian affair: he first thought Africa too hasty against Coelestius and defended Pelagius's artful confession at a Roman synod, reproving accusers including Hero and Lazarus. Aurelius of Carthage swiftly called a synod in reply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-vigilius:
Vigilius reigned from 537 to 555 and died at Syracuse on 7 June 555. He came from a distinguished Roman family: his father held the consul's title, and his brother was a senator. A deacon by 531, he was Boniface II's chosen successor, presented at St Peter's, but opposition made Boniface withdraw the designation and burn the decree the next year.

Agapetus made Vigilius his representative at Constantinople. Theodora tried to win him as an ally, promising the papacy and seven hundred pounds of gold, to avenge Anthimus's deposition and aid the Monophysites. After Agapetus died in April 536, Vigilius returned to Rome with imperial letters and money, but Silverius already held the see through the Gothic king. Belisarius then garrisoned Rome. Later he took a firm stand for Ephesus and Chalcedon in letters to Justinian and Patriarch Menas, approving Leo I and Anthimus's deposition. He wrote on discipline, including a decretal to Braga in June 538.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-praelatus-nul:
A prelate nullius wields near bishop's rule in a land that lies in no diocese. Such prelates spring from papal privilege alone, for only one above bishops can free a land from a bishop's rule. Their rights are near a bishop's, and they are taken to hold each power a bishop holds, unless canon law plainly bars it.

With no bishop's consecration, they may not ordain to sacred orders. They judge marriage cases as a bishop does, lift the call of banns, grant leave to hear confessions and preach, and hold back some cases for themselves. They publish indulgences and jubilees, rule the enclosure of nuns, and ask any bishop to confirm in their near diocese. With no special leave from the Holy See they may not call a synod, set synod examiners, give parish benefices, or absolve reserved cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-primicerius:
Primicerius, from primus in cera, first on the wax tablet, denotes the head of a class of officials' list. In later Roman times it was the term for the head of any administration: primicerius notariorum, primicerius protectorum, and the like. In church use it marked the Notarii and Defensores colleges' heads, which weighed heavily in the Roman Church's rule in later antiquity and the early Middle Ages.

When young clerics gathered in schools for training in church service across the West's districts, from the fifth or sixth century, their directors also commonly bore this title. Thus a Lyons inscription of 551 names a Stephanus primicerius scolae lectorum serving in the Lyons church. St Isidore of Seville treats the primicerius of the lower clerics' duties in his Epistola ad Ludefredum. From this post the primicerius also drew some powers over liturgical functions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priscianus:
Priscianus, Latin writer, was born at Caesarea and taught in the East under Anastasius I, from 491 to 518. About 512 he gave a praise poem of the emperor, which survives in 312 verses. He also rendered Dionysius's work of the same name in 1,087 verses, written under Hadrian.

Three works for a Symmachus, perhaps the consul of 485, treat numbers, coins, the metre of Latin comedies, and rhetoric. He also wrote a work on the Aeneid's verse, a treatise on accents, and a short work on declensions. But his fame rests on his eighteen-book grammar, antiquity's chief surviving grammar. The first sixteen, Maior, treat forms; the last two, Minor, treat syntax. They are dedicated to Julianus, consul and patrician, and in the preface Priscian owns his debt to Apollonius and Herodian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proconnesus:
Proconnesus is a titular see in Hellespont. The name marked an island in the Propontis' east part, between Priapus, now Kara Bogha, and Cyzicus. It also marked the island's capital, settled by Milesians or Samians. In 493 BC a Phoenician fleet in Darius' service burned it. In 410 Athenian ships under Alcibiades brought it, like Cyzicus, under Athens' rule. Later Cyzicus conquered it.

Proconnesus was famed for its white marble quarry, used to build nearby towns, above all Cyzicus, and the Mausoleus tomb at Halicarnassus. The quarry still works and gave the island its modern name Marmora. The old capital seems to be today's Palatia village. The island, a nahié of the Brousse vilayet, holds about seventy-seven square miles and 9,000 folk, nearly all Greek. In Byzantine times exiles were oft sent there, among them Stephen the Young and Patriarch Nicephorus. In 1399 Turks and Venetians fought there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prudentius:
Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes, began life in Spain under the name Galindo. He died at Troyes on 6 April 861. This encyclopedia entry follows a young Spaniard who fled Saracen persecution for the Frankish Empire. He changed his name to Prudentius, studied at the palace school, and rose to the see of Troyes shortly before 847. His fame rests on a fierce theological quarrel, the ninth-century debate over predestination.

Against Hincmar of Reims, Prudentius defended a double predestination in a letter of about 849. God destines some to reward and others to punishment, though not to sin itself. He also held Christ's death to be only for those actually saved. He pressed that view again in his work against John Scotus. The entry closes with the older lives and studies of this combative bishop, whose Spanish birth and Frankish career bridge two Christian worlds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publius-lentu:
Publius Lentulus is a fictitious person, and this encyclopedia entry unmasks him. He is said to have governed Judea before Pontius Pilate and to have written the Roman Senate a letter about Jesus. The letter calls Jesus a man of great power, whom the people name a prophet of truth and his disciples the Son of God. It credits him with raising the dead and healing the sick.

That portrait gives him a medium stature and a venerable aspect, so that beholders both fear and love him. His hair, the colour of a ripe hazel-nut, falls straight to his ears, then waves and curls over his shoulders, parted on top in the Nazarene manner. His brow is smooth, the letter adds, before breaking off in the surviving text. Von Dobschütz, Kraus and Harnack supply the scholarship that exposes the letter as a pious forgery, not a Roman document.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quadratus:
Quadratus stands first among the Christian apologists. This encyclopedia entry reports, on Eusebius's word, that he had heard the Apostles themselves. During Hadrian's visit to Athens in 124 or 125, Quadratus addressed the emperor with a discourse defending the Christian religion. All of it has vanished except one short passage quoted by Eusebius in his Church History.

Eusebius also claims, wrongly the entry says, that the appeal moved Hadrian to issue a favourable edict. Some scholars, noting the shared name, have identified the apologist with Quadratus the prophet, mentioned elsewhere by Eusebius. Bardenhewer's Patrology makes that guess, but the evidence is too slight to convince. Later mentions in Jerome and others, the entry warns, add nothing firm or merely enlarge Eusebius at will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphael-badiu:
Raphael Badius, a Florentine Dominican of the seventeenth century, was deeply versed in Tuscan and Florentine antiquities. This short encyclopedia entry notes that his researches made him expert in quaint and curious matters of history and saints' lives. He gave valuable help to the Jesuit Fathers Henschen and Papebroch in their labours on the Acta Sanctorum, the great collection of saints' lives. They acknowledge the debt themselves.

As chronicler of the Convent of Santa Maria Novella at Florence, Badius was also known to the historian and bibliographer Cinellus. Cinellus mentions his helpful knowledge of Florentine literature and writers with frequent gratitude. In 1681 he became Dean of the University of Florence. Quétif and Echard's history of Dominican writers supplies the entry's source on a scholar whose learning served greater projects than his own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratramnus:
Ratramnus, also spelled Rathramnus, was a Benedictine monk at Corbie, in the Department of the Somme. He ranks among the church authors of the ninth century. This encyclopedia entry dates his death only as after 868, since little is known of his life. His work is a treatise on the Holy Eucharist, De corpore et sanguine Domini. It was written at the Emperor Charles the Bald's request against a work of that title by Paschasius Radbertus.

Ratramnus set out to answer two questions. Do we see the Body of Christ in the Eucharist directly with our bodily eyes, or is it hidden from our senses? Is the Eucharistic Christ the same as the historic Christ? On the first question he distinguishes the invisible substance, truly the body and blood of Christ, from what the senses meet. Mabillon and Ernst's study of Paschasius supply the entry's sources on this Carolingian debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rector-potens:
Rector Potens, Verax Deus is the hymn for Sext in the Roman Breviary. This encyclopedia entry takes its theme from the noonday sun's great heat and light, at the day's sixth hour. Its prayer asks the Almighty Ruler to take the heat of passion from the heart. Baudot thinks the hymn probably by Saint Ambrose, noting that the hymns for Vespers, Terce and None, and probably Sext too, are his.

Bäumer's history of the Breviary complicates the claim. None of the three hymns appears in the oldest Benedictine cycle, while all three appear in the later Celtic cycle, so whatever probability supports Terce and None supports Sext equally. The entry notes that the second stanza rhymes throughout. For the authorship debate it refers readers to the companion hymn Rerum Deus Tenax Vigor, and for text, music and translation to Hymns Ancient and Modern, number 10.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-com:
Religious communities of the Name of Jesus covers three distinct groups sharing one dedication. The Knights of the Name of Jesus, also called Seraphim, were founded in 1334 by the Queens of Norway and Sweden to defend their lands against heathen invaders. They did not outlive the Reformation. The Sisters of the Name of Jesus form six congregations founded in nineteenth-century France, in dioceses including Besançon, Valence, Rodez, Toulouse, and Marseilles. They chiefly teach and nurse the sick.

The third group is the Confraternity of the Name of Jesus. It joined two older bodies: its Spanish counterpart and the Portuguese Confraternity of the Most Holy Name of Jesus. Andreas Díaz founded the Portuguese body in 1432. The merged confraternity dates from the sixteenth century. Popes Paul the Fifth in 1606 and Innocent the Eleventh in 1678 approved it, granted it indulgences, and set it under the Dominican general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhizus:
Rhizus was a titular see of Pontus Polemoniacus, suffragan of Neocaesarea, and a port on the Black Sea named by Ptolemy. Its history is unknown, but Procopius calls it a town of some importance, fortified by Justinian, and names it Rhizaion, as do the Notitiae Episcopatuum. From a suffragan of Neocaesarea it rose to an autocephalous archdiocese and finally a metropolitan see, on dates now uncertain.

As the Christian element shrank, the see sank to a simple exarchate. Today Rizeh, as the Turks call it, holds no more than four hundred Greeks among two thousand inhabitants. It exports oranges and lemons, and serves as capital of the Sanjak of Lazistan in the vilayet of Trebizond. Le Quien names three bishops: Nectarius at Nicaea in 787, John at Constantinople in 879, and the metropolitan Joachim in 1565.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhosus:
Rhosus was a titular see in Cilicia Secunda, suffragan of Anazarba, and a seaport on the Gulf of Issus, now Alexandretta, south-west of Iskenderoun. Strabo, Ptolemy, and Pliny place it in Syria, while Hierocles and George of Cyprus put it in Cilicia Secunda. Towards 200 Serapion of Antioch wrote a treatise on the Gospel of Peter for its faithful, who had turned heterodox over that book.

Theodoret tells of the hermit Theodosius of Antioch, who founded a monastery in the mountain near Rhosus before barbarian raids forced him back to Antioch, where he died. In the later Middle Ages the town and its fortress passed to the Armenians, and in 1268 Sultan Bibars took its castle from the Templars. Rhosus stands near the village of Arsous in the vilayet of Adana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ricardus-angl:
Ricardus Anglicus, Archdeacon of Bologna, was an English priest who served as rector of the law school at the University of Bologna in 1226. By new methods of explaining legal proceedings, he pioneered scientific judicial procedure in the twelfth century. His long-lost Ordo Judiciarius was found in manuscript by Wunderlich at Douai and published by Witt in 1851.

A more correct manuscript, later found at Brussels by Sir Travers Twiss, led Twiss to identify him with Bishop Richard Poor, who died in 1237, though the entry judges the evidence insufficient. A papal bull of 1218 calls him Ricardus Anglicus doctor Parisiensis, suggesting a Paris graduation, but no link to Oxford exists. His other writings include glosses on papal decretals and distinctions treating Gratian's Decree, and he must not be confused with Ricardus Anglicanus the physician.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-pullus:
Robert Pullus was a twelfth-century English cardinal, philosopher, and theologian who helped found Oxford teaching. Born in England about 1080, he seems to have studied at Paris in the early twelfth century. In 1153 he began teaching at Oxford, among the first celebrated teachers of the schools later organized as the university. After Henry II's death he returned to Paris, then went to Rome, where he became cardinal and Chancellor of the Apostolic See.

His influence always favoured orthodoxy against the rationalist tendency represented by Abelard, as Bernard's biography and his letters attest. His compendium, the Sententiarum Theologicarum Libri Octo, served for a time as the official theology textbook of western Europe. It was later displaced by Peter Lombard's Sentences. Compared with the Lombard, Robert leaned more to strict tradition. His Summa was first printed by Dom Mathoud at Paris in 1655 and reprinted in Migne. He died in 1147-50.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-romulus-augus:
Romulus Augustulus, deposed in 476, was the last Western Roman emperor, and his reign was purely nominal. After Valentinian III was murdered in 455, the Theodosian dynasty ended in the West. The Suevian Ricimer governed as real ruler for sixteen years. After Ricimer died in 472, his nephew Gundobad appointed Glycerius at Ravenna. The emperor Leo chose Julius Nepos, who forced Glycerius to become Bishop of Salona.

Nepos made Orestes magister militum and patrician, then sent him to restore order. Orestes instead turned his mercenaries on Ravenna, and Nepos fled to Dalmatia. Orestes entered Ravenna on 28 August 475, and his troops soon proclaimed his thirteen-year-old son emperor, called Augustulus. Orestes won Eastern recognition and made treaties. But his German warriors, denied a third of Italy, mutinied under Odoacer and killed Orestes at Piacenza in 476.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sagalassus:
Sagalassus is a titular see in Pisidia, suffragan of Antioch, and one of Pisidia's chief towns. It lies near the province's northwest boundary, in a fertile plain ringed by hills, on an affluent of the Cestrus, a river shown on its coins. Alexander stormed it after defeating its inhabitants nearby. Cneius Manlius ravaged the district and imposed a heavy war indemnity. After subjection to Amyntas, Tetrarch of Lycaonia and Galatia, it joined the Roman province of Pisidia.

Beyond that, its history is unknown, though most ancient geographers mention it. Until the thirteenth century the Notitiae episcopatuum list it as first suffragan of Antioch in Pisidia. Le Quien mentions four bishops: Jovius, Frontianus, Theodosius, and Leo. This formerly wealthy city is now a poor village called Aghiassoun, about twenty-three miles south of Isbarta. It has immense ruined monuments: theatre, portico, gymnasium, ramparts, tombs, and churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-amandus:
Amandus was one of Flanders' great apostles, born near Nantes about the end of the sixth century. At twenty he fled home and became a monk near Tours, resisting his family's efforts. Following divine inspiration, he went to Bourges, where under Bishop Austregisile he spent fifteen solitary years living on bread and water. A pilgrimage to Rome followed, and he was consecrated missionary bishop at thirty-three.

At Clotaire II's request he evangelized Ghent's idolaters, then all Flanders, suffering persecution with no success. Restoring a hanged criminal to life changed the people to reverence, bringing many converts. Monasteries at Ghent and Mount Blandin were erected, Belgium's first monuments to the Faith. Returning to France in 630, he incurred King Dagobert's enmity and was expelled. Dagobert later begged his return and sought him as tutor to the heir, but Amandus refused.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-euchari:
Eucharius was first Bishop of Trier in the third century's second half. According to ancient legend, he was one of Christ's seventy-two disciples. Sent to Gaul by St Peter with Valerius and Maternus, he came to preach the Gospel. They came to the Rhine and Elegia in Alsace, where Maternus died. His companions hastened back to St Peter, begging him to restore Maternus to life. Peter gave his pastoral staff to Eucharius, and Maternus returned to life on being touched with it.

Many Gentiles then embraced the faith. After the three had founded many churches, they went to Trier, where Eucharius settled. Among other miracles he raised a dead person to life. An angel announced his death and named Valerius successor. Eucharius died 8 December, bishop for twenty-five years. Valerius was bishop fifteen years, succeeded by Maternus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-exuperi:
Exuperius became bishop of Toulouse early in the fifth century, succeeding Silvius, and finished the basilica of Saint Saturninus that his predecessor had begun. Jerome praised his open-handed gifts to monks in Palestine, Egypt, and Libya, and his care for his own people while Vandal, Alan, and Suevi raiders ravaged the region. Living plainly himself, he gave what he had to the poor. He even sold the altar vessels, carrying the Host in a wicker basket and the Precious Blood in a glass vessel.

His lasting fame rests on a letter to Pope Innocent I asking about the canon of Scripture and points of church discipline. The pope's reply of February 405, Consulenti tibi, listed the canonical books as Catholics hold them today, including the deuterocanonical books. Claims that Innocent left those books out are mistaken.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-fulgent:
Fulgentius, born in 468 and dead by 533, became bishop of Ruspe in the North African province of Byzacene. He ranked among the Church Fathers for holy living, eloquence, and learning. His grandfather, a senator of Carthage, lost his property to the invader Genseric and was banished to Italy, though his sons later recovered land in Byzacene. Raised by his mother Mariana after his father's early death, Fulgentius learned Greek before Latin, memorized Homer young, and kept an excellent Greek accent all his life.

As a young man he managed his household wisely and rose to be procurator of the fiscus, the officer in charge of the provincial treasury. Stirred by Augustine's exposition of Psalm 36, he left worldly office for a monastery founded by Bishop Faustus, then became joint abbot with Felix after Faustus fled renewed persecution. Felix ran the house while Fulgentius taught the brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-honorat:
Honoratus, archbishop of Arles, was born about 350 in the north of Gaul to a pagan family. He died on 6 January 429, though some authors give the 14th or 15th. Converted with his brother Venantius, he sailed from Marseilles about 368 under the guidance of Caprasius to visit Palestine and the settlements of Syria and Egypt. Venantius died at Methone in Achaia, cutting the journey short, and the travellers returned to Gaul through Italy.

Encouraged by Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, Honoratus settled on the island of Lérins to live in solitude. Disciples soon gathered, and a monastery formed that later trained many bishops and church writers. After Patroclus was assassinated in 426, Honoratus was called to govern Arles, where Arian and Manichaean teachings had caused disorder. He restored order and orthodoxy while directing Lérins from afar, and he died in the arms of his disciple Hilary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hospiti:
Hospitius, also called Sospis, was a recluse said to have been born in Egypt early in the sixth century and dead at San-Sospis near Villefranche on 21 May 581. A monk in his native land, he came to Gaul and withdrew to a ruined tower on the peninsula of Cap Ferrat, a few miles east of Nice. People nearby often sought his counsel, and about 575 he warned them of a coming Lombard raid.

Seized by the raiders, his life was spared. He worked a miracle for one warrior who converted, took up religious life, and later told Gregory of Tours about the recluse. Gregory is the source for the scant details of Hospitius's austerities and many miracles. Foretelling his own death, Hospitius was buried by his friend Austadius, bishop of Cimiez, and he is still venerated in the diocese of Nice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-leontiu:
Leontius, bishop of Fréjus in Provence, was probably born at Nîmes late in the fourth century. He died in his episcopal town in 488, though some authorities give 443 or even 448. His ordination as bishop is uncertain, most likely between 400 and 419, and much about his life remains obscure.

Yet his holiness must have been widely known, since from an early date he was joined with the Blessed Virgin as patron of the Fréjus cathedral. He was probably a brother of Castor, bishop of Apt, and is not to be confused with Leontius of Arles, who lived later. The chief event of his episcopate was the founding of the monastery of Lérins early in the fifth century, and Honoratus, its founder, called him superior and father.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-macariu:
Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem from 312 to 334, must have died before the council at Tyre in 335, where his successor Maximus appears among the bishops. Alexander of Alexandria wrote to him among bishops warned against Arius, and Arius abused him in a letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, showing how hard Macarius opposed the teaching.

He attended the Council of Nicaea, where his name stands first among the bishops of Palestine. Two conjectures about his part there remain guesses rather than facts. One holds that he clashed with his metropolitan, Eusebius of Caesarea, over the rights of their sees, and that the council's vague seventh canon reflects a drawn battle. The other holds that Macarius, with Eustathius of Antioch, helped draft the Creed the council finally adopted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-magnus:
Magnus of Füssen, also called Mang, worked as a missionary in the Algäu region of southern Germany and died around 750. His story survives only in an old Latin Life whose dates clash with each other, so historians treat much of it with care. The entry comes from the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, a large English reference work on Catholic life and history.

According to that Life, Magnus travelled with the Irish monks Columbanus and Gall, later took charge of Gall's small community, and then moved east at a pilgrim's urging. Bishop Wichbert of Augsburg sent him to preach in the eastern Algäu, where he crossed the Lech and built a cell on the spot where the Füssen monastery later stood. Readers get both the mission tale and the reasons scholars doubt its early chapters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-maurus:
Maurus, deacon and disciple of Benedict, died in 584 and is pictured as an abbot holding a crozier, a book and censer, or the food measures his master gave him. Son of the Roman noble Equitius, he became Benedict's chief support at Subiaco and a model of obedience in Gregory the Great's Dialogues. His short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sorts fact from a much-attacked legend.

According to a Life blamed on his companion Faustus, Maurus sailed to France in 543 and founded the abbey of Glanfeuil, later named for him. Modern critics, led by Delehaye, call that Life a ninth-century forgery by Abbot Odo, though defenders remain. Patron of charcoal burners and coppersmiths, and invoked against gout and hoarseness, he remains a familiar figure in Benedictine devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-palladi:
Palladius holds the distinction of first bishop sent to Ireland, consecrated by Pope Celestine and dispatched in 431 to the Scots who already believed in Christ. Two short notes in the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine anchor the whole story. One has Palladius urging Celestine to send Germanus against Pelagian teaching in Britain. The other records his own mission. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sifts these fragments.

Later writers filled the gaps with legend, and the entry tests each claim against the thin record, separating Palladius from Patrick, whose larger mission soon overshadowed his. What survives is a pioneer sent to a Christian community already in being, not to a pagan island. Readers get a clear account of how little can be said with certainty, and why that little still matters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-paschas:
Paschasius Radbertus, theologian of Corbie, was born at Soissons in 786 and died in his monastery around 860. Abandoned as a child and raised by Benedictine nuns, he entered Corbie under Abbot Adalard and taught the younger monks for years. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a scholar who became abbot almost against his will.

Though only a deacon, he was chosen abbot after Isaac's death, then resigned after about seven years to return to study. His writings include a twelve-book commentary on Matthew, expositions of Psalm 44 and Lamentations, and a life of Adalard. Best known for his teaching on the Eucharist, he stands as a leading mind of the Carolingian revival, and the entry maps his books for readers tracing early medieval theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-peter-c:
Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, was born at Imola in 406 and died there in 450. Baptised, educated, and ordained deacon by Cornelius of Imola, he rose to Ravenna in 433, where his preaching earned him the name Chrysologus, golden-worded. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia draws on a ninth-century biography by Agnellus that admits how little is known.

Trusted by Leo the Great and favoured by Empress Galla Placidia, Peter refused to back Eutyches after the Monophysite teacher's condemnation at Constantinople in 448. Felix of Ravenna later gathered 176 of his homilies, short talks that explain Bible texts in plain, pointed style, though some pieces are later additions. The entry suits readers meeting a pastor whose sermons, not his politics, made his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-peter-u:
Peter Urseolus, born at Rivo Alto in 928 into the noble Venetian Orseoli, died at Cuxa on 10 January 987. He served the republic at sea against pirates, married the noblewoman Felicitas in 946, and fathered a son who also became doge. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia turns on one extraordinary day in Venetian history.

On 11 August 976 conspirators burned the palace of Doge Pietro Candiano, destroying San Marco, two other churches, and some three hundred houses. The next day the citizens chose Orseolo doge in San Pietro di Castello, and he accepted only from duty to his homeland. He rebuilt what fire had ruined, then left power for the monastery of Cuxa, where he died in the odour of sanctity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-remigiu:
Remigius, archbishop of Reims and apostle of the Franks, was born at Cerny or Laon in 437 and died at Reims on 13 January 533. Noted for learning and holiness while still young, he was chosen archbishop in his twenty-second year and made the conversion of the Frankish realm his life's work. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia centres on his friendship with King Clovis.

When sacred vessels stolen from Soissons church were returned, the goodwill between bishop and king showed itself plainly. After the battle of Tolbiac, Clovis asked Remigius to baptise him at Reims on Christmas Eve 496, before Frankish and Alemannic bishops and much of the army. Clovis then granted the see broad lands, and Remigius spent the rest of his long episcopate planting the faith across northern Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-virgili:
Virgilius, archbishop of Arles, died around 610 after a career pieced together from conflicting lives. An eighth-century life makes him a monk of Aquitaine, abbot of Lérins, and builder of two basilicas at Arles, yet that life largely copies the life of Maximus of Riez. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs Gregory of Tours against the later legend.

Gregory instead makes him abbot of St Symphorien at Autun, raised to Arles through Bishop Syagrius after Lizier. Zealous to convert the many Jews drawn to Provence by trade, Virgilius used force, and Gregory the Great wrote in 591 praising his intent while urging prayer and preaching instead. In 595 Gregory named him pontifical vicar, and the entry leaves his beginnings honestly tangled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-romanu:
Romanus is another crowded name in the martyrologies, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia works through its bearers one by one. First comes a Roman martyr named with three companions of Lawrence, martyred on 10 August 258. He was buried in the Catacomb of Cyriaca on the Via Tiburtina, his grave noted in seventh-century pilgrim guides.

Legend later turned that ostiary, or doorkeeper, into a soldier, and the Roman Martyrology now keeps him on 9 August. A second Romanus, deacon of Caesarea in Palestine, was martyred at Antioch in 303 or 304: when Diocletian's edict appeared he strengthened the Christians there and urged the fearful to stand firm. The entry keeps genuine tradition and later invention clearly apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-rufinu:
Rufinus appears eleven times in the present Roman Martyrology, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists each bearer with what little is known. A Roman martyr of 28 February died with companions now nameless, and an African martyr of 7 April is named in the Hieronymian Martyrology under 6 April. The note is a work of sorting, not storytelling.

Valerius and Rufinus suffered together at Soissons in the Diocletian persecution and are kept on 14 June, while a Rufinus martyred with Martia at Syracuse is kept on 21 June. Rufinus of Assisi, kept on 30 July and said to be its bishop and martyr, probably matches the bishop of the Marsi noted under 11 August, though his Acts are purely legendary. Readers learn how martyrologies grow by copying and confusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-rufus:
Rufus, like Rufinus, fills ten places in the Roman Martyrology, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia picks out the bearers with some historical footing. A group of martyrs at Melitene in Armenia, one named Rufus, appears already in the Hieronymian Martyrology under 19 April. The note then moves place by place through the calendar.

A Rufus with companions died at Tomi, later miscopied as Philadelphia, and is kept on 1 August. Two martyrs named Rufus at Capua are kept on 27 August, one of them also appearing as Rufinus, and the other said to have suffered with Carponius under Diocletian. Martyrs at Damascus follow on 25 September, and a legendary bishop of Metz on 7 November, whose name was inserted into the lists without solid warrant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saints-vincen:
Vincent and Anastasius give their name to the abbey of Tre Fontane, the Three Fountains, near Rome, where three sanctuaries stand together. The first, St Paul of Three Fountains, rises where Paul was beheaded by Nero's order. Legend says his severed head bounced three times, each bounce opening a fountain that still flows inside the church. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours a remarkable monastic site.

A second church, first Our Lady of Martyrs, stands over Zeno and his 10,203 fellow legionaries, martyred in 299 under Diocletian, and holds the altar called Scala Coeli, ladder of heaven. The abbey church itself, built by Honorius I in 626 and given to Benedictines to tend all three shrines, grew richly endowed. Pilgrims still visit a place where legend, relics, and monastic life meet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salvianus:
Salvianus, a Latin writer of fifth-century Gaul, was born of Christian parents and married a pagan woman named Palladia, who converted with her parents. Husband and wife then resolved to live in continence, and about 430 Salvianus joined the ascetics guided by Honoratus of Lérins. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a moralist of a falling empire.

Gennadius calls him a priest of Marseilles, and he lived and wrote in southern Gaul, probably a native of Trier, travelling in Gaul and Africa. His surviving works, nine letters and two treatises, show no knowledge of Attila's invasion or the battle of Châlons in 451. Against Avarice and On the Government of God, his two treatises, argue that Rome's disasters came from Roman sin, not from a blind fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctus:
The Sanctus, the Holy, holy, holy that closes the Preface of the Mass, is sung in nearly every rite by people or choir. It ranks among the oldest datable parts of the liturgy. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with Clement of Rome, who died about 104 and quotes Isaiah's words, adding that Christians cry them together in church. That passage gives the earliest evidence for the chant.

Clement does not say at which moment the people sang, but the Sanctus stands at the end of the Preface in every liturgy from the Apostolic Constitutions onward. Origen, who died in 254, supplies the next witness, again quoting Isaiah. The entry follows the hymn through Eastern and Western rites, its Benedictus addition, and its music, showing a single cry of praise shared across divided churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxo-grammati:
Saxo Grammaticus, Danish historian of the thirteenth century, wrote the Gesta Danorum, the deeds of the Danes. What little is known of his life comes chiefly from his own preface. His father and grandfather fought in the campaigns of Waldemar I, who ruled Denmark from 1157 to 1182. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia pieces a shadowy author together.

Saxo was a cleric, since no layman of the age would likely hold his theology and classical learning, and he probably studied abroad, perhaps at Paris. He mentions Bishop Asker's funeral of 1158 as happening in his own time, suggesting birth about 1150, possibly in Zealand, whose cause he favours. Archbishop Absalon of Lund urged the history, died in 1201 before it finished, and Saxo then turned to Absalon's successor Anders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sedulius:
A Christian poet of the 400s, Sedulius is known almost entirely through his verse. The scant facts of his life come from Isidore of Seville and a brief note in some manuscripts. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry presents him as a layman first devoted to philosophy in Italy. He later turned to sacred poetry. He probably wrote in Greece during the reigns of Theodosius II and Valentinian III.

His chief work, the Carmen Paschale, sums up the Old Testament in its first book. The four books that follow sum up the New Testament. A prose dedication addresses a priest named Macedonius. The entry praises the poem's skill and freedom. Sedulius assumes his readers know the Gospel story. He dwells instead on the thoughts and feelings it stirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sedulius-scot:
Sedulius Scotus, sometimes called the Younger, taught, wrote grammar, and commented on Scripture in the 800s. The tag sets him apart from an earlier Irish poet of the same name. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry sorts him out from five other men named Siadhal in the Irish annals. It places the best-known one among Irish teachers at Liège under Emperor Lothair. There he worked as a scribe, a poet, and a student of Greek.

Ninety of his poems survive in print. The entry names his chief works, including a treatise on rulers and commentaries on Scripture and grammar. It also follows the guess that he ended his days at Milan, following his countryman Dungal to Italy. The time and place of his death are unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-selinus:
Selinus, a titular see in Isauria near the Gulf of Adalia, was a port on the east side of Cilicia at a river mouth. Its perch on a steep rock, which gave it its Greek name, made it almost impregnable. The one known fact of its early history is that Trajan died there in 117. It then took the name Trajanopolis, but the old name won out, as coins and records show.

Later Selinus was joined to Isauria. In 198 a rebel leader named Longinus was seized there and sent to Constantinople. By the tenth century it counted as a small town. Today it is the little village of Selinti, with ruins of a theatre, aqueduct, market place, and baths. Four bishops are named, from Neon at Constantinople in 381 to Gheon in 458.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-septimius-sev:
Septimius Severus, founder of the African dynasty of Roman emperors, was born at Leptis Magna in 146 and died at York in 211. He came from a family that had gained Roman citizenship. Favored by Marcus Aurelius, he served at Rome and in the provinces, then commanded a legion on the Euphrates under Commodus. He married Julia Domna of a priestly family of Emesa, mother of Caracalla and Geta.

When Pertinax was murdered by mutinous soldiers, the Danube legions proclaimed Severus emperor at Carnuntum. He pressed east and west with a clear political vision, favoring provincials and working with iron will to reshape the empire on an eastern despotic model. The entry paints him as revengeful and cruel to opponents, swayed by a superstitious faith in his star-written destiny, and careless of Rome and Italy's interests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sergius-and-b:
Sergius and Bacchus, martyrs who died in the Diocletian persecution in Coele-Syria about 303, were officers of frontier troops. Sergius ranked first among the officers, Bacchus second. Their martyrdom is well attested by early martyrologies, early veneration, and historians like Theodoret. High in the favor of Caesar Maximian for their bravery, they fell from favor when they owned their Christian faith.

Under torture, Bacchus died from beatings with thongs. Sergius endured more, including a forced run of eighteen miles in shoes lined with sharp nails, before he was beheaded. Their burial place at Resaph drew pilgrims, and Justinian built churches for Sergius at Constantinople and Acre. The Constantinople church, now a mosque, stands as a great work of Byzantine art. Their feast falls on 7 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-severin-biniu:
Severin Binius, historian and critic born at Randerath in western Germany in 1573, died in 1641 after a career at Cologne. He studied at the gymnasium of Saint Lawrence, taught there for years, and, after ordination, took a doctorate in divinity at Cologne University. There he taught church history and discipline and served as rector from 1627 to 1630. He rose to canon of the cathedral and, in 1631, to counsellor and vicar-general of the archdiocese.

His fame rests chiefly on his edition of the Church councils. Earlier collections by Merlin, Crabbe, and Surius struck him as incomplete, lacking explanatory notes. With other scholars he prepared a new four-volume edition at Cologne in 1606. It gave the Latin text of council acts, decretal letters, and lives of popes, with copious notes. He was also known for charity to the poor, above all to needy students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-severus-sanct:
Severus Sanctus Endelechus was a Christian rhetorician and poet of the fourth century, probably of Gallic origin. His true name may have been Endelechius, with the other names taken after his conversion. A manuscript note calls him the teacher at Rome in 395 of Sallustius, corrector of Apuleius. He was a friend of Saint Paulinus of Nola, who dedicated his panegyric of Theodosius to him and owed him the idea of the work.

His surviving poem, On the Deaths of Oxen, is an idyll in thirty-three strophes. The shepherd Bucolus mourns his flock dying of contagion, while Tityrus leads a healthy flock through the epidemic. The miracle, Tityrus explains, comes from the sign of the cross traced on the animals' foreheads. Bucolus and his companion Aegon then decide to become Christians. The poem shows both pagan resistance in the countryside and the means of Christian preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidonius:
Sidonius, a Christian author and Bishop of Clermont, was born at Lyons about 430 and died at Clermont about August 480. His father and grandfather, both Christians, had been prefects of the Gauls. About 452 he married Papianilla, daughter of Avitus, who became emperor late in 455 and set up a statue of his son-in-law in Trajan's Forum. Sidonius honored his father-in-law with a panegyric when Avitus became consul.

After Avitus fell, Sidonius yielded to Majorian and praised him in turn. He then backed Theodoric II of the Visigoths and later Anthemius, whose second consulate he celebrated at Rome before becoming prefect of the city. About 470 he returned to Gaul and was elected Bishop of Clermont against his wishes, as the one man able to hold Roman power against Euric. With General Ecdicius he resisted until Clermont fell, abandoned by Rome, in 474.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigismund-alb:
A Moravian born at Mährisch-Neustadt in 1347, Sigismund Albicus became Archbishop of Prague and died in Hungary in 1427. He entered Prague University young and took a medical degree in 1387. Seeking to study law, he went to Italy and earned a doctorate at Padua in 1404. Back at Prague he taught medicine for twenty years. He became physician-in-chief to Wenceslaus IV, who recommended him for the Prague archbishopric when it fell vacant in 1409.

The canons appointed him, though reluctantly, and he held the see only four years, resigning in 1413 for Conrad's election. He later received the priory of Wissehrad and the title of Archbishop of Caesarea. He was accused of favoring the new doctrines of John Huss and Wyclif. He retired to Hungary during the Hussite wars and died there. Three medical works of his appeared after his death, on the practice of medicine, on health, and on plague.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silandus:
Silandus, a titular see in Lydia suffragan to Sardis, is mentioned by no ancient geographer or historian. Its coins survive, showing the Hermus river. It is the present village of Selendi, chief town of a district in the Smyrna province, on the banks of the Selendi stream, a tributary of the Gediz. Some inscriptions are found there, but no ruins.
