The bishop list given by Le Quien needs correction, the entry warns. Markus attended Nicaea in 325, Alcimedes attended Chalcedon in 451, Andreas attended Constantinople in 680, Stephanus in 787, and Eustathius in 879. One bishop assigned to Silandus at Constantinople in 1351 belongs instead to Synaus. The see appears in Greek bishop lists until the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silesius-ange:
Angelus Silesius, born Johannes Scheffer at Breslau in 1624, was a convert, poet, and controversialist who died in 1677. Son of a Lutheran Polish nobleman, he took doctorates at Padua in 1648 and became court physician to the Prince of Oels. Received into the Catholic Church in 1653, he took Angelus at confirmation and added Silesius, the Silesian, the name by which literature knows him. Ordained priest in 1661, he retired to the Breslau monastery of the Knights of the Cross.

His fame rests on two poetic works of 1657. The Soul's Spiritual Delight gathers over two hundred religious songs of great beauty, sung in Catholic and even Protestant hymn books. The Cherubic Pilgrim gathers over sixteen hundred rhymed couplets of deep religious thought in epigram form. A few couplets seem to savor of quietism or pantheism, but the entry insists they be read in an orthodox sense, for he was no pantheist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-magus:
Simon Magus, by Justin's testimony a Samaritan from Gitta, lived at Samaria when Philip the Deacon preached there after Stephen's martyrdom about 37 AD. By magic arts, for which he was called Magus, he had won a name and followers. He heard Philip and was baptized with his countrymen. His conversion, the entry argues, sprang not from inward faith in Christ as Redeemer but from selfish hope of greater magical power.

When Peter and John came to bestow the Spirit's outpouring, Simon offered money for power to confer the Holy Spirit by laying on hands, and Peter rebuked him sharply. The entry then sorts legend from history. Apocryphal Acts tell of Simon's contest with Peter and Paul at Rome and his fall from an attempted flight before Nero.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
Founded at Aachen in 1844 for poor, orphan, and destitute children, especially girls. The Sisters of the Poor Child Jesus grew from Clara Fey's rented house of February 1837, where she fed, clothed, and taught gathered children. Clara Fey, Leocadia Startz, Wilhelmina Istas, and Aloysia Vossen, schoolmates at Aachen, entered community life on 2 February 1844 under Clara's direction. Fifty children lived with the community, and several hundred attended day schools.

Cologne's Cardinal Geissel approved the rules in 1845, and houses opened in quick succession from Bonn to Vienna. Need for funds and bishops' requests added girls' high schools, domestic training, and famed church embroidery. During the Kulturkampf the congregation was expelled from Prussia, moving its mother-house to Simpelveld in Holland in 1878. By 1911 it counted 38 houses with over 2,000 sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded in England in 1840 by Cornelia Connelly, born Peacock in Philadelphia and converted to Catholicism in 1835, the Society of the Holy Child Jesus educates girls and women of all classes. Leo XIII approved the society in 1887 and confirmed its rules in 1893. Its constitutions follow Saint Ignatius, and teaching in day schools, boarding schools, orphanages, and colleges stands as its principal object.

A superior general at the Mayfield mother-house governs the society, elected by a chapter for six years, with America as its only province. The first house opened at Derby in 1846, then moved to Saint Leonards-on-Sea on Cardinal Wiseman's advice. Louise, Dowager Duchess of Leeds, gave the Mayfield estate in 1863 and land in Pennsylvania, where five sisters opened a Towanda school in 1862 before moving to Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophronius:
Sophronius was a fifth-century bishop of Constantina, or Tella, in Osrhoene, caught up in the doctrinal storms that split the Eastern Church. A relative of Ibas of Edessa and sharing his strongly anti-Monophysite leanings, he risked suspicion of Nestorianism, the heresy that divided Christ's person.

The entry follows him through a synod at Antioch in 445. Where a fellow bishop was deposed for alleged misconduct. And on to the Robber Council of Ephesus four years later. Where fantastic charges of magic and sorcery were laid against him. His case was deferred to a new bishop of Edessa, and the account leaves readers with a vivid glimpse of theology fought out as church politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritual-exe:
The Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius of Loyola is a short manual for retreats, first written in Spanish, and this long entry traces its text, translations, and use. The author's own manuscript is lost; the copy now called the autograph was made by a secretary but carries corrections in Ignatius's hand, reproduced by phototypy at Rome in 1908.

Two Latin versions appeared in the saint's lifetime, a literal ancient version and a freer, more polished rendering by Father Frusius, known as the Vulgate. And both were laid before Paul III in 1548 for approval. The entry follows the Exercises through examiners' praise, papal approval, and centuries of retreat practice, giving readers the textual history behind a book that shaped Catholic prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-acacius:
St. Acacius was a third-century bishop of Melitene, venerated by the Greeks on several days but chiefly on 31 March, and this entry weighs what can be known of him. Living under the persecution of Decius, he was hauled before the tribunal of Marcian to account for his faith, condemned to death. And, after much suffering, released from prison by the emperor, so it is unsure whether he died a martyr.

Famed for splendid doctrinal teaching and for miracles, he must not be confused with a younger Acacius, also bishop of Melitene, prominent at the Council of Ephesus, whose sainthood is doubtful. The entry draws on the Acta Sanctorum for March, and it models the care needed when two bishops share one name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agilulfus:
St. Agilulfus was abbot of Stavelot, bishop of Cologne, and martyr, dying in 750, though this entry warns that little about him is certain. The life written by a monk of Malmedy and printed by the Bollandists is, in their own judgment, quite untrustworthy, and the entry keeps fact and legend visibly apart.

Of good family and schooled under Abbot Angelinus at Stavelot, he became abbot there and soon after bishop of Cologne. Tradition says he urged the dying King Pepin not to leave the succession to his illegitimate son Charles Martel, and that his violent death followed as the prince's revenge. A letter of Pope Zacharias in 747 praises him for signing a charter of orthodox profession, and his relics now rest at Our Lady of the Steps in Cologne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agricius:
St. Agricius was bishop of Trier in the fourth century, about 332 or 335, and this entry follows a prelate tied to the city's claim to primacy. Local ninth-century tradition made him patriarch of Antioch, moved to Trier by Pope Sylvester at Empress Helena's request. And he appears at the Council of Arles in 314, signing just after its presiding bishop.

That signature, the entry argues, already signalled Trier's claim to lead Gaul and Germany, a claim his successor Maximin pressed at Sardica in 343. Athanasius, exiled to Trier in 335 or 336, found crowds of faithful and churches rising. And tradition credits Agricius with bringing the Holy Coat, a Nail of the Cross. And the body of St Matthias to Trier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-albertus-m:
St. Albertus Magnus, Albert the Great, was scientist, philosopher, and theologian, born about 1206 and dead at Cologne on 15 November 1280. This long entry explains his titles, the Great and Doctor Universalis, Universal Doctor, as tributes to genius and range. He mastered every branch of learning cultivated in his day. In knowledge of nature, he stood second to none save perhaps Roger Bacon.

Eldest son of the Count of Bollstadt, born at Lauingen in Swabia, he was praised by the contemporary Ulrich Engelbert as the wonder and miracle of his age. He was, in Ulrich's phrase, a man so divine in all knowledge that his time could rightly call him its marvel. The entry follows his Dominican career, his teaching, his writings, and his pupil Thomas Aquinas, giving readers the fullest portrait of medieval science's greatest name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alexius:
St. Alexius was a confessor whose veneration travelled from the Byzantine East to Rome and thence across western Christendom, and this entry traces both saint and legend. The earliest Syriac legend calls him the Man of God of Edessa, a native of Rome. While the Greek legend, older than the ninth century and the source of all later versions, makes him son of the distinguished Roman Euphemianus.

On his wedding night he secretly left his father's house for Edessa in the Syrian East, where for seventeen years he lived as a pious ascetic. As fame of his holiness spread, he fled Edessa, and Latin versions carried his story westward. Where Rome embraced it and the whole West followed, a legend the entry unpacks layer by layer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alypius:
St. Alypius was the bosom friend of St. Augustine, younger than the great bishop, and this entry follows a friendship that shaped both men's conversions. After studying under Augustine at Milan, Alypius first won notice as a magistrate in Rome, then gave up that honour to follow his master into the Church.

Curiously, no ancient catalogue lists him as a saint; Gregory XIII placed his name in the Roman Martyrology in 1584, on the strength of Augustine's own account of his life. His conversion began while Augustine was still a Manichaean, faltered when friends dragged him to the arena's savage games. And completed when, with Augustine, he heard the voice Tolle, lege, take and read, and opened St Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anastasius:
St. Anastasius was bishop of Antioch from 559, famed for learning and austerity, and this entry follows a prelate twice caught between emperors and doctrine. He angered Justinian by opposing imperial teaching about Christ's Body, faced deposition and exile when Justinian died. Justin II carried out his uncle's purpose five years later, installing Gregory in his place.

On Gregory's death in 593 Anastasius regained his see, chiefly through Pope Gregory the Great, who pressed Emperor Maurice and his son Theodosius to restore him or send him to Rome. Gregory's letters hint Anastasius was too soft in denouncing Constantinople's claim to universal bishopric, and he died in 598, succeeded, it is said, by another bishop of the same name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anatolius:
St. Anatolius was patriarch of Constantinople under Theodosius the Younger, and this entry presents a churchman whose career drew fire from every side. The heretic Dioscurus had backed his appointment hoping for support, but found in Anatolius a determined enemy who condemned him and his followers at the Council of Chalcedon.

How he died is disputed, though it seems the heretics killed him, with Baronius dating his death to 458 after eight years as patriarch. The great annalist censures him fiercely besides, for conniving with Dioscurus over his appointment, for claiming Constantinople's supremacy over Antioch and Alexandria against Nicaea's statutes. And for weakness in handling doctrine and appointments, a portrait the entry reports rather than endorses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ansegisus:
St. Ansegisus was born about 770 of noble parentage and died on 20 July 833 or 834, a Benedictine reformer of monasteries. This entry follows a youth who entered Fontanelle, also called St. Vandrille, in the diocese of Rouen at eighteen, under his relative Abbot Girowald, showing deep piety joined to great learning from the start.

On Girowald's recommendation Charlemagne entrusted him with reforming St. Sixtus near Reims and St. Memius at Chalons-sur-Marne, houses that soon regained their original splendour. Pleased with his success, Charlemagne made him abbot of Flay, or St. Germer, in the diocese of Beauvais, whose buildings threatened to collapse, and the entry follows a restorer who saved stone walls and monastic discipline together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-antoninus:
St. Antoninus was archbishop of Florence, born there on 1 March 1389. He died on 2 May 1459. This entry follows a man known also by his baptismal name Antonius, found in his autographs, in manuscripts, in printed editions, and in the bull of canonization. His fellow citizens finally kept the diminutive form, Antoninus, out of affection. His parents Niccolo and Thomasina Pierozzi stood high in Florence, and Niccolo served as a notary of the republic.

At fifteen, in 1404, Antoninus asked Blessed John Dominic, the great Italian reformer then at Santa Maria Novella, for admission to the Dominican order. He was accepted a year later. He was the first to receive the habit for the new convent of Fiesole, alongside Fra Angelico and Fra Bartolommeo, one to become famous as a painter and the other as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-apollinari:
St. Apollinaris Claudius was a Christian apologist and bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the second century. This entry follows a writer famed for polemical treatises against the heretics of his day. He showed their errors to be borrowed entirely from the pagans. Against the Jews he wrote two books, against the pagans five, and two on Truth.

His eloquent Apologia for the Christians, addressed to Marcus Aurelius, appeared in 177. It appealed to the emperor's own experience with the Thundering Legion, whose prayers won him victory over the Quadi. The exact date of his death is unknown, but it probably fell while Marcus Aurelius still reigned. None of his writings survives, and his feast is kept on 8 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-arsenius:
St. Arsenius was an anchorite, born at Rome in 354. He died in 450 at Troe in Egypt. This entry follows a man read in Greek literature, of a noble Roman family, said to have been a deacon of the Roman Church. When Theodosius the Great asked Gratian and Pope Damasus to find him a western tutor for his son Arcadius, they chose Arsenius. He reached Constantinople in 383 and tutored in the imperial family for eleven years.

During the last three of those years he also had charge of Arcadius's brother Honorius. Coming one day to see his pupils at study, Theodosius found them sitting while Arsenius stood talking to them. He would not tolerate that, and made the teacher sit and the pupils stand. Arsenius had been given a splendid establishment at court and lived in great pomp, but he felt a growing inclination to renounce the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-assicus:
St. Assicus was bishop and patron of Elphin in Ireland, a convert of St. Patrick who worked in iron for him. This entry follows the Tripartite Life of St. Patrick, where we read that Bishop Assic was Patrick's coppersmith. He made altars and square bookcases. He also made Patrick's patens, three square patens of which the writer had seen one at Armagh, one at Elphin, and one at Donoughpatrick near Tulsk.

Assicus was a most expert metal worker, renowned also as a bellfounder. Of his last days Archbishop Healy gives a graphic account. Assicus fled into Donegal, ashamed over a lie told either by him or, as others say, of him. For seven years he lived on the island of Rathlin O'Birne. Then his monks tracked him down and, after much labour, found him in the mountain glens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-athanasius:
St. Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria, confessor and Doctor of the Church, born about 296. He died on 2 May 373. This long entry calls him the greatest champion of Catholic belief on the Incarnation that the Church has ever known. In his lifetime he earned the title Father of Orthodoxy, by which he has been distinguished ever since. The chronology of his career remains for the most part a hopelessly tangled problem.

The fullest material for his life lies in his collected writings and in contemporary records. He was born, it would seem, in Alexandria, most probably between 296 and 298. Some assign 293 instead, as the more certain year of his birth. That date is apparently supported by the Coptic Fragment published by Dr. O. von Lemm among the memoirs of the imperial academy of sciences at St. Petersburg in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aunarius:
St. Aunarius, or Aunacharius, was bishop of Auxerre in France, born in 573 and dead in 603. This entry follows a man of noble birth, brought up in the royal court, who wished to enter the clerical state. He was ordained priest by St. Syagrius of Autun, and in time was made bishop of Auxerre. His administration is noted for disciplinary measures that throw light on the religious and moral life of Merovingian times.

He ordered solemn litanies in the chief centres of population each day, by rotation, and in the larger towns and monasteries on the first day of each month. He enforced regular daily attendance at the Divine Office for regular and secular clergy alike. He held an important synod of four bishops, seven abbots, thirty-five priests, and four deacons for restoring ecclesiastical discipline and suppressing popular pagan superstitions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-austremoni:
St. Austremonius was apostle and bishop of Auvergne, about 314. This entry follows a man certainly known only from a few brief sentences in St. Gregory of Tours. According to that authority, he was one of seven bishops dispatched from Rome to Gaul around the middle of the third century. He worked in Auvergne, and is said to have been Clermont's first bishop.

Gregory's own episcopal lists make it unlikely Austremonius predated the start of the fourth century, since his third successor died in 385. More likely, he lived at the same time as the three Aquitaine bishops who attended the Council of Arles in 314. He was no martyr. His cult started around the middle of the sixth century, when Cantius, a deacon, saw angels in a vision over his neglected tomb at Issoire on the Couze.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-avitus:
St. Avitus, Alcimus Ecdicius, was a distinguished bishop of Vienne in Gaul, from 490 to about 518, though some place his death as late as 525 or 526. This entry follows a man born of a prominent Gallo-Roman family closely related to Emperor Avitus and other illustrious persons, a family in which episcopal honours were hereditary. Southern Gaul's Catholic faith and Roman culture faced difficult times, and Avitus was a favourable influence there.

He worked with earnestness and success to extinguish the Arian heresy in the barbarian kingdom of Burgundy from 443 to 532. He won the confidence of King Gundobad and converted his son, King Sigismund, who reigned from 516 to 523. He also opposed Semipelagianism zealously, and the Acacian schism at Constantinople, and he asserted the authority of the Apostolic See as the chief bulwark of religious unity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benignus:
St. Benignus, date of birth unknown, died in 467, son of Sesenen, an Irish chieftain in what is now County Meath. This entry follows a boy baptized by St. Patrick, who became his favourite disciple and his coadjutor in the see of Armagh in 450. His gentle and lovable disposition suggested the name Benen, Latin for Benignus. He travelled everywhere with his master and assisted him in missionary labours, giving valuable help in forming choral services.

Known as Patrick's psalm-singer, he drew thousands to Christ by his sweet voice. Benignus is said to have helped compile the Irish code of laws, the Senchus Mor. He also supplied material for the Psalter of Cashel and the Book of Rights, and attended the synod that made the Apostle Peter's see the final court of appeal by canon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bercharius:
St. Bercharius, or Bererus, was abbot of Hautvillers in Champagne, born in 636. He died on 28 March 696. This entry follows a man descended from a distinguished Aquitanian family, instructed by St. Nivard, archbishop of Reims. Under Nivard's charge he advanced rapidly in virtue and learning, and, believing himself called to the ministry, he entered Luxeuil under St. Walbert, and by humble, faithful duty he soon excelled his fellow novices.

Back in Reims, he persuaded St. Nivard to erect the Hautvillers cloister, and Bercharius himself became its first abbot. Given up to prayer and meditation, he also taught his brethren contemplative living. Always zealous to spread the faith, he founded two cloisters in the Chalons-sur-Marne diocese, one for men at Puisye, or Moutier-en-Der, and one for women at Pellmoutier. Those institutions he enriched by donations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-caesarius-:
St. Caesarius of Nazianzus was physician, younger and only brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, born probably about 330 at Arianzus near Nazianzus. He died at the end of 368 or the start of 369. This entry follows a boy trained carefully by his saintly mother Nonna and his father Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus. His studies probably took him to Caesarea in Cappadocia, then to Alexandria's schools.

There his favourite studies were geometry, astronomy, and especially medicine, in which he surpassed all his fellow students. About 355 he came to Constantinople, already famed for medical skill. His brother Gregory, travelling home from Athens, appeared there about 358. Caesarius gave up a well-paid, honourable post and returned to his parents with Gregory. The capital, however, soon proved too great an attraction for him, and the entry follows him to an exalted position as physician at the court of Constantine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ceslaus:
St. Ceslaus was born at Kamien in Silesia, Poland, now Prussia, about 1184. He died at Breslau about 1242. This entry follows a man of the noble Odrowatz family, probably a brother — or at least a relative — of St. Hyacinth. He studied philosophy at Prague, then theology and law at the University of Bologna. He then went back to Cracow, serving as canon and custodian of the Sandomir church.

About 1218 he accompanied his uncle Ivo, bishop of Cracow, to Rome. Hearing of St. Dominic's great sanctity, who had recently raised Cardinal Orsini's nephew to life, Ceslaus and Hyacinth sought admission to the Order of Friars Preachers. They received the religious habit from St. Dominic's hands in the convent of Sabina. Their novitiate completed, Dominic sent the two young religious home as missionaries, setting up a monastery at Friesach in Austria on the way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-chromatius:
St. Chromatius was bishop of Aquileia, dead about 406 or 407. This entry follows a man probably born at Aquileia, and in any case brought up there. He was ordained priest of that church, and about 387 or 388, after Valerianus's death, became bishop of that important city. He ranked among his time's most celebrated prelates, in active correspondence with St. Ambrose, St. Jerome, and Rufinus, his illustrious contemporaries.

A scholarly theologian himself, he urged those three friends to compose many learned works. Ambrose was encouraged by him to write exegetical works. Jerome dedicated to him translations and commentaries written at his suggestion: the Books of Paralipomenon, Tobias, and the books of Solomon, and a commentary on Habacuc. In the bitter quarrel between Jerome and Rufinus over Origenism, Chromatius rejected Origen's false doctrines, yet attempted to make peace between them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-chrysogonu:
St. Chrysogonus was a martyr who suffered at Aquileia, probably during the persecution of Diocletian, was buried there, and was publicly venerated by the faithful of that region. This entry follows a name listed in the so-called Martyrologium Hieronymianum under two different days — 31 May and 24 November — with the topographical note, in Aquileia. Only the Weissenburg manuscript mentions the primitive topographical indication on the latter date.

The Echternach manuscript gives Romae natale Crisogoni, while under 23 November Chrysogonus appears again among the Roman martyrs. Very early, Aquileia's martyr came to be venerated in Rome instead, where a titular church in Trastevere still bears his name. That church, Titulus Chrysogoni, appears first in the signatures of the Roman Synod of 499, and the entry follows the transfer of his cult from Aquileia to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columbanus:
St. Columbanus was abbot of Luxeuil and Bobbio, born in West Leinster, Ireland, in 543. He died at Bobbio, Italy, on 21 November 615. This entry follows a man whose life was written by Jonas, an Italian monk of the Columban community at Bobbio, about 643. That author lived while Attala, Columbanus's immediate successor, was abbot, and his informants had been the saint's companions.

Mabillon's second volume of the Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti gives the life in full. An appendix on the saint's miracles, by an anonymous Bobbio community member, comes with it. Columbanus was born the year St. Benedict died, and was well instructed from childhood. Handsome and prepossessing in appearance, he drew the shameless temptations of several of his countrywomen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-deicolus:
Deicolus, elder brother of Gall, crossed from Ireland to the continent with Columbanus. He was one of the twelve companions on that missionary journey. Born in Leinster about 530 and trained at Bangor, he laboured with Columbanus in Austrasia and Burgundy. He then settled at Lure in the French Jura. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him to his death there on 18 January 625.

Too old at eighty to follow his expelled master further, he built a community at Lure. It lived under the Rule of Columbanus. King Clothaire II enriched it with land, woods, and fisheries. Tales gather around him: a cloak hung on a sunbeam, and wild beasts tamed. Yet the entry's spine is the abbey itself. Before his death he handed it to a young monk named Columbanus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-demetrius:
Demetrius held the see of Alexandria from 188 to 231. He is the first holder of that office about whom much is known at all. This entry makes the most of scattered evidence. It weighs Coptic and Arabic traditions against the steadier record of Eusebius and Jerome. One tradition claims he died aged 105. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 presents him as organizer as much as pastor.

Under him Egypt gained its first bishoprics beyond Alexandria. Three were his own making. The famous catechetical school passed to the young Origen, whom Demetrius appointed when Clement retired. He also wrote on the dating of Easter to the bishops of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem. The portrait is of a long-reigning bishop shaping a church that was growing beyond a single city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-didacus:
Didacus, known in Spanish as San Diego, rose from poor parents to a beloved Franciscan saint. This entry follows a life of humble posts held with striking effect. He was received as a lay brother at Arizafa. In 1445 he was chosen guardian of the Franciscan house on Fortaventura in the Canaries. That was an unusual honour for a layman. Later he served as infirmarian at Ara Coeli in Rome. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Alcala to 12 November 1463.

At Rome during Bernardine of Siena's canonization year, the sick he nursed were said to recover through his prayers. Recalled to Spain, he spent his last years in penance and contemplation at Alcala. Sixtus V canonized him in 1588. The entry honours service without rank: a brother, never a priest, remembered as a healer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eleutheriu:
Eleutherius, first bishop of Tournai, stands at the edge of firm history, and this entry marks that edge with care. Almost nothing certain survives about him beyond his office at the start of the sixth century. Before his elevation he lived at court with his friend Medardus, who foretold both a count's rank and a bishopric for him. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 tests rival claims about a predecessor named Theodore.

After Clovis converted in 496 with thousands of his Franks, Remigius of Reims organized the northern Gallic hierarchy, and Eleutherius likely took Tournai then. His biography as it stands was largely invented by Henri of Tournai in the twelfth century. The entry thus offers a first bishop glimpsed through court friendship, royal conversion, and much later invention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eligius:
Eligius, bishop of Noyon-Tournai, began at the goldsmith's bench and ended as a king's chief councillor. Born at Chaptelat near Limoges about 590, he trained under Abbo, master of the mint, then worked in Neustria under the royal treasurer Babo. Clotaire II set him to make a gold throne studded with stones, and his honesty so pleased the king that he became master of the mint at Marseilles. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Noyon to 1 December 660.

Under Dagobert he rose higher still, and envoys paid respects to him before the king. He used that influence to ransom captives of many peoples arriving daily at Marseilles and to pour alms on the poor. His success in bringing the Breton king Judicail to submit in 636 increased his standing further. The entry follows a craftsman's skill into statesmanship and charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eugendus:
Eugendus, fourth abbot of Condat in the Jura, spent his whole life inside the monastery he entered at seven. Born about 449 at Izernore, he learned reading and writing from his father, who had become a priest, then was given to Romanus and Lupicinus for education at Condat. He never left it again. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Condat to 1 January 510.

He copied his teachers so zealously that observers could hardly tell which he resembled more. Learned in Greek and Latin authors and deep in Scripture, he lived austerely yet refused priestly ordination out of humility. Made coadjutor by Abbot Minausius, he succeeded about 496. After fire destroyed Romanus's wooden house, Eugendus rebuilt it in stone and kept its humble spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-euthymius:
Euthymius the Great, abbot in Palestine for nearly a century of life, drew disciples from hermit cave to great monastery. Born at Melitene in 377, he was educated and ordained by Bishop Otreius, who set him over all the monasteries of the diocese. At twenty-nine he slipped away secretly for Jerusalem, lodging first at the laura of Pharan east of the city. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 473.

In 411 he withdrew with Theoctistus into the wilderness, living in a rough cavern by a torrent. Disciples gathered until the cave became a church and a monastery rose, left in Theoctistus's charge. A cure wrought for Terebon, son of the Saracen chief Aspebetus, spread his fame far beyond Palestine. Aspebetus, later priest and bishop, attended Ephesus in 431. The entry follows fame growing from solitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-so:
Francis Solanus, Franciscan missionary of South America, earned the title Thaumaturgus of the New World across twenty years of labour. Born at Montilla in Spain on 10 March 1549 to noble and pious parents, he entered the Franciscans at twenty and later served as master of novices at Arifazza. In 1589 he sailed for the New World, landing at Panama and crossing the isthmus toward Peru. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Lima to 14 July 1610.

His mission covered the vast, harsh regions of Tucuman and Paraguay, where he spared no fatigue, shrank from no sacrifice, and feared no danger. Success followed on a scale that made his name a byword for wonder-working. The entry sketches a friar whose twenty-year apostolate evangelized peoples at the far edge of Spain's American world, through hardship borne without complaint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fulgentius:
Fulgentius, bishop of Ecija in early seventh-century Spain, stands between two archbishop brothers in a family of saints. With Leander and Isidore of Seville, and their sister Florentina, he consecrated himself to the Church. Their father Severianus, a Roman of Cartagena, was later and doubtfully called an imperial prefect. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 admits exact details of Fulgentius's life are wanting.

Contemporary sources mention him only occasionally. Leander's Libellus for Florentina says he sent Fulgentius back to Cartagena, a move he regretted, fearing harm might befall his brother, and begged Florentina's prayers. What danger threatened is unknown. Probably through Leander, archbishop from 584 and power in the Visigothic kingdom, Fulgentius reached Ecija. The entry is a study in scant evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gatianus:
Gatianus, founder and bishop of Tours, spent half a century planting the church in the third Lyonnaise province. Probably born at Rome, he reached Gaul during the consulate of Decius and Gratus, in 250 or 251, and laboured amid innumerable pagan difficulties. At his death on 20 December 301, the church of Tours stood securely established. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 rests its account on Gregory of Tours.

A traditional school, leaning on legends untraced before the twelfth century, claimed Gatianus as one of Christ's seventy-two disciples, sent to Gaul in the first century by Peter himself. Learned and devout writers have refuted that claim, and Gregory's sixth-century testimony rules it out. The entry thus defends a third-century founder against a grander, invented pedigree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gaudentius:
Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia from about 387 to 410, succeeded the heresy writer Philastrius while away on pilgrimage. Returning from Jerusalem, he found Brescia's people bound by oath to accept no other bishop. Ambrose and neighbouring prelates, backed by Eastern bishops threatening to refuse him communion, obliged his unwilling return. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 preserves his consecration discourse, pleading youth and obedience.

From the East he brought precious relics of John the Baptist, the apostles, and especially the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, received at Caesarea from nieces of Basil. With relics from Milan and elsewhere, he filled a basilica he named Concilium Sanctorum, Council of Saints, whose dedication sermon survives. The entry joins reluctant bishop, relic bearer, and church builder in one portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gorgonius:
Gorgonius, martyr of Nicomedia in 304, held high place in Diocletian's household and died for refusing to hide his faith. Trusted often with matters of greatest importance, he stood among the first charged when persecution broke out. Constant in his profession, he suffered frightful torments with Dorotheus, Peter, and others, and was finally strangled. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows his body from sea to shrine.

Diocletian, determined Christians should not honour the relics as they usually did, ordered the bodies thrown into the sea. Christians recovered them anyway, and Gorgonius's body reached Rome. In the eighth century Chrodegang of Metz translated it to Gorze monastery, whence many French churches drew portions. The Revolution's general pillage scattered those relics. The entry joins court favour, torment, and a relic's long road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of:
Gregory of Nazianzus, doctor of the Church, paired a father's bishopric with a son's eloquence across the fourth century. Born at Arianzus about 325, he was one of three children of Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, and Nonna. His father had once belonged to the Hypsistarian sect, and his pious wife converted him. With Basil he studied at Caesarea in Cappadocia under Carterius, forging a friendship that shaped both lives and their age's theology. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Arianzus to 389.

From Caesarea he went to Palestine for rhetoric under Thespesius, then to Alexandria, where Athanasius, then exiled, held the see. Returning home about thirty, he weighed law or rhetoric against devotion to God. In May 381 he preached at Pentecost in St. Sophia's before one hundred and fifty bishops gathered to confirm Nicaea and appoint Constantinople's bishop. The entry follows a theologian formed by schools and councils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hegesippus:
Hegesippus, second-century writer known almost only through Eusebius, defended apostolic tradition against Gnostics and Marcion. In five books of simplest style, his Memoirs set out the true tradition of apostolic preaching, appealing to teaching handed down through successions of bishops. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places his feast on 7 April in the Roman Martyrology.

Jerome wrongly supposed him a historian, and later writers wrongly called him a Judaeo-Christian. Eusebius shows him a convert from Judaism, quoting Hebrew, familiar with the Gospel according to the Hebrews and a Syriac gospel, and citing unwritten Jewish traditions. Journeying to Corinth and Rome, meeting many bishops, he heard everywhere the same doctrine. The entry preserves a traveller who tested tradition by listening across churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-honorius:
Honorius, fifth archbishop of Canterbury after Augustine, carried the Gregorian mission into its second generation. He was elected in 627 and consecrated at Lincoln by Paulinus of York in 628. He died on 30 September 653, the last date alone certain. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes his feast in England's breviary supplement by decree of 1883.

Bede presents him as a Roman monk, a pupil of Gregory, most likely Benedictine. He either sailed with Augustine in 596 or joined the second band of 601. That apostolic company's fervent piety, the entry says, did much to convert Kent. When Justus died, Paulinus, fresh from Northumbria's conversion, alone among English bishops could consecrate him. Two letters of Pope Honorius I, kept by Bede, show Honorius and Paulinus seeking Roman guidance together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ildephonsu:
Ildephonsus, archbishop of Toledo until 667, defended Mary's perpetual virginity with a monk's pen and a bishop's authority. Born to a distinguished family, nephew of Eugenius, his predecessor at Toledo, he embraced monastic life at Agli despite his father's determined opposition. Still a simple monk, he founded and endowed a nunnery at Deibiensi villula. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 23 January 667.

Ordained deacon about 630 by Helladius, his abbot and later archbishop, he became abbot of Agli himself and signed the eighth and ninth councils of Toledo in 653 and 655. Called by King Reccesvinth late in 657 to Toledo's throne, he governed a little more than nine years and was buried in St. Leocadia's basilica. His life rests on his own writings and his successor Julianus's notice. The entry prizes scant, authentic detail over legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-irenaeus:
Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and father of the Church, linked the apostles' age to the second century through Polycarp's voice. He was born in proconsular Asia, or a nearby province, in the first half of the second century. Rival reckonings place his birth between 115 and 142. While very young he had seen and heard Polycarp at Smyrna. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him to Lyons, where Marcus Aurelius's persecution found him priest.

Lyons' imprisoned clergy sent him to Rome in 177 or 178 with a letter to Pope Eleutherius on Montanism, praising his merits warmly. Returning to Gaul, he succeeded the martyr Pothinus as bishop of Lyons. In the religious peace that followed, he divided his work between pastor and missionary, though data on the latter are brief and late. The entry preserves a bishop whose memory reached back to a martyr bishop's preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-januarius:
Januarius, bishop of Beneventum, is Naples' beloved martyr of the liquefying blood. Believed to have suffered under Diocletian about 305, he is known from Acts that are numerous, late, and untrustworthy. Bede's martyrology, about 733, epitomized the Acta Bononiensia, source of the Roman Martyrology's entry. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 stresses how little of his life and martyrdom is truly known.

At Pozzuoli, the martyrology says, Januarius with Festus, Desiderius, Socius, Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius suffered chains, imprisonment, and beheading under Diocletian. His body came to Naples, where his blood is kept in a glass phial. Set near his head, the blood becomes liquid and bubbles as though fresh. The liquefaction reference, the entry notes, was added much later. The breviary adds furnace and beasts the flames and animals spared.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-canti:
John Cantius, professor of theology at Cracow, fled parish responsibility and returned to the lecture hall he loved. Born at Kenty near Oswiecim in 1412, or 1403, son of pious country folk Stanislaus and Anne, he studied first in his native town, then at Cracow Academy. Professors and colleagues were won by his pleasant, amiable temper, always happy, yet serious, humble, and godly. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cracow to 1473.

Excelling in philosophy and theology, he graduated bachelor, master, and doctor, was ordained priest, and became professor of theology at Cracow. Superiors soon sent him to Olkusz as parish priest, but fearing parish work's great responsibility, he left very soon. He was again made professor of Sacred Scripture at Cracow Academy, holding that post with devotion. His feast falls on 20 October, and he lies under St. Anne's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-clima:
John Climacus, abbot of Sinai, wrote the Ladder after twenty years alone at the mountain's foot. Surnamed Scholasticus and the Sinaita, he was born, doubtless in Syria, about 525, and died on Mount Sinai on 30 March, probably in 606, though some say 605. Education fitted him for intellectual life, yet while still young he abandoned the world for solitude. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him to Sinai, then famed for holy monks.

Under the monk Martyrius he trained in Christian virtue, and after Martyrius's death he withdrew to a hermitage at the mountain's foot. There for some twenty years he studied saints' lives constantly, becoming one of the Church's most learned doctors. In 600, aged about seventy-five, Sinai's monks persuaded him to lead them. He governed as abbot with greatest wisdom, and his fame spread so far that the pope himself sought his counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joseph-cal:
Joseph Calasanctius, founder of the Piarists, gave up family perpetuation for free schools for poor children. Born on 11 September 1556 at Calasanza castle near Petralta in Aragon, he was youngest of five children of Pedro Calasanza and Maria Gastonia. He studied at home and at Petralta school, then classics at Estadilla. At Lérida he studied philosophy and law, earning a doctorate of laws, and theology at Valencia and Alcalá. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Rome to 25 August 1648.

His mother and brother died, and his father wanted him to marry and continue the family. God intervened, the entry says, with a sickness in 1582 that nearly killed him. Recovered, he was ordained priest on 17 December 1583 by Hugo Ambrose de Moncada, bishop of Urgel. He served at Albarracin as his bishop's theologian, confessor, examiner, and procurator, following the bishop to Lérida. From that career grew the Piarist schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-justus:
Justus, fourth archbishop of Canterbury, is known almost entirely through Bede. Among the second band of missionaries Gregory the Great sent, he arrived in 601 to reinforce Augustine, bearing relics, books, sacred vessels, and other papal gifts. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 627, with a question mark.

Whether he was secular priest or monk is uncertain. Bede stays silent, and only later Canterbury monastics claim him for their order. In 604 Augustine consecrated him first bishop of Rochester, and King Ethelbert granted the new see Priestfield and other lands by charter. After Augustine's death, Justus joined Laurence and Mellitus of London in writing to recalcitrant British bishops. Other charters naming him are of dubious authenticity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ladislaus:
Ladislaus, king of Hungary from 1077 to 1095, stands among his country's national Christian heroes. Son of Béla I, born in 1040, he was chosen by nobles after Geisa I's death, passing over Solomon, son of Andrew I. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Neutra to 29 July 1095.

He made peace with Solomon when Solomon gave up his claims, then imprisoned him at Visegrád after a revolt. Freed at Stephen I's canonization, Solomon revolted again in 1086 with heathen Cuman aid, and Ladislaus beat them, winning again over Turkish Cumans in 1089. In 1091 he marched into Croatia at his widowed sister Queen Helena's request, taking it for Hungary's crown. There in 1092 he founded Agram's bishopric, and the same year Grosswardein's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-machutus:
Machutus, first bishop of Aleth, sailed with Brendan for the Island of the Blest and evangelized the northern isles. Born about 520, probably in Wales, and baptized by Brendan, he became that holy man's favourite disciple, specially chosen for the oft-described voyage. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him from Llancarfan abbey to the sea.

No doubt he stayed some years at Llancarfan while Brendan lived there, and from there Brendan, Machutus, and many companions set out for the Blest Island. On a second voyage he visited September Island, Cizembra, off St. Malo, tarrying there, and evangelized Orkney and Scotland's northern isles. At Aleth, across from St. Malo, he put himself under the hermit Aaron, and on Aaron's death in 543 or 544 succeeded to the district's spiritual rule as first bishop of Aleth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mamertus:
Mamertus, bishop of Vienne from about 462, enlisted his learned brother Claudianus as his priest. Of unknown birth, he died shortly after 475. His brother Claudianus, the theological writer, had sound rhetorical training in youth and knew Eucherius of Lyons personally, suggesting the brothers came from a wealthy Gallic family near Lyons. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes Mamertus, like his brother, knew profane subjects and theology, and seems to have been married before elevation.

Elected and consecrated shortly before 462, he called his brother from his cloister and ordained him priest of Vienne. Sidonius Apollinaris describes the brothers' activity in one letter and addresses another to Bishop Mamertus himself. In 463 Mamertus disputed with Pope Hilarius over the privileges of Vienne's bishopric, a quarrel the entry follows into Gallic church politics. Little certain survives of his earlier life, but his episcopate stands documented in letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mary-franc:
Mary Frances of the Five Wounds of Jesus, a Neapolitan Franciscan tertiary, lived a hidden life of suffering and prayer. Born at Naples on 25 March 1715 to a harsh, grasping father and a gentle mother, she endured hard labour and ill treatment at home. At sixteen she refused a forced marriage to a rich suitor and instead entered the Third Order of St Francis, taking her long name from devotion to Mary, Francis, and the Passion.

Her body reportedly bore the stigmata, kept invisible at her own prayer, while on Fridays she felt the pains of the Crucifixion. She lived under a spiritual director, received Communion daily from childhood, and died at Naples on 6 October 1791. The entry draws a portrait of quiet endurance shaped by family cruelty and intense devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maximinus:
Maximinus, bishop of Trier in the fourth century, defended orthodox belief against Arianism from one of the empire's great seats. Born near Poitiers and ordained by St Agritius, he succeeded him at Trier in 332 or 335, when the city housed the western emperor's government. His office put him close to Constantine II and Constans, and he used that standing for the Nicene cause.

He sheltered the exiled Athanasius for two years and four months, welcomed the banished Paul of Constantinople, and turned away four Arian bishops who came to win Constans in 342. With Pope Julius I and Hosius of Cordova, he pressed for the Synod of Sardica in 343. He died in 349 or 352, condemned by name at the Arian synod of Philippopolis for his pains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-medardus:
Medardus, bishop of Noyon in sixth-century Gaul, moved his see to safety and doubled it by taking Tournai as well. Born at Salency about 456 to a Frankish father and a Gallo-Roman mother, he was ordained by the bishop of Vermand and chosen as his successor. Wars and barbarian raids troubled the region, so in 531 he shifted his seat from defenceless Vermand to fortified Noyon.

On the death of Eleutherius of Tournai, King Clotaire pressed him to take that diocese too, and the two sees stayed joined until 1146. Known for piety, learning, and charity, he visited the sick, ransomed captives, and won the king's trust. He died at Noyon on 8 June, about 545. The entry sketches a pastoral bishop steering a frontier church through violent times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mellitus:
Mellitus, bishop of London and third archbishop of Canterbury, carried the Roman mission into the kingdom of the East Saxons. He led the second band of missionaries that Gregory the Great sent to join Augustine in 601, bringing vessels, vestments, books, and relics for worship. Consecrated by Augustine soon after landing, he built his see at London and raised the church of St Paul there.

When King Sabert died, his pagan sons drove Mellitus out after he refused them the Eucharist at Mass. He fled to Gaul, returned after a time, and later succeeded Laurence at Canterbury, where he died on 24 April 624. Bede calls him nobly born, and the entry traces a missionary career of exile, return, and steady church building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-methodius-:
Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and writer martyred probably in 311, stands as the first systematic opponent of Origen. Jerome calls him bishop of Olympus in Lycia, and adds a doubtful claim that he later held Tyre, which no later Greek writer confirms. Eusebius omits him from his Church History, most likely because he attacked Origen's theories.

His surviving works show a broadly trained philosopher and theologian. The Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a dialogue on chastity, remains his best known piece. Other writings take up free will, the resurrection of the body, and the created world against Origen. He died at the close of the last persecution, under Maximinus Daja. The entry sifts conflicting reports to recover a formidable early critic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nazarius:
Nazarius, fourteenth abbot of Lérins, laboured against the last traces of paganism on the southern coast of France. He probably held office during the reign of the Merovingian Clotaire II, from 584 to 629. His name stands on the calendar of saints of the French Church for 18 November.

His chief recorded deed was an attack on a sanctuary of Venus near Cannes. He overthrew the shrine and raised a convent for women on its site. That house was later destroyed by Saracens in the eighth century. The entry is brief, resting on the Dictionary of Christian Biography and Gallia Christiana, but it sketches a monastic leader clearing pagan worship from a Mediterranean shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicephorus:
Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople from 806 to 815, championed the veneration of images in its second great contest. Born about 758 to the imperial secretary Theodore and his devout wife Eudoxia, he served at court and represented Empress Irene at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. He then founded a monastery on the Thracian Bosporus and gave himself to study and ascetic practice.

Raised from layman to patriarch in 806, he clashed with strict monks over pardoning a priest who had blessed an unlawful imperial marriage. Under Leo the Armenian he refused to yield on images, was deposed, and was banished in March 815. From exile he kept writing treatises for icons until his death on 2 June 829.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicetius:
Nicetius, bishop of Trier in the sixth century, rebuilt church life in Frankish Gaul after the disorders of the Migrations. Born late in the fifth century to a Gallo-Roman family, apparently in Auvergne, he entered a monastery young and rose to abbot. King Theodoric I esteemed him, even when Nicetius rebuked the king's wrongdoing.

Chosen bishop after Aprunculus, he restored churches, founded monasteries, and preached against Arian and pagan survivals. Letters, poems of Venantius Fortunatus, and reports from his pupil Aredius, preserved by Gregory of Tours, supply unusual detail. He died in 563 or more probably 566. The entry presents a vigorous pastor shaping a frontier diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nilus:
Nilus the Elder of Sinai, who died about 430, defended John Chrysostom and wrote widely on the monastic life. First known as a married layman and court officer at Constantinople, perhaps a praetorian prefect, he studied Scripture under Chrysostom before his first exile. About 390 or 404 he left his wife and one son, taking his other son Theodulos to Mount Sinai as a monk.

Saracens raiding the monastery seized Theodulos, meaning to sacrifice him, but sold him as a slave instead. Father and son were reunited through the bishop of Eleusa, who made Theodulos a church doorkeeper. Nilus wrote letters and treatises on ascetic discipline, prayer, and Scripture. The entry recovers a courtier turned desert father from scattered early sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-novatus:
Novatus, named on 20 June with his brother Timotheus, belonged to one of Rome's earliest Christian households. He was the son of Pudens and Claudia Rufina, and brother of Pudentiana and Praxedes. His grandfather Quintus Cornelius Pudens, a Roman senator, counted with his wife Priscilla among Peter's first converts in Rome, and the apostle lodged in their house.

Part of the modern church of St Pudentiana on the Via Urbana is thought to preserve the senator's palace or baths built by Novatus. The entry is short, resting on martyrology and topography rather than a life story. It suits readers tracing how a Roman family home became a church and how siblings' names cluster in the early calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-optatus:
Optatus, bishop of Milevis in Numidia, wrote the classic Catholic reply to the Donatist schism. Probably a pagan rhetorician before conversion, he answered Parmenian, successor of Donatus at Carthage, in a work Jerome counts at six books, written under Valens and Valentinian. The surviving text runs to seven books, with lists of popes and Donatist antipopes carried further.

His argument turns on the unity and universality of the Church, the validity of sacraments despite unworthy ministers, and the error of rebaptism. Augustine later drew on him heavily. A seventh book, unknown to Jerome in 392, looks like an appendix to a new edition. The entry maps the work book by book for readers tracing the Donatist controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pachomius:
Pachomius, who died about 346, founded communal monasticism in Egypt and replaced the solitary life with life in community. After time with the hermit Palemon, he settled at the deserted village of Tabennisi, where a vision bade him stay and build a monastery. Many eager for monastic life would come to him, the vision promised.

His elder brother joined him first, then others bent on solitary ways with small changes, such as meals in common. Pachomius handled newcomers wisely, sparing them the burdens of community life at first and carrying those loads himself. Disciples who grasped his plan soon multiplied, and houses under his rule spread along the Nile. The entry points readers to the full treatment under Monasticism for his rule and federated monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pammachius:
Pammachius, a Roman senator who died about 409, moved in the circle of Jerome, Paula, and Augustine. In youth he studied rhetoric beside Jerome, and in 385 he married Paulina, second daughter of Paula. He joined those who denounced Jovinian to Pope Siricius in 390, and later criticised Jerome's book against Jovinian, drawing two courteous replies.

After Paulina died in 397, he took the religious habit and gave himself to charity. With Oceanus he asked Jerome in 399 to translate Origen's De Principiis and to disown Rufinus's insinuations. Augustine thanked him in 401 for urging the people of Numidia, where he owned land, to leave the Donatist schism. Many of Jerome's commentaries were dedicated to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paschasius:
Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman Church about 500, is known almost wholly from Gregory the Great's Dialogues. Gregory calls him a man of rare holiness and a father to the poor. Until death he backed the antipope Laurentius, not from malice but from error and ignorance, the entry stresses.

After he died under Pope Symmachus, a demoniac was healed by touching his dalmatic. Later he appeared to Germanus of Capua at the hot springs of Angulus, saying he did penance there for his mistake and begging prayers. Germanus prayed zealously, and soon found him gone. Two books on the Holy Spirit long printed under his name are now assigned by Engelbrecht to Faustus of Riez. The entry weighs a holy life against a mistaken allegiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-perpetuus:
Perpetuus, eighth bishop of Tours, built a splendid basilica over the tomb of Martin and ruled his diocese for thirty years. From an illustrious family that gave Tours his predecessor Eustachius and his successor Volusianus, he was appointed about 460 and died on 1 January or 8 December 490, or 8 April 491.

Soon after his elevation he chaired a council of eight bishops gathered for Martin's feast, which issued rules of ecclesiastical discipline. He watched his clergy closely, removing unworthy priests, and raised monasteries and churches across Touraine. Above all he replaced the small chapel of Britius with a beautiful basilica in 470. His will, first printed in 1661, survives as a curious monument of fifth-century Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-cani:
Peter Canisius, a Dutch Jesuit, led the Catholic revival in German lands during the Reformation. Born at Nijmegen on 8 May 1521 to the wealthy burgomaster Jacob Canisius, he studied at Cologne and Louvain. He took his master's degree in 1540. He joined the Society of Jesus at Mainz in 1543 after the Spiritual Exercises under Peter Faber.

He founded the first German Jesuit house at Cologne, preached at Vienna and Prague, and opened colleges at Ingolstadt and Prague. As first provincial of Upper Germany he advised princes and diets, debated at Worms against Melanchthon, and refused the bishopric of Vienna three times. His catechisms taught generations. He died at Fribourg on 21 November 1597.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-petronius:
Petronius, bishop of Bologna in the fifth century, is known with certainty from only two early witnesses. Eucherius of Lyons praised him as renowned in Italy for virtue, and Gennadius records his noble family, whose members held high office at Milan and in the provinces. His father probably served as praetorian prefect in Gaul from 402 to 408.

Petronius practised asceticism from youth, visited the Holy Places at Jerusalem, and was elected bishop of Bologna about 432. There he built a church of St Stephen, modelled on the shrines of Golgotha and the Holy Sepulchre. He died before 450. The entry is frank about its thin sources, and it suits readers who want a careful fifth-century portrait rather than legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-philastriu:
Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, spent a wandering life preaching against pagans, Jews, and heretics before he settled into his see. He died before 397 and sat at the synod of Aquileia in 381. Augustine met him at Milan about 383. About 384 he compiled a catalogue of heresies, the Diversarum Hereseon Liber.

A sermon among Gaudentius's works purports to mark the fourteenth anniversary of his death. It tells how he renounced all like Abraham, travelled nearly the whole Roman world, and bore scourging for opposing Arians. At Milan he steadied the Catholic party under Ambrose's Arian predecessor. Dupin first doubted the sermon's genuineness, and Marx repeated the doubt. The entry weighs both the catalogue and the suspect sermon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-philip-of-:
Philip of Jesus, a Mexican Franciscan, died crucified at Nagasaki in February 1597 with the first martyrs of Japan. Frivolous as a boy, he joined the Discalced Franciscans, tired of monastic life, left in 1589, and tried trade in the Philippines, living a life of pleasure. He was readmitted at Manila in 1590.

Sailing for Mexico in July 1596 to be ordained, a storm drove his ship onto the Japanese coast. The governor seized ship and crew, and soldiers and cannon aboard fed suspicion that missionaries were agents of conquest. Hideyoshi, enraged, ordered the arrest of the friars. Philip was crucified with his companions, and the entry follows a wayward youth to a martyr's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pionius:
Pionius, martyred at Smyrna on 12 March 250, faced the Decian persecution with deliberate courage. Arrested on 23 February with Sabina and Asclepiades, the anniversary of Polycarp's martyrdom, he had spent the night in prayer and fasting. Knowing arrest was coming, he fastened fetters round his own neck and his companions' necks, lest onlookers think they meant to sacrifice.

Led to the forum on a great Sabbath, he addressed Greeks and Jews alike, quoting Homer, Moses, and Solomon against mocking apostates. He refused sacrifice under interrogation and threats, and was sent to prison. The entry, drawn from his Acts, preserves a vivid courtroom scene from the early Church's struggle under Decius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-placidus:
Placidus, disciple of Benedict, is remembered chiefly for a childhood rescue on a lake at Subiaco. Son of the patrician Tertullus, he was brought as a child to Benedict and dedicated to God under chapter 69 of the Rule. Gregory's Dialogues tell how Maurus, at Benedict's command, ran across the lake's surface and drew the drowning boy safely to shore.

Placidus certainly accompanied Benedict to Monte Cassino about 529, which his father was said to have given to the saint. Of his later life nothing is known. A famous Passion making him abbot and martyr is now shown to be the work of Peter the Deacon, a twelfth-century monk of Monte Cassino. The entry separates a beloved legend from a thin historical record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-porphyrius:
Porphyrius, bishop of Gaza, turned a pagan stronghold into a Christian city. Born at Thessalonica about 347, he spent five years in the Egyptian desert of Scete and five more in a cave near the Jordan. His health broken, he still visited the scene of the Resurrection often. His companion Mark the Deacon later wrote his life.

Ordained priest in 392, he guarded the relic of the Holy Cross. Made bishop of Gaza in 395, he found a tiny Christian community amid hostile pagans. He appealed to the emperor, won a rescript ordering the destruction of Gaza's temples, and raised a church on the site of the temple of Marnas. He attended the Council of Diospolis in 415 and died at Gaza on 26 February 420.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-possidius:
Possidius, bishop of Calama in Numidia, wrote the short life of Augustine and the list of his works. His birth and death dates are unknown, but Prosper records him alive in exile in 437, driven from his see by the Arian Vandal king Genseric with two fellow bishops. He tells us he enjoyed Augustine's unbroken friendship for forty years.

A monk of Augustine's monastery, he became bishop about 397 and founded a monastery at Calama on his master's pattern. At Carthage he challenged Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, to public debate, which Crispinus declined. A namesake cleric of Crispinus then tried to assassinate him. The entry draws a portrait of loyalty, scholarship, and courage in a divided North Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-proclus:
Proclus, patriarch of Constantinople, rose through the household of Atticus to lead the capital's Church. He died in 446 or 447. A lector in youth, he haunted the schools for rhetoric and became Atticus's secretary, receiving diaconate and priesthood from him. When Atticus died in 425, a strong party backed Proclus, but Sisinnius won the throne.

Sisinnius named him archbishop of Cyzicus, but the Cyzicans chose their own bishop, and no one forced Proclus on them. After Nestorius fell at Ephesus in 431, Proclus at last became patriarch, though a canonical bar nearly blocked him. He preached the famous homily on the Mother of God and worked for reunion with the Antiochenes. The entry follows a patient churchman to the top.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-raymond-no:
Raymond Nonnatus, a Mercedarian ransomer, was cut from his dead mother's womb, giving him his name. Born in 1200 or 1204 at Portello in Catalonia to a noble but poor family, he showed early piety and talent. His father set him to farm work, then let him take the Mercedarian habit at Barcelona from the founder Peter Nolasco.

Soon judged worthy to succeed his master as ransomer, he sailed to Algiers and freed many captives. When money failed he gave himself as hostage. His preaching won converts and enraged Muslim authorities, who ran him through a gauntlet and sentenced him to impalement. A hope of higher ransom commuted the sentence to prison, where his lips were pierced to stop his preaching. He died at Cardona on 31 August 1240.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-saturninus:
Saturninus, first bishop of Toulouse, was dragged to death by a bull for refusing sacrifice. Tillemont calls him one of the most illustrious martyrs France has given the Church. His Acts are very old, used already by Gregory of Tours. He reached Toulouse during the consulate of Decius and Gratus in 250 and soon gathered a small church.

To reach it he passed the capitol temple, and pagan priests blamed his passings for silencing their oracles. Seized one day, he refused sacrifice unshaken, and was tied by the feet to a bull that dragged him through town until the rope broke. Two Christian women buried his remains in a deep ditch. His successors gave him honourable burial, and the church of the Taur marks where the bull stopped.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sechnall-s:
Sechnall, also Secundinus, served as Patrick's assistant bishop and first bishop of Dunshaughlin. Born in 372 or 373 to Restitutus, a Lombard, and Liamain, sister of Patrick, he was one of nine brothers, eight of whom rose to bishoprics in Ireland. He seems to have studied in Gaul and accompanied Patrick to Ireland in 432.

Irish Annals first record Sechnall and his brother Auxilius arriving to help Patrick. In 433 Patrick named him first bishop of Dunshaughlin in Meath, and his learning and prudence made him assistant bishop of Armagh from 434 until death. When locals held a fair in his church enclosure despite his protest, thirteen horses, chariots, and drivers were swallowed by the earth. He died at Dunshaughlin on 27 November 457.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tarasius:
Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, steered the Church back to images at the Second Council of Nicaea. Son of the patrician prefect George and Eukratia, he served the state as imperial secretary and championed image veneration. When Paul IV died in 784, Empress Irene, regent for Constantine VI, faced a popular assembly before the Magnaura Palace.

The people proclaimed Tarasius most worthy, though he protested his unworthiness and the hazard of raising a layman. He accepted only on condition that a council settle the image question. Ordained through the grades, he presided at Nicaea in 787, which restored images and condemned iconoclasm. He died on 25 February 806, praised for charity, discipline, and firmness toward an unworthy emperor's marriage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tarsicius:
Tarsicius, a Roman martyr of the Eucharist, died rather than surrender the Sacrament to a mob. The only firm evidence is a poem by Pope Damasus. Damasus likens him to Stephen the protomartyr. Stephen died by stoning in Judea. Tarsicius, bearing the Sacrament, died at the hands of a pagan crowd.

He suffered death rather than give the Sacred Body to raging dogs, as Damasus puts it, and the tradition is undoubtedly historical. Nothing definite is known of his person, though comparison with Stephen may hint he was a deacon. A sixth-century addition to Pope Stephen's legend makes him an acolyte. He was buried in the Catacomb of Callistus, his death falling between the mid-third and early fourth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tychicus:
Tychicus, a disciple and constant companion of Paul, carried the apostle's letters to Asia. A native of the Roman province of Asia, probably born at Ephesus, nothing is known of his conversion. He appears beside Paul on the third missionary journey from Corinth through Macedonia and Asia Minor to Jerusalem.

He shared Paul's first Roman captivity and was sent to Asia bearing the letters to the Colossians and Ephesians. Paul meant to send Tychicus or Artemas to Crete to replace Titus, but Artemas seems to have gone, and during Paul's second captivity Tychicus was sent to Ephesus. Several cities claim him as bishop, including Colophon, Chalcedon, and Neapolis in Cyprus. His later career is uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ubaldus:
Ubaldus, bishop of Gubbio, gave his rich patrimony to the poor and restored monasteries across Umbria. Born at Gubbio early in the twelfth century to noble parents, he lost his father young and was schooled by his cathedral's prior, becoming a canon regular. Seeking stricter regularity, he moved to St Secondo's monastery in the same city.

Recalled to the cathedral, he became prior, then travelled to Vienna to study the fervent community of Peter de Honestis, whose statutes Paschal II had approved. Returning after three months, he introduced those rules at Gubbio. Serving in regularity, poverty, humility, mortification, meekness, and fervour, his fame spread widely. Elected bishop of Gubbio, he reconciled factions and protected his city. He died there at Whitsuntide 1168.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ursus:
Ursus, martyr of the Theban Legion, is patron of the principal church of Solothurn in Switzerland. Honoured from very early times, he is recorded in the Roman Martyrology with Victor on 30 September. Relics of him appear in many Swiss churches, and since the twelfth century the baptismal name Ursus has been common around Solothurn.

The legend by Eucherius of Lyons, classed by Delehaye among historical romances, says Ursus suffered cruel torments for refusing sacrifice to idols and was beheaded about 286 under Maximian and Governor Hyrtacus. Between 473 and 500 Victor's body was brought to Geneva by Queen Theudesinde, and about then a church likely rose over Ursus's remains. In 1519 his old coffin was found, an event commemorated at Solothurn and Bern.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vicelinus:
Vicelinus, bishop of Oldenburg and apostle of Holstein, evangelised the Wends and Slavs of the Baltic coast. Born at Hameln about 1086 and orphaned early, he was schooled at Hameln, then left secretly for Paderborn, where Hartmann housed and taught him. He soon surpassed his companions and helped run the cathedral school.

Called to Bremen as teacher and principal, Frederic the archbishop offered him a canon's place. He travelled to Laon in France in 1122 for further study, a journey Schirren doubts. Ordained by Norbert of Magdeburg, he was sent among the Wends, receiving a church at Lübeck in 1126 from Prince Henry. After Henry's death he worked from Wippenthorp among Holstians and Slavs, founding Neumünster monastery. He died on 12 December 1154.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-victorinus:
Victorinus of Pettau, an ecclesiastical writer martyred probably in 303, wrote the earliest Latin commentaries on Scripture. Bishop of Pettau on the Drave in Styria, hence surnamed Petravionensis, he was long wrongly listed as of Poitiers, since the Martyrology lists him on 2 November as Pictaviensis. Until the seventeenth century he was also confused with the Latin orator Victorinus Afer.

Jerome gives him a place among church writers, crediting him with commentaries on many books. These include Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, the Canticle, Matthew, and the Apocalypse, plus treatises against the heresies of his time. All his works have perished save extracts from Genesis and the Apocalypse, and whether these extracts truly come from his works is still debated. These extracts, with notes, are published in Migne's Patrology, volume 5.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vindicianu:
Vindicianus, bishop of Cambrai-Arras in the seventh century, emerges from legend only in a handful of certain acts. Tradition, from documents much later than his death, puts his birth at Beaulaincourt near Bapaume about 620 and his death on 2 March, probably between 693 and 712. Nothing is known of his early years.

On Aubert's death about 668 he was elected successor, and he certainly held the see under Thierry III of Neustria about 673. Certain deeds follow: translating Maxellende's body to Caudry in 673, consecrating Honnecourt monastery the same year, signing a Maroilles donation charter in 675, and consecrating Hasnon church. The Gesta's author admits he does not know how long Vindicianus ruled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wenceslaus:
Wenceslaus, duke, martyr, and patron of Bohemia, was murdered by his brother after favouring German clergy and the Latin rite. Born probably in 903 to Duke Wratislaw, a Christian, and Dragomir, a heathen, he was schooled in Christianity by his grandmother Ludmilla and at Budweis. After Wratislaw's death, Dragomir ruled as regent against Christianity.

Urged by the people, Wenceslaus took government, placed Bohemia under Germany's protection, brought in German priests, and favoured the Latin rite over a Slavic rite short of priests. He had vowed virginity and was famed for virtue, and Otto I gave him royal dignity and title. For religious and national motives, at Dragomir's instigation, Boleslaw murdered him at Alt-Bunzlau on 28 September 935. Repentant, Boleslaw moved his body to St Vitus in Prague three years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-winwallus:
Winwallus, abbot of Landévennec, founded a Breton monastery after a dream turned him from Ireland. His name takes some fifty forms, from Wynwallow and Wingaloeus to Guenole and Guingalois, and its original form is indistinguishable. His father Fracan, a British chieftain, fled Saxon invaders to Brittany, where Winwallus was born.

After hard struggle with his father's objections, he entered religion under Budoc on the Island of Laurels near Isleverte. He meant to sail to Ireland to study under Patrick, but a dream showed Patrick forbidding the journey and telling him to leave Budoc soon. With eleven companions, after austerities on Tibidi island at the Aven's mouth, he settled at Landévennec and founded a monastery on a rock. He died on 3 March, probably early in the sixth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-zenobius:
Zenobius, bishop of Florence and patron of that city, converted his pagan parents and served popes on missions. Born in Florence late in Constantine I's reign to pagan parents, he came early under Bishop Theodore, who baptised him. After much opposition he brought his father and mother to the Christian faith.

Embracing the clerical state, he rose rapidly to archdeacon, and his preaching gifts reached Ambrose. At Ambrose's instance Damasus called him to Rome and used him on important missions, including a legation to Constantinople. After Damasus died he returned home, resumed apostolic labours, and on his bishop's death was joyfully appointed successor. Ancient legends praise his saintly life and miracles, including raising the dead. He died in 337.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaus-ho:
Stanislaus Hosius, cardinal and prince-bishop of Ermland, became Poland's leading voice against the Reformation. Born at Cracow on 5 May 1504 to German parents, he spent youth at Cracow and Wilna. At fifteen, already versed in German, Polish, and Latin, he entered Cracow University and graduated Bachelor of Arts in 1520.

Bishop Peter Tomicki of Cracow, vice-chancellor of Poland, took him as private secretary and tutor to his nephews, then funded study at Padua and Bologna. There Hosius perfected humanities, theology, and jurisprudence under Lazaro Buonamico, Romulo Amasio, and Hugo Buoncompagni, the future Gregory XIII, beside fellow students Reginald Pole, Otto Truchsess, and Cristoforo Madruzzo. Doctor of both laws, he rose through Polish church and state to Trent, where he presided as legate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cyril-and:
Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessalonica, born in 827 and 826. They are called the Apostles of the Slavs. This entry follows their mission from start to finish, beginning as monks near Constantinople who served the Khazars and learned their language.

Next came a Moravian plea for teachers who could preach in Slavonic. Cyril devised an alphabet and, with Methodius, put the Gospels and liturgical books into Slavonic. The brothers reached Moravia in 863. German clergy distrusted their Slavonic liturgy, so Rome examined them. Adrian II approved their work and made them bishops. Cyril died at Rome in 869, and Methodius carried on as archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-felix-and:
Felix and Adauctus were martyred at Rome in 303, under Diocletian and Maximian. This entry retells their Acts, then tests them. Felix, a Roman priest ordered to sacrifice, was taken to the temples of Serapis, Mercury, and Diana, where his prayer shattered the idols. On the road to execution a stranger joined him, confessed Christ, and shared his crown.

Christians named the stranger Adauctus, meaning added. Scholars now read the Acts as a legendary embroidery on a misunderstood inscription by Pope Damasus. Yet veneration is very old, recorded in Gregory's Sacramentary and ancient martyrologies. Their church over the graves was unearthed again in 1905, and their feast is 30 August.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-fergus:
Fergus is the name of several saints, and this entry keeps three of them distinct. First is Fergus Cruithneach, the Pict, who died about 730 after mission work across Alba, raising churches in Strathearn, Caithness, Buchan, and Glamis, and attending a Roman synod in 721.
