Second is Fergus, bishop of Duleek, who died in 778. Third is Fergus, bishop of Downpatrick, who died in 583 and built a church at Killmbain, likely the first bishop of that see. Their feasts fall on different days, and the Martyrology of Donegal lists ten saints of the name in all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-gallicanu:
Three saints named Gallicanus share a feast on 25 June, and this entry separates them. The first was a Roman general against Persia who became consul. Converted to Christianity, he retired to Ostia, founded a hospital, and was banished to Egypt under Julian, where he lived among desert hermits.

The other two were bishops of Embrun in Gaul. Gallicanus I attended councils at Arles in 524 and Carpentras in 527. Gallicanus II sat at Orléans in 541 and is said to have consecrated a church at Embrun, though the Palladius who supposedly built it may never have existed. Relics of the martyr rest in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-gervasius:
Gervasius and Protasius, twin martyrs of Milan, are patrons of that city and of haymakers. This entry follows their story from its shaky Acts, which make them sons of the martyrs Vitalis and Valeria, scourged and beheaded under Nero. De Rossi instead places their death before Diocletian, perhaps under Antoninus.

What is firm is Ambrose's discovery of their relics in 386. Building a great basilica, he dreamed of the burial spot, dug in the cemetery church of Nabor and Felix, and moved the bodies to his new church, later San Ambrogio Maggiore. Some modern critics doubt the twins ever lived, reading them as a Christian version of the Dioscuri.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-gordianus:
Gordianus and Epimachus were martyred under Julian the Apostate in 362, and their joint feast falls on 10 May. This entry explains how they came to be paired. Gordianus, a judge moved by the priest Januarius, embraced Christianity with his household, was tortured, and was beheaded.

Christians laid his body in a crypt on the Latin Way beside Epimachus, lately buried there, and the cemetery took both names. Sorting the records is messy work, since several martyrs share each name. The Bollandists count five men named Epimachus, and writers still argue over whether a Roman Epimachus ever existed at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-hippolytu:
Hippolytus is a name worn by several martyrs, and this entry disentangles them. One Hippolytus, an officer in the Acts of St Laurence, is almost certainly the same man as Hippolytus the presbyter of Rome, whose grave lay near the cemetery that bears his name.

Quite distinct is Cassian, a teacher at Imola tortured to death by his own pupils with iron pens, later joined to Hippolytus by a hymn of Prudentius. Another Hippolytus belongs to a group of Greek martyrs in the catacomb of Callistus. A bishop Hippolytus of Porto, kept on 22 August, likely grew from the same tangle of legends. The group's feast is 2 December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-nazarius-:
Nazarius and Celsus are known first through a discovery, not a story. This entry stresses one firm fact. Ambrose found their bodies in a garden outside Milan, after the death of Theodosius in 395, and moved them to the Basilica of the Apostles. A Milan tradition must already have pointed to that garden.

Later legend, without historical footing, sets their martyrdom under Nero and sends Nazarius wandering through Gaul and Italy. A sermon praising them that passes under Ambrose's name is not genuine. Still, devotion endured: a fine fourth-century silver reliquary survives at San Nazaro, and their feast, shared with Victor and Innocent, falls on 28 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-nereus-an:
Four Roman saints share a commemoration on 12 May: Nereus, Achilleus, Domitilla, and Pancratius. This entry traces their names through fifth-century lists into the Martyrologium Hieronymianum. Nereus and Achilleus lay in the catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina, while Pancratius rested on the Via Aurelia.

Seventh-century pilgrim guides agree on both resting places, and the Gelasian Sacramentary names Nereus and Achilleus in the Mass of the day. Legends of their martyrdoms grew later and fill much of the entry, alongside the churches raised over their graves, including the fourth-century church of Pancratius that still stands in altered form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-quinctian:
Quinctianus is a name carried by several martyrs and one bishop, and this entry sorts them. One Quinctianus, named with Irenaeus on 1 April, is placed only in Asia Minor, with nothing more known. Another, a bishop, died a martyr in Africa under the Vandal king Huneric and is kept on 23 May.

A third belongs to a Catania group listed on 31 December, again with no details. A fourth appears among Roman confessors jailed in the Decian persecution of 250. The fullest figure is Quinctianus of Rodez, who fled the Arians to Gaul, backed Clovis against the Visigoths, and ruled Clermont until his death on 13 November 525 or 526.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-quirinus:
Several martyrs named Quirinus appear in the old martyrologies, and this entry works through them in turn. One Quirinus, buried in the catacomb of Pontian, is kept on 25 March, and his relics reached the Bavarian abbey of Tegernsee in the eighth century. A second, buried in the Praetextatus catacomb on the Appian Way, is kept on 30 April.

That second Quirinus figures as a tribune in the Acts of Alexander and Balbina. In 1050 Leo IX gave his relics to his sister Gepa, abbess of Neuss, whose Romanesque church still stands. A third Quirinus came from Pannonia to Rome, and a fifth, honoured at Malmedy on 11 October, rests on legend alone, with no trustworthy reports.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-tarachus-:
Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus were martyred about 304, in the Diocletian persecution. This entry weighs two accounts of their deaths against each other. Ruinart judged the first account wholly authentic, while Harnack doubted it and Delehaye classed the tale among martyrdom legends he called historical romances.

According to the Acts, Tarachus came from Cladiopolis in Isauria, Probus from Side in Pamphylia, and Andronicus from a leading family of Ephesus. Tried and tortured three times at Tarsus and Anazarbus, they were thrown to wild beasts that would not touch them, then killed by the sword. Their existence is not in doubt, and their feasts fall on 11 October in the Latin Church and 12 October in the Greek.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sulpicius-sev:
Sulpicius Severus, an ecclesiastical writer born of noble parents in Aquitaine about 360, died about 420. What little is known of his life comes from his friend Paulinus of Nola and from Gennadius. Trained in law, he won fame as an eloquent advocate, married a consul's daughter, and lost her to an early death.

After 390 he gave up his brilliant career and followed Paulinus into monastic retirement, despite his father's anger. A friend and disciple of Martin, he lived in southern France, was ordained priest, and late in life fell into Pelagianism, then atoned with lifelong silence. His Chronicle, Life of Martin, dialogues, and letters survive, the Chronicle being a prime source for Priscillianism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sulpitius:
Two bishops of Bourges bore the name Sulpitius, and this entry keeps them distinct. The first, Sulpitius the Severe, wrongly identified with the historian of Martin, rose to the see in 584. Gregory of Tours calls him a high-born senator of Gaul, gifted in oratory and verse, chosen after King Gontran refused simoniacal bribes from rival candidates.

He settled a parish dispute between Rodez and Cahors in favour of Cahors, attended Mâcon in 585, and died in 591, kept on 29 January. The second, Sulpitius the Pious, was born at Vatan of noble parents. He served as school director under Austregisilus, then as chaplain to Clotaire II's armies, and as bishop from about 624. He laboured for discipline, the poor, and the conversion of the Jews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syllabus:
A Syllabus is a collection of condemned propositions, and this entry treats two series: the errors condemned by Pius IX in 1864 and those condemned by Pius X in 1907. The first series began with a petition from the Provincial Council of Spoleto in 1849. Cardinal Pecci of Perugia, later Leo XIII, moved it, asking Pius IX to gather the age's chief errors into a constitution and condemn them.

Preparation opened in 1852 under Cardinal Fornari, then passed to the commission behind the Immaculate Conception bull. Gerbet's pastoral instruction of July 1860 grouped eighty-five errors. It pleased the pope, and became the groundwork for a new commission under Cardinal Caterini, which specified sixty-one errors. Three hundred bishops approved the list in 1862, a hostile Turin paper leaked it, and the pope waited out the storm before publishing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sylvester-mau:
Sylvester Maurus, born at Spoleto on 31 December 1619, was a Jesuit writer on philosophy and theology. He entered the Society in 1636 and taught humanities at Macerata. He held the philosophy chair there for three years and then at Rome. Later he taught theology at the Roman College, where he also served as rector.

Friends prized a mind both speculative and practical, and a doctrine noted for soundness. He lived by Paul's rule to be wise unto sobriety, and those who knew him held that he never lost his baptismal innocence. His works include four books of philosophical questions from 1658, a six-volume paraphrase of Aristotle from 1668, and a three-volume Opus theologicum of 1687.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synaus:
Synaus was a titular see in Phrygia Pacatiana, suffragan of Laodicea, about whose city almost nothing is known. Ptolemy places it in Great Phrygia, and Hierocles in the sixth century places it in Phrygia Pacatiana under Laodicea. Today it is Semao, chief town of a district near Broussa, with 5,000 Muslim inhabitants, a few inscriptions, and no ruins.

Le Quien lists its bishops from councils across nine centuries. Arabius sat at Chalcedon in 451, Pronimus at Constantinople in 553, and Stephanus at Nicaea in 787. Constantine sat at Constantinople in 869, partisans of Ignatius and Photius in 879, and Isaac in 1351. In 1394 the see was united to Philadelphia, after a period attached to Hierapolis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tamassus-cypr:
Tamassus was a titular see in Cyprus, suffragan of Salamis. It stood in the island's great central plain southwest of Soli, on the road to Tremithus. Copper mines nearby make it very probably Homer's Temese, the island's chief copper market in his day. Three villages, Pera, Episkopio, and Politiko, now occupy the site. Coin spellings confirm the form Tamassus.

Legends of Barnabas and Auxibius name St Heraclides as first bishop. He later moved to Salamis and was succeeded by the martyr Myron. Three further bishops appear in the record. Tychon attended Constantinople in 381, Epaphroditus Chalcedon in 451, and Nicetas appears in 1210. The Latins suppressed the see in 1222, and it was never restored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarsus:
Tarsus was a metropolitan see of Cilicia Prima, of Semitic origin. It appears in the campaigns of Salmanasar and Sennacherib. Greek legend links it with Sardanapalus, whose tomb, the Dunuk-Tach, survives there. In 401 BC, when Cyrus marched on Babylon, King Syennesis governed it for Persia. Already Greek, it grew ever more hellenized. Alexander nearly died there after bathing in the Cydnus.

Its literary schools rivalled Athens and Alexandria. Under the Seleucids it took the name Antioch and revolted against Antiochus IV about 171 BC. Pompey subjected it to Rome, and it flattered Caesar as Juliopolis. There Cleopatra and Antony met and feasted while building their fleet. Its greatest glory is as birthplace of St Paul, who took refuge there after his conversion. Its first bishop, Helenus, dates only from the third century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-telmessus:
Telmessus, or incorrectly Telmissis, was a titular see in Lycia, suffragan of Myra. It flourished on a bay of the same name, also called Glaucus sinus, west of Lycia. It was famed for a school of diviners, consulted by Croesus before war with Cyrus and by Alexander after Halicarnassus. It was also called Anastasiopolis for emperors of that name. Its ruins stand at Makri, a harbour town of 1,500, half Greek.

The acropolis survives, walled by Knights of Rhodes and Genoese, with a theatre and a curious rock-cut tomb. Makri takes its name from ancient Macra, the Isla Longa of medieval Italians at the gulf's entrance. Le Quien names two bishops: Hilary in 370 and Zenodotus at Chalcedon in 451, styled bishop of the metropolis of Telmessaei and the Isle of Macra. Lists keep it under Myra to the tenth century, then record Macra and Lybysium in 1316.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temnus:
Temnus was a titular see in Asia, suffragan of Ephesus. This Aeolian town near the Hermus appears on its coins. Set on a height, it commanded Cyme, Phocaea, and Smyrna. Under Augustus it was already declining, under Tiberius an earthquake destroyed it, and in Pliny's day it stood uninhabited. It was later rebuilt and became a suffragan of Ephesus. Le Quien names three bishops: Eustathius in 451, Theophilus at Nice in 787, and Ignatius at Constantinople in 869.

The see does not appear in the episcopal lists. Ramsay thought it identical with Archangelus, assigned to Smyrna from the tenth to the thirteenth century. Turks seized the fortress of Archangelus in 1413, calling it Kaiadjik, or small rock, on the plains of Maenomenus, now Menemen. Temnus and Menemen are doubtless the same, though Texier names Guzel Hissar north of Menemen. Menemen now holds 9,000 people, with 2,000 Greeks and 500 Armenians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-termessus:
Termessus was a titular see, suffragan of Perge in Pamphylia Secunda. This ancient Pisidian city, home of the Solymi whose name survives in Mount Solyma, appears in Homer and Strabo. Warlike, it kept independence under Persians and refused Alexander the Great, who dared not besiege it. Under Alexander's successors it kept autonomy, allied with consul Manlius in 189 BC, and enjoyed that alliance under Domitian. It later joined Pisidia province, then Pamphylia.

Its ruins show one of Asia Minor's richest cities, Hellenized from the fourth century BC. Bishops named include Euresius at Nice in 325, Timothy at Ephesus in 431, Sabinianus in 448, and Auxentius in 458. Timothy and Sabinianus bear the double title of Termessus and Eudocias, but Ramsay's view that the two names mean one city fails. In 458 Auxentius held Termessus while Innocentius held Eudocias, and tenth-century lists keep them distinct. When city and diocese vanished is unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thapsus:
Thapsus was a titular see in Byzacene Africa, a Phoenician market on the Byzacium coast in Africa Propria. It stood near a salt lake on a point eighty stadia from Lopadussa island, between Leptis Minor and Sullectum, with military and trading ports. In 46 BC Caesar defeated Pompey's generals and King Juba there, exacting 50,000 sesterces from the vanquished. Thapsus then became a Roman colony. Its only known bishop, Vigilius, attended Huneric's assembly at Carthage in 484 and was exiled with his colleagues.

Vigilius wrote several controversial works against Arians and Eutychians. The ruins at Ras Dimas, near Bekalta in Tunisia, hold a mole, a fortress, an amphitheatre, and large cisterns, with a Punic necropolis nearby.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-benedictu:
Zachary's song of thanksgiving at the birth of his son John the Baptist is the subject here, the Benedictus of Luke chapter 1, verses 68 to 79. It ranks with the Magnificat and the Nunc dimittis among the three great canticles opening Luke's Gospel. Jewish in form yet Christian in feeling, it praises God for keeping ancient promises and raising up salvation.

Scholars debate its making: Loisy guessed an older psalm lay beneath Zachary's additions, while others read the names of Elizabeth, Zachary, and John woven into its lines. Two halves emerge, thanksgiving for the Messiah's coming and prophecy of John's mission. Liturgical use, above all at morning prayer, explains why the Church still sings it daily.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-jesuits-t:
Ignatius Loyola's Company of Jesus, better known as the Jesuits, is introduced here, with companion articles on its history in four periods. Paul III approved the institute in 1540 under the bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae, Latinising Ignatius's Company of Jesus into Societas Jesu. Jesuit began as a reproach in 1544, for overuse of Jesus's name, and members later accepted it in a good sense.

Ranked as a mendicant order of clerks regular, the Society joined priesthood, religious rule, apostolic work, and life on alms. Formation, vows, missions, schools, and generals follow in outline, pointing readers to the period histories for detail. It serves as the gateway to the order's sprawling story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-pseudo-he:
A wrong name hides the man behind this work, a fourth-century Latin version of Josephus’s Jewish War. Scribes wrote Iosippus for Josephus, and a careless reviser made that into Hegesippus. The label is thus just the first author’s name badly copied. Best copies name Saint Ambrose as the man who made the version.

Once hotly fought over, Ambrose’s part in it now wins most scholars. The work was in use near his death in 398, and Jerome’s letter of 386 to 400 already notes it. Hints, such as Theodosius’s conquest of Britain about 370, fit an early work of Ambrose before he was bishop. Free in style, it cuts, adds, and reshapes Josephus throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-seven-sle:
Seven youths who slept for ages and woke to a changed world form the legend retold here, a tale told in many tongues. Symeon Metaphrastes gives it in Greek for July's Lives of the Saints. Gregory of Tours turned it into Latin, James of Sarug versified it in Syriac, and Chardry sang it in Anglo-Norman verse. Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend and an Old Norse fragment carry it further. 

Decius, emperor from 249 to 251, came to Ephesus enforcing laws against Christians with gruesome cruelty. Seven noble young men, named by Metaphrastes as Maximillian, Jamblichos, Martin, John, Dionysios, Exakostodianos, and Antoninos, fled, slept, and woke to a Christian empire. Names vary by version, but wonder at time's passage stays constant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-society-o:
Religious women devoted to girls' education, under perpetual vows, are the subject here, founded on 21 November 1800 by Madeleine-Sophie Barat. Suppression laws of 18 August 1792 had crushed French religious life, but reaction soon set in, restoring old orders and founding new ones in a second spring. Fathers of the Sacred Heart led the revival.

Father Léonor de Tournély first saw that a women's institute of the same name, teaching girls, would best restore religion in France. Barat's vision, schools, and worldwide spread follow, from Paris convents to missions abroad. For readers of women's education, the entry traces a congregation built on the belief that forming girls forms the future.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thennesus:
Island bishopric Thennesus, titular suffragan of Pelusium in Augustamnica Prima, is the tiny see described here. Cassian gives an exact portrait of the little island holding it: inhabitants lived solely by commerce for lack of arable land. Its bishop had just died when Cassian arrived, and election of a successor was under way.

Heron, another bishop, suffered condemnation at Chalcedon in 451 for refusing to anathematise Patriarch Dioscorus. In the eighth century Dionysius of Tell Mahré, Patriarch of Antioch, landed there, and about 870 monk Bernard found inhabitants almost all Christians. Today Tell-Tenis, at an island's tip in Lake Menzaleh near Suez Canal, keeps Roman ruins and tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodorich-ca:
Jesuit schoolman Theodorich Canisius, half-brother to Saint Peter Canisius, built colleges across south Germany. Born at Nimwegen in 1532, he died at Ingolstadt on 27 September 1606. At twenty-two he won Louvain's top academic honour, then followed his stepbrother into the Society, welcomed in Rome by Saint Ignatius himself. After his novitiate he taught theology at Vienna.

Munich's Jesuit College then made him rector, and his pupils staged Homulus, or Everyman, in Latin in 1562, one of Germany's first morality plays. Paul Hoffaeus took his place in 1565. Dillingen kept him for twenty years as head of college and academy, lifting studies and the spiritual training of pupils, and he served as university chancellor from 1565 to 1582.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophanes-ke:
Preacher Theophanes Kerameus, Archbishop of Rossano in Calabria from 1129 to 1152, is the homilist praised here. Kerameus means potter, a name borne by others too, which has bred dispute over who wrote his sermons. Ninety-one survive in manuscript, mostly on Scripture, written in Greek still widely spoken in Sicily and southern Italy.

Simple, natural, and lucid, they rank as masterpieces of pulpit skill and rare plain expositions of Bible texts for their age. Francesco Scorso, a Jesuit, first edited them with a Latin version and long notes at Paris in 1644, reprinted in the Patrologia Graeca. Gregory Palamas prepared a new edition at Jerusalem in 1860. Scorso wrongly placed Theophanes in the ninth century as Bishop of Taormina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophilus:
Bishop Theophilus of Antioch, apologist of the second century, is the churchman examined here. Eusebius's Chronicle sets his name beside Pope Soter, who ruled 169 to 177, and his successor Maximinus beside Eleutherus, 177 to 193. Lightfoot and Hort showed this means only that each flourished in the other's age, since Eusebius lacked exact Antioch dates like those for Rome and Alexandria.

Ad Autolychum, his only surviving work, proves he lived past Marcus Aurelius's death in 180, so Eusebius made no blunder, despite Harnack and Bardenhewer. Three books, really separate tracts, defend Christianity against pagan critics, argue God's unity and providence, and trace history from creation. For students of early apologetics, it remains a clear and vigorous voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophrastus-:
Physician and healer Theophrastus Paracelsus, reformer of medicine, is the restless genius portrayed here. Born near Einsiedeln on 10 November 1493, he died at Salzburg on 24 September 1541. Also called von Hohenheim and Eremita, he came of a Württemberg house holding Hohenheim castle till 1409. His father Wilhelm, doctor to Einsiedeln monastery, moved to Villach in Carinthia about 1502 and served as town doctor till his death in 1534.

Paracelsus learned first from his father, Bishops Paumgartner and Schacht, and alchemy from Abbot Trithemius of Sponheim. Long years in labs and on the road taught him more than schools. He scorned Galen, prized experience, dosed with minerals, and wrote in rough German that doctors loved and hated. His fame as healer and rebel endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-jes:
Thomas of Jesus, whose birth name was Thomas de Andrada, was a reformer and preacher born at Lisbon in 1529 who died at Sagena, Morocco, in 1582. Schooled by the Augustinian Hermits from ten, he entered the order at Lisbon in 1534, studied at Coimbra, and became novice-master. His drive for primitive observance met such resistance that he had to stop, though the later Discalced Augustinians trace their start to him.

In 1578 he attended the death of John III of Portugal, then was forced to follow Sebastian's army to Africa. Wounded and captured at Alcacer, he was kept by a Muslim master who tried kindness and then torture to turn him from the faith. By a shaft of midday light in his dungeon he wrote, day after day, Os Trabalhos de Jesus, meditations on Christ's sufferings that comforted his fellow prisoners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thuburbo-minu:
Thuburbo Minus was a titular see in Africa Proconsularis, subject to Carthage, now the Tunisian town of Tebourba. It stands on the left bank of the Medjerda, twenty-one miles by rail west of Tunis, on a hill that covers only part of the ancient site. Andalusian Moors rebuilt it in the fifteenth century, and its Roman amphitheatre stood until the late seventeenth century, when it was pulled down to build a bridge.

The town is famous as the place where Perpetua and Felicitas, with their companions, were arrested. Two of its bishops are known: Victor, who faced the Donatist Maximinus at the Conference of Carthage in 411, and Germanus, who signed the bishops' letter of 646 against the Monothelites. The entry also sketches its larger neighbour, Thuburbo Majus, and its four known bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiberius:
Tiberius, the second Roman emperor, reigned from AD 14 to 37 after a life spent in his stepfather's shadow. Born in 42 BC to Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, he became Augustus's stepson when his mother married the emperor. Augustus adopted him in AD 4 and made him coregent in AD 10. Hard and secretive by nature, he won little personal love, and historians long painted him as a bloody tyrant.

Recent judgement, the entry notes, treats him more fairly, as a ruler faithful to duty, just, wise and self-contained. He reformed every branch of government and built on Augustus's work, strengthening imperial power by refusing to have his authority renewed by the Senate. Opposition grew from his taciturn temper and from Sejanus, prefect of the guard, who alone held his trust, and treason trials darkened his later reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ticonius:
Ticonius, also called Tyconius, was an African Donatist writer of the fourth century who left a mark on St. Augustine. He held a milder Donatism than Parmenianus, admitting a church outside his own sect and rejecting the rebaptism of Catholics. Parmenianus wrote against him, and Augustine quotes that letter, while Gennadius gives almost all else we know of him.

Ticonius wrote Donatist apologies, De Bello Intestino and Expositiones Diversarum Causarum, citing ancient synods for his side. He also framed rules for finding the sense of Scripture, seven by the corrected count, eight as Gennadius gives them. He read the whole Apocalypse as picture language, not as literal fact, and denied a thousand-year reign on earth and a double rising of the dead. Augustine drew on his rules while turning from his sect, a debt the entry traces with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titulus:
Titulus began in pagan Rome as an inscription on stone, and later as the stone marking the bounds of a property. Under Trajan it meant at Rome the limits of a priest's jurisdiction, the seed of its church meaning. Baronius notes that a cross carved on a church marked it as Christ's property, just as the titulus fiscalis marked imperial property. Before Constantine, Christians met in private houses.

Those house churches, called ecclesiae domesticae, grew into the domus ecclesiae and then the dominicum, taking the name tituli from the founder who held the property for the Church. By the end of the third century Rome's Christian community had a central house serving as church, bishop's home, refectory, charity office, hospice and court. In the fourth century that centre moved to the Lateran palace, and the old tituli became the city's parish churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titus:
Titus, Roman emperor from 79 to 81, was born on 30 December 41, the son of Vespasian. Highly educated and a brilliant poet and speaker in Latin and Greek, he won military fame in the Jewish war of 69 and 70. In April 70 he marched on Jerusalem and took the city after a five-month siege, destroying it. He had wished to save the Temple, but a soldier's brand set it alight in the fighting.

As a ruler Titus surprised those who feared a cruel reign, since he had shared his father's court's excesses. His saying that a day without a kindness done was lost earned him the title of darling and delight of the human race. His short reign faced two disasters in Italy, the eruption of Vesuvius and a great fire at Rome, and he met both with generous relief before dying in September 81.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tius:
Tius, also called Tium, was a titular see subject to Claudiopolis in Honorias, on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor. Strabo counts it unremarkable except as the birthplace of Philetaerus, founder of the Pergamene dynasty. Its coins name Dionysius as founder, and the town held temples of Dionysus and Jupiter. Justinian's Novel 29 places it in Paphlagonia.

Le Quien names six bishops. They are Apragmonius at Ephesus in 431, Andrew in 518, and Eugenius in 536. Later come Longinus at the Sixth Council in 681, Michael at the Seventh in 787, and Constantine at the Eighth in 869, who wrote on the transfer of St. Euphemia's relics. The see appears in every list of bishoprics, and George Pachymerus notes that it escaped the Seljuk raids of 1269. The modern village of Filias stands on its ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tremithus:
A titular see, suffragan of Salamis in Cyprus, named by Ptolemy, Hierocles and George of Cyprus. Its bishops include St. Spyridon, a married shepherd present at Nicaea in 325, whose cult remains popular in the East, and Theodore, at the Sixth Ecumenical Council in 681, who wrote a life of St. John Chrysostom.

The usurper Isaac Comnenus was defeated here in 1191 by Richard the Lionheart, who then took Cyprus. The city was destroyed afterwards and survives only as the Greek village of Trimethusia in the district of Chrysocho, a quiet end for a see once prominent in Cypriot church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulric-zasius:
Ulric Zasius was a famed jurist born at Constance in 1461, who died at Freiburg on 24 November 1536. After studying at Tübingen he worked as episcopal notary at Constance, then as town clerk at Baden in 1489 and at Freiburg in 1493. From 1496 to 1499 he ran the Latin school at Freiburg. He then studied law at the university there, became lecturer in rhetoric and poetry in 1500, and professor of jurisprudence in 1506.

Zasius also served as clerk of court, legal adviser to the university, and imperial councillor. He brought humanist learning to law, scorning the tangled notes of the glossators and seeking to restore the genuine Roman texts. His quarrels with the theologian Eck at first drew him toward Luther's doctrines, though he later drew back. The entry sketches a scholar who joined civic office, teaching, and legal reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unigenitus:
Unigenitus is the famed apostolic constitution of Clement XI condemning 101 propositions drawn from Pasquier Quesnel. Quesnel's book began in 1671 as a short moral summary of the Gospels in French, with notes to aid meditation. It won approval from Bishop Vialart of Châlons, grew into an annotated French New Testament in 1678, and reached a fuller edition in 1693 and 1694, warmly praised by Noailles, Vialart's successor. Its Jansenist leanings soon drew fire.

After bishops and Louis XIV pressed for a firmer act than a brief, Clement named a congregation of cardinals and theologians in February 1712. Eighteen months of sifting produced the bull Unigenitus Dei Filius at Rome on 8 September 1713. The entry follows the bull's reception in France, where its condemnation of Quesnel split bishops, clergy, and parlements for decades and became a landmark of the Jansenist quarrel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valens-acidal:
Valens Acidalius, German by birth as Havekenthal, was a philologist, Latin poet, and convert to the Catholic Church. He was born in 1567 at Wittstock in the Mark of Brandenburg and died on 25 May 1595 at Neisse. After schooling at Rostock, Greifswald, and Helmstädt, he began medicine but gave most of his time to Latin classics, spending three years at Padua and Bologna and travelling through Italy's chief cities.

After taking his medical doctorate at Bologna he gave himself wholly to Latin letters. He came back to Germany in 1593, his health failing, and found a patron in Johann Matthäus Wacke von Wackenfels, himself a convert and chancellor to Breslau's bishop. In 1595 Acidalius became a Catholic and rector of the Breslau gymnasium, dying a few weeks later. A brief life of a gifted scholar cut short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valerianus-ma:
Valerianus Magnus, of the noble Magni family, was born at Milan in 1586 and died at Salzburg on 29 July 1661. He took the Capuchin habit at Prague and served as provincial there. In 1626 he was named apostolic missionary for Germany, Hungary, and Poland. Emperors Ferdinand II and III respected him greatly, as did King Wladislaw IV of Poland, who used him on diplomatic missions.

Landgrave Ernst of Hesse, converted at Vienna in 1652 and acquainted with Valerian, summoned Capuchins to St Goar on the Rhine. Ernst attended the disputation between Valerian and Haberkorn of Giessen at Rheinfels in 1651. When the Jesuit Johann Rosenthal attacked Valerian's claims in that debate, a sharp literary quarrel between Capuchins and Jesuits followed. The entry traces Valerian's missions, writings, and controversies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valerius-maxi:
Galerius, a native of Illyria, was made Caesar on 1 March 293 by Diocletian, whose daughter Valeria he married. Diocletian in turn adopted his son-in-law. Galerius began life as an illiterate shepherd and remained a man of violent temper, fond of pleasure and small in politics. Yet he proved an able soldier and a loyal, devoted aide to Diocletian.

When Diocletian split the empire between two Augusti, Diocletian and Maximian, and their two Caesars, Galerius received the Danube lands, with his residence at Sirmium, though he worked chiefly in the East. From 293 to 295 he campaigned against Germans on the lower Danube and beat them repeatedly. The entry follows his Persian wars, his rise to Augustus, and his persecution of Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-cae:
César de Bus was a French priest who founded two congregations devoted to teaching Christian doctrine. Born at Cavaillon in 1544, he first served in the king's army against the Huguenots, then spent years in poetry, painting, and, in Paris, a life of pleasure.

After his brother's death he obtained a church benefice, then returned to a better life and was ordained in 1582. Distinguished by charity, preaching, and catechizing, he conceived a congregation of priests to teach the faith, founding the Doctrinaires at L'Isle in 1592. Approved by Clement VIII in 1597, the congregation reached Avignon the next year. He also founded a women's order, the Daughters of Christian Doctrine, later the Ursulines. Pius VII declared him Venerable in 1821, and five volumes of his familiar instructions were published in 1666.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ces:
Cesare Baronius was a cardinal and church historian whose Annales Ecclesiastici earned him the title of Father of Ecclesiastical History after Eusebius. Born at Sora in the Kingdom of Naples in 1538, he studied law at Naples before St Philip Neri steered him. Reluctantly at first, into church history, setting him to lecture on it at San Girolamo.

His great work answered the Lutheran Magdeburg Centuriators, thirteen volumes that claimed the Catholic Church had strayed from early teaching. Baronius drew on Rome's libraries, unpublished documents, monuments, coins, and inscriptions, revising his lectures again and again. His defence of papal rights angered Spain, which had his Annals condemned. Yet in the conclaves of 1605 he came within a few votes of the papacy, an honour he worked to avoid. He died at Rome in 1607.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veni-creator-:
Veni Creator Spiritus is the most famous hymn invoking the Holy Spirit, assigned in the Roman Breviary to Vespers and Terce of Pentecost and throughout its octave. The Church also sings it at the gravest solemnities: elections of popes, consecrations of bishops, ordinations, dedications of churches, synods and councils.

Coronations of kings, as well as at the opening and close of the school year. Much of the entry is textual history. It compares the older text, attested no earlier than the ninth century and printed in the Vatican Gradual of 1908, with the Breviary text revised under Urban VIII for classical metre. A 1899 decree of the Congregation of Rites fixed the Eastertide doxology for use in every season, and the entry traces the older doxology's links with the hymn Beata nobis gaudia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veni-sancte-s:
Veni Sancte Spiritus, called the Golden Sequence, is the Pentecost sequence sung at Mass from Whit Sunday through the following Saturday. Its ten stanzas share a persistent rhythmic close in the sound ium, a feature copied in English by the hymnologist Neale. Neale's version ranks just behind Brother Caswall's, found in both Protestant and Catholic hymnals.

Authorship is the entry's main puzzle. Older writers gave it to King Robert II of France or to Hermann Contractus. Manuscripts show it cannot predate the middle of the twelfth century, which makes Stephen Langton a likelier candidate, with Innocent III also proposed. The discussion weighs manuscript dates, later hands, and rival ascriptions without settling the question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-verecundus:
Verecundus was bishop of Junca in the African province of Byzacena during the Three Chapters dispute of the mid-sixth century, over writings said to have Nestorian leanings. When Pope Vigilius's Judicatum provoked near-universal anger, pope and Emperor Justinian agreed to settle the question at a general council in Constantinople.

Verecundus went there with Primasius of Hadrumetum, reaching it in mid-551, and both men stood against Greek bishops' pledges and threats to condemn the Chapters. Standing by Vigilius, they joined him in excommunicating Theodore Askidas and deposing Patriarch Mennas in August 551, then followed the pope's flight to Chalcedon that December. Verecundus, an ardent champion of the Chapters to the end, died shortly afterwards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vigilius:
Vigilius of Tapsus was a bishop in the African province of Byzacena. Named in the list appended to Victor Vitensis's history among bishops present at the 484 conference of Catholic and Arian bishops summoned at Carthage by the Vandal king Huneric. Beyond that fact almost nothing certain is known of his earlier or later career, though he is conjectured to have fled to Constantinople when Catholic bishops were exiled from Africa.

His writings show an active part in the Eastern Church's controversies. Undoubtedly his is a dialogue against Arians, Sabellians, and Photinians, with Athanasius, Arius, Sabellius, Photinus, and Probus as speakers, and a five-book treatise against Eutyches summarizing the case against Eutychianism. Many other works are attributed to him without sufficient evidence, including treatises against the Arian deacon Maribadus and bishop Palladius, and twelve books on the Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vitus-miletus:
Vitus Miletus, originally Müller, was a Catholic theologian born at Gmünd in Swabia in 1549 and dying at Mainz in 1615. He studied at Rome's German College from 1567 to 1575, addressed Gregory XIII as students' dean in 1573, was ordained at St John Lateran on Easter Saturday 1575. Took his doctorate at Bologna that June on his way home.

Summoned to Mainz by Elector Daniel Brendel von Homburg, he worked at reforming the clergy, then was sent to Erfurt to help Suffragan Bishop Nicolaus Elgard restore Catholicism. His Lenten sermons of 1579 on the Eucharist drew sharp controversy with Protestant preachers. Sent to Rome in 1582 to fetch the pallium, the archbishop's woollen vestment, for a new archbishop, he served successive archbishops on important affairs, including monastic visitations. As spiritual counsellor defended the faith by preaching and writing until death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-damas:
William Damasus Lindanus was a Dutch bishop and scholar who defended Catholic teaching in the Low Countries during the Reformation wars. Born at Dordrecht in 1525, he died at Ghent in 1588. He read philosophy and theology at Louvain, polished Greek and Hebrew at Paris, took his licentiate in 1552, and took orders the same year. Posts followed as Scripture teacher at Dillingen, vicar-general at Utrecht, royal counsellor, and inquisitor in Friesland.

Philip II named him first Bishop of Ruremonde in 1562, though local hostility kept him from his see until 1569. He reformed the diocese, applied Trent's decrees, fled heretic attacks more than once, and quarrelled with the Duke of Alba. In 1588 he moved to Ghent and died three months later. His works include Panoplia Evangelica, a defence of Trent, and dialogues for ordinary readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-duran:
William Durandus was a medieval canonist and the leading writer on liturgy of his age, called Speculator from his great law book. Born about 1237 at Puimisson in Provence, he died at Rome in 1296. He read law at Bologna under Bernard of Parma, taught at Modena, and was called to Rome by Clement IV, who made him subdeacon and gave him canonries at Beauvais and Chartres. As papal auditor he drafted decrees for the Second Council of Lyons in 1274.

Durandus governed Romagna for the pope, crushed a rising under Guy of Montefeltro, razed Guy's fortress, and founded Urbania in its place. Elected Bishop of Mende in 1286, he took residence only in 1291, leaving his nephew in charge meanwhile. His Rationale Divinorum Officiorum of 1286, in eight books, remains the standard medieval guide to Roman rite, vestments, Mass, hours, and the calendar, with rich symbolic readings of each rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zacharias-chr:
Zacharias Chrysopolitanus was a Premonstratensian exegete famed for his Gospel harmony. Born at Chrysopolis, Besançon, he died about 1155. First headmaster of Besançon's cathedral school, he then joined the Premonstratensians at Saint Martin's Abbey in Laon. His Unum ex Quattuor, or On the Harmony of the Evangelists, joins the four Gospels with grammatical and etymological notes on Greek, Hebrew, and some Latin words. It was introduced by three prefaces on the Gospel's relation to Jewish law, philosophy, and evangelist symbols.

Zacharias credits the original harmony to Ammonius of Alexandria and leans chiefly on Latin Fathers. His 181 chapters show early Scholasticism at work, pressing always for the Bible's literal sense. In one notable break from Ammonius he has Christ journey again to Samaria after the triumphant entry into Jerusalem. His taste in choosing patristic passages compares favourably with Aquinas's Catena Aurea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zengg-modrus:
Zengg-Modrus is the Hungarian diocese suffragan to Agram, joining the sees of Zengg and Modrus. Its foundation year is unknown; Miraeus, about 1150 to 1160, was its first bishop. The See of Modrus was established at Corbavia in 1185, and Pius II moved it from Corbavia to Modrus under Turkish pressure, giving it the Modrus name. Urban VIII united Zengg with Modrus, and Gregory XVI confirmed the union in 1836. Until 1600 the see was suffragan of Spalato, later of Gran, then of Kalocsa; since 1852 it belongs to Agram.

The diocese covers Fiume, parts of Agram county, and the Military Frontier, divided into five archdeaconries, fifteen vice-archdeaconries, and 137 parishes. Mass and services use ancient Slavic by papal privilege. Two chapters belong to Zengg and Modrus, with one collegiate chapter at Fiume. The seminary stands at Zengg, established by Bishop Osegovich in 1857. Tersato, a pilgrimage place, lies near Fiume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zosimus:
Zosimus was a Byzantine historian of the fifth and sixth centuries, whose birth and death dates are unknown. Nothing further is known of his life beyond that he was a lawyer connected with Constantinople's treasury and an upholder of paganism. Formerly assigned to the fifth century's first half, he is now generally taken as a contemporary of Emperor Anastasius I, who reigned from 491 to 518.

He may be identical with the Sophist Zosimus of Gaza or Ascalon named by Suidas, though Suidas mentions no historical work by that Sophist. He evidently meant to continue but was prevented, perhaps by death. His work is a chief authority for fourth-century Roman history. A heathen devoted to the old gods, he blamed Rome's decay on the abandonment of ancient worship and held to pagan superstitions such as stellar influence and soothsaying.
cessions-of-land-by-indian-tribes-to-the:
C. C. Royce's paper appeared in the First Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, printed at Washington in 1881, with Indiana as its worked example. He begins with the legal character of Indian title. Did Native peoples hold more than a tenancy at will? Were they open to removal whenever white neighbours wished? Royce reviews what courts and governments had ruled since the discovery of America.

A map of Indiana fronts the study. Royce then lists treaty cessions one by one, with dates. The Sac and Fox cession of 1804 comes first. Winnebago cessions of 1829 and 1832 and a Pottawatomie cession of 1832 follow. He shows how they overlap. Step by step, nearly a whole state changes hands on paper.
china-and-the-manchus:
Herbert A. Giles, Cambridge professor of Chinese and a former consul at Ningpo, told the story of Manchu China from its origins to its fall. Giles begins with the Nü-chên and Kitan nomads north of Korea, then follows the fall of the Ming dynasty and the Manchu conquest. Chapters march emperor by emperor: Shun Chih, K'ang Hsi, Ch'ien Lung, and on through the troubled nineteenth century.

Foreign wars, rebellions, and court weakness fill the later reigns, until the boy emperor Hsüan T'ung gives way to Sun Yat-sen and the republic. Giles writes brisk, opinionated history for general readers, with a pronunciation guide and a list of works consulted. The book captures what Edwardian Britain knew, and guessed, about China.
christopher-and-columbus:
Elizabeth von Arnim, billed only as the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden, published her twin novel with Doubleday, Page in 1919. Anna-Rose and Anna-Felicitas, seventeen-year-old twins, cross the Atlantic on the liner St. Luke in wartime. They are orphans, half German and half English, and aliens everywhere. Under a rug on the second-class deck they rename themselves Christopher and Columbus, off to discover a New World.

Mr. Twist, their unwilling escort to America, finds his charge complicated at landfall. The man meant to receive the twins, Mr. Dellogg, has inconveniently died. Twist resents a corpse for spoiling his plans, and knows he is unreasonable. The twins love him simply anyway, as the frontispiece shows. Comedy and pathos share the voyage, in von Arnim's lightest wartime manner.
christopher-columbus:
Mildred Stapley Byne's Christopher Columbus, from the True Stories of Great Americans series, tells the discoverer's life for young readers. Lowell lines on the title page set the theme. Europe's wise men sneered that all knowable earth was known, until one man from Genoa refused, and sailed toward an unknown world.

Chapters follow Columbus from his youth and his season of waiting through Isabella's decision. They continue through the cry of land, the natives of the new land, and the return in the Nina. Later chapters cover the second and third voyages, the return in disgrace, public sympathy, the last voyage, and the courage of Diego Mendez. Byne writes plainly and admiringly, making Columbus a hero of persistence for school readers.
coriolanus:
William Shakespeare's Coriolanus, his Roman tragedy of pride, appears in this old-spelling electronic text, prefaced by the same printer's notes used across this Shakespeare set. Caius Martius, named Coriolanus for his victory at Corioli, despises the Roman plebeians and their tribunes. The people, hungry for corn, despise him back.

Banished, he joins his enemy Aufidius and marches on Rome, where his mother Volumnia pleads him out of vengeance and into death. The middle scenes show the tribune Brutus charging that disdain mangles true judgment and robs the state of integrity. Shakespeare's coldest political play studies honor, class hatred, and a hero whose virtues fit war and ruin peace.
cratylus:
Plato's Cratylus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, perplexed its own editor, who ranks it with Plato's best in fancy, humor, and style while doubting anyone has dispelled uncertainty about its aim. Hermogenes and Cratylus dispute whether names are correct by nature or by convention. Socrates, between them, improvises etymologies by the hundred.

Greek words are unfolded into hidden meanings, gods' names parsed, and letters assigned sounds and characters, until Socrates wonders whether language grew up largely independent of any name-giver. The dialogue founded the philosophy of language while mocking its own method. Jowett's introduction guides readers through the jest and the seriousness, which remain entangled by design.
dear-brutus:
J. M. Barrie's play Dear Brutus opens in a darkened room where its two chief characters, the stage directions say, are Darkness and Light. Outside lies Lob's moonlit garden, and Lob, an elfin old host, has gathered a house party of discontented guests. Each regrets some turning taken years before. Barrie builds the play on one wish: what if life offered a second chance?

In Act Two, the guests wander into a magic wood that appears for one midsummer night, and each lives the other life. The drunk becomes a great man, the childless woman gains a daughter, and the painter meets the family he never had. The wood grants wishes only to show that character travels with the traveler. Readers and audiences get Barrie's gentlest argument: people mostly become again what they already were, which makes the play's comedy tender rather than cruel.
doe-osti-17052061-international-nuclear-:
Milestone report ANL/NSE-26/21, dated July 15, 2026, links four cost tools into one workflow for comparing nuclear plant costs across countries. Jia Zhou of Argonne, with partners from Idaho and Brookhaven labs, led the work. The tools cover capital cost estimation, international adjustment, cost reduction over time, and levelized cost of energy.

A case study uses the AP1000 reactor design. China localization and learning effects are priced, then the same levers are applied to a United States build to see how much of the cost gap they close. Tentative small modular reactor estimates for the United States are also run through the framework. A remaining gap stays unexplained, the authors note.
doe-osti-2584736-design-and-fabrication-:
Miranda Gottlieb's May 2025 Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report, LLNL-TR-2006470, covers the design and fabrication of a thyristor built with ion implantation. A thyristor is a solid-state switch made of four alternating p-type and n-type layers. Qinghui Shao and Caitlin Chapin served as principal investigators for the work.

Gottlieb explains how the device turns on with a small pulse, conducts in one direction only, and stays either fully on or fully off. The report then works through fabrication choices, including how to mask the wafer during implantation. It compares silicon dioxide and metal masks for a boron implant at 180 kiloelectronvolts, finding the oxide mask must be much thicker but works best in the process. Such switches suit high-power loads where reverse current could cause damage.
doe-osti-2997320-ion-traps-and-packaging:
The Chimera project closes with Sandia report SAND2025-11897R, led by Melissa Revelle with Matthew Delaney, Eric Ou, and co-authors, on packaging ion traps with other technologies on one chip. Trapped ions drive leading quantum computers and atomic clocks. Scaling them is blocked by bulky external lasers, clashing materials, and fabrication limits.

Chimera pursues heterogeneous integration: traps, silicon photonics, and detectors built as separate best-in-class pieces, then joined. Sharing one control surface for light and ions also cuts vibration effects, steadying the trap. Process runs showed the risky steps working better than feared: front and back trench etches landed well, and a metal pad etch came out as drawn. Trap parts were photographed after etching, with and without back lighting, as the record of progress.
doe-osti-2997607-affinity-of-ldr-organic:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00569, by William Jolin, Benjamin Pershing, and Andrew Boggess, dated September 2025, measures how strongly regulated organic chemicals stick to cement materials and activated carbon. Hanford's glass plant cannot vitrify all of its low-activity waste, so cement forms are being weighed as a supplement. Federal rules do not yet count cement binding as a standard treatment for these organics, so proof matters.

Fifteen compounds were chosen to span different chemical behaviors. Single-compound sorption tests ran for eleven of them; mixtures tested whether compounds help or hinder each other's uptake. Naphthalene vanished even from sealed control samples, a loss the report flags rather than hides. Cast Stone, with and without activated carbon, was the test solid. Results feed the case for or against cement as an approved treatment.
doe-osti-2998334-wind-driven-direct-air-:
Georgia Institute of Technology final report on award DE-AR0001414, led by Ryan Lively, covers the WEDAC project from May 2021 to March 2025. WEDAC aims to pull carbon dioxide straight from the air using wind alone. Its contactors are 3D-printed structures loaded with amine chemicals that grab carbon dioxide as air passes through, with no fan power needed.

Prototype work broke the cycle into steps: adsorption, air removal, Joule heating to release the gas, collection, and cooling before the module reopens. Performance testing finished in late 2024 on small laboratory units, quantifying captured carbon dioxide, heating and cooling rates, and adsorption times. The filing closes the award with a passive design whose operating cost is mostly the heat pulse, a tempting trade where wind is steady and power is dear.
doe-osti-3007885-hfir-activity-workbook-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory user guide ORNL/TM-2025/4274, by Jose Salcedo-Perez, Hailey Green, Zain Karriem, and Ariel Marquez, dated December 2025, documents the HAWK software tool. HAWK stands for HFIR Activity Workbook Generator, serving the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge.

The guide walks users through the inputs the generator needs. Material definitions carry long alias lists, so names like Al 6061, 6061-Al, and Aluminum 6061 all resolve to one material. Cycle dates and composition data feed the workbook that reactor staff use for activity calculations. Clear input rules keep those workbooks consistent between analysts, and the guide shows the data formats the tool expects.
doe-osti-3010478-final-technical-report-:
Final technical report for DOE grant SC0024462, by Kevin Huffenberger of Florida State University, covers testing whether CMB-S4 inflation measurements would survive different foreground models. The reporting period ran July 2023 to March 2025, though active work stopped a year earlier when Huffenberger moved to Texas A&M.

The enemy is galactic dust, whose polarized glow can swamp the faint B-mode signal of primordial gravitational waves. Comparing Planck dust data with the team's own magnetohydrodynamic simulations showed the dust polarization matches strongly supersonic turbulence. A filament-based model also characterized parity-odd foreground signals that could fake cosmic birefringence. CMB-S4 was cancelled, but the methods transfer to BICEP, the South Pole Telescope, and the Simons Observatory.
doe-osti-3015295-eliminating-the-need-fo: Cooling without refrigerants is the subject of a short CRADA final report, LBNL-2001727, dated December 16, 2025. Berkeley Lab contact Melanie Sonsteng ran the lab side, with Calion Technologies, on 100,000 dollars of DOE support. Calion's ionocaloric cycle uses liquid and salt-based materials to pump heat, aiming at a zero global-warming-potential platform, unlike vapor compression systems. The team mapped an ionocaloric heat pump and chiller for efficiency, power density, and temperature lift, and tested the separation step, named as the largest technical risk. One patent application, solely Calion's, is listed.
doe-osti-3022915-optimization-of-boron-c:
An LLNL paper by Matthew Wehler and colleagues optimizes how boron carbide ceramic is densified for use as sputtering targets at the National Ignition Facility. Sputtering sources must be dense and compositionally controlled, since thin boron carbide films coat components inside the fusion experiments. Direct current sintering is the consolidation method under study.

The experiments vary composition in a systematic sweep. Powders were prepared with carbon black nanoparticles, graphite, or amorphous boron additions: carbon and graphite each at 0.0 through 0.5 atomic percent, and boron at boron-to-carbon ratios from 4:1 up to 9:1, each series with an additive-free control. Mixtures were milled, sonicated, dried overnight at 80 degrees Celsius, and crushed before sintering under standard conditions. Density readings decided which recipe wins.
doe-osti-3068739-final-technical-report-:
Cindy Rubio-Gonzalez of the University of California, Davis, closes the ComPort project in this final report, dated April 28, 2026, under award SC0022182. The funding ran from September 2021 to August 2025. ComPort built testing methods to guard software when it is ported, moved from one computer type to another. Modern supercomputers mix many chip kinds, and that mix can quietly bend the numbers a trusted science code produces.

The team shipped five open-source tools and six papers, one winning the Hans Meuer Award for best paper at ISC High Performance 2023. CIGEN hunts input ranges that expose compiler-made number mismatches. FPLearner uses graph neural networks to tune mixed-precision programs, speeding prior tuners by about 25.5 percent on average. MUPPET applies mutation testing to squeeze out more speed.
doe-osti-3374010-an-introduction-to-vari:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24940, issued June 15, 2026, by Ian Jaegers of the lab's Primary Physics group, teaches the basics of variational calculus to engineers. Variational calculus finds the curve or function that makes a quantity as large or small as possible, a need that turns up across physics and design work. Jaegers wrote the guide as a living document, meant to be updated over time and read next to standard textbooks, not in place of them.

The guide builds the core cases step by step from one master equation, then works through concrete examples the reader is urged to solve along the way. A sample problem asks for the extremal function of a sample functional with fixed end values. The plain layout aims to let an engineer apply the methods to a system of interest without wading through a full math text.
doe-osti-3376409-emerald-connections-wea:
A final report for award DE-EE0010271, prepared by Resource Innovations, reviews the Emerald Connections Weatherization Plus Health pilot. Emerald Cities Collaborative held the award, with Alexis Washburn as project director. The pilot served low-income homes in Lynn, Massachusetts, and Seattle, Washington. Standard weatherization often walks away from the worst homes. Rot, moisture, or health hazards force a deferral, and the family gets nothing. This pilot added flexible health funds to break that pattern.

The Lynn arm shows the shift most clearly. Action Inc. auditors could blend the pilot's flexible money with federal weatherization funds and National Grid support. Homes once turned away got served. Once inside, crews could do more per home than the standard menu allows. Seattle partners included the city housing office and El Centro de la Raza. The review is careful: the short run time clouds any final grade on the model.
edward-macdowell-a-great-american-tone-p:
John Fielder Porte praises Edward MacDowell as America's great tone poet in a life and music study from E. P. Dutton of New York in 1922. Two verdicts front the book: Massenet calls MacDowell sincere and personal, a poet of exquisite harmonies, and Grieg names him the ideally endowed composer. MacDowell's own Columbia lectures supply a long extract on the spirit in nature.

Porte works through the piano music piece by piece. The Woodland Sketches, Op. 51, and New England Idyls, Op. 62, stand high in his judgment. A forest study for technique earns cooler words: fine rhythm training, but not the master's best. Dance of the Gnomes closes one set at a fiery presto. The book pairs biography with close, opinionated criticism, and it helped fix MacDowell's place as the first American composer Europe took seriously.
euthydemus:
Plato's Euthydemus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, is part comedy and part the oldest treatise on logic, as its introduction claims. Two sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, arrive in Athens boasting they can teach virtue and refute anything. Socrates asks them to demonstrate on the young Cleinias while his lover Ctesippus watches.

The brothers produce fallacies by the dozen: whatever is, cannot not be; fathers are dogs; learning is learning what you already know. Socrates, pretending earnestness, says he was the more decided because they seemed to jest. Beneath the clowning sits Plato's serious purpose, distinguishing real teaching from verbal victory. Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations later catalogued the very tricks laughed at here.
fables-for-the-frivolous:
Fables for the Frivolous, by Guy Wetmore Carryl and illustrated by Peter Newell, retells La Fontaine with apologies, as the subtitle says. Carryl's contents are a parade of paired adjectives. The Ambitious Fox meets the Unapproachable Grapes. The Persevering Tortoise faces the Pretentious Hare. Patrician Peacocks, an Arrogant Frog, and the Impecunious Cricket fill out the menagerie. The 1898 volume reprints pieces from Harper's periodicals, Life, and Munsey's Magazine.

Each fable is a short verse comedy with a moral turned sideways. Carryl was the American master of the form, a light versifier of real technical brilliance. His animals speak drawing room American. The morals land as jokes first and sermons never. Newell's illustrations match the wit line for line. The book remains the frivolous fable's high water mark in English: Aesop rewritten by a man who had been to the club and found it wanting.
father-sergius:
Leo Tolstoy opens Father Sergius in Petersburg in the eighteen-forties, when Prince Stepan Kasatsky, a brilliant Guards officer engaged to a maid of honor, shocks society by entering a monastery. His reasons lie inward: learning his fiancee had been the emperor's mistress broke his pride and his worldly faith together. Kasatsky becomes the hermit Sergius.

Fame follows him into retreat, and temptation arrives as a beautiful visitor he escapes only by cutting off his own finger, which falls to the floor before the pain comes. Later failures humble him into anonymous wandering and service. Tolstoy wrote the story late, as a fierce examination of pride wearing the mask of holiness.
four-plays-of-aeschylus:
Aeschylus stands at the head of Greek tragedy, and this volume gives four of his plays in English verse. The Suppliant Maidens, The Persians, The Seven Against Thebes, and Prometheus Bound are translated by E. D. A. Morshead. A frontispiece shows Hera and Prometheus from a red-figure vase.

The sampled speech comes from Eteocles in The Seven Against Thebes. The ruler who steers the ship of state, he says, must keep watch against the treachery of sleep. If things go wrong, one name bears the bruit from street to street: Down with Eteocles. He calls on boys, elders, and men in their prime to rise in aid of the city.
good-things-to-eat-as-suggested-by-rufus:
Rufus Estes published his own cookbook at Chicago in 1911, a collection of recipes for meats, game, fowl, fish, puddings, and pastries. He had cooked in the Pullman Company's private car service and was then chef for the subsidiary companies of the United States Steel Corporation in Chicago. A signed portrait leads the book. Before the recipes, he tells his life in a short sketch.

Estes was born in Murray County, Tennessee, in 1857, a slave, and given the name of his master, who owned his mother's family of nine children. His rise from bondage to a famed chef's post frames the recipes with quiet force. The dishes are rich, formal, and practical, the fare of fine rail travel. The book is now prized twice over: as a cookbook, and as the work of one of the first Black chefs to publish under his own name.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PaulingLinus_Pa: A research note dated April 7, 1973 concerns a quotation about insanity attributed to Linus Pauling. The quote appeared in Arthur Herzog's article 'Faking It' in the Saturday Review. Pauling, the Nobel Prize-winning chemist, was often quoted on subjects far from chemistry. The note records a researcher checking one such attribution. It gives the article, the magazine, and the date, but not the quote itself or the note-taker's conclusion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PostalServiceUS:
The Bureau of Chief Postal Inspector issued this final report in September 1968. Its subject is the mailing of firearms under allegedly fictitious names. Mail-order guns moved through the postal system under names that inspectors believed were invented, and the bureau investigated the practice as a system, not a single case.

The Oswald rifle had been bought by mail under the name A. J. Hidell, which made this subject a live one for years after Dallas. A 1968 report shows the Post Office still working the problem at full scale. It records the bureau's findings on how fictitious-name orders were placed and what could be done about them. For readers, it is the administrative sequel to a famous purchase.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WatergateManusc: Harold Weisberg turned from the Kennedy case to Watergate in a set of manuscript pages. The draft covers G. Gordon Liddy's transfer to the Committee to Re-elect the President, Nixon's campaign organization. Weisberg wrote with the same suspicion of official stories that marked his assassination books. The pages show him drafting an account of how a burglar moved inside a presidential campaign.
govdocs-archive_org-oswald-spengler-hera: Oswald Spengler, the German historian known for The Decline of the West, wrote a study of Heraclitus, the early Greek thinker. Heraclitus taught that all things flow and change, and only fragments of his words survive. The edition includes a foreword by Rodolfo Mondolfo on how to interpret him. Spengler reads the fragments as one mind's whole view of the world, not as scattered sayings.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
As the Soviet war in Afghanistan wound down in the late 1980s, four powers circled the country's future. A New Phase in the Great Game follows the United States, the Soviets, India, and Pakistan as each tried to shape a new Afghanistan.

The Great Game was the old name for rivalry over Central Asia, and the briefing book argues it never really ended. Declassified records show diplomats and intelligence services backing clients and blocking rivals while Afghans bore the cost. The collection serves readers who want the end of the Soviet war told from the files of all four capitals.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_china_Ch: China's Tibet Problem: The Contentious History - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In the 1950s the Soviet missile program was a hard target for American intelligence, meaning a secret very hard to penetrate. James E. David edited this briefing book, number 695, published in February 2020. It covers United States efforts against that program through 1957.

The failures are candid. Washington learned of the first Soviet ICBM test from a Soviet press release. News of the second came from a remark made to a French politician. Sputnik's launch caught the United States unaware until the satellite was in orbit. The record shows an intelligence system learning, expensively and in public, how much it did not know.

For sixty-five years the United States has tracked objects in orbit, building a space surveillance network to watch an ever more crowded sky. James E. David and Charles Byvik edited this briefing book, number 824, published in March 2023. Its title asks the network's three basic questions.

What is up there, where is it, and what is it doing: that is the daily work of cataloging satellites and debris. The documents span the effort from the early space age to today's congestion. Readers get the unglamorous backbone of space power, the tracking that makes both military planning and collision warnings possible.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Castle BRAVO, detonated at Bikini Atoll in 1954, yielded far more power than its designers predicted and spread fallout over inhabited islands and a Japanese fishing boat. This briefing-book page marks seventy years since that shot, which its title calls the worst nuclear test in United States history. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the test documents are not described. BRAVO's legacy includes sick Marshall Islanders, a dead fisherman, and the modern politics of nuclear testing compensation.

Twice in 1979 and 1980, American warning systems reported Soviet missile attacks that were not happening, and United States forces went on alert. This briefing-book page presents the record of those false warnings. A companion Archive volume on Colonel Odom's four a.m. phone call covers the same alert system in detail. The evidence here is the title alone. The episodes remain the standard cautionary case in nuclear safety: minutes of confusion, inside a system built to react in minutes.

The United States Air Force filmed its own preparations for nuclear war, and some of that film has been declassified. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in March 2023, built around those movies. One shows the crew of an American bomber at work.

Evidence here is short, so description stays plain. Films made for training and morale show nuclear war as a job: checklists, uniforms, calm voices. That ordinariness is the historical point. Moving images of crews rehearsing the end of the world reveal how completely the mission had been normalized inside the service that would fly it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Argentine generals seized power on March 24, 1976, opening seven years of military rule and mass repression. Briefing Book number 752, edited by Carlos Osorio and published in March 2021, asks a narrower question: what did the United States know before the coup, and when did it know it?

The documents show American officials had ample warning that a coup was being plotted, and kept a channel open to the plotters themselves. The Ford administration knew the military planned grave abuses against human rights. One episode stands out: the American ambassador stopped a pre-coup visit by a former deputy director of the CIA. For readers, the papers shift blame from surprise to choice, showing a government informed early and engaged anyway.
grace-harlowe-s-return-to-overton-campus:
Grace Harlowe returns to Overton in this 1915 volume by Jessie Graham Flower, after her college course is done. The contents open with a midsummer pilgrimage and a welcome guest. Jessica's wedding is on the list, and Emma Dean returns. A strange applicant appears, and the girls found the Harlowe House Club. A Semper Fidelis reunion gathers the old crowd.

Grace's return lets Flower show what her girls do with their training: they build a home and a club for the girls who come after them. Evelyn Ward arrives as a freshman, a new Grace in the making. Old friendships are tested by distance and change. The book closes a long series arc with warmth, and it honors the idea that school ties can be kept for life by work and love.
grass-of-parnassus:
Andrew Lang called his 1888 verses Grass of Parnassus, rhymes old and new, a modest title for polished occasional poetry. The contents sort poems as Deeds of Men, Rhodocleia, and Hesperothen, that last group returning to Homer's Phaeacia and the Sirens. Seekers for a city, the White Pacha, and Colonel Burnaby open the heroic section.

Lang writes of Burnaby and the Gordon relief expedition, twilight on Tweed, Clevedon church, and a strange rose that blossoms only in fairy tales heard at a nurse's knee. History, classics, and border scenery blend in his light forms: ballades, rondels, and songs. The volume shows the scholar-poet Lang between his translations of Homer and his fairy books.
greek-romances-heliodorus-longus-achille:
Rowland Smith translated three surviving Greek novels of love and adventure in one volume. Heliodorus wrote the Ethiopics, Longus wrote Daphnis and Chloe, and Achilles Tatius wrote Clitopho and Leucippe. All three date from the Roman imperial centuries.

Lovers are separated by pirates, storms, false deaths, and jealous rivals. Heliodorus opens in mid-action and unwinds his plot backward with great skill. Longus tells a gentler tale of two foundlings growing into love on Lesbos. Achilles Tatius favors lush description and narrow escapes. Together these romances show the ancient novel learning to entertain at length.
gutta-percha-willie-the-working-genius:
George MacDonald, the Scots teller of fairy tales, wrote Gutta-Percha Willie as the story of a working genius: a boy whose gift is to make and mend. Arthur Hughes drew the eight pictures. The contents trace Willie's path: who he was, his education, an apprenticeship, and a trade. One chapter marvels that Willie learned to read before he knew his letters. Another sends him digging, to find what he did not expect.

Willie turns his hands to shoeing a horse, to water power, and to a nest in the ruins. His grandmother and a wise Mr. Shepherd guide his mind while his hands learn. MacDonald's point is tender and plain: real genius may live in a workshop, and work done with love is a kind of genius. The tale is a Victorian hymn to honest craft, told for the young.
holberg-comedies-by-holberg-jeppe-of-the:
Ludvig Holberg, often called the Danish Moliere, wrote the three comedies gathered here in English. Jeppe of the Hill wakes a drunken peasant as a lord for a day. The Political Tinker mocks a craftsman who thinks he can run the state. Erasmus Montanus skewers a student drunk on Latin learning.

Each play turns one human folly into laughter with a kind edge. Peasants, burghers, and scholars all get their turn under Holberg's whip. The jokes still land because pride and pretence have not changed. These plays founded a stage tradition in Scandinavia and remain its comic bedrock.
in-search-of-gravestones-old-and-curious:
W. T. Vincent, head of the Woolwich District Antiquarian Society, wrote In Search of Gravestones Old and Curious in London in 1896. The book holds one hundred and two illustrations. Chapters trace how gravestones evolved and how they grew more artistic. Walks in Kent supply many examples.

Later chapters visit Ireland, Scotland, and lands abroad. Vincent argues for reform and for preserving old stones. A middle passage notes our instinct to tread lightly where the dead sleep. He also treats rules for churchyards. Antiquarians get a field guide drawn from long tramps.
josephus:
Josephus is Norman Bentwich's study of the ancient Jewish historian, published at Philadelphia in 1914. Bentwich had already written on Philo-Judaeus of Alexandria. Nine chapters run from The Jews and the Romans to a conclusion. A bibliography, a list of abbreviations, and an index support the text.

Two chapters follow Josephus's life to the fall of Jotapata and after his surrender to Rome. Others treat his works, his relation to earlier writers, and the Jewish Wars. Bentwich also sets Josephus beside the Bible and later Jewish history. A final chapter reads his apology as a defense of Judaism. The book introduces a writer whose histories remain a chief source for his age.
lives-of-girls-who-became-famous:
Sarah Knowles Bolton wrote these lives for aspiring girls in 1914. She had earlier written Poor Boys Who Became Famous. Her preface insists life is earnest activity, not a play-day. Goethe and Jean Ingelow supply mottoes about energy and work.

Bolton offers George Eliot and Rosa Bonheur as grand examples. Elizabeth Fry visited the poor and the prisoner instead. Mrs. Stowe and Miss Alcott lightened their parents' burdens by writing. Rich readers, like Baroness Burdett-Coutts, must bless the world generously. Mary Lyon's persistency shows poor girls what purpose can accomplish. Work is heaven's hest, Jean Ingelow's quoted line declares.
maitre-cornelius:
Maitre Cornelius is a tale by Honoré de Balzac, in Katharine Wormeley's translation. It opens on All Saints' Day, 1479, in the cathedral of Tours. Vespers are ending, and darkness fills the unfinished towers. Archbishop Hélie de Bourdeilles rises to bless the faithful.

In that candlelit gloom Balzac sets his medieval mystery. Cornelius is the aged treasurer and moneylender of King Louis XI. His hoarded gold and secret house draw young lovers into danger. A young nobleman risks all to reach the girl he loves. Balzac blends history, romance, and his great theme of money. The tale is the Human Comedy's medieval chapter.
mediaeval-lore-from-bartholomew-anglicus:
Robert Steele gathered Mediaeval Lore from Bartholomew Anglicus, with a preface by William Morris. Bartholomew was an English friar of the 1200s who wrote a vast store book. Steele picks its most curious entries for modern readers.

Morris opens by fighting the old view of the middle ages. That age, he says, was no mere chaos between two bright eras. He credits new study of history and art for the change. The lore itself ranges over beasts, plants, stones, and the skies. A picture of thinkers on Mount Olympus fronts the book. Keats lines on holy air and water set its mood.
menexenus:
Menexenus is a short dialogue attributed to Plato, presented here in Benjamin Jowett's translation. In it, Socrates recites a funeral oration over Athens's war dead. He claims, with a straight face, that Aspasia taught it to him. The speech praises Athens in the grand style of public oratory.

Jowett's appendix, printed with the text, weighs doubts about which Platonic works are genuine. Funeral speeches, he notes, are exactly the kind of writing most open to forgery. He explains how unknown works easily gained a famous author's name. Read together, speech and appendix raise sharp questions about rhetoric, patriotism, and authorship.
moon-of-israel-a-tale-of-the-exodus:
H. Rider Haggard set this tale of the Exodus in ancient Egypt, narrated by the scribe Ana. His author's note argues a bold thesis about Pharaoh. The real Pharaoh of the Exodus, he suggests, was the usurper Amenmeses. Amenmeses held the throne briefly between Meneptah and Seti II, and his body has never been found.
